Germany asks UN top court to throw out Israel arms export case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:21:56 UTC
19:21:56 KST

Germany asks UN top court to throw out Israel arms export case
THE HAGUE, Sept 7 - Germany asked the International Court of Justice on Monday to throw out a case brought by Nicaragua which accuses Berlin of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention because it supplies arms to Israel.
Berlin suspended weapons exports to Israel for a few months in 2025 but they have since resumed. A U.S.-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025 halted large-scale fighting that had devastated Gaza, but it has not ended Israeli strikes.
Nicaragua and Germany are both signatories of the Genocide Convention which includes an obligation on states to act to prevent possible genocides - but it is unusual for the court to hear cases where neither party is directly involved in the conflict at the heart of it.
Israel rejects genocide allegations as politically motivated and says its military campaign has targeted the militant group Hamas, whose attack on Israel triggered the war in October 2023.
ARGUMENT OVER JURISDICTION
Nicaragua's claim builds on the case South Africa brought against Israel for allegedly committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
In an interim ruling in 2024, the ICJ said it was plausible Israel violated some rights guaranteed under the Genocide Convention during its assault on Gaza.
Israel opposes that case and says it respects international law and has a right to defend itself. The main genocide case is not expected to be heard in full until late 2029.
Germany told the ICJ, also known as the World Court, on Monday that Nicaragua had not taken the proper steps before turning to the court and that much of the claim falls outside the jurisdiction it has under the genocide treaty.
"Germany respectfully requests the court to reject Nicaragua's claims," Julia Monar, legal adviser of the German foreign ministry, told the judges.
Nicaragua, which broke off diplomatic relations with Israel in 2024 over the war in Gaza, will have a chance on Tuesday to argue why the case should move forward.
A ruling on Germany's objection to jurisdiction is expected later this year. Even if the case can continue, it is expected to take years before a final ruling on the merits.
The ICJ is the United Nations' top court which deals with disputes between states and alleged violations of numerous international treaties. Its rulings are final and without appeal. REUTERS

Lithuania orders checks on all grain from Russia and Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:21:00 UTC
19:21:00 KST

Lithuania’s agriculture minister has ordered checks on the origin of all grain transported from Russia and Belarus through the country to prevent the possible transit of grain stolen from Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, the Agriculture Ministry said.
Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika formally asked the State Food and Veterinary Service to immediately investigate the origin of all grain transported in transit from Russia and Belarus, including both feed and food-grade grain.
“Uniform checks must be applied to all consignments of grain transported from Russia and Belarus, regardless of their intended use,” Mažeika said in a statement. “We must do everything to ensure that our country’s infrastructure is not used for the transit of stolen Ukrainian grain.”
Since May last year, Lithuania, Ukraine and the United Kingdom have been implementing the Grain Verification Scheme, under which mandatory laboratory testing is conducted on feed grain held in customs warehouses, according to the ministry.
But changes in monitored traffic flows indicate that some shipments may be moving under simplified direct-transit procedures or being declared as food-grade grain to avoid inspections, the ministry said.
Mažeika called for closer cooperation between the State Food and Veterinary Service and the Customs Department to ensure timely information on transit flows and identify and inspect high-risk shipments before they leave Lithuania.
The State Food and Veterinary Service last week took samples from a grain shipment at the port of Klaipėda and will have them analysed at a laboratory in France to establish their country of origin, the service said.
Aistė Prielgauskaitė, a spokeswoman for the service, said authorities suspect the grain may have originated in Ukraine rather than Russia, as stated in the accompanying documents. If confirmed, the grain could have been stolen from Ukraine and transported through the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, she said.
Prielgauskaitė told BNS that grain samples were taken Thursday from a customs warehouse in Klaipėda. The laboratory analysis is expected to take two to three weeks.
Mažeika previously told BNS that Russia might seek to export Ukrainian grain through ports in Latvia and Lithuania.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk applauded the German far right’s win in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, a result that sent shockwaves through the country’s political establishment and around Europe.
“Well done!” Musk wrote on X in response to Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel’s acclamation of lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. Siegmund thanked the billionaire for his “support” and floated future cooperation, saying Germany could again become “a place worth investing in” if the party takes power in Saxony-Anhalt.
Musk has championed the AfD for years, including during Germany’s 2025 federal election campaign. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has had a turbulent relationship with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and publicly attacked him this spring over Berlin’s criticism of U.S. policy toward Iran, posted a screenshot without commentary on Truth Social of Sunday night’s projected result.
Advertisement
The AfD ultimately took 43.8 percent and 39 of 83 seats — three short of an outright majority — delivering its strongest-ever state election result and moving closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since World War II.
The result had the party’s allies around Europe exulting. Italy’s right-wing Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini congratulated his “friend” Weidel and declared: “Another Europe is possible.” Austrian far-right leader Herbert Kickl said voters had torn down the political “firewall” around the AfD, while Spain’s Vox leader Santiago Abascal wrote on X that the result was “a great hope for Germany and Europe.”
Hard-right Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe called the AfD “an inspiration.” Dutch far-right leader Geert Wilders also congratulated the party after the election results rolled in.
Notably, Britain’s preeminent populist-nationalist leader Nigel Farage had not publicly commented on the result as of Monday morning, with France’s far-right leaders Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella also remaining tight-lipped.
Mainstream shock
While Musk and Europe’s right rejoiced, centrist and left-wing heavyweights around the continent sounded the alarm.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland could celebrate the result. French Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad called it “a grave moment in Europe,” warning that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be a solution.”
Advertisement
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed, called the AfD’s return a “catastrophic demonstration of the blindness of Europe’s centrist politicians” and said: “This disaster is their doing.”
Giorgia Meloni’s coalition in Rome was split: Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, leader of the pro-European conservative Forza Italia, declared the result “extremely bad news,” putting him at odds with coalition partner Salvini.
By Monday morning, Meloni, French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had not publicly weighed in — nor had EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa.

Taiwan, Belize launch disaster risk management project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:18:04 UTC
19:18:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TaiwanICDF and two Belizean government ministries launched the Belize Multi-Hazard Risk Management Capacity Building Project on Aug. 27 in Belmopan, Belize.
Under the project, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management and the Ministry of the Public Service and Disaster Risk Management will establish a cross-ministerial mechanism for integrated disaster management. The initiative will bolster the country’s capacity to respond to disasters such as floods and wildfires, according to TaiwanICDF.
TaiwanICDF project manager Lin Li-shan (林莉珊) said the initiative focuses on three main areas: strengthening cross-agency disaster early warning platforms and coordination mechanisms, expanding resilient community development and disaster preparedness capacity, and introducing automated wildfire monitoring technologies.
Lin said the project will establish disaster risk maps for 15 newly selected communities prone to floods and wildfires, promote community-based disaster preparedness and multi-hazard response training, and install three automated ground-based wildfire early warning stations in high-risk areas. It will also use remote sensing and ground observation data to develop wildfire risk assessment models and establish carbon monitoring sites.
This approach will gradually expand Belize’s nationwide early warning coverage, Lin added.
Minister of Sustainable Development Orlando Habet said Taiwan-supported early warning systems have already produced results. Through inter-ministerial cooperation, Belize aims to adopt a multi-hazard risk management approach and strengthen wildfire prevention and preparedness, he said.
Minister of Public Service Henry Charles Usher said Belize faces recurring hazards every year, including hurricanes, floods, storm surges, droughts, and wildfires. Although disasters cannot be prevented, proper preparation and training can significantly improve communities’ ability to respond, he said.
Usher called the memorandum of understanding an important step toward strengthening national disaster preparedness and local resilience.

Gwangju Biennale’s Taiwan Pavilion highlights new media art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:17:26 UTC
19:17:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The 16th Gwangju Biennale, one of Asia’s leading contemporary art events, opened Saturday (Sept. 5), featuring a Taiwan Pavilion titled “Instance Dungeons: Gray Zone.”
Founded in 1994 to commemorate the May 18 Gwangju Democratization Movement, the biennale champions human rights, democracy, and community.
Over three decades, the exhibition has evolved into a global platform challenging Western-centric artistic narratives while tackling issues including climate change and social justice.
Singaporean artist and curator Ho Tzu Nyen serves as artistic director for this edition.
A recipient of the Chanel Next Prize, Ho is known for his critiques of Asian modernity and geopolitics, with past presentations at the Venice Biennale, Sao Paulo Art Biennial, and Cannes Film Festival.
Titled “You Must Change Your Life,” in reference to German poet Rainer Maria Rilke, the main exhibition features 43 artists and collectives exploring creative practice as a vehicle for transformation.
The main exhibition features Taiwanese performance artist Tehching Hsieh (謝德慶), whose disciplined, yearlong performances turn lived time into creative material. Taiwanese American artist James T. Hong (洪子健) is also featured.
Curated by Chen Hsiang-wen (陳湘汶), former artistic director of the Taipei Digital Art Center, and Lin Hsiao-yu (林曉瑜), the Taiwan Pavilion showcases eight artists and artist duos examining how algorithms, digital interfaces, and virtual spaces reshape contemporary culture and power structures.
Artist Li Yi-fan (李亦凡) joins the pavilion following his presentation “Screen Melancholy” at the 2026 Venice Biennale. His work at Gwangju uses online conspiracy theories to examine whether fabricated information can nevertheless provoke genuine fear and desire.
Chang Wen-hsuan (張紋瑄) connects wartime memories from Taiwan and South Korea while examining the effects of information overload on memory. Cheng Hsien-yu (鄭先喻) uses light beams that track visitors to explore the meaning of attention, observation, and surveillance.
Cheng Ting-Ting (鄭亭亭) examines the distance between mediated images of war and lived experience. Hsu Che-yu (許哲瑜) and Chen Wan-yin (陳琬尹) revisit memories of Taiwan’s former nuclear weapons program.
Juan Po-yuan (阮柏遠) uses artificial intelligence to reconstruct military ruins and historical archives, revealing how algorithms can misread the past. Lin Yu-liang (林瑜亮) examines how information shapes human perception and action.
Su Hui-yu (蘇匯宇) combines cinema and artificial intelligence to revisit collectivism, patriarchy, and national narratives.

Taiwan’s new F-16Vs are built, not ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:17:08 UTC
19:17:08 KST

Taiwan’s first two F-16V Block 70 fighters left the United States on Aug. 17, but as of Sept. 3 they had still not arrived at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung, and Taiwan’s military had not publicly disclosed an exact arrival time.
They are built but not yet delivered. Even after they arrive, they will not yet be an operational capability.
Taiwan has spent years recovering from production delays. The harder test begins after production.
The aircraft must reach Taiwan, be accepted, integrated, and used for training before they add real capacity to the Air Force. What happens to these first two jets may indicate what the remaining 64 will face.
First clock
Taiwan signed a contract in 2019 for 66 new-build F-16C/D Block 70 fighters, with completion originally expected by the end of 2026. The program fell behind after COVID-19 disrupted production and supply chains, and Lockheed Martin had to rebuild its F-16 line in Greenville, South Carolina.
By October 2025, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) acknowledged that completing all 66 aircraft in 2026 would be difficult. Lockheed Martin responded by running two shifts, with production operating as much as 20 hours a day.
The effort produced the first two aircraft, tail numbers 6727 and 6728.
That is where one delay ends and another begins. The first was about building the aircraft. Now it is about getting them to Taiwan.
Ferrying fighters across the Pacific is not simply a matter of distance. Taiwan’s first F-16s made the same journey in 1997, requiring 19 aerial refuelings across the route: nine on the Fort Worth-to-Hawaii leg, six to Guam, and four on the final approach to Taiwan.
The Block 70’s conformal fuel tanks extend range, but the fighters still need tankers, maintenance stops, and suitable weather.
The current aircraft spent more than five nights at Hickam Air Force Base in Hawaii, longer than the 1997 stopover there. Reports on Aug. 26 placed the jets at Guam and expected same-day arrival in Taiwan, but unsettled weather pushed the timeline back again.
A reported Aug. 28 arrival also came and went. By Aug. 30, aviation enthusiasts were still waiting outside Chihhang Air Base, watching an empty runway.
Separate delays
The F-16V program now contains several separate issues that should not be treated as a single delay.
In June, lawmakers questioned whether Taiwan’s AN/ALQ-254 Viper Shield electronic warfare system complied with a 2012 Legislative Yuan requirement tied to US Air Force equipment standards.
Koo argued that the requirement applied to Taiwan’s earlier Block 20 upgrade, not the new Block 70 purchase, and pointed to other Block 70 operators using the same system.
It remains unconfirmed whether the internal suite is even installed on the first two aircraft.
There is no evidence that this dispute caused either the production or ferry delay. It is a separate procurement question and should be judged on its own.
Cost sharing
Taiwan also helped finance F-16V-related development after the United States and Egypt withdrew, and it recovers part of that contribution when other countries later buy systems covered by the investment.
A National Audit Office review through October 2025 put the contribution at about US$319.85 million, with US$245.23 million paid or under US review and US$74.62 million still outstanding.
This is cost sharing, not an open royalty on every F-16V sold. Taiwan is recovering part of an earlier investment while still waiting for the aircraft it ordered for itself.
The 66 new-build fighters are costing about NT$247.2 billion, or roughly US$7.7 billion.
What Taiwan bought
Taiwan already has F-16A/B fighters upgraded to the F-16V Block 20 standard under Peace Phoenix Rising. AIDC says it completed delivery of 139 upgraded aircraft in December 2023.
The 66 aircraft being built under Peace Phoenix Soaring are different. They are new Block 70 fighters, with systems such as the APG-83 AESA radar and conformal fuel tanks.
Taiwan is not simply replacing older fighters. It is adding a newer version to the F-16 fleet it already operates.
Those systems matter. But they add no operational capacity while the aircraft remain unavailable to Taiwan’s Air Force.
The strategic question is not whether 66 F-16Vs can match the PLA’s much larger air fleet. They cannot, and that was never the point.
What matters is how much extra capability these aircraft will add, and how quickly Taiwan can turn that capability into a usable force.
After delivery
Taiwan’s revised schedule now calls for all 66 aircraft to be delivered in 2027 and 2028. The first test is production.
Once the aircraft begin arriving, another clock starts: acceptance, integration, and training before they are ready for operations.
The first two aircraft offer an early look at how Taiwan handles the gap between buying a weapon and putting it to use.
The Viper Shield dispute, the ferry delay, and the production schedule are separate issues, each with its own timeline. But the Air Force has to absorb the results of all three.
A revised delivery schedule does not make the aircraft obsolete. A weapon that has been paid for is not the same as one that has arrived, and neither is the same as one that is ready for use.
Two jets can wait out a typhoon. Taiwan’s Air Force cannot wait indefinitely for the rest of the fleet.
The real test is whether the remaining 64 aircraft move from production to Taiwan, acceptance, integration, training, and operational readiness on schedule.

Red Cross says it has records of over 11,000 missing people in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:17:02 UTC
19:17:02 KST

Adama Bamba, Mohammad Kara Maryam, and Lina Altawell
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said Monday that it has records of more than 11,000 active cases of missing people in Sudan, including over 9,000 documented since fighting erupted in April 2023.
ICRC spokesperson Farid al-Hamid told the Sudan Tribune that the committee continues to work with the Sudanese Red Crescent to determine the fate of missing people.
“The agency’s tracing operations clarified the fate and location of 613 registered missing individuals in the first six months of the year,” he said.
The committee also helped more than 38,500 people separated from their families restore contact with them, according to al-Hamid.
He added that the ICRC trained emergency teams on burying bodies in a way that allows their identities to be determined later.
“In the capital alone, reports indicate more than 20,000 bodies have been recovered and buried without formal records or documentation, leaving families with little certainty over the fate of their kin,” Al-Hamid said.
He said the ICRC is holding bilateral and confidential talks with all parties to the conflict in Sudan to ensure respect for international humanitarian law.
The committee also trained hundreds of officers and armed personnel on international humanitarian law during the first half of this year, al-Hamid said, expressing concern over the continued impact of fighting on civilians.
Since April 2023, Sudan has been gripped by a war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

China issues national guideline to boost classical industries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:16:41 CST
19:16:41 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on promoting high-quality development of renowned traditional industries in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China on Monday issued its first national guideline on boosting the high-quality development of time-honored industries such as silk, tea and porcelain, targeting 50 leading enterprises with annual revenues exceeding 10 billion yuan (about 1.48 billion U.S. dollars) each by 2028.
The guideline, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and five other government departments, also aims to shape 100 national consumer brands and build several industrial clusters with an annual output of over 100 billion yuan by 2028, and to foster world-class enterprises and renowned brands by 2030 as these industries move up the global value chain.
Developing established industries with profound Chinese features, which also cover traditional Chinese medicine, brewing, arts and crafts, and the "four treasures of the study" -- writing brush, ink stick, paper and inkstone, is an effective way to expand domestic demand and boost consumption, as well as an important vehicle for passing on Chinese civilization and strengthening cultural confidence, according to the guideline.
Representative sectors of these traditional industries now boast about 25,000 enterprises above the designated size, employing nearly 3.5 million people and generating about 8 trillion yuan in annual revenue, MIIT Vice Minister Xie Yuansheng told a media conference on Monday. "Time-honored industries are the crystallization of Chinese civilization and national treasures," he said.
The guideline comes as China seeks to turn its cultural heritage into market competitiveness. Feng Haicang, an official with MIIT's consumer goods industry department, noted that about 90 percent of China's silk products are exported, but mainly as raw materials or original equipment manufacturer goods, with domestic brands having limited pricing power in the global market.
To help classical industries embrace innovation without losing tradition, the guideline calls for building "industrial brains" in major production areas, applying artificial intelligence to decode traditional craftsmanship, and constructing smart tea factories, smart pharmacies, intelligent kilns and digitalized breweries.
"Embracing AI does not mean abandoning old craftsmanship, but giving millennia-old techniques a pair of technological wings," Xie said. In silk weaving, AI-assisted design can now generate thousands of patterns in minutes, he added.
On consumption, Xie said Chinese consumers are shifting from "buying more goods" to "seeking better services and experiences," and that revitalizing these industries requires coordinated efforts in products, scenes and channels to help time-honored craftsmanship "come alive, go viral and reach every household."
Specifically, the guideline encourages integrating heritage industries with culture, tourism, wellness and rural vitalization, and supports global launches of heritage brands, access to duty-free channels, and international recognition of carbon footprint accounting for silk, tea and porcelain products.
The move is expected to be part of China's broader push to expand domestic demand, which the Central Economic Work Conference listed as the top priority this year.
The country will hold the first national exposition of time-honored industries in east China's Hangzhou City in late October, Xie said. ■

China improves investment mechanism to advance rural revitalization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:16:36 CST
19:16:36 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled a plan to improve its investment mechanism for rural revitalization as part of broader efforts to boost agricultural and rural development, the country's agriculture ministry said Monday.
Jointly issued by multiple government bodies, including the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, the National Development and Reform Commission and the People's Bank of China, the plan calls for stronger fiscal and financial support and increased social capital participation. The goal is to steadily boost investment in rural revitalization and further optimize the investment structure for agriculture, rural areas and farmers.
By 2030, the country aims to have basically established a rural revitalization investment mechanism aligned with agricultural and rural development conditions, featuring a well-balanced structure, sound approaches and an emphasis on both efficiency and effectiveness, according to the plan.
Emphasizing the leading role of government funding, the plan outlines measures to fully leverage bonds, loans and insurance to support agricultural and rural development, while calling for coordinated efforts by governments, financial institutions and social capital.
Favorable pricing and subsidy policies will also be rolled out in a more coordinated and effective manner, according to the plan.
Addressing issues concerning agriculture, rural areas and farmers remains a top priority on China's development agenda, with advancing rural revitalization across the board serving as a key task.
To this end, the outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) stresses improving the effectiveness of policies aimed at strengthening agriculture, benefiting farmers and enriching rural areas. It calls for improving related mechanisms and policy frameworks, facilitating the two-way flow of resources between urban and rural areas, and injecting greater vitality into agricultural and rural development. ■

Cocoa rises for 6th consecutive month amid El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:16:07 UTC
19:16:07 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Cocoa prices extended their positive trend for a sixth consecutive month, rising 25.5% per metric ton in August to $6,771 on global markets due to the impact of El Nino and concerns over a potential supply crunch in West Africa.
Geopolitical risks and climate issues fueled supply concerns, with significant increases across commodity prices last month, especially in agricultural products.
Wheat rose 21% per bushel as escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions threatened Black Sea grain trade, with a near-complete halt in grain loading operations in the Black Sea due to hostilities between the two countries, as well as port closures.
Corn climbed 16% due to declining production in Brazil and a falling US harvest, while strong Chinese demand for soybeans and declining production in South America increased its price by 8.5%.
Rice jumped 9.2% as adverse weather conditions and below-average monsoon rains in major rice producers in Asia, especially in India, fueled concerns over yields and reduced future supply expectations.
Coffee fell 1% per pound due to increased rainfall forecasts in Brazil, while sugar surged 21.5% on rising oil prices, as sugarcane is one of the raw materials used in ethanol production.
Cotton rose 13.9% due to hot weather and drought in cotton-producing regions of the US.
Cocoa reversed course this year after plummeting last year, surging 25.5% to $6,771 per metric ton.
Cocoa saw its fastest annual decline, at 48.1%, last year due to easing drought concerns in West Africa and increasing harvests.
The commodity sharply declined in January and February 2026, making a poor start to the year, but prices jumped 14.3% in March, 8.2% in April, 9.9% in May, 29.4% in June and 6.3% in July.
Daniela Corsini, senior economist at Italian banking group Intesa Sanpaolo, told Anadolu that the Middle East war drove up energy costs, while problems due to climate change and record-breaking temperatures amid El Nino affecting harvests drove up cocoa prices.
Corsini stated that supply disruptions in West Africa could worsen even further in the coming months, while El Nino intensified the annual Harmattan winds that affect the region, threatening cocoa trees.
“Thus, several analysts have trimmed their forecasts for a global surplus in 2026-27 and some have also warned about the risk of a global market flipping again into deficit due to strengthening demand, especially in Asia,” she said.
Oran van Dort, commodities analyst at Rabobank, told Anadolu that the 2026/27 harvest contributed to the cocoa rally beginning earlier this year.
Dort stated that the risk of El Nino and the slow crop development and flowering in the Ivory Coast and Ghana played key roles in the rally.
“In my view, too much of the current narrative is being driven by media coverage of a worst-case El Niño scenario and concerns over a poor mid-crop, which in turn may be fueling speculative bullishness,” he added.

Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:16:06 UTC
19:16:06 KST

Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
The Venice Film Festival hosted the world premiere of My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile, a documentary by Russian-born American filmmaker Julia Loktev. The film follows journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta as they find themselves in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In this latest chapter of her documentary epic about Russian journalists, Loktev explores how her subjects struggle to find their footing and keep doing their work despite the challenges of life abroad. Film critic Anton Dolin reviews the film for Meduza.
An unwitting déjà vu. With a flicker of dread, you realize you’re about to sit through six hours of documentary footage on a subject you’ve already studied in exhaustive detail — and lived through yourself. Then the film draws you in: you start worrying about the people on screen and can’t tear yourself away. By the end, your head is full of thoughts you want to share with readers and future viewers alike — until you remember that a year and a half ago, you already wrote about Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends.
I flip through that piece, nodding along, and find myself agreeing with what I wrote. The important things have already been said. What is there to add? Do I really need to retell the “plot” that pushes the film’s characters — journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta — into forced emigration and scatters the action across a dozen locations?
At the time, I wrote that I was watching Loktev’s nonfiction epic as my own story. That’s not exaggeration: you’re reading this piece by a film critic convicted in absentia and designated a foreign agent by Russian authorities, writing for a publication that Russia has declared an “undesirable organization.”
What’s more interesting is something else. Over more than a year in theaters, My Undesirable Friends has found viewers across a striking range of countries — from Iran to the United States, from Belarus to Israel — who recognize themselves in this unusual film, an iPhone-shot chronicle of shattered hopes seen through the eyes of young Russian liberal journalists.
Unconventional in every respect, the film has landed on numerous “best of the year” lists, won best documentary at the Gotham Independent Film Awards, and made the Oscar shortlist. Loktev seems to have captured the spirit of the times — the “last air” referenced in the subtitle of the first part of My Undesirable Friends.
At roughly 12 hours total, the project invites comparisons to a great Russian novel — or any novel of similar sprawl — whose sheer volume is at once intimidating and comforting. A simpler analogy is a TV series: My Undesirable Friends is divided into 10 chapters, and that’s no accident.
But watching it in a theater matters. The deliberate clash between the homemade, chronicle-like iPhone footage and the sheer scale of the runtime and the screen captures an essential paradox: the tragic, almost grotesque imbalance between the smallness of a person under political persecution and the unencompassable scale of the historical machine that grinds any one of us to dust.
There’s something else, too. You don’t step into the theater to unwind — you’re condemned, in effect, to live there for a while, growing close to characters who mature and change before your eyes. A cold, detached gaze is almost impossible. The film demands your empathy. By the end, these “undesirables” become your friends, too.
Loktev, absent from the frame, shoots and edits without hurry, without compressing time, letting air into other people’s claustrophobic spaces — perhaps not the last air after all, since everyone ultimately manages to escape and survive. Her touch is delicate enough to reveal her as more than a sympathizer. As Novaya Gazeta put it, she’s an accomplice.
It’s not only a TV series or a novel that can stretch across long, endless hours — life does too. When you’re caught in the thick of events, especially shocking and dramatic ones, you lose the ability to see them from a distance. Film has that resource. By giving shape to the formlessness of reality, My Undesirable Friends reveals patterns and, carefully, step by step, leads its lost, hapless émigrés toward the light — maybe not toward the triumph of good over evil, but at least toward clarity.
The credits seem to separate “characters” from “performers.” The former are listed by diminutive first names, without surnames — they’re friends, after all. The latter are real people. Who is playing whom? Playing, or, on the contrary, shedding a social mask and setting aside a professional role to let real emotion through?
In the film’s first chapter, set in spring 2022, Anya — Anna Nemzer — is in Israel, bewildered, preparing to leave for Georgia. Ksyusha (Ksenia Mironova) and Lera (Valeria Ratnikova) are in tears, trying to check into a random hotel in Istanbul. Alesya (Alesya Marokhovskaya) and Ira (Irina Dolinina) look around uncertainly in Prague. And Lena (Elena Kostyuchenko), her voice full of horror, states the inevitable: to file truthful reports from Ukraine, she’ll have to quit Novaya Gazeta.
By the end, each character’s arc feels complete, even though all of them — young, full of energy and even hope — remain at a crossroads on their own path, far from any imagined destination. The film does have one unqualified advantage over life: it gets to end with closing credits.
The Venice Film Festival, where Part II of My Undesirable Friends is having its world premiere, is hosting several other monumental documentaries this year: Sergei Loznitsa’s three-hour Imperium, Alex Gibney’s four-hour Musk, and Mariano Llinás’s five-hour Life of Jorge Luis Borges. Loktev’s runtime sets a record even against that field — and this is only half the entire film. Apparently only films this uncompromisingly detailed, this painstakingly thorough, can answer the unasked questions of a disoriented viewer.
A brief digression: this summer’s most unconventional box-office hit was Christopher Nolan’s three-hour The Odyssey, whose sheer length did nothing to deter audiences. The characters of My Undesirable Friends wander uncharted seas and hostile islands while their own Trojan War rages on. They don’t have a single chance yet to sail off into the sunset.
Loktev’s film, though, moves past the two basic plots in Borges’s classification cited above: it isn’t a siege story (that was Last Air in Moscow), and it isn’t a homecoming that can only be dreamed of. The third Borgesian plot is the search. Ksyusha, Lera and Anya, Lena, Alesya and Ira are searching not just for a safe harbor but for the lost meaning of their work — and, with it, of their existence. Loktev, stitching scattered misadventures into a patchwork of a unified narrative, helps them find that meaning, but does so, fortunately, without moralizing or drawing categorical conclusions.
Tel Aviv and Riga, Tbilisi and Amsterdam, New York and Prague, Istanbul and Washington, and finally — how could they not appear? — Moscow and Kyiv… Ksyusha, stone-faced, walks out of the courthouse where her fiancé, Ivan Safronov, was sentenced to 22 years in prison. Lera fantasizes about The Hague, where she imagines herself reporting live on air during Putin’s trial. Anya discusses the news with her father over Zoom, then tries to locate the spot in her body that reacts to the sale of her grandmother’s apartment — somewhere near the solar plexus.
Meanwhile, Lena and her girlfriend, Yana (Yana Kuchina), seriously discuss Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB)‘s plans to kill Lena, then, just to be sure, tell their fortune with a book — a random volume of Harry Potter that happened to be at hand. Rowling’s grim fairy tale also appeared in the first part of the film. It’s easier to imagine yourself fighting dementors and death eaters if you’re still hoping for a happy ending.
Warning: this video contains explicit language.
The climax arrives in the fourth, penultimate chapter. While Lena works on a book with the provocative title Moya Lyubimaya Strana — “My Favorite Country” (in the Russian edition, the word “favorite” is censored with asterisks, leaving readers plenty of room for interpretation) — TV Rain lands at the center of a scandal in Latvia, where opposition television journalists who had fled Russia had obtained a broadcasting license. Twice, they let the phrase “our army,” referring to the Russian army, go out on air. For that, they would lose their right to work and their visas — exiled once again.
Loktev tells this story from start to finish, without omissions, foregrounding the internal and external chaos of everyone caught up in the conflict. A single possessive pronoun becomes the apple of discord. There’s no room for compromise. The two sides in the standoff speak different languages — and no, not Latvian and Russian. The rift runs far deeper than a linguistic misunderstanding.
Surprisingly, it’s this episode that dots the i’s. The resolution itself is ambivalent: in the moment, Latvian authorities win, while a later court ruling overturns the fairness of their decision. But more than two years have passed since then, and TV Rain relocated to the Netherlands long ago, where it now broadcasts — probably for the best, for everyone involved.
It’s exactly then, in the winter of 2022–2023, that it becomes clear opposition journalists from Russia no longer have an “ours” on either side of the border. But that also means their moral choices are made without regard for “their own.” At this point My Undesirable Friends — “my,” another possessive — finally takes shape as a film about choice and the act of claiming agency. This is what the characters were searching for all along: not a home, not a job, not stability, but an inner anchor that would let them keep doing their work, whatever stood in the way.
Navalny’s killing — Lera cries reading the news at her monitor. Trump’s inauguration — Ksyusha, in Washington, finds herself in the middle of the celebrations. This story has no ending and can’t have one. Sometimes, it turns out, you don’t need a resolution — a setup is enough. New characters appear: former TV Rain journalist Petya (Peter Ruzavin) and his Ukrainian wife, Natalka (Natalia Humeniuk, the former head of the Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske). Blurring the increasingly faint line between journalism and activism, they find support in each other. However irresponsible their dreams for the future may be, the path they’ve chosen is perfectly clear. Petya goes off to fight for Ukraine, and his personal story opens a new chapter.
For all its chronicle-like quality and seeming neutrality, My Undesirable Friends restores, as if by a wave of a magic wand, faith in the idea that everyone has power over their own tomorrow — even if the day after tomorrow is shrouded in impenetrable fog. It’s probably an illusion, but the kind of illusion that, even in the worst of times, makes life feel meaningful.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea
September 7, 2026
Russia and North Korea on Monday cut the ribbon on the first road bridge linking the two countries as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen their strategic partnership.
The crossing spans the Tumen River and marks another expansion of transport links between the two countries.
Where is the new bridge?
The road crossing is near the existing Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge commissioned in 1959 following the Korean War.
Russia and North Korea already have direct rail and air connections, but until now there had been no road bridge between them.
The new bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life. Relatives of Novichenko attended the opening ceremony.
Construction began in April 2025 after the project was agreed during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.
Why is the road bridge being opened now?
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the new crossing should boost economic development, tourism and employment.
"I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," the TASS news agency quoted Mishustin as saying by video link at the opening ceremony.
Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened considerably since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
North Korea sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion launched in 2024.

How to Watch the Apple September Event (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Another Apple event is almost here, though this one will likely feel a little different than the September events of lore. It’s the first Apple event since CEO Tim Cook’s departure, and might be the first time the public gets a taste of how the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, can slip into those shoes.
The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern). You can watch the stream right here on this page, or on Apple’s website and YouTube channel. Apple will also stream the event on its Apple TV devices and Apple TV+ streaming service. Leaks and rumors have left just about everyone expecting news about Pro-level iPhones and a long-awaited Apple foldable device.
Since the Covid pandemic, Apple has eschewed live presentations, instead inviting media and employees to the Apple campus to watch prerecorded videos of all its product announcements. WIRED will have reporters on the ground—you can follow along with all the action on our live blog, which will go live the morning of the event. WIRED will also have a roundup of everything the company announces for your perusal right after the event.
What to Expect
Thanks to leaks from sources like Bloomberg, the event is widely expected to be the moment Apple finally announces its long-rumored foldable iPhone. It’s bound to be pricey, with rumored estimates sitting around $2,000.
Apple is also expected to focus on premium products, chiefly the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4. That means Apple may push the launch of its base iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027. The move likely stems from increased manufacturing costs and limited product availability due to the ongoing memory crisis. It's also an effort to build hype for Apple’s more premium—and expensive—products, and maybe entice customers to sign up for the company’s new iPhone leasing program. We’ll likely see the mid-tier iPhone 18e at that spring event, alongside a second-gen iPhone Air.
New AirPods may also be on the table, though Apple’s heavily rumored AirPods Pro with cameras—designed to be the “eyes” of Siri for AI-powered visual assistance—could be delayed to later this year or to 2027.
If you’re hoping for new iPads, Macs, or home devices, well, you may have to wait a little longer. Apple announced a new Mac Mini and Mac Studio at the end of August, but the company may debut new home products, a new iPad Mini, and new MacBooks during events in October.
As for snagging devices right after Apple announces them this week, unconfirmed reports suggest the company will open iPhone preorders on September 12, a day later than it usually offers them, out of respect for the victims of 9/11. The following week is likely when the company will drop the final, official versions of its software, like iOS 27 and macOS 27.

Details emerge of 36th Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:15:00 EEST
19:15:00 KST

Details emerge of 36th Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting
The 36th meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format) will take place remotely, co-chaired by the defence ministers of the UK and Germany.
Source: European Pravda, citing its own sources
Details: The Ramstein meeting, 36th since its establishment, will take place in video format co-chaired by UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius – as has been the case since the US stepped back from its coordinating role following the change of administration.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby are expected to participate.
The meeting is due to begin at 16:00 Kyiv time.
Ahead of the meeting, Ukraine submitted a list of urgent air defence needs to NATO, and Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara held a preparatory call with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
The last meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group was held on 18 June at NATO Headquarters in Brussels and was co-chaired by the United Kingdom and Germany.
Following the meeting, Pistorius announced that Ukraine would receive a three-digit number of air-to-air missiles from German stocks. He also said the two nations would jointly produce ground robotic systems.

Japanese Premier Takaichi seeks talks with Trump before his meeting with China's Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:14:51 UTC
19:14:51 KST

Aamir Latif
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is seeking a meeting with US President Donald Trump before the latter's expected meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported on Monday.
Takaichi would prefer to speak with Trump before his meeting with Xi when she visits New York for the UN General Assembly later this month, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported on Monday, citing a Japanese government source.
Japan is seeking to coordinate with the US on China amid concerns about a possible rapprochement between the two major powers, as Xi and Trump are expected to meet in Washington on Sept. 24.
Tokyo, according to sources, is emphasizing dialogue rather than insisting on a particular format for the talks.
Japan fears that Trump may make concessions to China on issues such as Taiwan to secure economic gains ahead of the November midterm elections in the US.
Such an outcome, a Japanese government source said, could affect Tokyo's security and economic interests.
According to the latest schedule from the UN, Takaichi and Trump are both set to deliver addresses on Sept. 22.
If Takaichi is unable to meet Trump while in the US, she is likely to seek out a phone call with him around the time of the Washington-Beijing summit.
Diplomatic relations between Tokyo and Beijing have been strained under the Takaichi government after she suggested in parliament in November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could prompt a military response from Japan.
Separately, Takaichi is mulling reshuffling her Cabinet and ruling party executives as early as Sept. 16, according to Kyodo News.

Belgian prosecutors detain former reasearcher and probe alleged Chinese espionage at bankrupt chipmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:14:09 UTC
19:14:09 KST

The suspected leak of gallium nitride chip technology from bankrupt firm BELGAN to a China-based rival comes amid a wave of investigations into suspected Chinese espionage across Europe.
Belgian prosecutors have detained a Chinese-Belgian national in connection with an espionage investigation linked to China, the Federal Prosecutor's Office has announced.
The suspect was detained in May, as he was about to board a flight to Beijing, though authorities disclosed the arrest only now.
Prosecutors are investigating charges of espionage, participation in a criminal organisation, misuse of company assets and unlawful disclosure of trade secrets in connection with Belgian semiconductor company BELGAN BV, which went bankrupt in 2024, leaving 400 employees without jobs.
According to prosecutors, the 52-year-old suspect held a senior research position at BELGAN while also serving as a director of a Chinese company with similar manufacturing activities, financed by a Chinese investment fund.
"The investigation may point to the unlawful transfer abroad of specialised intellectual property and trade secrets relating to the production of gallium nitride chips," the Federal Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.
The technology is used in electric vehicles, aerospace and military applications.
Prosecutors confirmed to Euronews that a second suspect is being sought in the case. Authorities have carried out searches and seized data storage devices. According to Belgian public broadcaster RTBF, the detained man denies the charges against him.
Belgian authorities had already begun investigating BELGAN's 2024 bankruptcy. The company, which was developing a new generation of chips, was partially acquired by Hong Kong-based Chinese investors, who appointed managers to the Belgian firm.
The same investors reportedly set up a similarly focused company in China, GaNkool, and transferred sensitive licences and technologies to it.
Chinese espionage cases on the rise
Several China-related espionage investigations have been launched across Europe in recent months. In June, a Canadian intern of Chinese origin was arrested in Mons, Belgium.
The suspect worked in IT at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe and had access to sensitive data.
In 2025, Jian Guo, a former assistant of Chinese origin to German far-right lawmaker Maximilian Krah at the European Parliament, was sentenced to five years in prison for passing sensitive EU documents to Beijing.
And in the United Kingdom, two British-Chinese dual nationals were convicted and jailed this summer for surveilling exiled Hong Kong dissidents on British soil.

Belgian football federation refuses to back Infantino’s FIFA re-election bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:13:20 UTC
19:13:20 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The Royal Belgian Football Association (RBFA) said on Monday that it would not support Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for another term as FIFA president, citing concerns over transparency and governance.
The federation said its decision was based on two “fundamental pillars” on which FIFA had so far failed to demonstrate transparency.
The first relates to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which was shelved after criticism. The RBFA said several important decisions and assessments concerning the project had not been supported by sufficient justification, raising questions about the transparency and governance of the process.
It said it remained aligned with UEFA in seeking clear answers about FIFA’s decision-making and next steps.
The second issue concerns the red card shown to US forward Folarin Balogun during the World Cup, a case in which the Belgian federation said it was directly involved. FIFA had suspended the red card after US President Donald Trump urged Infantino to review the case.
Despite explicit requests for a clear justification of the decisions taken and clarification about how similar situations would be handled in the future, the federation said it had yet to receive a satisfactory response.
“For the Belgian Football Association, it is essential that such cases are handled transparently and rigorously, in the interests of FIFA, good governance and the credibility of international football, with clear guarantees for the future,” it said.
The federation has asked FIFA to place the Balogun case on the agenda of the next FIFA Council meeting on Oct. 15. RBFA President Pascale Van Damme is a member of the council.
“My team at the RBFA communicated calmly and constructively with FIFA, during and after the World Cup, to obtain clarification in the Balogun case,” Van Damme said.
“Two months after the events, we note that our questions remain unanswered,” she added.
Van Damme said the federation was seeking the necessary explanations and wanted to explore possible improvements to FIFA’s existing procedures so similar cases could be handled “clearly, consistently and efficiently” in the future.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:12:22 BST
19:12:22 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.
Attending a misconduct hearing
Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).
Please note the following conditions of entry:
- any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)
- any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time
- priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)
- any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing
- members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session
- no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing
- any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing
- where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment
- no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time
- no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient
- we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible
- members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted
If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.
Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.
Private hearings
Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.
Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:
- all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private
- a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing
- specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness
- specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome
If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.

Upcoming police appeals tribunals

Anti-immigrant protesters clash with UK police over new boat arrivals (VIDEOS)

Anti-immigrant protesters clash with UK police over new boat arrivals (VIDEOS)
Right-wing protesters have clashed with police in the British city of Portsmouth as they tried to prevent a group of newly arrived migrants from being processed, videos from the scene show.
A small boat which departed Normandy in France with some 140 asylum seekers aboard was intercepted by the UK authorities in the English Channel and escorted to Portsmouth, British media reported on Sunday.
The news prompted hundreds of anti-immigrant activists to head to the city in Hampshire in south-eastern England. The demonstrators blocked roads in the area in an attempt to prevent buses from delivering the migrants to a Home Office processing center in the village of Manston in Kent.
The protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore face masks, chanted: “Stop the boats” and “Send them back.”
Footage from the scene captured minor scuffles between the activists and police armed with riot shields. The demonstrators were also filmed throwing objects at the officers.
Riot police clash with protestors in Portsmouth after small boat arrival. Shot for @PApic.twitter.com/JavKFpfVVa
— Jamie Lashmar (@jamie_lashmar) September 6, 2026
Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, who recently founded the Patriot Platform group, said in a live stream from the scene that “we will not accept this anymore.”
BREAKING:
The police and anti-migration activists are facing off with each other in the sea near Portsmouth.
After the police started splashing water on the activists, they responded with the same measure. The activists are there to block illegal migrants from being disembarked…
“This is no longer an option to tell us that the boat numbers are down. This isn’t about the numbers being down… this is about understanding that this has to come to an end now,” Thomas, who is an associate of prominent British right-wing activist Tommy Robinson, said of the flow of migrants from the other side of the channel.

The demonstrators said they intended to continue blocking the roads all night, but ended the rally at around 3 AM local time after police obtained a dispersal order and warned that officers would begin making arrests, according to The Guardian.

A British government spokesperson said that “we condemn the intimidating and thuggish behavior we are seeing tonight. The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”
A similar protest, also staged by Patriot Platform, took place in Dover on Saturday, with activists blocking roads out of the UK’s busiest international ferry and passenger port. The local councilor described the action as “coordinated” and “illegal.”
Some 33,000 people, mostly adult men, arrived in the UK in small boats between July 2025 and 2026, making up around 88% of all illegal migrants entering the country, according to government data. During the same period in 2024 and 2025, the number of asylum seekers crossing the channel stood at 41,000.
A YouGov poll published in August showed that 69% of Britons believe immigration over the past decade has been too high, while 43% said it had been mostly bad for the country, up from 33% in 2016.

AfD to push for restoring ties with Russia after state election victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:10:34 UTC
19:10:34 KST

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-chair Tino Chrupalla said after the party’s decisive victory in the election to the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag (state parliament) that it would pressure Berlin to restore relations with Russia and change its sanctions policy.
"We want to have good relations with Russia again," Chrupalla said in an interview with ARD TV channel. According to him, sanctions policy needs to change. "The AfD will have to address this issue primarily in the Bundesrat (the chamber representing Germany’s federal states), by putting pressure on the German federal government," he stressed.
At the same time, Chrupalla noted that the AfD wants to govern in Saxony-Anhalt following its election victory and seek partners to do so. "We will send offers of talks to all parties. Then we will see who rejects the hand we are extending," he explained. "I believe the CDU needs to ask itself what conclusions it should draw from this disastrous election result," the politician added. According to Chrupalla, the goal is to "continue providing stable government in Saxony-Anhalt, and opposition parties also bear responsibility for this."
"Talks will begin this week. This is our top priority, and I expect that Ulrich Siegmund will become our minister-president and be elected by the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag," Chrupalla said. A change in the region’s political course is crucial, he said. "We want to overcome divisions," the AfD co-chair concluded.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election was held on September 6. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive victory with 43.8% of the vote. This was the AfD’s best-ever result in any German state, doubling its share of the vote from the previous state election five years ago. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came in second, losing more than half of its vote share compared with 2021. The Christian Democrats received just 17.2% of the vote, the CDU’s worst-ever result in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) came in third with 9.3% of the vote. The Greens received 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%. The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance - Reason and Justice) also cleared the threshold to enter the Landtag with 5.3%.

UN urges ‘accountability’ after 23 die in US immigration custody in 2026

UN urges ‘accountability’ after 23 die in US immigration custody in 2026
- The UN rights chief reported 23 deaths in US immigration custody in 2026 and demanded accountability for these fatalities.
- The UN urged the US to stop deportations to dangerous locations like Haiti and to ensure due process for removals to third countries.
- Concerns were raised about ICE's plan to buy electric shock gloves, which may increase violence during enforcement operations.
AI generated
Geneva – The United Nations rights chief on Sept 7 demanded accountability for swelling numbers of deaths in US immigration custody, and urged Washington to halt deportations to places where people face “irreparable harm”.
Speaking before the UN Human Rights Council, Volker Turk highlighted that “four more people have died in US immigration custody since my last update to this council” in June.
That meant there had been “a total of 23 deaths in 2026 alone”, he said, insisting that “there needs to be accountability for these deaths”.
US President Donald Trump has made combating illegal immigration a top priority of his second term, with the authorities rounding up thousands of people and expanding detention centres.
A joint report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights in June said the rate of people dying in ICE custody has reached its highest level in over a decade amid the crackdown.
The UN rights chief on Sept 7 also called out a range of other US immigration enforcement practices, including forcing migrant returns to dangerous places and to countries they had no connection to.
“I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries,” he told the council.
Turk also voiced alarm at the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s reported plans to “equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves”, warning this would “increase the violence associated with their operations”.
The plan to purchase the shock gloves, which was first reported by The Associated Press, calls for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the ICE parent agency, to spend US$10 million to US$20 million (S$12.6 to S$25.3 million) on what are described as “distraction and de-escalation” devices.
ICE has been criticised for a series of fatal shootings during enforcement operations, including those of two American citizens in Minnesota in January who were involved in anti-ICE protests.
Critics have focused on the forceful tactics used by ICE agents in rounding up migrants and on an alleged lowering of the standards of training for new recruits. AFP

Hainan’s resort city of Sanya to strengthen environmental measures under new Chinese code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:08:55 UTC
19:08:55 KST

HAIKOU, China, September 7. /TASS/. The southern Chinese resort city of Sanya on the coast of Hainan Island plans to strengthen its environmental measures in accordance with China's new Environmental Code, the Hainan Daily newspaper reported.
The newspaper noted that the legislation took effect on August 15. It is expected to provide an important boost to Sanya's high-quality development. The new measures could help restore natural vegetation, expand mangrove forests, and increase populations of various local wildlife species. Another key objective is to develop modern environmentally friendly infrastructure, including a more extensive network of electric vehicle charging stations and convenient cycling routes.
The article noted that Sanya is a city with excellent environmental conditions, surrounded by tropical forests and boasting pristine beaches and numerous bodies of water. One of the goals is not only to create even more favorable living conditions, but also to harness the city's green potential to develop new modern industries and advance promising business projects.
To successfully achieve these goals, Sanya plans to continuously strengthen its legal and regulatory framework, carefully work out the details of the relevant measures and improve their effectiveness. Such efforts, the article stressed, are aimed at creating a "calm and orderly urban environment," which it compared to an "invisible but extremely important form of soft power." In practice, this will include tougher measures to combat noise pollution, stronger monitoring of residential conditions, and the introduction of "precise, intelligent, and systematic methods." These measures are expected to reduce the environmental impact of construction sites, as well as industrial and commercial activities.
The new strategy includes fines for violations and sets deadlines for remedying environmental damage. At the same time, continuous real-time monitoring mechanisms using smart technologies will be strengthened. Local cafes and restaurants will also face more effective oversight of their equipment to prevent smoke and unpleasant odors. To this end, officials from the relevant government agencies are expected to provide businesses with tailored recommendations, helping them properly install kitchen exhaust systems and lay pipelines in accordance with official standards.
At the same time, the modernization is intended to avoid imposing excessive costs or obstacles on businesses, while encouraging the expertise sharing and improvements in service quality. Air, water, and soil pollution will also be punishable through criminal prosecution and court proceedings. Meanwhile, to ensure that the legal provisions are put into practice and reach beyond "a limited audience," the authorities plan to raise legal awareness among ordinary residents and tourists – both urban and rural – through a series of specific measures, including special lectures and notifications on social media.

Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon says her pro-Palestine stance is still costing her film roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:08:28 UTC
19:08:28 KST

Oscar-winning US actor Susan Sarandon said she continues to lose film roles because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, with some talent agencies still discouraging filmmakers from hiring her.
Sarandon made the remarks at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, where she was promoting her latest film, The Echo Chamber.
“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she told a news conference.
“But that’s the power structure. I think among people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome,” she added.
The 79-year-old actor said she believed public understanding of Palestine and the relationship between Israel and the US had changed significantly since Israel’s war on Gaza began in 2023.
“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,” she said.
“That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel. Nobody really understood that.”
Sarandon said reluctance to hire people who publicly criticise Israel remained particularly strong among major studios.
She thanked The Echo Chamber director Andrea Pallaoro for casting her despite what she described as warnings from within the industry.
“In terms of doing this film, I thank Andrea for that, because he didn’t listen to the warnings,” she said.
Sarandon was dropped by talent agency United Talent Agency in 2023 following remarks she made at a pro-Palestinian rally in New York.
Directed by Pallaoro, The Echo Chamber is an Italian-Belgian production starring Sarandon, Luca Marinelli and Alicia Vikander. The film is competing for the festival’s top prize, the Golden Lion.
Sarandon won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in the 1995 film Dead Man Walking. Her other prominent films include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Bull Durham and Thelma & Louise.

Macklemore backs Palestine at Ed Sheeran shows, prompting removal petition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:07:25 UTC
19:07:25 KST

US rapper Macklemore used his opening performances for Ed Sheeran in New Jersey to deliver a forceful pro-Palestinian message, prompting an Israeli-American organisation to call for his removal from the remaining dates of Sheeran’s tour.
Performing before crowds of more than 80,000 at MetLife Stadium on Friday and Saturday, Macklemore wore a keffiyeh and performed his 2024 song “Hind’s Hall” as images from Gaza and the occupied West Bank appeared on screens around the venue.
“I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he told the crowd during Friday’s performance.
He also spoke about the broader principle behind his message, saying everyone should have the right to “freedom,” safety and peace.
‘Free Palestine’ message draws backlash
Macklemore repeated his message during Saturday’s show, again wearing a keffiyeh and leading the crowd in chants of “Free Palestine” before performing “Hind’s Hall.”
He also called for freedom for Palestine, Cuba, Congo, Sudan and Iran and described US Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a “terrorist organisation.”
Addressing Jewish members of the audience, Macklemore said opposition to Israeli policies should not be equated with hostility toward Jewish people.
“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is criticism of you,” he said.
He added that his message was about “peace, love” and ensuring people are treated with dignity, respect and equality.
At least one message shown on the stadium screens read: “Holocaust survivor says stop the genocide in Gaza.”
Following the performances, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition urging Sheeran and organisers of his Loop Tour to remove Macklemore from his remaining appearances.
The organisation argued that the concert was intended as a musical event rather than a political rally and accused Macklemore of using the platform to promote what it described as a “one-sided political agenda.”
The petition also asked organisers to clarify whether Macklemore’s remarks, visuals and performance had been approved beforehand and called for clearer rules governing political messages during future shows.
The story behind ‘Hind’s Hall’
Released in 2024, “Hind’s Hall” takes its name from Hamilton Hall at Columbia University, which was occupied by pro-Palestinian student protesters and renamed in memory of Hind Rajab, a Palestinian child killed in Gaza in January 2024.
The song became one of Macklemore’s most prominent political statements, with the rapper using his music to criticise US support for Israel and express solidarity with Palestinians.
His appearances at MetLife Stadium extend that activism to one of the world’s largest concert stages, putting the Israeli war on Gaza and Palestinian rights at the centre of a major US music event.
