How to Read the Room
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Every room has a parallel conversation running underneath what appears on the surface. It’s a pulse, a vibe, a temperature. This undercurrent of unspoken behavior delivers data instantly, but only if you can decipher it.
Neuroscientists, psychologists, anthropologists, and linguists have studied subtle behaviors for years in a quest to unravel the mystery of how humans create meaning together. I’ve spent the last decade training others how to spot invisible signals, detect who holds power, identify which relationship will influence a decision, spot who has already made up their mind, and decipher who is lying.
These are the very skills you need to read the room—and they are all learnable. Here are four science-based approaches to improve your ability to do this:
Declutter your mind to get an accurate read
Your mood influences your judgment, and cognitive load distorts what you see. Happy people tend to predict positive outcomes and underestimate negative risks. Stressed minds can find hostility in neutral interactions, according to research by Australian psychologist Joseph Forgas. Landmark work by J.A. Easterbrook showed that emotion and strain reduce the range of cues we can take in and process.
Overload your mind, and you will misread the room. Heightened cognitive load, the baggage you carry into a meeting or conversation, distorts what you see. When your mind is cluttered with thoughts of a fight with your spouse or an unfinished project, you stop observing what’s happening and start reading others through the prism of your own stress. In this mindset, a flat “thanks” can become a slight, and a colleague’s distraction can feel like contempt.
When a room feels like it’s turning against you, the first question worth asking is whether the room changed or your bandwidth did.
Manage what you transmit
Every gathering has a vibe. While that may sound like astrology, science tells us it’s brain circuitry, and that we probably catch each other’s moods far more often than we think.
Yale neuroscientists led by Joy Hirsch paired strangers face-to-face and used brain imaging to track what transferred when one person watched emotionally charged videos while the other person watched only the video-watcher. The second person began to mirror the video-watcher’s emotional state, even though they never saw the videos themself.
A 2023 study in Communications Biology timed the process: strangers watching television together synchronized their emotional responses within 850 milliseconds. The synchronization ran strongest during positive moments, suggesting joy travels freely while we keep our darker feelings hidden.
The emotional state you bring into a room can also shape how everyone else behaves before anyone has consciously registered that you’re anxious or angry. An anxious person can make people rush or interrupt others more frequently. A contemptuous person can license cruelty and make dismissive jokes or harsh judgment feel acceptable. A calm person can reduce the temperature long enough for rational thought to return.
The message? Manage your own state of mind before you attempt to manage anyone else’s.
Take note of who is missing in the room
A group’s intelligence is not the sum of its IQs. Research by Carnegie Mellon Professor Anita Williams Woolley into the collective intelligence of teams found that group performance had less to do with average or maximum individual IQ than with collaboration. She found that strong groups have good communication skills, open minds, and an equal flow of ideas among participants. A room where one person dominates may feel decisive, but it may be losing intelligence in real time.
Watch who grabs attention and who recedes into the background. Who gets interrupted? Who is allowed to finish? Who tried to get into the conversation and then gave up? The smartest thing to do, for the group, is to allow everyone to speak and to be heard.
Read body language like a pro
Amateur room readers imbue simple gestures with definitive meaning: crossed arms signal defensiveness, eye contact suggests honesty. The pros observe changes from baseline and look for clusters of behavior that point in the same direction.
Science tells us how badly shortcuts deceive us. For example, many people believe that liars avoid eye contact. Researchers at an international airport asked 338 passengers from 81 countries to tell the truth or lie about their travel plans on camera. The liars held eye contact longer—deliberately, a beat past comfortable. Meanwhile, honest people, nervous under questioning, glanced away and looked guilty.
Fidgeting is also meaningless as a single gesture. Let’s say someone taps their foot in a meeting or plays with their pen nervously. Maybe that’s their norm. The behavior only becomes a signal when their pattern shifts. The savvy room reader asks what triggered the shift from baseline and watches for a cluster of behaviors. Did a particular question cause them to shift their posture, stop their normal foot-tapping, and freeze their blink-rate? That’s worth noting.
The question is never, “What does this gesture mean?” The better question is, “What does this gesture mean here, from this person, under these conditions?”
Room reading is a powerful skill that’s part social observation and part emotional intelligence.
As you start to see people and interactions more clearly, you’ll alter your own behavior accordingly. And when you do, many more doors will open because you won’t be guessing what the moment requires.

As Trump locks in oil deal, Venezuelans ask: What happened to elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The White House has said the sweeping oil deal between the U.S. and Venezuela would make elections ‘possible’ in a country long battered by economic and other problems.
- President Trump and interim President Delcy Rodríguez, however, will not commit to when an election might be held.
- ‘We were expecting elections,’ said one Caracas resident. ‘This pact with Trump entrenched the dictatorship that he himself declared war on.’
WASHINGTON — President Trump has locked in a deal to develop Venezuela’s vast oil resources, an arrangement the White House says will bring a country battered by years of economic collapse to a “place where elections are possible.”
But the agreement — backed by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a holdover from the Nicolás Maduro government that Washington deems “illegitimate” — is raising new uncertainty about how entrenched the unelected government may become.
In January, when the U.S. military captured Maduro, Trump did not say how long a democratic transition would take but said Rodríguez was “gracious” and “essentially willing to do what we think is necessary.”
Asked by The Times on Wednesday what was stopping him from demanding Venezuela set a firm election date, Trump was blunt: “I just don’t think they are ready yet.”
“It’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship and we’re getting along great with the government,” Trump said. But he said an election would happen “soon.”
Under the deal, the U.S. government is partnering with an oil producer to create a new company, North American Blue Energy Partners, to develop 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. NABEP will have rights to the fields for 100 years.
For many Venezuelans, the lack of urgency around elections — set against a deal that gives the United States majority control over roughly a third of the country’s oil reserves — is starting to feel like a broken promise.
“They tell us we have to wait two years, maybe more, while in the meantime they do business with a government that wasn’t elected, that was imposed on us, and that we don’t want,” Carlos Pérez, a 23-year-old automotive mechanics student, told The Times.
Antonio Marchetti, a 45-year-old plumber and electrician, said that while he sees the removal of Maduro as a “good thing,” the oil deal makes it seem as though Trump’s plans were those of a “cowboy, the invader John Wayne,” all along.
“We were expecting elections,” Marchetti said. “This pact with Trump entrenched the dictatorship that he himself declared war on. But to get rid of Maduro, he left the rest and did business with them. It disgusts me.”
The frustrations go beyond Venezuela. In Washington, Republican lawmakers have praised the oil deal, while calling Rodríguez an “interim dictator” who cannot be trusted.
María Corina Machado, the exiled leader of the Venezuelan opposition and a recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, on Thursday raised her own worries about what the oil deal means for the future of Venezuela.
In a video message, Machado stopped short of criticizing Trump’s oil deal, but acknowledged concerns about a pact negotiated with an “illegitimate” government.
“Venezuelans know that there can be no development without strong institutions and a government elected by popular vote,” she said. “That is the only real guarantee of success and stability for any large-scale investment.”
A plan in the works
Trump administration officials have characterized the deal as an economic lifeline that will eventually stabilize a country and prepare it for free and fair elections.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the United States is facilitating talks between Venezuela’s interim government and Dinorah Figuera, an opposition figure leading Venezuela’s 2015 National Assembly, the last democratically elected legislature recognized by the United States.
Broken pumps, rusted pipes, ghost towns mark Venezuela’s once vibrant oil hub. It will cost billions to restore the industry.
Machado has been left out of those talks. They are expected to resume in mid-September.
Rubio says that for any election to be “credible,” the voting system will require an overhaul and political parties will need time to organize. Steps also must be taken to ensure the country has a free press.
Echoing Rubio’s comments, the White House said Friday that Trump wants elections held at the “right time,” but that his top priority is to bring Venezuela “back from the dead and rebuild the country after it was incompetently ruled by a nasty dictatorship.”
On Wednesday, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited Caracas, Rodríguez declined to set a firm date for an election, but added, “I have worked tirelessly to ensure that Venezuela is ready and prepared when the time comes for its electoral process, which will take place — have no doubt about that: There will be an electoral process.”
The open-ended approach to holding an election, however, has drawn criticism from former Trump administration officials, who argue the lack of a timeline essentially lets Rodríguez govern indefinitely.
“Here’s my fear: It makes us Delcy’s partner, and gives the president a reason to want her to remain in power,” Elliott Abrams, who served as U.S. special envoy to Venezuela during Trump’s first term, told The Times.
He contended that the White House so far appears to prefer a pliant interlocutor, and Rodríguez, he says, will do “whatever Trump tells her to do.”
If an election is to take place in Venezuela, a nine-month runway for preparation is likely to be expected, Abrams said.
In Washington, some Republican lawmakers have continued to call for elections in Venezuela, arguing that Rodríguez cannot be trusted.
“The only way we will have a prosperous Venezuela is with the end of the murderous regime and the return of democracy,” Rep. Carlos A. Gimenez (R-Fla.) wrote on social media. He also called Rodríguez an “interim dictator.”
There’s a lot that’s not immediately clear about President Trump’s deal giving the United States a stake in Venezuela’s vast oil reserves.
In an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said he does not necessarily think elections should happen before the oil agreement is finalized, but he said they “need to proceed rapidly.”
“I believe they should proceed no later than midway through next year,” he said.
Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) said he is working with Trump and Rubio to ensure “free, fair and transparent elections as soon as possible.” He did not, however, say what would constitute “soon.”
Mixed views on economic hope
In the Lake Maracaibo region, an area that would see renewed investments under the oil agreement, Junior Araujo — a 47-year-old oil worker — sees a “wonderful opportunity to be reborn.”
Araujo, the father of three, is in desperate need of a better economic outlook. He works 120 hours a week and earns only $20. For his family, food alone usually costs about $150 a week.
“We have to get creative and find new ways to make ends meet through side jobs like selling clothes and making yogurt,” he said. “That’s our real financial situation.”
For Araujo, the hope for a better economy does not take away his frustrations with the government.
“We’re neither happy nor dancing here, all our benefits have been taken away from us,” he said. “Our main problem is the current government; we need to restore our institutions.”
Nazareth Lezama, a 35-year-old teacher, also sees the oil deal as an economic opportunity but remains concerned that the current government may not have negotiated the best price or conditions for Venezuela. She added this has happened in the past.
“We must be clear that this regime destroyed the oil industry,” she said, adding that Venezuelans “need elections to choose leaders based on merit.”
Marchetti, the plumber from Caracas, says the oil deal is a “100-year chain” on Venezuelans imposed by Trump. He said it has become the “last straw” for him, and he has decided to leave Venezuela and emigrate to Europe.
“With all the pain in my heart, I will leave everything behind. I have a European passport; it won’t be easy to start a life from scratch, but there is no hope left here,” he said.
He does not know where he will land yet. But he knows he needs to leave Venezuela.
“This ship is sinking,” he said.
Times staff writer Ceballos reported from Washington. Special correspondent Mogollón reported from Caracas.

Trump's economic record is working against him in the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Trump’s economic record is working against him in the midterms
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump’s trade wars, tax cuts and immigration crackdown have driven up prices on everyday goods and gas.
- With inflation elevated and gas prices surging amid the war with Iran, voters give Trump dismal marks on the economy as Republicans brace for midterm losses.
- Some GOP candidates are embracing Trump and touting his policies but others are distancing themselves from the president.
WASHINGTON — A sporadic global trade war led by President Trump is fueling inflation across the U.S. economy, elevating prices on everyday goods, as the war with Iran sends the price of gas on a roller coaster.
Aggressive tax cuts have pushed the national debt past $40 trillion, driving a growing crisis in the bond market. And an unprecedented immigration crackdown is disrupting the labor supply in agriculture, construction, hospitality and food processing, raising prices even further.
Approaching the halfway point of Trump’s second term, a president who won reelection based on a promise to turn the economy around now faces a reckoning in the midterm elections centered largely on his economic record.
Trump’s economic agenda has emerged as an increasingly awkward liability for Republicans heading into the November elections, leaving lawmakers to defend policies that have delivered political pain at home, even as the White House argues they will pay off in the long run.
Polling on Trump’s handling of the economy has remained in precariously low territory throughout the summer, entering Labor Day weekend with less than a third of Americans supporting his job performance on their most pressing concerns. One recent poll, from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, found that only 22% perceive the economy in a good or fair state.
And Americans’ confidence in the economy is unlikely to improve much ahead of election day, Nov. 3, in part because bad economic news has shown to sink confidence fast. Good news takes much longer to win people back, experts said.
“Voters’ opinion of the economy has mostly hardened,” said Aaron Klein, chair of economic studies at the Brookings Institution. “People vote the economy of the spring and summer, not November.”
Good news has been harder to come by.
Heading into the holiday weekend, Trump dismissed communities opposed to data-center construction as “backwards and poor.” A rapidly escalating trade dispute with Canada threatens Republican gains in battlegrounds along the northern border that could determine control of the Senate.
And fresh polling found that more than 90% of Americans believe corruption is rampant in Trump’s government, even as the president spends hundreds of millions of dollars on vanity projects across the capital.
Susan Collins, the incumbent Republican senator from Maine seeking another term in a strategically critical race, chastised the Trump administration for its latest trade spat with Ottawa as “making the job harder” of securing reelection.
“There’s just nothing good you can say about them,” Collins said of the tariffs.
Trump has pushed back on criticisms of his record, declaring the country has “the greatest economy we’ve ever had” and touting what he calls a manufacturing boom, all while distancing himself from potential midterm losses.
“I’m not affected by the election,” Trump told reporters last week. “I’m not running. But my party’s running, and I’m going to help my party.”
But Rep. Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican and speaker of the House, said last week that the midterms would serve as a referendum on Trump’s presidency.
“Even though his name isn’t in the midterm, his legacy is,” Johnson said. “The America First priorities and principles are. His administration is.”
Several embattled incumbents fear that’s the case and are distancing themselves from the president. Several Republican lawmakers — including Reps. Tom Barrett of Michigan and Zach Nunn of Iowa — plan on skipping a midterm GOP convention called by Trump for this week in Texas.
Joanne Hsu, director of the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers, said that gas prices were a chief frustration among Americans, and found that consumer sentiment soured rapidly once it became clear the conflict in Iran would not be short-lived.
“Consumers are absolutely not feeling great about the economy right now, and the factors that are underpinning their frustrations with the economy at this time are factors that are pretty tough to turn around on short notice,” Hsu said.
Even if the Iran conflict reached a resolution, confidence in the economy is likely to change only when the prices are reflected at the gas station, she said.
“When it comes to the views of the economy, it’s really about what’s happening to my wallet,” Hsu said.
During a White House press media briefing on Thursday,Vice President JD Vance acknowledged the Iran war has led gas prices to rise and that he does not know when Americans can expect those prices to go down.
“The reason gas prices are so high now is because the Iranians are shooting at commercial shipping,” Vance said. “Gas, frankly, could have been much, much higher were it not for our efforts. But I am not going to make a promise about when it is going to return to $3.”
The day after Vance spoke, diesel hit a record all-time high of $5.85 a gallon. In California, it sold for as much as $7.71.
Yet Trump has tried to downplay the economic pressure the war in Iran is placing on Americans, in particular as the Strait of Hormuz — a vital shipping corridor for oil and gas — remains under threat by Iranian troops.
“We have the Strait of Hormuz in extremely good shape,” Trump said, adding that the U.S. Navy has escorted ships through the channel. “A lot of oil is coming out. That’s why you haven’t seen the price of oil going the way they thought it might have to go.”
Trump on Monday also touted an agreement with the Venezuelan government to develop a vast amount of the South American country’s oil reserves. Asked how he sees the deal affecting American consumers, Trump said: “Ultimately prices are going to come down.”
“Now, will it happen before the election? I can’t tell you that. But I think people are very smart,” he said.
For some Americans, the economic pressures are a key driver ahead of the midterm elections.
Monica Escalante, a home care provider who is a member of the United Domestic Workers union, said she started feeling the pinch on her wallet after Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on a number of products she buys at the grocery store. Gas, she noticed, became harder to cover after the Iran war started.
Escalante, who lives in Bakersfield, said she also has to drive her client to the grocery store, and that mileage reimbursements are not enough to cover her costs.
“It’s really hard when I don’t have the money for gas, and she doesn’t have the money for gas. Then it is like: What do we do?” she said. “It is either she’s borrowing or I’m trying to figure out how I can get gas in my tank.”

Press review: US may revive Russia-Ukraine talks as Dutch push on frozen assets grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. US envoys meet with Vladimir Putin in Moscow as Washington seeks to revive Russia-Ukraine peace talks; the Netherlands is pushing the EU to use frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine despite opposition within the bloc; and US-backed oil deals are expanding foreign involvement in Venezuela as the country seeks to revive production. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: US mediation may revive prospects for renewed Russia-Ukraine talks
US presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on September 5 for their first visit to Russia in the past seven months. They spent more than three hours at the Kremlin discussing Washington’s peace proposals with Russian president Vladimir Putin before continuing consultations with Vladimir Zelensky. Jared Kushner said Donald Trump had instructed his team to prepare a package of documents for a peace agreement between Moscow and Kiev. According to Kushner, Washington ultimately hopes to return the negotiations to a trilateral Russia-US-Ukraine format.
The very fact that contacts have resumed after a lengthy hiatus is already a positive signal, political scientist Andrey Kortunov told Izvestia. In his view, the duration of the talks indicates that the dialogue was substantive: if Moscow and Washington had merely been reiterating their previous positions, there would have been no need for a three-hour meeting at the Kremlin.
At the same time, the durability of any agreements brokered by Donald Trump remains in question. The upcoming US congressional elections could significantly alter Washington’s policy toward Russia and Ukraine, Ivan Loshkarev, associate professor at the Department of Political Theory at MGIMO University, told Izvestia.
Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at HSE University, told Vedomosti he is skeptical about the possibility of a "diplomatic breakthrough," as the positions of the main parties to the conflict -- Kiev and Moscow -- remain far apart. At the same time, Suslov said that interim agreements could be reached on resuming the active phase of the negotiation process.
"Fundamentally, the discussion most likely concerned the resumption of direct Russian-Ukrainian contacts in one format or another -- this is how all previous rounds of Mr. Witkoff’s diplomatic activity ultimately concluded. However, preparations for such contacts could take the entire fall, or even longer if the parties so choose," Dmitry Novikov, associate professor at the Faculty of World Economy and International Affairs at HSE University, told the newspaper. He recalled that several months elapsed between Anchorage and the first Russian-Ukrainian contacts.
The EU responded positively to the US envoys’ visit Izvestia writes. However, despite calls from Europe to resume direct dialogue with Moscow, Brussels has yet to take any concrete steps. Individual European countries should become involved in the dialogue on their own, Czech member of the European Parliament Ivan David told the newspaper.
European countries will remain outside the main negotiation process in the near future, political scientist Evgeny Mikhailov believes. If Washington succeeds in making progress in the dialogue between Moscow and Kiev, the EU will have to adapt to the situation -- even if its own policy toward Ukraine remains unchanged.
Izvestia: Netherlands pushes EU to revisit use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine
The Netherlands intends to push for the transfer of frozen Russian assets to Ukraine, the country’s embassy in Moscow told Izvestia. However, there is no consensus on the issue within the European Union itself. Belgium, whose Euroclear depository holds the bulk of Russia’s reserves, has once again voiced opposition. Belgian officials warned of serious legal risks and a potential blow to the reputation of the entire European financial system. The Hague’s initiative, which has also been joined by Spain, Poland and Sweden, has received no public endorsement from other countries.
"The use of frozen assets to support Ukraine is something the Dutch government has consistently advocated," the country’s embassy in Russia told Izvestia. "Together with Poland, Spain and Sweden, we have asked the European Commission to develop a solution for the use of assets frozen at the international financial company Euroclear. This is necessary because Ukraine requires both short-term and long-term financial support," the embassy added.
The main dispute concerns the procedure for seizing the reserves themselves. The European Commission has repeatedly rejected proposals for outright confiscation, considering the use of profits generated by the assets alone to be legally safer, Izvestia writes.
Belgium is concerned that the seizure of sovereign funds could violate international law. Bulgaria, Hungary, Italy, Malta, Slovakia, France and the Czech Republic have also opposed confiscation.
Political scientist Egor Sergeev believes that the Netherlands’ latest initiative is merely another stage in a debate that the European Union will continue to revisit. According to him, the EU has been consistently seeking a way to secure long-term financing for Ukraine while placing the smallest possible burden on its own budgets, which is why the issue of confiscating Russian assets periodically returns to the agenda. At the same time, the expert told Izvestia he doubts that the current round of negotiations will produce any concrete decisions: the EU has already established a number of mechanisms that effectively use frozen Russian reserves as financial collateral. However, the likelihood that the assets will be returned to Russia also remains extremely low.
Vedomosti: US oil push may revive Venezuela’s output but full recovery remains years away
Contracts awarded under President Donald Trump’s August 31 deal with Venezuela to control 65 bln barrels of its oil, covering the development of three fields by US-based Chevron and Italy’s Eni, are unlikely for now to significantly increase production and do not threaten China’s interests in the country. However, the transfer of 17 fields for 100 years to North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) affects Chinese assets and threatens both Caracas’ debt payments to Beijing and Venezuelan oil supplies to China, although these losses are not critical for the Chinese, experts surveyed by Vedomosti agreed.
The return of international companies to Venezuela will help further boost the country’s recovering oil production, as has already occurred in other countries. With Western assistance, Caracas could return to the peak production levels seen 30 years ago by around 2035, energy expert Kirill Rodionov told the newspaper.
However, investment by the two companies alone is not yet on the scale needed to rapidly "cure" Venezuela’s oil industry, which has been deteriorating since 2018; the country needs hundreds of billions, rather than tens of billions, of dollars, Viktor Kheifets, editor-in-chief of the Latin America journal, believes.
At the same time, the projects awarded to Chevron and Eni are not among the Chinese projects that were being developed before the change of power from Nicolas Maduro, who was abducted in January, to interim President Delcy Rodriguez, an expert at the Financial University under the Government of Russia, Igor Yushkov, told Vedomosti.
China has already recovered the bulk of the principal on Venezuela’s debt, with mainly interest payments remaining, which even the previous authorities in Caracas considered excessive, Kheifets noted. Caracas owed Beijing $10-15 bln out of a total external debt of $150-200 bln, according to a June estimate by S&P Global Energy.
At the same time, Beijing has significantly reduced its dependence on Venezuelan oil in recent years, Kheifets said. However, these supplies generated high margins for Chinese buyers because of the discounts, Yushkov noted. "Refining in China will be less efficient without advantageous Venezuelan and now Iranian oil. The United States has deprived Beijing of such profitable suppliers, even though alternatives remain available," he said.
Vedomosti: AfD lands record result in Saxony-Anhalt, putting Merz under pressure
Elections to the local parliament (Landtag) were held on September 6 in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with the country’s main opposition party, the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD), the clear favorite. According to an exit poll released by broadcaster ARD after voting ended, the AfD is leading the election in Saxony-Anhalt with 44.5% of the vote - its best result in the history of Landtag elections. Experts told Vedomosti that attempts to keep the AfD out of power could produce an unstable government and further benefit the party, whose record showing reflects broader economic, institutional, and social discontent, while the setback could intensify pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In theory, the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt could unite against the AfD or form a minority government, senior research fellow at the Institute for International Studies at MGIMO University Artyom Sokolov told the newspaper. However, the expert explained that such a government would be unlikely to remain viable, while the AfD would benefit either way, as it could argue that it was being deliberately kept out of power and that the firewall (Brandmauer) policy was leading to an ineffective government. For Merz, the AfD’s victory represents a serious blow that could prompt members of his CDU party to call for his resignation.
The AfD’s success cannot be explained solely by the migration issue or the oft-cited "nostalgia for East Germany," Vladislav Belov, deputy director of the Institute of Europe at the Russian Academy of Sciences, noted. Rather, it reflects a combination of accumulated distrust toward federal institutions and traditional parties, a sense that eastern German interests are not sufficiently recognized, and contemporary concerns including the state of the economy, energy costs, migration, education and infrastructure.
As for Merz’s own political future after the election, the expert believes that the CDU has no interest in replacing the chancellor. Merz currently serves as an anchor for maintaining stability within the coalition, which, despite its difficulties, will continue to function.
Kommersant: OPEC+ leaves October production quotas unchanged amid Hormuz uncertainty
The seven-member OPEC+ alliance, whose influence over the oil market has weakened because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has kept October oil production quotas at September levels. Market participants told Kommersant that producers are still falling short of their current output targets, making an increase in quotas unlikely in the coming months.
October production quotas for the alliance’s largest producers - Saudi Arabia and Russia - will remain at 10.478 mln barrels per day (bpd) and 9.949 mln bpd, respectively. Iraq’s quota will stand at 4.431 mln bpd, followed by 2.676 mln bpd for Kuwait, 1.628 mln bpd for Kazakhstan, 1.007 mln bpd for Algeria, and 841,000 bpd for Oman.
The next OPEC+ meeting is scheduled for October 4. Kommersant’s sources believe producers will also maintain the current level of production at that meeting.
As Kommersant’s sources noted, OPEC+ decisions remain largely formal for now because, in practice, partners are producing well below their target levels due to the situation in the Middle East. The alliance’s influence on the market is currently severely constrained by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has left a significant share of the world’s oil production trapped, and this situation is unlikely to be resolved in the coming months. As a result, the sources believe production quotas for OPEC+ members will most likely remain unchanged through the end of the year.
Igor Yushkov, expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, told Kommersant there is no point in deciding to increase OPEC+ production while Middle Eastern oil remains trapped in the Persian Gulf and the capacity of Russia’s export infrastructure remains constrained.

Continental divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
26 minute listen
Leônidas Borges de Oliveira drove the first 300 miles of the world’s longest road trip alone. The date of his departure, in early 1928, meant that the young Brazilian army officer also had the road almost entirely to himself. This gave him time to think about what he had taken on. The vehicle beneath him, a donated Ford Model T with a decade of delivering newspapers on the odometer, chattered with ease over alternating segments of fresh gravel and steaming asphalt that constituted Brazil’s new highway, connecting Rio de Janeiro with São Paulo. On both sides of the road, Oliveira surveyed the deforested Paraíba Valley, which had hosted the world’s first coffee boom – ranks of bean-fruiting bushes whose product had reached global markets in 60-kilo sacks on the backs of mules. Oliveira was among the first to see his nation at highway speed, and velocity could make the eroded landscapes of the past feel irrelevant. He believed he was chasing the future.
His compatriots shared his optimism. With shining medals around his neck and a new Swiss chronograph on his wrist, Oliveira departed from Rio to the fanfare of two brass bands and a flourish of civic oratory. He arrived in São Paulo to cheering crowds and a press corps keen to follow his automotive exploits. Oliveira’s rapid progress on this first leg, not to mention his countrymen’s enthusiastic support, fortified his resolve to push on to his final destination: the United States’ capital at Washington, DC.
Oliveira’s inspiration to make the long drive sprang from a novel idea, first proposed in 1923: the construction of an automotive highway that would link up the Western Hemisphere with a long ribbon of asphalt. Nobody knew exactly where the proposal had originated, and some official reactions in Latin America were tepid, but the popular response revealed an accelerating enthusiasm, and auto makers moved to capitalise on it. In 1924, the US Department of Commerce, which was headed by former auto executives, welcomed delegates from 19 Latin American nations to the largest promotional junket the US had organised to date, including a greeting at the White House by President Calvin Coolidge and a month-long highway tour that circled from New York to North Carolina and Minnesota to Michigan. The objective was to promote what Americans were calling a ‘Highway of Friendship’ – a Pan-American road, from the northern reaches of Alaska to the tip of Tierra del Fuego, over which they hoped to see unfettered automotive travel and the emergence of stronger hemispheric cultural bonds.
Scores of intrepid adventure motorists were electrified by the possibility of such a road, and they believed the best way to support the proposal was to drive it, even before contractors had broken any ground. Oliveira, short in stature but ruggedly muscular, sought a little personal glory, he confessed, and none could blame him for that. But the notion that most resonated with his irrepressible idealism was the raw concept of unrestricted mobility, the agency and facility to go anywhere in the world a person cared to go. The last Western nation to abolish slavery, Brazil codified in its 1891 constitution every citizen’s right to move about the landscape without legal or physical restraint, and to reside, work and form relationships wherever they chose. For Oliveira, the highway and the car represented the medium and the means that could make free movement an achievable reality on a new scale. His long, goodwill drive was launched to celebrate these ideals, and to make them concrete.
What Oliveira ultimately wanted was an authentic Pan-American Union, two continents without passports, without customs, and without official barriers at the hemispheres’ many successive borders. Nearly a century later, the fraternal ideals that underpinned this dream and gave birth to the Pan-American Highway might appear unimaginably distant, subverted by nativist sentiment – but, in fact, remain alive in one of the two continents the road was supposed to link.
First, Oliveira had to prove it could be done. A few dozen had tried to reach the US before him. In fact, the first to road-test potential routes for such a highway were not American drivers in new American cars but Argentines and Brazilians piloting either luxury European sedans entirely inappropriate to the terrain or topless American jalopies of dubious reliability. Nobody had succeeded in – or even committed to, as Oliveira had – driving the entire expedition without a detour, that is, on the actual ground without placing one’s vehicle on the afterdeck of a ship or on a railroad flatcar to surpass a series of known, impenetrable topographies. Everyone told him, and kept telling him all along his route, that what he proposed was impossible. Brazilian highway officials doubted he would get out of Brazil.
He soon learned why he had so many doubters. Over his excursion, he found little mileage as easy as the Rio to São Paulo highway. The way was treacherous, and motorists had died in previous attempts. Indeed, Oliveira’s gruelling daily toil did not let up until he entered the US state highway system almost a decade later. His drive proved not only the world’s longest to date in accrued distance at 17,769 miles but also arguably the longest ever in elapsed time.
Oliveira’s convictions kept him and two later companions at their task, plodding north, year after year. At every opportunity, he spoke with energy about the dreams surrounding the construction of a highway connecting the continents, of an imminent hemispheric fraternity, and his remarks were published approvingly in papers in every nation he passed through. At his arrival in Washington, however, US officials insisted that what he claimed to have done was impossible. Most were considerate enough not to say it to his face, and he had the honour of meeting President Franklin Roosevelt and speaking to a large audience at the Pan-American Union building. But almost nobody believed Oliveira’s claims. Engineers from the US Bureau of Public Roads had struggled to walk segments of the route, let alone motor along it. And they rejected his maps, which they described as not inaccurate but belated. The Americans had already projected the official route through spaces their surveyors had not yet dared to go.
Where the road ran out, his men disassembled their vehicles, packed the components onto mules, and marched them on foot
The evidence, however, suggests that Oliveira did exactly what he said he did. He arrived in Washington in early 1938 with a 500-page logbook of his itinerary, as well as photographs of himself and his companions posing with every mayor, governor and head of state they met along their route. They took informal photos at train stations, each city’s name in prominent signage, to prove they’d been there. The streets of most towns and villages they passed through had never seen a car before, and Oliveira’s team was welcomed as conquering heroes. The Brazilians even had a formal portrait done in Managua with the Nicaraguan revolutionary Augusto Sandino, who was possibly the biggest obstacle to intercontinental automobile travel from 1927-33. Sandino had thwarted, captured and even shot previous automotive adventurers who’d dared to pass through his territory. The photo, taken while Sandino was in peace negotiations, was his last; he was assassinated two days later at a military camp, gunfire that Oliveira claimed to have heard himself.
In truth, Oliveira didn’t literally drive on four tyres over the entire route, though he cut no geographic corners. Where the road ran out or became too steep or narrow, his men disassembled their vehicles (he now had two Model Ts), packed the components onto mules, like sacks of coffee, and marched them on foot until the terrain again became drivable. As further proof, every step of the way, Oliveira’s maps detailed his progress, and he gifted copies of his charts to any state or national government that would receive them.
Beleaguered by a whisper campaign in Washington against his drive, Oliveira returned to Brazil disillusioned, and he rarely talked about his extraordinary excursion during the rest of his life, which was spent at the lowest rungs of Brazil’s consular service. Despite his inimitable effort, he had been disbelieved and called a charlatan. Even though he never seemed to raise the question himself, some at home wondered if his nationality, or worse, his likely African and Indigenous ancestry, played a role in his rejection as a legitimate explorer. And, despite substantial publicity, Oliveira’s expedition was largely forgotten, even in Brazil, not to be recovered in historical memory until this century.
The Pan-American Highway that Oliveira hoped to pioneer was indeed born in a burst of fraternal rhetoric. Officially, however, the road was never just about driving a car from Patagonia to Alaska, or vice versa, for the mere amusement of tourists. It was to be a modern network connecting every national capital, from Ottawa and Washington to Santiago and Buenos Aires. And this was to be only a beginning. The network was to then expand until it reached every province and shore, facilitating trade and resource extraction, breaking down old stereotypes and softening contested borders in friendly cultural exchanges. The ideals remained potent for half a century, and in 1966 the US declared the entire US interstate system part of the Pan-American Highway network.
In a strictly material sense, this greater project has been a remarkable success, millions of miles of functional automobile paths that have revolutionised movement and left few spaces inaccessible to wheels. By 1915, the US paved a road from Canada to Mexico. In 1917, Peru pushed its first highway into the Amazon Basin. Already by 1925, Venezuelans could drive over the Andes in comfort, and from 1931 Cubans could motor the full length of their island. The US built a primitive road across Canada to Alaska in 1942, during the war, and Mexican contractors reached Guatemala in 1950. The overall progress was extraordinary. Ironically, however, the key link in the system through Central America, over which the US took control and about which there was incomparable publicity, was the slowest to advance. Not till 1962 did the US-built highway reach Panama City. And not far beyond the Panama Canal, the road came to a sudden halt at the boundary of an almost mythical space between Panama and Colombia known from 1955 as the Darién Gap. Since about 1980, not a single mile of progress has been made to close it.
The Pan-American Highway would harden national borders almost everywhere it went, rather than open them
The idealised Pan-American Highway has a troubled history that in some essential features parallels Oliveira’s ill-starred excursion. The road was announced in celebration and extraordinary idealism; it was pursued despite extreme exertions, diplomatic squabbles and ballooning expenses; and its construction spanned an unexpectedly long period, essentially a century. But the project sputtered out in disappointment and forgetting. Remarkably, the highway ended in a broadly held false memory. If Brazilians forgot Oliveira’s record road trip, Americans seemed to remember that we finished the highway. Even today, two thirds of the North Americans I’ve asked if it’s possible to drive from North to South America think that the Pan-American Highway was inaugurated and has long been open to general traffic. This historical confabulation formed early. American tourists in the 1970s, some pulling camping trailers, drove south in full expectation of crossing the intercontinental divide to vacation in South America. When they passed through the Native village of Chepo in eastern Panama, locals kindly informed them that there was no road through, but third- and fourth-generation US motorists could not seem to comprehend the idea of no road, so on they went. One Chepo resident sardonically observed that, within days, every driver returned north by the same road they’d come on. Set straight about the highway’s incompleteness by their own experience, some expressed a sense of having been defrauded by all the official highway hoopla.
And just as Oliveira’s trip did not end in increased American brotherhood, the Pan-American Highway would harden national borders almost everywhere it went, rather than open them. If getting from one border to the next became increasingly easy, at the borders themselves, the road’s arrival threw up political, cultural and material barriers – walls, fences and even the Darién Gap itself, which at first was a geographical barrier universally condemned. By the late-1970s, the Gap came to be embraced as a permanent fixture by Panamanian officials, US diplomats and international environmentalists. The best current explanation for the highway’s unfinished status, the reason that Panama and Colombia are the only two bordering nations on Earth without an automotive connection of even the most rudimentary kind, is that Panama refuses to build a road they believe would serve as a superhighway for Colombian immigrants. The Gap is their border wall.
Before highways connected the nations of the Americas, many borders were illegible – nobody quite knew where the lines were, and states made little effort to monitor human ingressions into national territory. These official absences at the border reflected rather open policies toward immigration and naturalisation before the 1920s. Brazil’s constitution, like those of other Latin American nations, rejected colonialism’s restrictions on migration and guaranteed free entry to anyone ‘when and how he may choose, independently of passport.’ Many Latin American nations paid immigrants to come, and gave them free land on arrival. Even in border towns like the two Nogales – one in the Mexican state of Sonora, and the other in Arizona, US – people knew where the border was, but movement across it was brisk and unregulated. Residents shopped, courted, and attended school with little regard for the line, which ran down the middle of a broad, shared main street, and the cities’ two mayors shared fire-fighting resources and cooperated on policing crime. At Ellis Island, the first US federal processing centre for immigrants, and at other official entry points, millions arrived each year literally undocumented, without passports, visas or birth certificates. Their names, identities and even nationalities listed on ship manifests were whatever they cared to declare, and customs officers waved through nearly all of them with little ceremony beyond a hasty medical check.
Popular attitudes toward immigrants had fluctuated with economic conditions but, for decades, flaring anti-immigrant sentiment had had little effect on general policy. True, the US barred the entry of prostitutes in 1875, convicts and the insane in 1882, and polygamists in 1891, but other than the 1882 blanket ban on Chinese nationals, most legislation had rather narrow targets against individuals defined as undesirables. Otherwise, the doors were mostly open. Policies, however, changed abruptly in the 1920s, and the highway’s promotion had some impact on the reversal. The same year that Coolidge spoke in favour of building the highway, he also declared that ‘America must be kept American,’ and US Congress passed the broadly restrictive Johnson-Reed Act, whose discriminatory quotas reduced immigrant arrivals by a harsh 80 per cent. Latin Americans were not included in the act, but already by 1929 the US began detaining and repatriating individuals of Mexican descent, some of whom had been born in the US.
Changes in attitudes and policies were not restricted to the US: Mexico and Central America followed suit almost immediately. Panama barred West Indians from entry in 1926. In the early 1930s, Mexico not only halted Chinese immigration but expelled without due process thousands of Chinese residents, many of whom had established successful, multi-generational businesses. In some cases, border restrictions seemed to arrive simultaneously with the highway. Costa Rican officials, who had recently promoted their open borders, established their first, land-based immigration controls just as the US constructed the highway connecting the nation to Nicaragua and Panama in the late-1930s.
The barriers to migration were national, ethnic and racial, created to turn back the poor and car-less
Significantly, restrictions on entry did not apply to tourists. Nor to adventurers. At the time of Oliveira’s drive, one could still cross borders without being aware of them but, increasingly, legal admittance to a nation required both passports and visas, and the red tape could be thick. Still, Oliveira found no insurmountable official barriers to his expedition’s actual progress. Indeed, the best way to identify yourself as a safe holidaymaker, or a legitimate explorer – someone who posed little threat of overstaying one’s welcome – was to arrive at the border by car. The automobile signalled one’s status and, if passage by car was fast on the highway, entry was almost certain – if not quick and painless – once at the border.
But it was migrants, not tourists, who became the primary long-distance users of the Pan-American Highway and its tributaries. Despite motel construction and flashy campaigns promoting national scenic sites, automotive tourists never showed up in significant numbers on the road. This had less to do with the quality or unfinished status of the highway than with its extraordinary length. Boosters touted the highway as the world’s longest, expecting that moniker alone to draw motorists toward distant adventures, but the Pan-American Highway proved too long for the average American’s two-week paid vacation. Reporters imagined Ohio suburbanites driving to Rio de Janeiro as if on a whim. But a drive to South America, even without the inevitable hassle of shipping one’s car around the Darién Gap, was a commitment of many months, even if going just one way. The few who did get as far as Panama typically sold their cars to US military personnel in the Canal Zone and sailed or flew home because they could not face the hardship of driving all the way back.
So those who took to the road in their millions didn’t come in cars with sunglasses on their noses. Rather, they sought new homes far from the places of their chance births. The majority moved on foot from rural areas to the largest cities in their own nations, the great urban migration that began in the 1930s, explained in part by new industrial jobs but greatly facilitated by new roads. Others went greater distances to settle in neighbouring nations: Colombians to Panama City; Nicaraguans to San José; Paraguayans and Bolivians to Buenos Aires. The most adventurous made the long trip to the US. While the highway made movement overland for migrants on foot substantially easier, once they arrived at a border, they typically came up against formidable legal obstacles. Even if they had secured the proper papers, they might be rejected because, without cars, they were identified as poor migrants. The administrative barriers to migration were national, ethnic and racial in character but, most specifically, they were created to turn back the poor and car-less.
Hence, migrants circumvented officials by crossing borders where there were no roads. Nicaraguans arrived within view of Costa Rica on chartered buses that left them on a lonely highway that paralleled the border. Under the cover of night, they walked into Costa Rica where another bus picked them up and dropped them in San José the same day. Migrants moving north through Guatemala avoided the Mexican immigration office on the bridge over the Suchiate River, crossing the same on rubber rafts for a small fee, often within sight of authorities. To get across the US border, there were dozens of ways to get around official barriers, most of them now facilitated by Mexican cartels.
The longest walk still takes place in the Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama. Despite its distance and dangers, the Gap has been the most attractive point of entry onto migrant trails north because, without a road, neither Colombia nor Panama place officials or enforcement at the border itself, making it North America’s soft underbelly. Here, despite the hazards of the Gap, which includes a two-week trudge that has proven fatal for some, once at the border, you can walk across entirely unopposed. In the past, if Panama caught illegal migrants walking into the nation, they gathered them in jails and then marched them right back over the Gap. In recent years, with as many as a half a million coming through annually, including tens of thousands of children, Panama finds it easiest to put migrants on buses headed north, withholding passports until they arrive at the Costa Rican border.
Important elements of the highway’s original ideals have endured even in the face of the dominant, contrary trends in immigration policy. Strikingly, beginning in 2010, nations in South America that in the past had been at war, often over the very boundaries that separated them, states whose individuals still retain an often palpable dislike for one another, came together to agree that, for the purposes of immigration, their borders would essentially cease to exist. Agreements strove to recharacterise immigration as a solution rather than a problem: the free movement of people was likely to decrease national tensions, enhance labour allocation, and recognise migrants’ basic human dignity by eliminating discrimination in work, healthcare and civil rights. While the EU seemed to be suffering setbacks, such as the loss of the UK, South America quickly gained an almost universal adherence.
Hence today in South America, all those highways built at such great cost to connect national territories finally arrived at the destination to which Oliveira and others hoped: a union of American states. South America now houses the world’s largest free immigration zone, where the citizens of member nations, in addition to the familiar human rights of speech, religion, and assembly, now enjoy the basic right of free movement, to live, labour, and build (or reunite) families in any member country they choose. Regardless of their poverty, they can relocate to another nation without passports or visas and, upon arrival in their newly chosen home, they can start a business, send remittances, and enrol their children in public schools. Educational credentials are universally recognised, and new residents can be registered in national retirement programmes with credit for time employed in their nation of origin. And with just two years of residency, immigrants are eligible to apply for full citizenship. Nine nations have agreed to most of these terms, the exceptions being Venezuela, due to political challenges, and Suriname and Guyana, who are not yet parties to the treaty. The changes, of course, have not gone uncontested, particularly by conservative leaders such as Javier Milei, who insists on Argentina’s sovereign power over immigration, has suggested an Argentine Brexit, and even threatened Argentines with a loss of citizenship at home if they leave. Still, even in Argentina, the basic terms of the agreement hold, despite Milei’s populist bluster. The contrast with the US’s rising walls and Panama’s persisting Gap could not be starker.
In 1932, the Darién Gap was wider than it is today, and it was the only place that Oliveira was forced to backtrack. He attempted to drive it even though the Colombian military had told him it was impossible. Broad swamps and malarial fevers forced the Brazilians to place their disassembled Fords on the deck of a boat for the first and only time. Oliveira, who might be in the running for the most optimistic person to have ever lived, opined that the Pan-American Highway would never be built overland though the Gap. The topography, he believed, was just too difficult. On that point, he was wrong. Humans have built roads through, over, and under terrain far more difficult than the Gap: Mexico’s Durango to Mazatlán Highway conquers the Sierra Madre with 63 tunnels and 115 bridges, one of them 400 metres high; the Faroese have tunnelled 600 feet below the Atlantic Ocean to connect their remote islands, one segment of which includes the world’s first subseafloor roundabout.
In Panama, politics more than topography stand in the way of completing the road. The reality Oliveira could not yet see was that the fraternal ideals of free exchange and movement that he’d actively championed would die north of the Gap, foiling the highway’s long-anticipated completion. The South, however, has come to embrace Oliveira’s unswerving idealism, which would have pleased him. The myriad roads built across the South American continent in the past century, all without US help, permit the free flow of not just money, goods, ideas and wildlife, for which walls are mostly meaningless, but of human bodies, outside of whom no real meaningful rights exist. In South America, constitutional guarantees to free movement extend beyond national borders. Hence, a driving motive of the Pan-American Highway has now gone half the way there, but from the opposite direction its conceivers intended.

Thousands of canceled flights and closed airports: travel to Indonesia threatened by a volcanic eruption

2026-09-07
12:59:42 EEST
18:59:42 KST

Thousands of canceled flights and closed airports: travel to Indonesia threatened by a volcanic eruption
Kyiv • UNN
Seven airports have been closed in Indonesia, and more than 270,000 passengers have been affected by the eruption of Anak Krakatau. Authorities expect further eruptions.
In Indonesia, around 2,300 flights have been delayed, canceled or diverted due to the eruption of Anak Krakatau volcano, and the effects of the transport collapse have already affected more than 270,000 passengers. UNN reports this, citing Reuters, AP and Indonesian services.
Seven airports remain closed, including two in the Jakarta area. Authorities are warning of a high likelihood of further eruptions.
Details
As of September 7, seven airports are not operating, including the capital’s main international airport, Soekarno-Hatta, and Halim Perdanakusuma in Jakarta, as well as airports in the provinces of Lampung, Banten and West Java.
Initially, a decision was made to close eight airports due to the spread of ash. One of them, Atung Bungsu in South Sumatra, resumed operations on the morning of September 7.
Authorities warned that it is difficult to predict the exact time when air traffic will be fully restored. The decision will depend on wind direction, weather conditions and the concentration of volcanic ash in the air. More than 270,000 passengers have currently been affected by flight cancellations.
The scale of the transport crisis continues to grow
While Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation previously reported that approximately 170,000 passengers had had their trips disrupted, the latest figures show that the number has exceeded 270,000. Overall, around 2,300 flights have been canceled, delayed or diverted.
The situation remains particularly difficult at Soekarno-Hatta Airport, which handles Jakarta’s main international passenger traffic. There alone, the effects of the eruption have affected around 1,000 flights. A number of major carriers, including Singapore Airlines, Malaysia Airlines, AirAsia and Lion Group airlines, canceled or postponed flights to Jakarta. Some passengers were forced to spend the night in terminals. Airlines provided people with food and drinks and, in some cases, arranged transfers to hotels.
To ease pressure on the transport system, Indonesian authorities placed five alternative airports into 24-hour operation. They are planned to be used to receive flights that cannot operate due to the closure of airspace around the capital.
The eruption of Anak Krakatau volcano: how it unfolded
The most intense phase of the eruption of Anak Krakatau volcano, located in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began late in the evening of September 4 and lasted about 25 hours. According to Indonesia’s Geological Agency, the continuous phase of the eruption has already ended; however, as of September 7, periodic emissions of volcanic ash, underground tremors and other signs of activity are being recorded. Experts consider the likelihood of further eruptions to be high.
During the most active phase, the ash column rose to a height of up to 15 kilometers. Volcanic ash was also detected in the airspace around Jakarta, posing a direct threat to civil aviation.
What difficulties has the country faced because of the volcanic ash
The effects of the eruption have already been felt beyond the transport sector. Volcanic ash fell in Jakarta and in the provinces of Banten, West Java and Lampung. Local residents were urged to wear protective masks and goggles, avoid prolonged outdoor exposure, cover water reservoirs and exercise caution on the roads because of reduced visibility. The media also report cases of eye irritation among the population.
As of September 7, Jakarta schools have switched to remote learning. Educational institutions in neighboring regions affected by the ash have also been authorized to make similar decisions.
The eruption has also affected fishing. Some local fishermen have refused to go out to sea.
At the same time, ferry services across the Sunda Strait continue to operate. Ships have been ordered not to approach Anak Krakatau closer than three kilometers.
What is the situation in Indonesia now
The third of four volcanic hazard levels is in effect for Anak Krakatau. The public is prohibited from approaching the volcano closer than three kilometers. The main risks remain new explosive eruptions, falling fragments of volcanic rock, heavy ash, and possible lava flows.
At the same time, Indonesian authorities are currently not detecting any immediate threat of a tsunami.
Context
Anak Krakatau, whose name translates as "child of Krakatau," formed in the caldera of the legendary Krakatau volcano after the catastrophic eruption of 1883. The tsunami caused by the volcano then claimed the lives of more than 36,000 people. In December 2018, the partial collapse of Anak Krakatau also triggered a tsunami in the Sunda Strait. More than 400 people died as a result of the disaster.
In addition to Anak Krakatau, activity was also recorded on September 6 at Mount Semeru in East Java, approximately 850 kilometers away. The third hazard level has also been established for Semeru.
Despite the simultaneous activity of several volcanoes in Indonesia, the authorities attribute the current large-scale disruptions to air traffic and airport operations specifically to the eruption of Anak Krakatau.

Over 400M acute pesticide poisonings occur worldwide each year: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:58:28 UTC
18:58:28 KST

Dilara Hamit
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Between 402 million and 433 million cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning occur worldwide each year, including around 11,000 fatalities, according to a new study.
The research, published Sept. 2 in the journal Frontiers in Public Health, estimates that approximately 46% of the world’s farming population is affected by pesticide poisoning annually.
Researchers based the figure on a global farming and occupational population of approximately 934 million people. The greatest estimated number of non-fatal cases was recorded in southern Asia, followed by southeastern Asia and eastern Africa.
The study updated an earlier systematic review by examining scientific literature published between 2006 and 2023 and supplementing the findings with data from the World Health Organization’s Mortality Database.
It covered 139 countries, including 62 represented in 214 scientific articles and another 77 covered through WHO mortality records.
The publications reviewed directly documented around 369,600 annual cases, including more than 9,100 deaths. Researchers then produced global estimates by combining national figures with regional population data.
The authors said the findings demonstrated that acute pesticide poisoning remained a major global public health challenge despite international efforts over the past two decades to reduce the harmful effects of pesticide use.
Global pesticide consumption increased from around 1.8 million tons in 1990 to 3.8 million tons in 2023. Usage rose by 210% in the Americas and 185% in Africa during that period, while declining by 5% in Europe.
The researchers warned that the burden of non-fatal poisoning, particularly among farmers and farmworkers, has received insufficient attention because international monitoring and policy measures have tended to focus on fatalities and intentional self-poisoning.
They also said official figures may significantly underestimate the problem, as many affected people do not seek medical treatment because of financial constraints, limited access to health facilities, fear of losing work or inadequate reporting systems.
At the same time, the authors acknowledged that extrapolating results from surveys conducted in high-risk agricultural areas or using non-specific symptoms could lead to overestimates.
The study also cited inconsistent definitions, limited national data, small sample sizes and the absence of standardized reporting systems as important limitations. Some countries were represented by only one publication.
The researchers called for standardized surveillance and reporting protocols and stronger national monitoring systems.
They also urged governments to implement international recommendations to phase out highly hazardous pesticides where risks cannot be adequately controlled, saying such action could substantially reduce the global poisoning burden.

How will France's school ban on phones play out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:58:24 UTC
18:58:24 KST

- Paris principal warns of practical challenges in enforcing ban saying it was enacted just as school year started leaving little time to plan
- Parents group stresses need to educate students on digital risks rather than just restrict access
When French high school students walked through the gates for the new school year last week, they entered classrooms under a new rule: their phones were off-limits during the school day.
France has extended its existing restrictions on mobile phones in middle and high schools, bringing students aged roughly 15 to 18 under the measure for the first time.
The ban took effect with the start of the 2026-27 school year on Sept. 1. It is part of a broader government effort to reduce young people’s exposure to screens and social media.
But while the principle is straightforward, its implementation is not.
Schools have been left to decide how phones will be stored, when exceptions can be made and how violations will be handled. Some are using lockers or individual pouches, while others are relying on students to keep phones switched off and inside their bags.
At the High school des Metiers Nicolas Louis Vauquelin in Paris, principal Carole Zerbib said the challenge was turning a national rule into something that works in the daily life of a school.
The law was enacted just days before the start of the school year, she said, leaving schools little time to devise plans.
 
- ‘A difficult measure to implement’
For Zerbib, the first challenge is practical: what happens to phones once students enter the school.
At Vauquelin, students are expected to keep their phones switched off and stored in their bags. The school is relying primarily on students’ responsibility and trust, she told Anadolu.
But storage and confiscation can create additional work. If a student violates the rule, the phone may be confiscated and taken to the administration, where it must be stored securely and its confiscation and return recorded.
“There is a risk of theft, loss or damage,” Zerbib said, noting that managing phones can require additional staff time.
The French Federation of Parents’ Councils shared with Anadolu concerns about how the measure will be applied from one school to another.
Mustafa Ozcelik, vice president of the parents council, said schools do not have the same facilities, equipment or human resources, creating a risk that implementation could vary across the board.
The parent council, he said, supports exceptions for medical needs, disabilities and specific educational requirements.
‘A rule is accepted when it is understood’
The measure has not been popular among students, according to Zerbib, who said enforcement could be particularly difficult during breaks.
The school plans to offer activities including chess, board games and choir as alternatives to phone use.
Zerbib said the rule is more likely to be accepted when students understand why it is being introduced.
Ozcelik echoed the view saying removing phones is not enough.
He said high school students are older and more independent than middle school pupils, and that schools should therefore focus on teaching them how to regulate their own digital use rather than relying solely on restrictions.
“The high school is a space for autonomy, maturity and critical thinking,” he said, arguing that a blanket approach risks overlooking the educational role schools can play in helping students.
This includes teaching students about social media, notifications, algorithms, cyberbullying and data protection.
What the government wants
The government has presented the measure as a way to improve concentration, learning and school climate.
Ozcelik acknowledged that limiting phone use during lessons could have positive effects.
But he said a phone ban alone could not address all the factors affecting concentration and school success, pointing to issues such as fatigue, sleep, learning conditions, school climate and social and family difficulties.
Zerbib also expects the measure to have positive effects, particularly on concentration and direct interaction among students.
She said reducing social media use could also help reduce bullying.
Beyond the school gates
Zerbib said families and adults also have a role in setting limits around screen use and warned that the measure would have limited value if students simply compensated at home for the time spent without their phones at school.
Ozcelik said protecting children and adolescents from digital risks should involve more than restrictions, including greater responsibility for platforms.
“Our objective is not simply to make the phone disappear from the high school,” Ozcelik said.
“Our objective is to allow young people to learn to control it and gradually become autonomous in digital use.”

UAE builds alternative trade, energy routes after Iran attacks, official says
The United Arab Emirates is building alternative routes for its energy exports and trade to ensure they are not "held hostage" by the ongoing war with Iran, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Monday.
The conflict has significantly impacted the oil-rich Gulf Arab states, including the UAE as Tehran fired missiles at the country and attacked its oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity," Gargash told the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi.
The UAE has been expanding port capacity along its eastern coast, as well as pipelines, railways and trade routes for alternative corridors, he said.
Gargash added that while relations with Iran could be restored, rebuilding trust with its neighbours after the attacks may take decades.
"A functional relationship with Iran can and must be restored, but rebuilding trust is another matter," Gargash said.
The UAE, a critical economic lifeline for Iran, had suspended all financial and economic transactions with the Islamic Republic in August, citing military escalation by Tehran and missile threats.
Gargash also criticised the Gulf Arab states for their response to the Iranian attacks, saying their collective action fell short.
"For many years we broadly agreed on the nature of the challenge posed by Iran," he said.
"The problem was therefore not a lack of understanding. Where we fell short in confronting this historic challenge was translating this shared understanding into sufficiently united and strategic response."

Amsterdam canal swim raises record €3m for ALS research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:57:07 UTC
18:57:07 KST

Amsterdam canal swim raises record €3m for ALS research
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More than 3,300 people swam 2km through Amsterdam’s canals on Sunday and raised a record €3 million for research into the muscle-wasting disease ALS. Last year’s event brought in just under €1.73 million.
Swimmers set off from the Keizersgracht in groups every few minutes and finished at the Marineterrein, next to the maritime museum. A shorter 750-metre swim for children and less experienced swimmers took place earlier in the day.
Among the participants were 12 people who have ALS, some swimming under their own power and others towed through the water by family and friends. Television presenter Beau van Erven Dorens, radio host Marieke Elsinga, actress Monic Hendrickx and singer Maaike Ouboter also took part.
Hellespont origins
 The event grew out of a 2011 fundraiser in which a group of friends swam the Hellespont in Turkey in memory of a friend who had died of ALS, raising €90,000.
The first Amsterdam edition followed in 2012, when some 1,100 swimmers, including the then Princess Máxima, raised €740,000.
ALS, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, causes progressive loss of muscle control and has no cure. Most patients die within three to five years of their first symptoms. Around 500 people in the Netherlands are diagnosed every year, according to broadcaster NOS.
Donations remain open until the end of September and the final total will be announced on October 1.

Majority of Spaniards unhappy with government's handling of Ceuta crisis, poll shows
MADRID, Sept 7 - Nearly nine in 10 Spaniards blame Morocco for the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta in late July, while a majority rate Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's handling of the crisis as "bad" or "very bad", according to an opinion poll released on Monday that also showed a drop in support for Sanchez's party.
The 40dB poll of 2,000 people for El Pais newspaper and radio station SER also recorded an increase in voting intentions for the conservatives and the anti-immigration, far-right Vox party, in line with several other polls conducted after the deadly border surge into Spain's North African enclave.
• For 89% of respondents, Morocco bore the most responsibility for the crisis, followed by human-trafficking groups (75%), the spread of disinformation on social media (74%), the migrants who decided to cross (73%) and the Spanish government (72%), the 40dB poll found.
• Only 14.2% rated Sanchez's handling of the crisis positively, with two-thirds of those surveyed saying his response was too slow.
• The combined voting intentions for the conservative People's Party and Vox hit 50.2%, leading their potential right-wing alliance to breach the 50% mark for the first time in an opinion poll during this legislature. The centre-left bloc fell to 36.1%.
• The PP rose to 32.4%, from 32% in the previous 40dB poll in July, and Vox to 17.8% from 17.2%, while Sanchez's Socialist Party dipped to 27.6% from 28%.
• About 27% of respondents named Vox as the most capable party on the issue of immigration, ahead of the Socialists at 18.4% and the PP at 13.9%.
• Seven out of 10 chose tighter border controls over protecting vulnerable migrants and 82% backed increasing fences and surveillance at Spain's borders. REUTERS

First road bridge opened between Russia and North Korea
According to Current Time, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song took part in the ceremony via video link.

The Russian and North Korean authorities say the bridge is intended to expand trade and tourism.
Until now, the only land connection between Russia and North Korea was the Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge.
Construction began on April 30, 2025. The agreement to build the bridge was signed in June 2024 during Vladimir Putin’s visit to North Korea.
