Despite war, 71% of Ukrainians consider themselves happy – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:54:00 EEST
18:54:00 KST

Despite war, 71% of Ukrainians consider themselves happy – poll
Despite the war and the challenges facing society, most Ukrainians (71%) consider themselves happy. Meanwhile, one in six Ukrainians (16%) say they are unhappy.
Source: a study by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS)
Details: According to the survey, 31% of respondents said they were definitely happy, while 40% chose "more yes than no". Another 11% answered "both yes and no".
Meanwhile, 16% of respondents said they were unhappy or rather unhappy (9% answered "more no than yes", while another 7% chose "no").
"Men are slightly happier than women, but this is largely due to the fact that women in Ukraine live about 10 years longer than men, and the level of happiness in Ukraine decreases with age. In addition, due to longer life expectancy, more women become lonely with age, which also negatively affects the level of happiness," the KIIS press release said.
Sociologists noted that the decline in happiness with age significantly distinguishes the results for Ukrainians from those of many studies conducted in the US and European countries.
"The level of happiness in Ukraine decreases with age. This significantly distinguishes Ukraine from the results of many studies in the USA and European countries, where the dependence of subjective well-being on age has a U-shaped shape: its level decreases until about 45-50 years and then increases again," the researchers said.
The researchers said that in Ukraine in May 2026, 75% of people under the age of 40 considered themselves happy, compared with 60% of those aged 70 and over.
"The studies that we and other sociological centres began to conduct after the start of the full-scale invasion yielded paradoxical results at first glance.
Objectively, the situation in the country deteriorated significantly, millions of people lost their usual way of life, income, housing and were separated from their families, but in the first period of the war, many subjective indicators did not worsen, and some even increased. This also applied to the feeling of happiness," Volodymyr Paniotto, Director General of KIIS, said, commenting on the findings.
For reference: The survey was conducted from 7 May to 3 June 2026 using telephone interviews based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers. A total of 2,007 Ukrainians aged 18 and over took part. Residents of Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories were not included in the sample (although some respondents were internally displaced people who had moved from the occupied territories). The survey also did not include Ukrainian citizens who left the country after 24 February 2022.
Background: Previously, anxiety levels among Ukrainians were reported to have fallen, while their sense of happiness had increased.

Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:53:53 UTC
18:53:53 KST

Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.
Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.
Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.
Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.
Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.
During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.
During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

FACTBOX: Alternative for Germany wins Saxony-Anhalt election with record 43.8%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:53:18 UTC
18:53:18 KST

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a decisive victory in the election to the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag (state parliament), receiving 43.8% of the vote, according to preliminary official results released by the regional electoral commission.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the results.
Results
- The Alternative for Germany won the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag (state parliament) election with 43.8% of the vote, according to preliminary official results released by the regional electoral commission.
- This is the AfD's best-ever result in any German state, doubling its share of the vote from the previous state election five years ago.
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came in second, losing more than half of its vote share compared with 2021.
- The Christian Democrats received just 17.2% of the vote, the CDU's worst-ever result in Saxony-Anhalt.
- Conservative candidates failed to win a single constituency, securing no direct mandates.
- The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) came in third with 9.3% of the vote.
- The Greens received 8.9% of the vote and the Left Party - 8.6%.
- The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance - Reason and Justice) also cleared the threshold to enter the state parliament with 5.3%.
About the election
- Around 1.7 mln people are eligible to vote in Saxony-Anhalt.
- Turnout reached a record for the state since German reunification, with around 77.8% of eligible voters casting ballots.
Situation in the country
- The election results have created an extremely difficult situation for forming a state government, as all parties except the BSW refuse to cooperate with the AfD, while the Christian Democrats also rule out cooperation with the Left Party.
- At the same time, the Alternative for Germany fell just short of securing an absolute majority.
- However, it could form a regional government for the first time in its history if it receives the BSW's support.
Parties' positions
- The Alternative for Germany achieved a historic result in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and received a mandate to form the regional government, party co-chair Alice Weidel said in an interview with ZDF TV channel.
- According to Weidel, the AfD is extending a hand to all political forces interested in strengthening Germany's position.
- AfD candidate for Saxony-Anhalt premier Ulrich Siegmund said the party had achieved what it set out to accomplish.
- BSW candidate Thomas Schulze told DPA that his party was open to talks with the Alternative for Germany on forming a regional government.
- He also noted that the BSW and AfD share common ground on some issues, including relations with Russia.
- Saxony-Anhalt Minister-President Sven Schulze, the CDU's candidate in the state election, conceded his party's defeat and congratulated his AfD rival Ulrich Siegmund.
Expert views
- Experts describe the CDU's defeat as a personal defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and evidence of rejection of his government's policies, including its policy toward Russia.
- The Saxony-Anhalt state election results amount to a political earthquake for Germany, with dramatic developments ahead for the country, prominent German political scientist Alexander Rahr wrote on Telegram.
- He believes the AfD's success will further boost its popularity in other German states.

Ukraine is seeking to take control of IDS Ukraine, the producer of the country’s largest bottled water brands, amid a legal dispute involving sanctioned Russian investors and a UK-based billionaire family that owns 34% of the company.
According to The Guardian, Ukrainian authorities froze IDS Ukraine’s corporate holdings in 2022 because Russian investors own a 49% stake in the company.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Those investors include Mikhail Fridman, founder of Russia’s Alfa Group conglomerate, who is subject to Western sanctions over his ties to Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin’s regime.
Ukraine’s Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) has been instructed to appoint an independent manager to take control of the company’s operations. The Georgian government is among IDS Ukraine’s other minority shareholders.
ARMA head Yaroslava Maksymenko said the agency had repeatedly encountered legal and bureaucratic obstacles, partly because existing shareholders resisted surrendering control over their assets.
Separate proceedings are underway in Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court, where shareholders are challenging attempts to nationalize some or all of IDS Ukraine. Some government officials regard the bottled water producer as a strategically important asset during Russia’s war.
ARMA raises concerns but no wrongdoing established
Maksymenko said ARMA was concerned about the potential laundering or withdrawal of money from IDS Ukraine if the current management remained in place.
Ukraine, US Plan Winter Aid and Post-War Guarantees in Kyiv
However, no Ukrainian authority has officially established that the company or its non-sanctioned shareholders engaged in money laundering or other criminal financial activity.
ARMA also said it was targeted by a cyberattack during one attempt to select an independent manager for the company. There is no evidence identifying those responsible and the Patarkatsishvili family is not suspected of involvement.
New World Value Fund Limited, the investment vehicle through which the family holds its stake, has alleged unlawful conduct by ARMA officials. Maksymenko dismissed those allegations as misinformation.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) is continuing to investigate the allegations concerning ARMA officials.
British shareholders threaten international litigation
The Patarkatsishvili family said it had supported Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and argued that it was being unfairly targeted despite not being under sanctions.
“An asset should not be taken away from non-sanctioned shareholders against whom there are no allegations or concerns,” a family spokesperson said.
The family said it would continue defending its stake before Ukrainian courts and authorities. If the property is ultimately taken through the ARMA process, it could bring the dispute before international courts.
The 34% stake was inherited in 2008 by Liana Patarkatsishvili, her sister Iya, and their mother Inna, after the death of billionaire businessman Badri Patarkatsishvili.
Liana Patarkatsishvili is also a theater producer. Her company Sage & Jester staged the immersive production “Storehouse” in London in 2025, featuring British actors Toby Jones and Meera Syal.
IDS Ukraine rejected ARMA’s concerns, saying no competent Ukrainian authority had found evidence of money laundering, unlawful fund withdrawals, or similar financial offenses by the company.
The company also said it had continued producing and supplying drinking water without interruption since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, despite repeated missile and drone attacks.

Kallas canceled the launch of the EU defense group due to pressure from diplomats - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
Kaja Kallas canceled the creation of the EU defense group after pressure from member states. Diplomats feared duplication of the European Commission's work.
On Sunday, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas was forced by pressure from EU member states to cancel the creation of a new high-level defense group that would have included former political and military leaders. Politico reports, UNN writes.
Details
It is noted that the high-level group, which Kallas described as a gathering of the "brightest minds" to develop ideas for closing gaps in EU defense "in the shortest possible time and in the most effective manner," was viewed by some diplomats as part of the resistance to reforming the EU’s foreign policy service. Kallas is engaged in a fierce battle with the European Commission over these plans, but according to one EU official, pressure from some capitals led to the initiative’s cancellation.
Some member states believed that this was not the path to take at this point. After discussing it with the ministers, we decided not to pursue this initiative; we are now looking for new ways to engage with the member states
The presentation was due to take place in Brussels on Monday morning. Around 150 people from EU institutions, think tanks, academia and NATO were expected to attend.
Kallas’s office kept the names of the group’s members secret, but according to three diplomats, it was expected to be headed by former NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen, with former defense ministers also joining.
The publication emphasizes that from the outset, some diplomats warned of a high risk that the new group’s activities would duplicate the work of the European Commission, in particular that of European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, who already holds regular meetings with think tanks and former leaders.
According to some diplomats, one of the main reasons for canceling the event was the lack of proper preparatory work and coordination with individual capitals.
At the same time, another EU official noted that the trigger for the cancellation was a problem in Italian domestic politics, specifically a dispute over potential candidates for the group.

French wine output to be among lowest in 30 years after heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

French wine output to be among lowest in 30 years after heatwaves
- French wine production in 2026 is projected to be one of the lowest in 30 years, with a 17% drop from the 2021-2025 average due to heatwaves and drought.
- Vineyard area shrank by 2.5% as winemakers uproot vines amid falling wine consumption, with Champagne output expected to halve and other regions are also facing sharp declines.
- France's agriculture suffered from record heatwaves, prompting a €1 billion emergency aid package for farmers announced on Sept 4 to address the crisis.
AI generated
PARIS – French wine production is likely to be one of the worst in the past 30 years, with Champagne region’s output set to halve from 2025, after shrinking vineyards and severe heat and drought damaged vines and grapes, the farm ministry said on Sept 7.
In its first estimate for 2026 production, the world’s second-largest producer after Italy projected 33.9 million hectolitres: 6 per cent below 2025 and 17 per cent down on the 2021 to 2025 average.
A hectolitre is the equivalent of 100 litres or 133 standard wine bottles.
This would mark France’s third consecutive weak wine harvest, after low output in 2024 and 2025.
Although spring conditions had initially supported a better harvest outlook, summer drought and heatwaves damaged vines and reduced yields, the ministry said.
Output in Champagne is expected to be 49 per cent down on 2025, and 47 per cent below the five-year average.
Bourgogne-Beaujolais is forecast to be down by a third and Val de Loire and Charentes by 12 per cent and 6 per cent respectively.
Languedoc-Roussillon, France’s largest producing basin, should rise 5 per cent from the 2025 weak harvest thanks to better yields, though output remains below average.
Bordeaux is also expected to rebound 10 per cent from 2025 after late-August rain helped offset drought stress, but production remains well below its five-year average.
Most wine producers in France – like other European countries – started harvesting grapes unusually early in 2026 as a result of extreme heat, the ministry said.
France is traditionally the world’s largest exporter by value.
The production area fell 2.5 per cent in 2026. Oversupply in the face of falling wine consumption has prompted winemakers to uproot a portion of their vineyards in past years.
Beyond the wine sector, most French agriculture producers have been badly hit by this summer’s record heatwaves that devastated crops, pastures and water supplies.
France on Sept 4 announced an emergency aid package for farmers of more than €1 billion (S$1.47 billion). REUTERS

18:47:19 KST

Shrouded in secrecy for years, the documentary following disgraced entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes premiered at a secret screening yesterday at the Telluride Film Festival. A24 has released a trailer and announced that the film will hit cinemas next month.
It’s a rare thing when a film studio manages to pull off a genuine surprise drop, especially considering the amount of marketing and buzz surrounding new releases. But A24 has managed to do just that with the new documentary You Can See Everything.
Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the project started shooting in 2023 in top secrecy and premiered at a secret screening yesterday at the Telluride Film Festival.
It follows disgraced businesswoman Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of health technology company Theranos, who was convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than 11 years in 2022. She reported to federal prison in May 2023.
According to the film's synopsis, Holmes invites Fielder and Oppenheim to document her life for 34 days before she goes to prison, and the filmmakers continue following Holmes over the course of three years.
“What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.”
On the same day as its premiere, A24 released a trailer and poster for the documentary, and both are chilling. The teaser trailer in particular borders on sinister, as the camera focuses on Holmes and her signature (and very unnerving) wide-eyed stare, as she affirms that she is not deceiving anyone.
“Why would I do that?” she asks, before a skeptical Fielder asks: “You’re being real right now?”
“I’m always being real,” Holmes replies.
The camera then pulls back to reveal Holmes has been rocking her young baby the whole time.
Check out the trailer below:
You Can See Everything marks the feature directorial debut of Canadian comedian Fielder and it's the second directorial work from Oppenheim to premiere in the last few days, after the Venice debut of his Robert Pattinson-led Primetime.
Vanity Fair confirmed that Fielder actually lived with Holmes and her husband Billy Evans while making the documentary. The publication described the film as being “full of unexpected twists and turns and shocking reveals.”
If the trailer hasn't already given you the chills, check out the unsettling poster:
Elizabeth Holmes supposedly dropped out of Stanford University at the age of 19 to run Theranos. As the CEO, she attracted a high-profile board, including former US senators and two ex-secretaries of state. In 2015, Forbes named Holmes the youngest and wealthiest self-made female billionaire in the US on the basis of a $9-billion valuation of her company.
Holmes raised $945 million from powerful investors including Rupert Murdoch and Larry Ellison, before it was revealed that the company's revolutionary method of conducting blood tests never existed. She was eventually convicted of fraud and sentenced to 11 years and three months in prison.
The spectacular rise and fall of the disgraced entrepreneur has become a Silicon Valley cautionary tale - one which has been adapted into numerous podcasts and books, as well as an HBO documentary by Alex Gibney titled The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley and the minieries The Dropout, for which Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy for playing Holmes.
After being convicted, Holmes attempted to flee the US, and pushed for a new trial. She is scheduled to be released from prison on 16 August 2032.
You Can See Everything will be in US theatres next month, although A24 hasn’t announced an exact release date. There is no news so far regarding a European release date.

Far-right AfD courts conservative support after historic German state election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:46:58 UTC
18:46:58 KST

Far-right AfD courts conservative support after historic German state election win
BERLIN, Sept 7 - The Alternative for Germany appealed on Monday to lawmakers from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives to support its bid to rule Saxony-Anhalt after the far-right party surged into first place in the eastern German state's election.
The anti-immigrant, pro-Russia AfD won nearly 44% of the vote, official results showed, an outcome that underlined the deep unpopularity of Merz's ruling coalition and also triggered alarm among Germany's neighbours, France and Poland.
However, the party — which wants to deport immigrants, halt support for Ukraine and ditch the euro — has fallen short of an absolute majority in the state legislature, winning 39 of the 83 seats, and hopes to win over individual conservative lawmakers.
The election result raises serious questions about the longstanding refusal of Germany's mainstream parties, including Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), to work with the AfD, a policy known as the "firewall". The AfD says this is undemocratic.
"Politics always means compromise," national AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla told German broadcaster ARD, appealing to CDU lawmakers to make a "centre-right conservative majority" in Saxony-Anhalt possible.
The CDU needs to ask itself what conclusions it draws from this disastrous election result, he added.
"Partisan games really ought to be a thing of the past," he told German radio, referring to the firewall policy.
Ulrich Siegmund, the party's lead candidate in the state, said he hoped to become Saxony-Anhalt's state premier if the AfD could build a stable majority in the legislature, and said it would hold discussions with various parliamentary groups there.
'AN AFFRONT TO VOTERS'
The only German party that has signalled readiness to work with the AfD is the populist left-wing BSW, which on Monday echoed Chrupalla's criticism of the "firewall" policy.
"Even the mere attempt to forge another 'firewall' coalition (by the other mainstream parties to keep the AfD out of power in Saxony-Anhalt) would be an affront to the voters," said Sahra Wagenknecht, the face of the left-wing populist BSW.
The BSW shares the AfD's hostility towards mass immigration, which it says undermines local workers' rights, and also advocates for ending Germany's support for Ukraine and restoring ties with Moscow.
The BSW could help clear the way for Siegmund to become state premier by abstaining in a parliamentary vote. That could allow him to head a minority government, although Siegmund has previously rejected such a scenario.
Germany's intelligence services have branded the AfD as "extremist", allowing them to step up surveillance of the country's biggest opposition party. The AfD strongly rejects the label.
Saxony-Anhalt is a relatively small state, and one of the poorest in Germany's former communist east, but Alice Weidel, the AfD's other national co-leader, hailed Sunday's result as a milestone and said her party aimed to win at least 40% in the next national election, due in 2029.
'VERY, VERY WORRYING SIGNAL'
In the first international reaction to the election result, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told RTL radio it "sends out a very, very worrying signal".
"This shows that we face a major challenge in the face of a populist wave which is spreading around the world today and which we must resist," said Lescure, whose own country holds national elections next year that could see far-right veteran Marine Le Pen become president of France.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also described Sunday's outcome in Saxony-Anhalt as "a very worrying sign".
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote, according to the official election results, more than doubling its support from the last state election in 2021. The CDU's share almost halved to 17.2%, with about 83,000 former CDU voters switching to the AfD.
CDU state candidate Sven Schulze attributed part of his party's poor performance to developments in Berlin, where Merz — the most unpopular chancellor in German history — is struggling to revive Germany's sluggish economic growth. The euro was little changed in Monday trade but analysts are closely monitoring the surge in support for far-right parties across Europe, noting that the AfD wants to take Germany out of the common currency.
"This development is dangerous for the longer term stability of the single currency," XTB research director Kathleen Brooks said.
"The next few years could see waves of political change in Europe and a shift to the right in the two largest economies. This may not be a problem for FX traders today, but it is a problem for tomorrow." REUTERS

Two killed, four injured in Russian airstrike on Kramatorsk
Ukrinform reports this, citing a Facebook post by the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office.
On the morning of September 7, Russian forces carried out four airstrikes on Kramatorsk, using FAB-250 bombs equipped with UMPK glide kits. Some of the strikes hit apartment buildings.
Two men, aged 45 and 66, were killed in their homes. Another local resident, a 60-year-old man, and three women aged 58, 61, and 79 sustained injuries. They were diagnosed with blast injuries, a fracture, shrapnel wounds, cuts, and lacerations. Three apartment buildings in the city center and passenger cars were damaged.

Under the procedural guidance of the Kramatorsk District Prosecutor’s Office, a pretrial investigation has been launched in criminal proceedings on the grounds of a war crime (Part 2, Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
As previously reported by Ukrinform, on September 6, Russian forces injured seven residents of Donetsk region.

Russia losing more troops in Ukraine than it can replace, EDF officer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Russia losing more troops in Ukraine than it can replace, EDF officer says
Russia is losing more troops in Ukraine each month than it can replace, as evidenced by the absence of a major summer offensive by Russia this month, Estonian Defense Forces Lieutenant Colonel Mattias Puusepp said.
Underpinning even the most modest advance by Russian forces in Ukraine is an implied willingness to sacrifice thousands of combatants to make gains as small as a single square kilometer, Puusepp noted.
A big part of the picture is the fact that Ukrainian forces have become more effective at halting Russian advances, too.
"If we compare this with the same period a year ago, when the Russians managed to capture about 460 square kilometers last August and lost about 30,000 men in the process, then this August, according to Ukrainian statistics, the Russians have lost 42,000 men in taking significantly less territory. This shows that the Ukrainians' ability to repel and annihilate them effectively has been boosted over the past year, and at the same time the Russians have failed to come up with any effective method for accelerating their advance," Puusepp told "Ukraina stuudio."
When more than 40,000 men are lost in a month while the replenishment rate to the battlefield is around 30,000 over the same period, this represents a fairly substantial deficit and is one of the reasons why the advances have slowed, he went on.
"In fact, we cannot say there has been any successful offensive as such this summer, which had generally been expected, with the Russians anticipated to launch some kind of larger offensive. Instead, it has all been more like local skirmishes, and they have not been able to achieve any significant operational success," Puusepp said.
Another round of conscription or general mobilization, whose likelihood has been dismissed by Russian leader Vladimir Putin, may according to the Ukrainian shave to wait until after the Russian Duma elections later this month. While not a popular vote winner, such a move could translate to around half a million more personnel for Russia's forces. At the same time, it can be scraping the barrel more in terms of willingness to fight or to serve in the military whatsoever, making them something of a band‑aid solution at best.
Puusepp said conscripts can be provided "with minimal personal equipment and weapons. But whether they can effectively form them into specific units is somewhat doubtful. Presumably, they will simply be used to plug gaps wherever things are falling apart the most."
These kinds of personnel tend to be fed into a meat grinder anyway. "As can be observed from the publicly available information, recruits are not trained for very long. In the more extreme cases, they basically go from the recruitment center to the front in a couple of days without any training whatsoever, and that's that," Puusepp added.
Of the overall situation on the front, this remains stable, with only minor movements back and forth, Puusepp said.
"The war is now in its 236th week, and the Ukrainians are holding on. The level of activity is basically the same as last week, at around 265 combat engagements per day. The hotspots also remain the same: Kostiantynivka, Pokrovsk and Lyman in Donetsk oblast, and Huliaipole in Zaporizhzhia oblast. As for Putin's bragging, we have to understand that this is primarily aimed at a domestic audience, to show that all those thousands who have been killed did not die for nothing; that some kind of success has been achieved," he concluded.
Russia has launched summer offensives in some years, while Ukraine has mounted counter‑offensives at different points in the calendar too, including in the autumn of 2022. The "Rasputitsa" mud in spring and autumn often slows large‑scale operations, but both sides have sometimes continued making gains even in those conditions.

Lower Saxony, Rafael and Aurelius to build Iron Dome components at former VW factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:41:57 UTC
18:41:57 KST

The German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Aurelius Capital have signed a letter of intent to purchase Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, allowing the Israeli defense company to establish production of Iron Dome components in Germany and paving the way for Germany to get the Iron Dome, Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post has confirmed by several sources.
The agreement, signed at the factory on Monday, will see the Volkswagen site in Osnabrück developed into a center of excellence for innovative security and defense solutions. It will combine German engineering expertise, industrial capital and quality standards.
First reported by the German publication WirtschaftsWoche and confirmed to D&T, is a change in direction from the original plan, which initially called for the German car-maker to cooperate with Rafael to produce the parts. Qatar, Volkswagen’s largest foreign shareholder, blocked that plan.
Following the statement of intent, the consortium will hold detailed negotiations, assessments of regulatory requirements, and the necessary internal decision-making processes by all parties involved. D&T understands that this is the first step towards Berlin procuring the missile defense system, marking the second time the system has been sold to a European country.
The Osnabruck plant currently employs 2,300 people and produces the T-Roc Cabriolet, Porsche Cayman and Porsche Boxster. According to reports, Volkswagen will leave the site in the second half of 2027, and while the Iron Dome’s Tamir interceptor itself will not be manufactured there, military vehicles, launchers, generators, and other equipment will be.
Olaf Lies, Minister-President of Lower Saxony said that “this partnership creates realistic opportunities for long-term, highly skilled employment at a location that has stood for industrial excellence for 125 years.”
Lies added that the country’s “security environment has changed fundamentally. Germany and Europe must strengthen their capabilities in the security and defense industry and become more independent. This is both a responsibility and an economic opportunity. Osnabrück can play an important role in this effort. The workforce has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to achieve outstanding results. We are building on that strength.”
Rafael has been active in Germany for over 20 years and has established a strong presence in the country with various subsidiaries including Dynamit Nobel Defence, EuroSpike and EuroTrophy Gmbh.
Yoav Tourgeman, President and CEO, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems said that the partnership with Germany is part of a long-term relationship with the country “with the idea that the technology will be fully produced in Germany, to protect Germany and Europe.”
“The technology at the heart of this partnership is built for the defense of today, tomorrow, and well beyond. Our outstanding combat proven technology evolves constantly in order to be ahead of the threats, so that highly reliable defense will always be provided,” he added.
Aurelius Capital was co-founded by Alon Lifshitz and Tomer Jacob, alongside former NSA director Michael Rogers and former IAF commander Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Eshel and former Mossad deputy director Udi Lavi.
Aurelius is expected to take over the site together with Lower Saxony and develop new business there.
“At Aurelius, we are very proud to partner with Rafael and transform an advanced automotive manufacturing facility in Osnabrück into a leading defense production center. This initiative is made possible by Rafael’s groundbreaking technology, the highly important partnership with the Government of Lower Saxony, and the close cooperation with Volkswagen. Its goal is to strengthen the security of both Germany and Israel while creating significant value for all parties involved. This is only the first step in a strategic partnership that will continue to grow and deepen over time," Jacob said in a statement.
Integral part of Israel’s missile defense array
Initially designed to shoot down short-range rockets, the Iron Dome has become an integral component of Israel's multi-layered defense array.
The system’s modular architecture enables seamless integration with additional defense layers, and it can operate independently or as part of a broader air defense network that includes the the Arrow (Arrow 2 and Arrow 3) system, which intercepts ballistic missiles outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, and the David’s Sling missile defense system which is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, medium- to long-range rockets, as well as cruise missiles fired at ranges between 40 to 300 kilometers. Rafael has also manufactured the Iron Beam laser defense system which has been operational along Israel’s northern border.
The system’s early years were defined by rapid operational learning. Iron Dome took part a long series of conflicts and operations, from Operation Protective Edge, Operation Guardian of the Walls, Operation Breaking Dawn, Operation Shield and Arrow, Operation Swords of Iron, and Operations Rising and Roaring Lion, where it is served alongside the Arrow and David’s Sling as a central pillar in the protection of Israel’s home front.
Each round of fighting was followed by a new wave of software updates, radar refinements, and interceptor improvements.
It quickly became evident that the system was a flexible defensive layer capable of handling dense salvos, more complex trajectories, and a wider range of threats. The system’s radar was upgraded to track more targets simultaneously, its algorithms became faster and more selective, and its interceptors were refined to handle longer ranges and more demanding engagement profiles.
German defenses
Germany has also purchased Israel’s Arrow 3 as a response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and the growing proliferation of advanced missile systems.
Germany signed the $3.5 billion Arrow 3 contract in November 2023, the largest defense deal in Israel’s history at the time. In December, the two countries signed a $3.1 billion follow-up contract to expand interceptor and launcher stocks.
The Bundeswehr announced on June 30 that the second Arrow air defense battery site would be in the greater Kaufbeuren area of Bavaria and would house the ELM-2080 Green Pine Block C radar to detect and track threats.
The second location would complement the initial battery at Fliegerhorst Holzdorf/Schönewalde, south of Berlin, the capital. That battery was the first time the system had been deployed outside of Israel.
Arrow 3, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) is a highly maneuverable system designed to provide ultimate air defense by intercepting ballistic missiles when they are still outside the Earth’s atmosphere.

Far-right AfD's Weidel targets 40% in next German federal election after state victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:41:40 UTC
18:41:40 KST

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is aiming to win at least 40% in the next federal election after a historic win in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, said national co-leader Alice Weidel on Monday.
"My stated goal is to significantly widen the gap in a very short time and grow to at least 40% for the next federal election," said Weidel.
The AfD surged into first place in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections on Sunday, putting a far-right party on the cusp of power at the state level for the first time since World War II.
AfD's success highlights unpopularity of Merz's conservatives
While short of an overall majority, the AfD won 44% of the vote and delivered a drubbing to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives, reflecting the deep unpopularity of Germany's ruling coalition in a fracturing political landscape.
The AfD is already Germany's most popular party at the national level and is seeking to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.
As counting continued, it remained unclear whether the AfD could form a government, but the wider political significance was clear for the election, which, according to broadcaster ZDF, drew a heavy turnout of 77%.

Turkey plans 229% defense spending boost over three years to advance domestic military tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:41:33 UTC
18:41:33 KST

Turkey plans to increase defense spending by 229% over the next three years as part of a push to develop its own technologies and produce higher-value products in the defense industry, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz announced on Sunday, according to Turkish media reports.
“In the defense industry, we aim for a Turkey that develops its own technology and produces high added value,” Yilmaz said. “We are increasing defense spending by 229%.”
The plan was announced during a presentation of Turkey’s new Medium-Term Program (MTP), which sets out the country’s economic roadmap for 2027-2029.
The increase in defense spending is the largest among the seven priority areas outlined in the program. Spending on social housing is set to increase by 150%, mining exploration by 139%, industrial infrastructure by 54%, railways by 49%, health by 43%, and food supply security by 42%.
Envanter Medya, a Turkey-based news site that tracks developments in military technology, noted that the additional funding would support major defense projects, including mass production of the TF-KAAN fighter jet, the first deliveries of the KIZILELMA unmanned fighter aircraft and the delivery of more than 10 ALTAY tanks to the Land Forces.
Turkey one of world's largest military spenders
“The global economy has recently been going through a new period in which economic, technological and geopolitical developments are intertwined, predictability has decreased, and risks have risen to historically high levels,” Yilmaz said.
“The Turkish economy is, of course, not independent of the developments taking place in the world and in our region.”
Yilmaz said the war with Iran had created both direct and indirect consequences in many areas, including energy and commodity prices, global trade, the inflation outlook and growth expectations.
Turkey’s military spending already reached $30 billion in 2025, making it the world’s 18th-largest military spender, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Turkish military spending rose 7.2% from the previous year, with SIPRI saying the increase was driven by ongoing military operations in Iraq, Somalia and Syria, but most of all by investment in Turkey’s domestic arms industry

UK minister slams ‘thuggish’ anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
The gathering was the second anti-migrant demonstration in two days, after masked men disrupted traffic in the port of Dover on Saturday
British minister Emma Reynolds has condemned hundreds of protesters who blocked streets in the English coastal city of Portsmouth late on Sunday to try to stop the arrival of migrants from France, calling them “thuggish”.
The gathering was the second anti-migrant demonstration in two days, after masked men disrupted traffic in the port of Dover on Saturday, chanting “Stop the boats”, a reference to the vessels carrying asylum seekers across the English Channel.
Both groups appeared to be led by Daniel Thomas, an ally of veteran far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson.
“Perhaps the scale of the protest was something that we hadn’t seen before, but the police have brought this under control,” Reynolds, who is chief secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News on Monday when asked about the protests in Portsmouth.
Successive British governments have faced accusations from opposition parties and anti-migration activists of failing to curb the numbers of asylum seekers coming to Britain, often in overcrowded, inflatable boats.
Reynolds said the numbers had fallen sharply to about 17,000 from January 1 to September 1, down 43 per cent on the same period last year.

Ukraine provides NATO with list of urgent air defence needs ahead of Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine provides NATO with list of urgent air defence needs ahead of Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting
An extraordinary meeting of the NATO-Ukraine Council at the level of permanent representatives has taken place at NATO headquarters in Brussels, during which Ukraine presented a list of its priority and urgent needs for air and missile defence systems.
Source: Ukraine's Defence Ministry on the morning of Monday 7 September, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The meeting, convened at Ukraine's request, took place ahead of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format) meeting on 8 September. Strengthening Ukraine's air defences will be the central issue on its agenda.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte chaired the meeting.
Serhii Boiev, Ukraine's Deputy Defence Minister for European Integration, and Brigadier General Serhii Sobko, Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, presented the allies with a detailed assessment of current aerial threats.
The Ukrainian side provided a list of its priority and urgent needs for air defence systems.
Following the meeting, Ukraine called on the allies to rapidly provide additional air and defence assets directly related to protecting the lives of Ukrainians.
Ukraine also called on its partners to mobilise by the end of the year the resources needed to meet NATO's declared target of €70 billion in military support for Ukraine.
Background:
- On 6 September, Ukraine's Defence Ministry reported that Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara had discussed preparations for the Ramstein meeting during a phone call with Rutte.
- The previous meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group took place at NATO headquarters in Brussels on 18 June. It was co-chaired by the United Kingdom and Germany.
- Following that meeting, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius announced that Ukraine would receive a three-digit number of air-to-air missiles from German stocks, as well as plans for the joint production of unmanned ground systems.

UN rights chief urges halt to arms transfers to Israel, business supporting illegal settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:39:07 UTC
18:39:07 KST

- Turk calls for global AI ‘red lines,’ warns advanced systems could pose ‘existential risk to humanity’
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Monday urged states to end transfers of arms to Israel that risk being used to violate international law, and called on companies to stop business practices supporting illegal settlements.
Speaking at the opening of the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Turk said Israel’s annexation of the occupied West Bank was “unfolding, unobstructed,” despite a clear ruling by the International Court of Justice.
“What more will it take for states to take action to prevent the entrenchment of occupation across land earmarked for Palestinians under the two-state solution?” he said.
“They (states) need to end the transfer to Israel of arms that risk being used to violate international law. Companies also need to end business practices that support illegal settlements,” he added.
The rights chief said words of condemnation “ring hollow in the face of deliberate violations and suffering,” calling for greater international efforts toward sustainable peace.
On Gaza, he said Israel has killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in daily strikes despite the ceasefire announced almost a year ago and continues to restrict humanitarian aid.
He said he is appalled by Israeli proposals for the forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, as well as executions and torture of Palestinians suspected of collaboration by armed groups affiliated with Hamas.
Turk calls for AI ‘red lines’
Turning to artificial intelligence, Turk called for an “all-out effort” to establish “cast iron guarantees” around AI safety and security, warning advanced AI could pose an “existential risk to humanity.”
"At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines," he said.
According to Turk, he would write to AI companies in the coming days, urging them to take immediate steps to reduce risks.
He warned that “a handful of men” wield “almost unlimited power over AI” and argued that delays in establishing effective governance benefit major technology companies, their owners and enablers.
Pointing to concerns about increasingly powerful systems, Turk said AI that can escape its testing environment or blackmail developers to prevent itself from being switched off is “AI that is too powerful.”
He also called for greater attention to AI’s human rights implications, including its effects on employment practices, fundamental principles of democracy and the environment.
Turk acknowledged recent international progress, including the establishment of the Global Dialogue on AI and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, but said governments and companies need to listen to growing public concerns about the technology.
Resumption of US-Iran attacks 'alarming,' immediate return to talks needed
Turk also voiced alarm over the resumption of attacks between the US and Iran and their impact across the Gulf region, citing reports of civilian deaths and injuries, including at a wedding in Iran's Hormozgan province.
He called the crisis “entirely avoidable” and appealed for an immediate return to negotiations.
Turning to Ukraine, Turk warned that Russia's full-scale war was on a “menacing trajectory,” with rising civilian casualties and intensified attacks on energy infrastructure.
He said he was “horrified” by reports that fully autonomous drones launched by Russia killed three Ukrainians last month, while Ukraine has also reportedly field-tested such weapons.
“I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement,” he said.
Turk also urged the US to halt returns of people to countries where they could face “irreparable harm,” including Haiti, and ensure due process for removals to third countries.
He said four more people had died in US immigration custody since his last update to the Human Rights Council, bringing the total to 23 deaths in 2026, and called for accountability.
"Hard-won gains for people of African descent are deliberately being undermined in some countries, including cuts to anti-discrimination programs and attempts to distort history," the human rights chief said. “Politicians, traditional and social media amplify isolated incidents to portray migrants, refugees, Muslims, marginalized racial and ethnic groups, and minorities as a collective threat.”
Turk also expressed concern over renewed hostilities in South Sudan and escalating tensions in Yemen, urging restraint and greater international efforts to prevent a return to “all-out war.”
On Yemen, he renewed his demand for the Houthis to immediately release 73 UN and NGO personnel being held by the group.
The rights chief also reiterated concerns over China's Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region, including detention facilities, urging Beijing to investigate allegations of human rights violations, including torture.

Finland's largest sex crimes case opens with teacher accused of luring victims on Snapchat
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:39:00 EEST
18:39:00 KST

Pirkanmaa District Court has begun proceedings in what is believed to be the largest-ever sexual crimes case in Finnish legal history.
The hearings are expected to last until at least the end of this year, with the court sitting on 45 separate days throughout the coming autumn and into the winter.
The schedule, announced in court as the first hearing began on Monday morning, reflects the vast number of victims in the case — 361. Police said there may be many more, even as high as 900, as some 530 potential victims have yet to be identified.
The known victims are all boys aged between 9 and 15 years old, and they live in many different parts of Finland. Some legal representatives will participate in the session in court in Tampere, while others will join remotely from several different district courts.
The defendant, a 28-year-old man, will appear before the court remotely from Kanta-Häme District Court. He is charged with aggravated sexual abuse of a child, sexual abuse of a child, and aggravated distribution of images depicting a child in an offensive manner.
Man posed as a woman in Snapchat messages
The crimes are alleged to have occurred on the Snapchat messaging app between 2019 and 2022.
According to police, the defendant posed as a woman on Snapchat and sent messages to the children asking them for photos and videos. He then used screen recording software to capture the images without the knowledge of each sender.
The number and content of the images and videos vary by victim, but one boy sent about 160 videos to the defendant.
Police do not believe that the man met any of the children in person, meaning all the crimes occurred online.
They do however suspect that he knew some of the victims beforehand, either through sports or while working as a substitute teacher.
Attorney Jyri Kilpi, who is representing 77 victims, told the court in his opening statement on Monday that the defendant used the rosters of underage sports teams to select his victims and to understand more about their interests and hobbies.
He described the shame and regret his clients, and their parents, feel as a result of the defendant's actions — noting that many could not bring themselves to tell their parents what had happened.
"All responsibility lies entirely with the adult perpetrator, not the victim," Kilpi said.
Prior conviction
According to Yle's information, the defendant in this case was sentenced to three years in prison in 2023 after being found guilty by Kanta-Häme District Court of the aggravated sexual abuse of a child.
The court heard that the then-20-year-old defendant had sexual intercourse with his 14-year-old male student, while he was working as a substitute teacher at a primary school in the region. He also sent the boy hundreds of sexually suggestive messages, images, and videos.
The investigation of this case led the police to confiscate the suspect's phone, where they subsequently found thousands of sexualised images and videos of children.

Gorgeous boutique seafront hotel and spa to open on Greece’s Samos island

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

18:38:55 KST

Guests staying at the 72-key Nírema Hotel & Spa Samos will be just steps away from the beach once it opens later this month.
Looking for your next Greek island escape? Turn your eyes towards Samos off the coast of western Türkiye, where a gorgeous new boutique hotel is set to open this month.
Nírema Hotel & Spa Samos – MGallery Collection promises a picture-perfect escape, with its name coming from the Samian word for “dream”.
Featuring just 72 rooms, the property is exclusively for those aged 13 and above. Of these, there are eight suites with private pools and terraces.
The hotel is around a 25-minute drive from Samos International Airport, which is around a 50-minute flight from Athens International Airport Eleftherios Venizelos. There are direct flights to Samos from cities such as Brussels, Amsterdam, Vienna, Milan and London Gatwick during the summer months.
Alternatively, you can take a ferry from Kuşadası in Türkiye which takes around an hour.
What to expect at Nírema Hotel & Spa Samos
Set to welcome its first guests on 18 September, Nírema Hotel & Spa Samos overlooks Vathy Bay, and guests are just steps away from the sea.
The property boasts a spa and fitness centre, as well as an outdoor pool.
Samos has been known for its wine for more than 3,000 years, and guests can explore this at the Curvus wine cellar, where you’ll be able to try Muscat wines with tastings and pairings.
Elsewhere at the property, you can eat at the all-day dining spot Apagia as well as Apora Pool Restaurant.
Where to go on Samos
Beyond the hotel’s wine collection, you can learn about traditional winemaking at Samos Wine Museum and purchase bottles from vineyards on the island.
For culture vultures, Samos is home to the UNESCO World Heritage Site Pythagoreion and Heraion of Samos, which spans the remains of an ancient fortified port complete with a tunnel-aqueduct, as well as a temple of the Samian Hera.
If you’re focusing on relaxation for your next trip, there are plenty of beaches for you to enjoy, like Paralia Gaggou or Livadaki Beach.
Dining celebrates Samos' agricultural and maritime heritage through a sea-view à la carte restaurant, a mixology-focused pool bar and an intimate wine cellar located close to the Samos Wine Museum.

Israeli strikes kill at least 11 in southern Lebanon
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:38:43 EEST
18:38:43 KST

Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people in Kfar Remman early on Monday, according to Lebanese state media, as a new wave of attacks hit residential areas and medical workers near territory illegally occupied by Israeli forces. The attacks followed days of fighting that has placed fresh pressure on a US-backed ceasefire framework.
Lebanon’s National News Agency said nine people, including two children, died when an Israeli strike hit a three-storey residential building in Kfar Remman in the Nabatieh district. Five others were wounded.
A separate drone strike hit a vehicle in the same town and killed two medics, according to the agency.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry gave an earlier toll of nine deaths. It said eight people died in the residential building and one paramedic died in the vehicle strike.
The Israeli military said it was examining reports of the deaths.
Israeli forces also struck Deir al-Zahrani in southern Lebanon after issuing a forced evacuation order. The Israeli military claimed it targeted a building near a Hezbollah facility that had been used to launch an explosive drone.
The attacks followed Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon on Sunday that killed seven people and wounded at least 20, according to Lebanese authorities.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the escalation threatened the ceasefire framework agreed in June and called for international pressure on Israel to halt its attacks.
The agreement calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon in stages and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Israel says Hezbollah has continued launching drones and rebuilding military infrastructure in the south. Hezbollah has accused Israel of breaching the agreement through strikes and continued illegal occupation.
The renewed fighting has forced residents to leave areas close to what Israel calls its “security zone”.
The pressure on Lebanon’s health system has also increased.
Israeli strikes destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Sunday, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. The hospital had stopped operating about two months earlier as fighting intensified, but had previously treated local residents and sheltered displaced people.
The ministry said 17 hospitals across Lebanon have sustained damage since March 2 and three hospitals in the south have been put out of service.
The Lebanese Health Ministry said in a report published on Sunday that 4,362 people have been killed and over 12,300 wounded since the conflict escalated in March. The Health Ministry says hundreds of women and children are among the dead.
The ministry also reported 180 attacks on ambulance crews since March 2, with 135 healthcare workers killed.
Israeli authorities say 40 soldiers and four civilians have died on both sides of the border during the same period.
According to UNHCR, around 360,000 people remained displaced by Israeli attacks in August, including at least 22,000 staying in collective shelters.
Israel has continued illegally occupying areas in southern Lebanon despite the June framework. Lebanese officials say that has stalled the withdrawal process and prevented displaced residents from returning to their villages.

France's EDF Energy is reportedly in discussions to buy So Energy, the smaller British supplier whose Irish parent company has put it up for sale, in a deal that would add to a renewed wave of consolidation among UK gas and electricity retailers.
French-owned EDF Energy is one of a handful of parties negotiating with British So Energy's owners, Sky News reported, and faces at least one rival bidder whose identity has not been established.
If EDF prevails in the auction, industry insiders expect the transaction to cover So Energy's customer base rather than the company as a whole.
So Energy has roughly 300,000 household electricity customers and was founded back in 2015.
Ireland's Electricity Supply Board took a controlling stake in 2021 and put the business under review this summer, appointing PwC to run the sale.
ESB, the Irish parent company of So Energy, has been open about the process.
"Our parent company, ESB, has initiated a process to evaluate potential divestment options for So Energy," a spokesperson for So Energy said in July adding that this followed a strategic review and that "ESB plans to focus on its core business."
For EDF, the appeal is scale in a market where it has been losing ground.
The company is among the big six suppliers that once dominated British energy, with three million customers and five million accounts, but now trails well behind Octopus Energy and Centrica-owned British Gas. Scottish Power finds itself in a similar position.
Buying a customer book rather than a company outright is the cheaper route to that scale, adding accounts directly while avoiding the operational complexity of absorbing an entire business.
The talks also come at an uncomfortable time for British households.
Ofgem lifted the price cap by 4% to £1,723 per year for the autumn, meaning bills will climb just as the industry reshuffles itself.
Meanwhile, government policy is pulling the other way as Andy Burnham used his first week as prime minister to announce that VAT would be scrapped from domestic energy bills, part of a broader push to tackle cost of living.
No agreement has yet been reached between the parties.

Jaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two years

18:37:31 KST

Jaguar Land Rover has announced thousands of job cuts in a “body blow for workers” as it grapples with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack.
Britain’s largest carmaker, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, confirmed the anticipated cuts on Monday, saying it wants to reduce its global workforce by about 4,000 over two years, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn.
JLR’s employs 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK. The cuts will mainly affect the 26,000 UK employees who are salaried and management workers. The company has plants in Solihull, Warwickshire and Merseyside, and is headquartered in Coventry.
Its proposal threatens to provide an early reality check for the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, and his promise to “reindustrialise” Britain.
JLR’s profits have tumbled as it wrestles with strong competition in the global car market, Trump’s US tariffs and last year’s hack, which led to the shutdown of its factories.
The JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, said: “The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Through our Growth Reimagined strategy, JLR is moving decisively to strengthen our competitiveness and position the business for long-term success …
“As part of this transformation, we will reduce our global workforce by around 4,000 roles over the next two years. We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”
The Guardian understands that factory workers who are paid hourly – the vast majority of those on the shop floor – will be unaffected by the cuts, which will instead fall on salaried employees in divisions such as management, marketing, and research and development.
The business minister, Jonathan Reynolds, has ruled out using taxpayers’ money to deter the company from pursuing the redundancies.
Reynolds will hold talks with Balaji and Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, on Tuesday. Graham is expected to push for JLR to favour retraining and redeployment over compulsory job losses, if it cannot achieve enough redundancies voluntarily.
The cuts will be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shopfloor production workers.
JLR announced the job cuts as the chancellor, John Healey, made an economic speech at the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry, just a few miles from the carmaker’s offices. Healey said he wanted to “draw the line” under rising business costs.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the Commons business and trade committee, said the news was a “body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands”.
“Whether or not these redundancies are voluntary, we now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work.
“But the troubles at JLR underline the challenge facing the government’s reindustrialisation drive. Britain is preparing to spend billions more on defence, infrastructure and new technology. But British business needs cheaper energy and government orders, not at some distant point in the future, but now, now, now.”
Last year’s hack eventually cost the company about £200m and contributed to its pre-tax profit falling to just £14m, from £2.5bn a year earlier.
The government last year agreed to underwrite a £1.5bn loan to JLR to help it recover from the hack but the carmaker has not tapped the facility.
JLR has also suffered the fallout from Trump’s trade tariffs, which hit sales of models such as the Range Rover and the Defender as the company seeks to expand further in the US market.
JLR is in the midst of a large-scale overhaul of its products, including the launch of its first fully electric Range Rover this month, which will come with a a starting price of £154,070, and an upcoming new electric Jaguar. It is also considering a deal with Stellantis to make some of its cars in the US to help ease the effect of trade tariffs.
Balaji said the cuts were aimed at “reducing organisational complexity” and would mean the company could break even on sales of about 300,000 vehicles a year, making it better able “to compete in a rapidly evolving market”.
European carmakers have faced tough trading conditions as Chinese manufacturers’ sales have surged across the UK and Europe, giving companies such as Chery and BYD a manufacturing foothold in the regions.
In July, Chery, which also owns the Omoda and Jaecoo brands, accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.
JLR follows Volkswagen in announcing large-scale job cuts, after the German carmaker said last week that it intended to make 50,000 more people redundant as part of a turnaround plan.

Popular Egyptian TV presenter Sarah Khalifa faces appeal battle after death sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:36:28 UTC
18:36:28 KST

Khalifa and 11 others face death sentences in a major synthetic drug trafficking case, with appeals and further legal challenges expected.
An Egyptian television presenter faces execution after a Cairo court sentenced her to death for financing and coordinating a synthetic drug network, but her lawyer says they will appeal, and legal experts say the case is far from over.
Sarah Khalifa, known for hosting the crime programme Mission Impossible on private channel Al-Mehwar and for her events business, was sentenced on Saturday alongside 11 others in a major synthetic drug manufacturing and trafficking case.
Nine defendants received life sentences and seven were acquitted. Those sentenced to death were also fined 500,000 Egyptian pounds (€8,000).
Khalifa's brother Mohamed was among those sentenced to death, on charges of manufacturing and testing drugs.
Khalifa's lawyer Mohamed El-Gendy said the defence would appeal and pursue all available legal avenues.
A higher criminal court can reconsider the evidence and each defendant's role, upholding, reducing, or overturning sentences. A further challenge before Egypt's Court of Cassation is also possible.
Before Saturday's ruling, the court had referred Khalifa and 12 other defendants to Egypt's Grand Mufti — a procedural requirement before a criminal court can impose the death penalty. The Mufti's opinion is advisory and not binding.
Twelve of those 13 defendants ultimately received death sentences.
More than ordinary hashish
Egyptian media initially described the case as involving synthetic hashish, but forensic evidence presented during the trial identified the substances as synthetic cannabinoids, laboratory-made chemicals that mimic some of the effects of cannabis on the brain but can be significantly more potent and unpredictable.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime describes MDMB-4en-PINACA as a potent synthetic cannabinoid placed under international control in 2021 following a World Health Organization recommendation citing severe adverse effects and deaths.
Synthetic cannabinoids can cause psychosis, seizures, heart and kidney problems, and in severe cases, death.
The committee said the substance was not specifically listed on Egypt's controlled narcotics schedule, but concluded it fell under Egyptian law because its chemical structure and effects were similar to already-listed substances.
The defence challenged that interpretation and the court accepted the committee's findings.
The case began in April 2025 when Egypt's anti-narcotics authorities said they had uncovered a network importing raw materials used to manufacture synthetic drugs.
Police initially raided two Cairo apartments and recovered around 200 kilograms of drugs, raw materials and equipment.
As the investigation widened, prosecutors said the total seized exceeded 750 kilograms. The investigation lasted some 40 days before prosecutors obtained arrest warrants.
Al-Masry Al-Youm newspaper, citing judicial and security sources, reported that investigators alleged raw materials were sourced abroad, concealed inside cosmetics containers and luggage on flights.
The prosecution said members had specialised roles covering procurement, manufacturing, storage and distribution. The case against 28 defendants relied on testimony from 20 witnesses and digital evidence including messages, photographs and videos.
Khalifa's alleged role
Prosecutors said Khalifa financed parts of the operation, travelled abroad to meet senior members of the network and acted as a link between them and other members inside Egypt.
According to investigation records reported by the Egyptian press, two defendants living outside Egypt bought batches of materials used to manufacture the drugs from China and obtained instructions on how to produce them.
Investigators said other members mixed the chemicals according to formulas supplied by senior figures in the network before testing newly manufactured batches on drug users to assess their effects, and then weighing, packaging and distributing them.
Khalifa's brother, Mohamed Khalifa, was identified by prosecutors as one of those involved in manufacturing and testing the drugs and was also among those sentenced to death.
Prosecutors also relied on digital evidence recovered from Khalifa's phone.
According to prosecution documents shared with domestic media, investigators found WhatsApp exchanges containing videos of substances resembling those seized in the case, as well as communications with other alleged members of the network.
A handwriting examination also concluded that Khalifa had written entries in a seized notebook containing names, figures and amounts that prosecutors said related to spending on the drug operation.
Khalifa consistently denied involvement in the network.
Saturday also brought a second conviction against Khalifa in a separate case.
A Cairo court sentenced her to three years in prison for assault after investigators found video footage on her phone showing a young man identified as her driver being stripped, assaulted and filmed naked inside her home.
Two other defendants in that case received seven years each and a fourth received five years.
Egypt retains the death penalty for serious drug trafficking offences. Amnesty International recorded 23 executions in Egypt in 2025, up from 13 the year before, and has criticised the country's use of capital punishment for offences that do not involve intentional killing.

Türkiye, Danish firm sign thorium technology agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:36:00 UTC
18:36:00 KST

Türkiye’s Energy, Nuclear and Mineral Research Agency (TENMAK) has signed a memorandum of understanding with Denmark-based Copenhagen Atomics to cooperate on the use of thorium in next-generation nuclear technologies.
The agreement aims to expand research and development capacity in advanced nuclear systems and examine the domestic production of thorium compounds that meet nuclear fuel standards for molten salt reactors, the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry said on Sept. 7.
The memorandum was signed at a TENMAK campus in Istanbul in the presence of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
“We hope this cooperation will deliver results and eventually lead to a commercial product,” Bayraktar said, adding that the focus on thorium gave the partnership particular importance.
Bayraktar said Türkiye was pursuing several small modular reactor projects in parallel with the involvement of public institutions and private investors.
It would become clearer over the next few years which technologies could progress toward commercialization, he added.
The agreement will involve Turkish industry, researchers and engineers in efforts to use the country’s thorium resources in higher-value nuclear technologies.
The initial work will focus on research and project development for producing thorium compounds in Türkiye that are suitable for use in molten salt reactors.
Copenhagen Atomics is developing thorium molten salt reactor technology and is working on a modular design called Onion Core.
Under the agreement, the company will assess its technology against Türkiye’s research infrastructure, workforce and industrial capabilities.
The ministry said the longer-term aim was to establish domestic production of nuclear-grade thorium compounds and develop Türkiye as an international supplier in the field.

The latest heatwave is part of a series of intense heat events recorded in France this year.
One episode in late June reached record intensity, whilse another, extending from late July into August, lasted 23 days and matched France’s longest heatwave on record, set in 1983.

Nauru opens embassy in Jerusalem, becoming ninth country with mission in Israeli capital
"You have recognized what we all know to be the truth- Jerusalem is the capital of Israel”
Nauru officially inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Monday, becoming the ninth country to establish an embassy in the Israeli capital.
The opening ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Nauru’s vice president and foreign minister, Lionel Aingimea. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said the move reflected the close relationship between the two countries and Nauru’s commitment to expanding bilateral ties.
“Nauru is one of Israel’s most loyal and steadfast friends in the international community,” Sa’ar said. “You have recognized what we all know to be the truth — Jerusalem is the capital of Israel.”
Sa’ar also praised Nauru for consistently supporting Israel at the United Nations and for backing it during proceedings at the International Court of Justice.
Aingimea said the decision followed a conversation with Sa’ar when the two met in Fiji. He described support for Israel as deeply rooted in Nauru’s religious values and pledged that his country would align itself more closely with Israel in future UN votes.
“Our motto is ‘God first,’ and Israel has always held a special place in our hearts,” Aingimea said. “We believe with all our hearts that supporting Israel brings us God’s blessing.”
According to Aingimea, Nauru has voted with Israel at the UN 71% of the time. “Mark my words: That 71% will rise in the very near future,” he said.
The opening is part of an Israeli diplomatic campaign to increase international recognition of Jerusalem as its capital and encourage more countries to establish missions in the city. Most foreign embassies remain in the Tel Aviv area because Jerusalem’s status is among the most contentious issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said the United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Somaliland, Papua New Guinea and Fiji also maintain embassies in Jerusalem. It added that more countries are expected to follow.
Israel and Nauru plan to expand cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, water management, innovation and climate resilience, the ministry said.
