====================================================================================================

Who needs unity? The collapse of the Third Bloc parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:33:59 UTC
18:33:59 KST

The three parties of the “Third Bloc”, the group of small right-leaning and centrist political factions in Israel trying to push for a broad unity government which launched with great fanfare at the start of the election campaign, are reaching the final stretch before candidate lists are submitted with a resounding political failure. It sounded promising, looked intriguing, and familiar, experienced politicians took the reins, recruited high-profile names and promised to offer the public exactly what it was supposedly looking for: an alternative that did not clearly belong to either political camp. But when the moment of truth arrived, it became clear there were almost no buyers for that product.
Ayelet Shaked, whose name was mentioned throughout the campaign as one of the figures who might fit into that political space, ultimately announced that she would stay out. In a Facebook post Sunday evening, she effectively also offered an explanation for the broader failure of the “third bloc.”
“I had hoped that after October 7, the political reality in Israel would change,” she wrote. But, according to her, this time too “the political system is converging around the same patterns of camps and boycotts, two blocs that in my view are tearing the country apart.”
Shaked explained that she still believes in a “broad cross-bloc government,” but acknowledged that she does not see a realistic way to establish such a government under the current political circumstances.
“I did not see a realistic way to represent you properly. If there had been one, I would have said: Here I am,” she wrote to supporters who had urged her to return to politics.
In that sense, her decision to remain outside may be the sharpest expression of the state of that political niche: It seemed there was demand for a party that would refuse to choose absolutely between the two camps, but as the deadline for submitting candidate lists approached, it became clear that the desire for “unity” was very difficult to translate into seats. Shaked, at least, chose not to take the gamble and join one of the parties now fighting for its political survival.
It began with Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein’s Unity party, continued with Hili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel’s Zionist Home-Reservists party, and may now end with Benny Gantz’s Blue and White. Gantz, who removed himself from the anti-Netanyahu bloc and sought to create an independent political space, was in many ways one of the founders of that “third bloc.” But the other two parties have already collapsed and disappeared from the map, while Blue and White itself is now fighting for survival.
After Shaked’s decision to stay out, Gantz’s options narrowed further. There is currently no natural partner with whom he could merge or join forces, and discomfort is growing even among the few remaining lawmakers in his faction. They do not want to be dragged into a race that could end below the electoral threshold and cost the entire camp votes. Knesset lawmaker Michael Biton, one of Gantz’s closest associates for years, is expected to announce his retirement. Despite everything, Gantz is insisting for now on going all the way.
Erdan discovered how hard it is to build a party
Gilad Erdan entered the race with the ambition of leading a new political line, one that would try to leave behind the division of recent election campaigns into “only Bibi” and “anything but Bibi.” He presented the idea of “unity” as a particularly sought-after product after the October 7 massacre and the wars that followed, but failed to translate the slogan into real political power.
The way the party was managed also raised quite a few questions. Precisely during the critical days before the candidate lists closed, Erdan was abroad, and even before that the campaign seemed to be operating at limited intensity. On August 29, ynet obtained information that Erdan had decided to dismantle his campaign headquarters and that, without a significant merger, he would not continue in the race.
“That is a total and unparalleled lie,” one of his associates responded at the time. “Everything is working as usual. Not one person has moved.”
But as the days passed, it became clear that the information had been correct. In a sense, Erdan himself had already anticipated the difficulty before setting out.
“Building a party is much more complicated and difficult than I thought,” he said before deciding to run independently.
Yoaz Hendel’s reservists party also sought to position itself as part of that same politically unaffiliated space. To Hendel’s credit, he was among the few politicians who actually served hundreds of reserve-duty days since October 7. He seemingly had a clear political story to tell, but after three years of ongoing war even that sentiment was no longer enough on its own to sweep voters along.
The main problem was the message. Hendel, Tropper and their people struggled to provide a simple answer to the voter’s most basic question: What exactly will you do the day after the election? Will they join a government led by Netanyahu? Will they give Gadi Eisenkot the 61 seats he needs? Or will they try to force a unity government — and if so, how exactly?
As the questions multiplied, the message became blurred. In the end, the public was not convinced.
The person who may have benefited most from the collapse of the “third bloc” is Gadi Eisenkot. Not necessarily because he actively worked to dismantle it, but because developments worked in his favor. Erdan’s party evaporated, and he managed to draw Hili Tropper into his own slate. In doing so, he reduced the risks.
Now one major task remains for him: move Gantz out of the way. But here, the story is no longer only political. The relationship between the two is burdened by accumulated grievances, personal tensions and considerable frustration built up over the years.
After they parted ways, and after Eisenkot built himself a new political home, the possibility that Gantz will insist on running to the end could turn the battle between them from an electoral threat into a personal and public confrontation.
Thus, within just a few weeks, the promise of a meaningful “third bloc” has almost completely evaporated. What initially looked like a political space that could reshape the balance of power has, as candidate lists are about to be submitted, turned into a graveyard of new parties — and another reminder that in Israeli politics, there is often a vast distance between an idea that sounds good and actually crossing the electoral threshold.

Türkiye posts fastest growth in electricity demand among IEA members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:32:11 UTC
18:32:11 KST

Türkiye’s electricity demand grew by an average of nearly 5 percent annually between 2005 and 2024, marking the fastest increase among member countries of the International Energy Agency (IEA), according to the agency’s Türkiye 2026 Energy Policy Review.
Türkiye’s strong economic and population growth is reshaping the country’s energy needs.
With electricity demand expected to continue rising in the coming years, Türkiye’s National Energy Plan projects electricity consumption to reach 510 terawatt-hours by 2035.
The report noted that the rapid growth in electricity demand, coupled with the expansion of renewable energy capacity, highlights that grid infrastructure, storage, flexibility and demand-side management, rather than generation capacity alone, will be among the most critical issues facing Türkiye’s energy system in the years ahead.
The IEA report also noted that growth in electricity demand has been driven primarily by economic activity, particularly in the industrial and services sectors.
Rising demand and expanding renewable energy capacity are expected to place additional pressure on the country’s power grid.
Renewable energy sources are expected to play an increasingly important role in meeting growing electricity demand.
Renewables accounted for 43 percent of Turkey’s total electricity generation in 2025, and the share is targeted to rise to 55 percent by 2035.

MADRID, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Real Madrid suffered its first defeat of the season, Barcelona maintained its perfect start and Athletic Bilbao thrashed Atletico Madrid. Here are four things we learned from the weekend's La Liga action.

4. Aubameyang looks like a summer bargain
Villarreal remains without a win under new coach Inigo Perez after a 3-2 home defeat to Deportivo La Coruna, with Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang again proving decisive for the promoted side.

China releases 5-year development plan for information, communications sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:30:58 CST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued a development plan for the information and communications industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to promote high-quality development of this sector.
By 2030, a new-generation communications network with comprehensive coverage and leading performance is expected to be fully established, according to the plan, while adding that efforts will be made to accelerate the development of a technologically advanced, secure and controllable information and communications industrial system.
Meanwhile, an agile and efficient governance system integrating technology and management is expected to be effectively established, and network and data security capabilities featuring all-domain coordination and practical application will be significantly enhanced, the plan said.
The industry's empowerment level and degree of globalization will be further improved, laying a solid foundation for basically achieving modernization of the information and communications sector by 2035, the plan added.
The plan also outlines 13 key indicators, including achieving information and communications industry revenue of 4.1 trillion yuan (about 604.8 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030, cumulative investment of 3.8 trillion yuan in information infrastructure, and an average annual growth rate of 7 percent in total telecommunications business volume.
By 2030, there will be 50 5G (including 5G-A) base stations per 10,000 people, intelligent computing power will reach 9,800 EFLOPS, and the 5G user penetration rate will reach 95 percent, the ministry said.
EFLOPS, or ExaFLOPS, is a unit of computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second. ■

Iran war: How US consumers spent an additional $100bn on fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:30:44 UTC
18:30:44 KST

Iran war: How US consumers spent an additional $100bn on fuel
The average US household has spent $763 extra on fuel in six months, as the US-Israel war on Iran pushes up fuel costs across all 50 states.
US consumers have paid an additional $100bn for petrol and diesel in the six months since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, according to a tracker from Brown University’s Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs.
Across the country, the added cost works out to roughly $763 per household, based on an estimated 131 million households nationwide.
The war on Iran has been unpopular in the United States, with a majority of Americans blaming President Donald Trump for the rise in fuel prices. Trump has dismissed concerns about rising fuel prices in an interview with Reuters news agency, saying: “If they rise, they rise.” He has instead tried to shift the blame by accusing oil companies of “price gouging”.
Trump claimed that the war would last four to five weeks, but it has entered its sixth month, with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.
Petrol accounts for the larger share of the cost because Americans use far more of it than diesel. The price of petrol has climbed 39 percent, from about $2.98 to $4.15 a gallon ($0.79 to $1.09 per litre). Diesel has jumped even more sharply, rising more than 60 percent from $3.67 to $5.90 per gallon ($0.97 to $1.56 per litre).
Where are fuel prices highest in the US?
Fuel prices vary significantly by state. Prices are highest on the West Coast, especially in California, where high fuel taxes and carbon pricing programmes were already pushing costs up before the war even started.
According to the American Automobile Association, California has the nation’s highest average petrol price at $5.85 per gallon ($1.55 per litre), followed by Washington state ($5.51), Hawaii ($5.39), Alaska ($5.03) and Oregon ($5.01).
Indiana has the country’s lowest petrol price at an average of $3.43 per gallon ($0.91 per litre).
The map below shows a state-by-state breakdown of petrol prices. Hover over each state to see the percentage increase from before the war to now.
How higher fuel costs drive up the price of food
Oil and gas touch nearly every stage of the food chain, from fertiliser and tractor fuel on farms to refrigeration and insulation in cold storage to plastic packaging and truck fuel for transport.
As oil prices rise, these added costs accumulate at each step: production, storage, packaging and delivery.
By the time food reaches supermarket shelves, those additional costs are passed on to consumers as higher prices.
In lower-income countries, where populations spend a far greater share of their earnings on food and import large quantities of grain and fertiliser, rising oil prices could rapidly translate into food shortages.

Melike Pala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Germany told the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Monday that it significantly restricted arms exports to Israel between August and November 2025, with no export licenses issued initially and later approvals limited to equipment that could not be used in the Gaza Strip.
Addressing the court during hearings on Germany's preliminary objections to a case brought by Nicaragua, a German representative said Berlin closely monitored the situation in Israel, Gaza and the wider region and adapted its export licensing policy accordingly.
"The figures for licenses granted for the final export of arms to Israel fell significantly in the period from 8th of August to 23rd of November 2025, during which the federal government restricted its arms exports to Israel, in fact, no arms export licenses for final export to Israel were issued in the period from 8th of August to 12th of September," the representative said.
However, German newspaper Der Spiegel reported last week that the country approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) worth of military equipment exports to Israel in the first half of this year amid its ongoing genocide in the Gaza Strip.
The German side argued the restrictions followed an Israeli military push at the time and were intended to ensure that arms exports remained compatible with international humanitarian law.
Germany also said that when processing of export applications resumed in late 2025, the decision was linked to a ceasefire agreement reached in Gaza.
Berlin claimed that its export licensing policy is subject to continuous review by government authorities and judicial scrutiny by German courts.
Nicaragua accuses Germany of violating its obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention and international humanitarian law by providing political, financial and military support to Israel, as well as by suspending funding for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
Germany rejects the allegations and argues that the ICJ lacks jurisdiction to hear Nicaragua's claims.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

18:29:54 KST

A weekend of protests in Portsmouth and Dover has exposed deepening tensions over Britain's Channel crossings, even as the government insists arrival numbers are falling.
The UK government branded hundreds of demonstrators as "thuggish" after they blocked roads in an attempt to prevent asylum seekers leaving Portsmouth on Sunday.
The protest came after around 140 migrants arrived by small boat, as tensions over Channel crossings continue to mount.
"We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we saw in Portsmouth last night," a spokesperson for the UK's Home Office, said in a statement.
"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy but it must never cross a line into disorder."
Footage showed demonstrators, many dressed in black with their faces covered, confronting police officers holding riot shields as they formed a cordon around buses carrying the migrants to a processing centre.
Officials said the transfer was ultimately completed successfully.
Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones told the BBC it was a "wake up call" for the UK government.
Jones said that "people have a right to peaceful protest" and that was "largely" the case last night but "there were crimes committed and they will now be investigated and I would not be surprised if there are arrests that come off the back of the footage that was captured as evidence".
The Conservative MP said "hundreds" were acting lawfully and warned it was a "wake-up call to the government... that the British people are fed up with the lack of control of our borders".
Sunday's protest followed a similar demonstration on Saturday, when masked crowds blocked access to the Port of Dover.
French authorities said the vessel carrying the 140 migrants had departed from the Baie de Seine in Normandy — an unusually long and riskier route compared with the boats that typically depart from closer to Calais and land near Dover.
Arrivals in the county of Hampshire, where Portsmouth is located, remain extremely rare.
Another local Conservative MP Joe Robertson called the development "extremely concerning," questioning whether smugglers were opening new routes for larger vessels.
The unrest comes despite recent data suggesting crossings are slowing. The Home Office said Channel arrivals in August fell to their lowest level since records began in 2018, with migrant numbers at their lowest since 2020.
The average number of passengers per boat has been rising in recent months. Some 16,513 migrants have crossed the Channel by small boat so far this year.
It is a small fraction of overall arrivals in Britain which total over 800,000 - most of which come through legal routes on student or work visas.
The issue continues to fuel support for the Reform UK party, underscoring how migration remains one of the most volatile political issues across Europe.

DNA Business: A Gene Gold Rush | Storyteller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:25:14 UTC
18:25:14 KST

[NOTE: DNA Business: A Gene Gold Rush available until October 5, 2026.]
What if the most intimate information about who we are had become a commodity?
Once the exclusive preserve of elite scientists and medical laboratories, DNA can now be decoded by anyone — with a simple home testing kit. A handful of tech start-ups, including Ancestry, 23andMe and MyHeritage, have turned our desire to know where we come from, who we are related to and what diseases we might be vulnerable to into a global, highly lucrative business.
But how reliable are the answers these companies provide? Behind the seductive promise of discovering our origins or predicting our health risks lie methods whose scientific validity is questioned by leading geneticists. And there is an even bigger issue: what happens to our DNA once we have handed it over?
In 2019, an estimated 26 million people worldwide had taken a direct-to-consumer DNA test. By the end of 2026, that figure is expected to have nearly doubled, reaching close to 50 million. Many believe they are simply buying information about themselves. Few realize that their genetic data can become a valuable asset — collected, stored and potentially sold to pharmaceutical companies to fuel medical research and drug development. Regulation is struggling to keep pace. In some countries, certain insurers can already consider genetic-test results when deciding whom to cover—and at what price. Could other financial institutions one day seek access to the same extraordinarily sensitive information?
Through compelling personal stories, undercover investigation and interviews with leading geneticists, researchers and lawyers, this film exposes the hidden economy growing around our DNA.
This is no longer simply a story about science. It is a story about privacy, identity, money and power — and about the extraordinary possibility that, in the future, our genes could determine not only who we are, but how the world treats us.

Ebola burial teams endure exhaustion, hostility from communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Yuma Adolphe and his team have one of the most difficult jobs in the fight against Ebola in Congo's Ituri province, the epicenter of the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease. They are responsible for ensuring that those who die from Ebola receive safe and dignified burials, a task that requires them to dig graves, prepare bodies and handle coffins almost every day.
But as authorities struggle to contain the outbreak, which has killed nearly 3,200 people among more than 6,600 confirmed cases, the burial teams say they are reaching their limits. Their workload is growing, while hostility and fear in affected communities make an already dangerous job even harder.
"It is difficult, but we try to push ourselves beyond our limits," Adolphe told The Associated Press (AP).
Since the outbreak began in mid-May, authorities have deployed small burial teams like Adolphe's to Ebola hotspots, where they work on the front lines of efforts to contain the rapidly spreading disease. The workers are paid $20 a day for handling some of the most dangerous and emotionally difficult tasks in the response.
Despite the exhaustion and risks, members of the burial teams say they remain committed to protecting their communities, knowing that safe burials are essential to preventing further transmission of the virus.
For Adolphe and his colleagues, the work is grueling, but they see it as a necessary sacrifice to help keep their communities safe.
"We have to look at our own mental well-being, and physically the fatigue mounts, but we keep going to ensure the community is protected."
But their work is in the crosshairs of locals' frustration with the outbreak, which has not only taken their loved ones but also prevented them from observing traditional burial rites.
Health workers exclusively handle the bodies because Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids of infected people.
Experts say the bodies of victims still contain considerable amounts of active virus and can spread infections further.
Since May, health workers and burial teams such as Adolphe's have been attacked by bereaved families across the front line of the outbreak.
"Usually, the body is handed over to the family, who can handle it however they wish, in accordance with our African customs," Adolphe said. "But in this situation, it's difficult to let the family handle the body as they please. They are deprived of certain rituals, and that's what leads to misunderstandings."
Jeanne Alasha, adviser to the military governor of Ituri on health and humanitarian affairs, said that "as for those who continue to assault the teams, they are committing offenses punishable by law."
Ituri province, where the outbreak is concentrated, is also at the center of the rebel conflict in eastern Congo. The province is under a military government appointed by national civilian authorities in Kinshasa.
Shortly before noon last Friday, Justine Abineno, a chorister, was buried in Ituri. Abineno had died of Ebola. She had complained only of slight headaches before going to a hospital, where she was diagnosed with Ebola, her mother said.
A catechist presided over the ceremony, which was attended by dozens of people, as a team of burial specialists in scrubs and boots stood by.
Abineno's mother, Sofia Wanito, said doctors only allowed her to see the body through the window of the hospital ward, and she was not allowed to touch the coffin.
"In the past, we didn't die like this. I could not even cover her with the sheets myself and pay a final tribute," Wanito said.
The Ebola outbreak is spreading across six provinces in eastern Congo under some of the most difficult conditions imaginable, fueled by rebel violence, displacement and intense population movements. A weak health care and surveillance system also challenges responders, as do insufficient contact tracing and laboratory testing.
Efforts to contain the outbreak have also been complicated by the lack of an approved vaccine or treatment for the rare Bundibugyo virus causing it. Authorities have started vaccinating frontline health workers with the Ervebo vaccine, which the World Health Organization (WHO) says could offer some protection against Ebola, but there is no conclusive evidence that it would work against the current virus.
Health authorities say the true scale of the crisis is likely three times as high as official statistics suggest as the disease continues to outpace efforts to contain it. WHO has said the outbreak is projected to surpass the deadliest in history, West Africa's 2014-16 outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people.
Frontline health workers in eastern Congo have gone on multiple strikes to demand pay for their work, complicating efforts to stop the outbreak.
Benjamin Muhindo, another burial team member, said his family worries that he might bring the virus home. For him, though, a bigger priority is ensuring the proper burial of victims, he said.
"Burials during this Ebola epidemic are very complicated, as we are working under pressure and constantly racing against the clock," Muhindo said.
Trauma experts say the high number of cases and deaths are only one side of the outbreak's impact at the personal and communal levels.
"The trauma of this outbreak doesn't stop with the case count," said Rose Tchwenko, Mercy Corps country director in Congo. The chain of transmission will only be broken by "an integrated holistic response," which includes a social response to bereaved families and frontline workers, she added.
After the burial on Friday, Adolphe said he was very tired but more worried about the community than anything else.
"We have no choice," he said. "We are here to safeguard our community."

China injects over €45 billion into state banks and insurers as growth slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:24:28 UTC
18:24:28 KST

China's finance ministry is leading a combined 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) capital injection into eight state-owned banks and insurers, a coordinated effort to strengthen balance sheets strained by weak lending, low interest rates and government instructions to prop up the stock market.
Beijing has reached for its chequebook.
The Chinese finance ministry is advancing a 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) package to businesses, announced on Sunday through statements from the companies involved and reported by state news agency Xinhua, making it one of the larger interventions in China's financial system this year as growth slows.
The Chinese banks take the bulk of it, roughly 290 billion yuan (€37.2bn), intended to preserve their capacity to keep lending as Beijing presses them to increase support for economic activity.
Xinhua reported the injection would strengthen the institutions' "sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities and ability to serve the real economy."
The Agricultural Bank of China is pursuing a private placement of A-shares worth up to 160 billion yuan (€20.5bn) and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China up to 100 billion yuan (€12.8bn), with the finance ministry among the investors.
Unusually, so is the China National Tobacco Corporation, which operates the state tobacco monopoly and the Export-Import Bank of China which will receive 30 billion yuan (€3.85bn).
Insurers account for the remaining 70 billion yuan (€9bn).
China Life Insurance Group, the country's largest life insurer, gets 35 billion yuan (€4.5bn) and China Taiping Insurance Group 7 billion yuan (€900mn).
The People's Insurance Company of China plans to raise up to 15 billion yuan (€1.9bn) through a private placement to the ministry, China Export and Credit Insurance Corporation receives 10 billion yuan (€1.28bn), and China Reinsurance Group is raising 3 billion yuan (€385mn).
Insurers have been squeezed from two directions as years of low interest rates have eroded investment returns, while the government has directed them to put money into Chinese equities.
The currency has been moving in the same direction.
The Chinese yuan reached its strongest level against the US dollar since January 2023 on Monday, trading at around $0.149, a firmer exchange rate that also happens to blunt a long-standing American complaint about Chinese currency management, weeks before talks in Washington.
Beijing's busy month
The capital injection is not the only move Beijing is making this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is reportedly preparing to bring a large delegation of business executives to his Washington visit on 24 September, according to sources cited by news agencies.
It would be a notable departure from customary practice.
Xi rarely travels with corporate leaders, many of whom lost standing after the regulatory crackdowns on technology, education and property that began in 2020, and the last comparable delegation accompanied him to the US more than a decade ago, in 2015.
Washington's response has also been curious.
"The White House is not tracking a Chinese CEO delegation," a US official said, without explaining what tracking meant in this context, leaving the statement short of either confirmation or denial.
The gesture would be reciprocal in any case.
When US President Donald Trump visited Beijing in May, he brought a roster of American CEOs including Elon Musk, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang. Bringing Chinese counterparts to Washington would signal a willingness to invest and trade with the US, while handing the White House potential economic wins before November's midterm elections.
Expectations for the summit itself remain modest, with the two sides still divided over which products should count as non-sensitive under trade arrangements.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng are due to meet in early September to work on deliverables.

New high-speed train service links Antwerp, Brussels Airport and Leuven with Cologne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:24:16 UTC
18:24:16 KST

Antwerp, Leuven and Brussels Airport are now directly connected to Germany via a new ICE high-speed train service. The first train arrived at Antwerp Central this morning, following stops at Brussels Airport and Leuven. The trains will now run twice a day in both directions between Antwerp and Cologne.
New high-speed train service links Antwerp, Brussels Airport and Leuven with Cologne
The first ICE train was given a warm welcome at the three Belgian stations on Monday morning. The train arrived at its final destination, Antwerp Central, at around 9.30 am, half an hour behind schedule. The ICE trains operated by the German railway company Deutsche Bahn can accommodate over 400 passengers.
Route and timetables: In Germany, the trains depart from Cologne, with a stop in Aachen. In Belgium, they stop at Liège, Leuven, Brussels Airport and Antwerp. Passengers travelling from Antwerp can reach Cologne by ICE in approximately 2 hours and 20 minutes. From Brussels Airport, the journey takes less than 2 hours; from Leuven, approximately one and a half hours. The trains arrive in Cologne at around 1.30 pm and 9.30 pm.
Tickets for journeys between Antwerp and Cologne are available from 29.99 euros. For Leuven and Antwerp, this is the first permanent direct high-speed rail link to Germany. Brussels Airport is once again connected to the high-speed network for the first time since 2015. Passengers travelling with Belgian flag carrier Brussels Airlines can combine train and flight on a single ticket.
Partnership with Belgian Rail NMBS
Deutsche Bahn is partnering with Belgium’s state-owned rail company NMBS to realise this ICE service. The NMBS will operate half the services. The Cologne–Antwerp route is the second ICE service between Belgium and Germany. Eight ICE train services already run daily between Germany (Frankfurt, Cologne, Aachen) and Belgium, stopping in Liège, and terminating at Brussels South.
Eurostar high-speed trains also run between Belgium and Germany.

Penghu tests drone deliveries to remote islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:24:03 UTC
18:24:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Penghu County Government said Monday it was testing the use of drones to deliver supplies to remote communities.
The county and National Penghu University of Science and Technology launched test flights from Magong City to Jibei Islet. The program is intended to provide residents with a reliable supply of daily necessities in the future.
The pilot flight took off from the university campus, with Earthbook CEO Hsu Wei-cheng (徐偉城) demonstrating the drone’s setup. NPU President Lee Wen-hsi (李文熙) and local officials attended the event.
Lee said the drone was designed to withstand strong winds and followed a route mapped using weather forecasting data. He said additional wind-resistance tests were scheduled for February.
Hsu said the drone can travel up to 120 kilometers and is controlled from an operations center on campus. He said the farthest of Penghu’s 19 inhabited islands is 40 km away.
The drone has a carrying capacity of 3.5 kilograms and can reach Jibei in 15 minutes while traveling at 100 kph, Hsu said.
The university said the test flight was successful. It plans future flights to Hua, Tongpan, and Hujing islets.
Deputy Magistrate Lin Chieh-hsing (林皆興) said only 19 of the county’s islands have permanent residents and transportation to many can be disrupted by poor weather. He said drones and unmanned vessels were necessary to provide access to medical care and daily necessities.

Gongwin canine cancer drug set to enter Taiwan market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:40 UTC
18:23:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Gongwin Biopharm Holdings Co.’s new animal cancer drug has received marketing approval from the Ministry of Agriculture to treat melanoma in dogs, Liberty Times reported Saturday.
Melanoma develops from pigment-producing cells and is one of the most common cancers in dogs. It can occur on the skin, toes, and in the mouth, with oral melanoma accounting for more than 80% of cases and being particularly aggressive, according to SBM.
Gongwin’s Gwa103 uses a mechanism called intratumoral drug ablation to destroy cancer cells. The drug selectively enters malignant cells, helping reduce damage to surrounding healthy tissue, according to Anue.
Current treatment relies mainly on surgery and chemotherapy. Because canine melanoma often develops in the mouth and limbs and can affect large areas, surgery may require the removal of additional tissue.
Gongwin has signed letters of intent to collaborate on the drug with more than 100 animal hospitals across Taiwan. The drug can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other cancer therapies, according to UDN Money.
After completing labeling, supply chain arrangements, and hospital onboarding, the company plans to begin supplying the drug in stages in accordance with regulatory requirements. It will also provide clinical training for veterinary teams.
Gwa103 is also eligible for conditional marketing approval in the US, where Gongwin has obtained authorization to conduct clinical trials. The company also plans to expand into other major pet markets, including Australia, Japan, China, and Hong Kong.
Fortune Business Insights said the global veterinary oncology market was worth NT$91.9 billion (US$2.9 billion) in 2025. It estimates the market will grow at a compound annual growth rate of 10.7% from 2026 to reach NT$225 billion by 2034.

Chi Mei to feature 8 rare string instruments in Kaohsiung concert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:35 UTC
18:23:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — This year’s Chi Mei Music Festival will culminate Nov. 14 with a concert featuring eight rare string instruments from the Chi Mei Museum collection at the National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts, also known as Weiwuying, per a press release.
The concert, titled “Mountains and Waters, Rain and Storms: A Feast of Masterpieces by Brahms and Dvorak,” will feature pianist Liu Meng-chieh (劉孟捷), French conductor Victorien Vanoosten, music director of the Toulon Opera, and the National Taiwan Symphony Orchestra (NTSO).
Liu, who specializes in the works of Brahms and received an Avery Fisher Career Grant, will perform Brahms’ Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor. Vanoosten will conduct Dvorak’s Symphony No. 8 in G major with the NTSO, according to the museum.
One of the most notable instruments will be a 1674 viola by Austrian luthier Jacob Stainer featuring a lion-head design. The museum described it as one of only four surviving Stainer lion-head violas in the world. The NTSO’s principal players will use the eight instruments during the concert, adding depth to the orchestra’s middle and lower registers.
This year’s festival is centered on Johannes Brahms (1833–1897). Brahms was a major figure of the Romantic era who combined the formal structures of the Classical period with the emotional language of 19th-century Romantic music, per the press release.
The festival program covers different periods of Brahms’ musical career and places his works alongside those of composers who influenced him or were his contemporaries, including Beethoven, Schubert, Robert Schumann, Liszt, and Wagner, as well as Dvorak.
The festival is curated by Chiao Yuan-pu (焦元溥), a writer and producer who holds a doctorate in musicology from King’s College London. The museum said this year’s festival features 13 instruments from the Chi Mei collection across its concerts, including works by Stradivari and Guadagnini and examples from the German and Austrian violin-making traditions.

Middle East: Israeli strikes kill several in Lebanon

Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case
Germany's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel, should be thrown out.
The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted."
Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
"Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges.
Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings.
It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court.
Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law.
"Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said.
The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza, where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year.
However, Germany only instituted this policy in 2025, and continued to ship defensive equipment worth hundreds of millions of euros this year.
Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution
Iran's Foreign Ministry issued a warning against any country participating in security operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X.
Baqaei noted Tehran's diplomatic relationship with Seoul, saying that Iran "places great importance on its friendly relations with the Republic of Korea."
The comments come after South Korea's presidency on Friday said it had not reached a decision on sending forces to the Strait of Hormuz to help ensure free navigation of the waterway.
South Korea has been facing pressure from the Trump administration to make military contributions relating to Iran and has been accused of turning down any request for assistance.
"We are closely communicating with the international community, including relevant countries, to help restore peace and stability in the Middle East as soon as possible and to ensure the free passage of all vessels, including those of our country, through the Strait of Hormuz," Yonhap news agency cited South Korea's Foreign Ministry as saying in a statement.
Shipping traffic in Strait of Hormuz drops following US-Iran strikes
Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has dropped to the lowest level since May , according to data analytics platform Kpler.
According to its latest figures, an average of 10 commodity vessels, transited the vital shipping route over the past 10 days.
Kpler recorded the number on Sunday, which was down from the 15 vessels on Friday and the 13 seen on Saturday.
The drop in maritime traffic comes amid strikes targeting tankers by the US and Iran.
On Saturday, US forces hit three Iranian oil tankers, following Iranian attacks on US warships in the region.
In retaliation, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it has targeted three oil tankers travelling what it said ewas an unathorized route in the strait.
The strikes over the weekend represented a "major escalation in maritime conflict," the Reuters news agency cited maritime intelligence firm Marisks as saying.
"Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," Marisks noted.
"Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage and materially elevated for US-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman," the firm said

Reports of at least 10 dead following overnight Israeli strikes
Overnight Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed at least 10 people, including two children, health officials said.
Earlier, Lebanon's National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israeli warplanes struck a residential building in Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon.
The agency reported that a separate drone strike struck a vehicle with two medics inside, however, the Associated Press cited the Health Ministry as saying the strike on the car killed one paramedic and wounded two others.
Israel's military has not commented on these latest strikes, but Israel's Foreign Ministry released a statement on X referencing the militant group.
"Repeated drone attacks. Weapons storage. Terror infrastructure. Command centres embedded in civilian areas. Hezbollah continues attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon. These violations will not be accepted," Israel's Foreign Ministry wrote on X.
The ministry said that Hezbollah had violated the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire agreement, under which, the militant group would be disarmed.
"Hezbollah continues attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon," the ministry said.
On Sunday, Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun pushed for Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks.
Despite a peace agreement that came into effect over two months ago, flare-ups are continuing between Israel and Hezbollah.
The US, Germany and several Arab countries consider Hezbollah a terrorist organization, whereas the EU only deems Hezbollah's armed wing a terror group.

Thousands gather in Belgrade for funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:22:05 KST

Thousands gather in Belgrade for funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic
BELGRADE, Sept 7 - Thousands of people gathered in front of a church in Belgrade to pay respects to former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic who died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Mladic remains a revered figure among many Serbs in Serbia and in Bosnia's autonomous Serb Republic, despite his convictions linked to his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and in the siege of Sarajevo.
People carrying Serbian flags and pictures of Mladic wearing a traditional Serbian military cap arrived in front of the church to light candles early on Monday, hours before his scheduled burial.
Free bus services were offered from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
Mladic's coffin was displayed inside the church and six men, mainly war veterans from Serbia and Bosnia, took turns guarding it. Mladic's wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
"Time will tell, time is the best judge who will show what kind of person is who and to whom," said Belgrade resident Jovan Vincic, who had come to the church.
CONFLICTS TRIGGERED BY BREAK-UP OF YUGOSLAVIA
Mladic's death has stirred up strong feelings linking back to the break-up of Yugoslavia and the ethnic conflicts that ensued in the Balkans.
Mladic was found guilty by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the U.N.-designated enclave.
He was also convicted over the 43-month siege of Sarajevo, during which about 10,000 people were killed.
Last week, EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos postponed her visit to Serbia because of what she said was the "glorification" of Mladic after his death, including the use of a government plane to return him to Serbia.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic dismissed those statements, but did not say whether he would attend Monday's funeral.
The service was scheduled to be conducted by the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church at noon, after which Mladic will be buried in a nearby cemetery beside his daughter, who died in 1994.
In Sarajevo, meanwhile, the funeral rekindled painful memories of the war.
"It is really horrible that this is taking place there (in Belgrade) because I know there are normal people who are against it," said Zdravka Gvozdjar, a retired pharmacist whose 9-year-old son was killed during the Sarajevo siege by a grenade fired by the Mladic-led forces, one among more than 1,000 children killed in the city.
"Mladic ... only deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be ... promoted as a hero," she said. "He should be remembered only as a butcher." REUTERS

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:22:03 UTC
18:22:03 KST

Cricket Australia is set to proceed with the partial privatisation of the Big Bash League despite opposition from New South Wales and Queensland.
States will be allowed to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.
What's next?
A formal announcement is expected to be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday in concert with several of Australia's cricket stars.
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.
Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.
The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.
It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.
However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.
The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.
The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.
This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.
Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.
But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.
South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.
New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.
Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.
In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.
Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.
It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.
In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.
Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

"Russia's imperial ambitions will not end with Ukraine," Finnish defence minister says

12:20:46 EEST
18:20:46 KST

Finland must respond to the threat from Russia calmly, but also firmly and decisively, Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) said on Monday.
Häkkänen made the remarks during his opening address at the 257th National Defence Course, which brings together leaders from government, the media and academia to discuss national security issues.
"Russia's imperial ambitions will not end with Ukraine," Häkkänen said. He added that Moscow is seeking to restore at least the spheres of influence it had during the Soviet era.
Häkkänen described the Russian threat as long-term and unpredictable, with his remarks coming as Finland completes its eastern border fence.
"The time to strengthen Finland's national defence is now," Häkkänen said, noting that the impact of Europe's increased defence spending will only become visible in practice in the 2030s.
Finland is also investing in counter-drone capabilities together with Sweden.
"This is a significant and historic step in closer Finnish-Swedish cooperation. It is also a testament to the Nordic countries taking responsibility for their own defence," Häkkänen said.
The defence minister also welcomed the growth in Finnish defence exports. Last year, 479 export licences were granted, while the value of completed exports was around 700 million euros.
Eastern border fence completed
Finland has completed a 200-kilometre barrier along its eastern border with Russia this autumn.
The project affected thousands of Finns, with around one thousand landowners receiving compensation. The fence is designed to prevent unauthorised entry. Construction began after the asylum seeker situation in 2023, when thousands of migrants crossed the border, prompting Finland to close its eastern border crossings.
The Finnish government still considers it possible that the threat of instrumentalised migration could return.
The project cost 356 million euros, with maintenance expected to cost a further 1.5 million euros a year.

US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, outlining a pathway toward renewed peace talks and expressing hope for a trilateral format soon.
The two envoys outlined their assessment during remarks in Kyiv, a day after meeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 6.
Kushner told reporters that Washington had consulted both sides about reviving three-way negotiations. "One thing Steve and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format," he explained. "We've spoken with both parties, and so hopefully we'll have progress on that very soon."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Witkoff stated that Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had dispatched the pair to reopen talks. "The President asked Jared and me to come here and to restart conversations, negotiations, because this is so important to him," he noted.
Kushner characterized the Moscow talks as constructive and substantive, with both delegations posing questions about the elements of a durable settlement.
Witkoff, who has made about eight visits to the Russian capital to meet Putin, emphasized the role of personal ties in ending the war. He and Kushner have traveled there together at least three times. "Relationships are critical in terms of solving conflicts like this," Witkoff declared.
The envoys met Putin first to gauge Moscow's position and briefed Zelenskyy's team on the discussion. Witkoff stated that their task is to bring the two sides together, narrow the issues between them, and build reliable communication channels.
He described the previous 48 hours as a constructive start and expressed confidence in an eventual resolution.
The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first trip to the Ukrainian capital, which they reached by train after their aircraft landed in Poland. Ukraine had readied its airports to receive the delegation by air, but Russian strikes ruled out a direct landing.
At the railway station, they were met by senior Ukrainian officials, including presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Serhii Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
The timing carries added weight as winter nears, with Moscow calculating that Ukrainian resolve will weaken through the cold months and that Putin's willingness to negotiate will fade until the season ends in mid-March.
The Kyiv talks followed directly from a marathon session in Moscow the previous day. There, Witkoff and Kushner spent more than three hours with Putin—three hours and 10 minutes in all—focused primarily on approaches to ending the war in Ukraine.
Officials on both sides framed the exchange as substantive and unusually frank, and the delegation was reported to have arrived with a range of settlement proposals. The discussions extended beyond Ukraine to potential large-scale US-Russian economic projects.
The Moscow visit unfolded under a temporary arrangement on strikes. Putin had ordered Russian forces to refrain from hitting Kyiv for three days from midnight on September 5, and Zelenskyy signaled Ukraine's readiness to observe a matching halt on cities tied to the negotiations.

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:18:01 UTC
18:18:01 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield, the Ryazan Oil Refinery, and three Russian air defense assets during an overnight operation in Russia on September 6, with fires reported at both the airfield and refinery.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 6, Ukrainian forces targeted the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region. A fire was recorded at the facility, which the General Staff said is involved in supplying the Russian armed forces.
The Ryazan refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with a design capacity of around 17 million metric tons of crude per year. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense manufacturer, said its FP-1 drones struck equipment at two major primary crude-processing units at the refinery.
The company reported hits on the distillation columns of the ELOU-AVT-6 unit, the refinery’s largest primary processing unit with an annual capacity of 8.5 million metric tons, as well as equipment at the AVT-3 unit, which has a capacity of 3.1 million tons per year.
Together, the two units account for more than 77% of the refinery’s primary oil-processing capacity, according to Fire Point.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield in Russia’s Rostov region. The General Staff reported a fire in the area of the facility but said the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Three Russian air defense assets were also hit in the Rostov region—a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
The Podlet radar is designed to detect low-altitude and small aerial targets, including drones and cruise missiles. The Pantsir-S1 is a short-range air defense system combining surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters, drones, and precision-guided weapons.
The strikes were part of a broader overnight Ukrainian drone operation that targeted at least 14 Russian regions, as well as temporarily occupied Crimea and areas over the Black and Azov seas. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed 258 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, while Moscow and the surrounding region were left untouched under a temporary airspace arrangement during US envoy visits.

The death toll from devastating flash floods and mudslides at the Nepal-China border has climbed to 1,398, with over 5,500 people remaining missing, official statistics showed on Monday.
Of those missing, 850 are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said that 1,355 bodies have been recovered so far, while around 5,000 people, including 589 foreigners, remain missing.
More than 13,000 people have been rescued from the flood-hit areas.
Chinese authorities said at least 43 people have been confirmed dead, while 519 others, including 261 foreigners, remain missing in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
Nepal’s Cyber Bureau has launched an investigation into social media abuse targeting people affected by last month’s river floods, local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.
Following a warning from Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the bureau formed a 10-member team to investigate social media users accused of posting abusive and hateful comments against those affected.
Shah warned in a Facebook post that those who mocked or harassed people suffering in the aftermath of the disaster would face consequences, adding that the government would take a tough line against such behavior.
Authorities said they are compiling profiles of people who have posted insensitive comments about flood survivors.
Many families searching for relatives who went missing in the floods are using social media to appeal for help. Their posts, however, have been met with a slew of hostile and demeaning comments.
“People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals,” Shah wrote. “The government will show no leniency towards them.”
The abuse continues despite the prime minister’s warning.
 
At least one person has been arrested for posting hateful comments on social media against those affected by the floods.
According to local law, those found guilty can be fined up to Rs100,000 or sentenced to up to five years in prison, or both.

Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:15:40 UTC
18:15:40 KST

Russia flew hundreds of warplane sorties against a small group of Ukrainian sea drones, according to the ArmyInform. The drones belong to Group 13, a Ukrainian military-intelligence unit. The unit is running out of Russian warships to sink and now strikes land targets from the sea, its commander, known by his call sign Thirteenth, said.
Years ago, Russia entered its all-out war against Ukraine with a commanding navy and treated the Black Sea as its own. A country left with almost no warships has since answered with cheap robot boats, turning expendable machines into the tool that now contests that sea.
More than 500 sorties to hunt one small drone group
Group 13 hunts Russian warships with Magura sea drones—uncrewed attack boats. Russia flew more than 500 aircraft sorties against a group of eight to 10 Magura drones at the time, the commander said. Moscow spent more on locating the drones than the unit's entire mission cost, he added. Missions have grown longer, too. What once took a day now takes three, four, or five days.
Biggest Magura sea drone doesn’t ram ships. It carries other drones and stays out seven days
The commander split the unit's rise into three stages: victory at sea, an end to Russian air dominance over the water, and now strikes on land from the sea. The bar set in 2023 and 2024 is unrealistic to hold in the Black Sea today, he said, because there are no ship targets left, and what remains is harder to reach. A struck S-400 air-defense system does not pay off like a sunk warship, he added.
The bill for Russia
The damage runs past destroyed hardware. Each Russian sailor killed leaves a family pension to pay and training to write off, the commander said. He pointed to the Syrian Express, Russia's sea supply line to Syria. It once ran a short route and now goes through the Baltic Sea, and the whole bill runs into the millions, he said.
The unit's capabilities came together in a strike on the Ivan Khurs, a Russian reconnaissance ship, its first target. The later sinking of the missile boat Ivanovets killed 40 Russian crew in minutes, the commander recalled. He expects the unit to be remembered as revolutionaries, likening its sea drones to the first tanks more than a century ago.

Germany seeks to dismiss Nicaragua's Gaza genocide case at top UN court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:14:51 UTC
18:14:51 KST

Germany seeks to dismiss Nicaragua's Gaza genocide case at top UN court
Germany is set to ask the International Court of Justice on Monday to dismiss a case accusing Berlin of "facilitating genocide" in Gaza by supporting Israel after the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas militants. The details of the case, filed by Nicaragua in 2024, have not yet been made public.
Germany will Monday ask the top United Nations court to toss out a case brought against it by Nicaragua, which has accused Berlin of "facilitating genocide" with its support of Israel.
Lawyers for Germany will kick off four days of hearings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the court based in The Hague that rules on disputes between countries.
Read moreGermany denies aiding 'genocide' in Gaza, says Israeli security at 'core' of foreign policy
The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel's offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment.
The court threw out Nicaragua's request in April of that year, saying "the circumstances, as they now present themselves" did not justify emergency orders.
The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule in the case or that Nicaragua's argument does not stack up.
Berlin has filed so-called "preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims" presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement.
The detail of Berlin's case has not yet been made public.
Genocide claim
After Germany presents its case on Monday, Nicaragua will respond before both countries get another chance to address the court on Wednesday and Thursday.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was "pathetic" to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons.
Nicaragua's ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court: "Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide."
Germany retorted that Nicaragua's case was "grossly biased", strongly denying the accusations that it was in breach of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
Read moreWhy is it so hard to talk about Palestine in Germany?
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza in response to the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks against it by Hamas militants.
Due to its Nazi past, Germany has placed Israel's security "at the core" of its foreign policy, its representative told the court in the 2024 hearings.
Germany said its arms trade with Israel was subject to "detailed scrutiny ... that far exceeds the requirements of international law".
This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies.
The ICJ's rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them.
For example, it has ordered Russia to stop its invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Nepal holds day of mourning for more than 1,300 killed in floods
Nepal flags fly at half-mast to mark a day of mourning after catastrophic Himalayan floods kill more than 1,300.
Nepal is holding a national day of mourning to remember more than 1,300 people who died in last month’s catastrophic floods.
Government offices in Nepal and missions abroad are flying the national flag at half-mast on Monday, the 13th day since the floods, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Relatives hold cremations without bodies for Nepal’s missing flood victims
- list 2 of 3Photos: UN urges global aid after China, Nepal floods kill over 1,300
- list 3 of 3China, Nepal race to find thousands still missing 12 days after floods
In the Hindu tradition, it is the final day of the mourning period, during which close family members stay at home and relatives visit to pay their respects. On the final day, rituals are held to pray for those who died.
The government has not planned any wider events for this day of mourning because search teams are still looking for survivors and resources are limited.
“There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas,” Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Center (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency.
A huge wall of mud and rock, triggered by a glacier breaking off, collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet region on August 26, causing flooding that killed at least 1,380 people and left more than 5,500 missing.
In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel at a hydropower site on Saturday. The others rescued were two hydropower workers from another tunnel on Friday, as well as a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.
President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, is touring flood-hit areas on Monday and will survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.
In Kathmandu, family members gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the speeding up of the search for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower projects and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekoshi River or buried by the debris.
Sumana Shrestha stood with her family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.
Her husband, a consulting geologist, was supposed to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The two-and-a-half-storey office was buried by debris.
“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”
Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site.
He said authorities sent only a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”
Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Molchanova was 22 at the time, living in Russia and studying design at a university; she had come to the United States on a trip and spoke little English.

How Molchanova ended up in Epstein’s “cult” and got pulled into his financial schemes

Epstein regularly coerced Molchanova and other women who had become dependent on him into sex, and he expected them to bring him new potential victims. Molchanova says she refused to take part in this kind of procuring, and his attitude toward her worsened as a result. He constantly demanded that she explain how she could be useful to him and often isolated her from the outside world.
Epstein also monitored her spending, Molchanova said, giving her less than $3,000 a month, though the amount varied. He dictated what she wore, how long her hair should be, which doctors she could see, and who she could spend time with. In 2013, he even arranged a sham marriage for Molchanova to another woman. He is known to have used this tactic more than once within his “cult.”
In 2014, Epstein’s lawyer, Darren Indyke, registered a company called JSC Interiors in Molchanova’s name — she said that Epstein presented it as a way to launch her design business. In reality, she carried out only a handful of design-related tasks, such as putting together flower arrangements, while Epstein kept JSC Interiors under his own control, using it to move money and carry out other transactions without the knowledge of its nominal founder.
Molchanova says she only learned about this years later. Bank of America, where the company held its account, clearly turned a blind eye to actions Epstein allegedly took in her name, she says, and she later became the lead plaintiff in a collective lawsuit against the bank brought by women harmed by the financier. A court recently approved a settlement in the case, under which Bank of America agreed to pay a total of $72.5 million to dozens of plaintiffs. The bank denies facilitating crimes related to human trafficking for the purposes of sexual abuse.
Indyke and Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, also deny any wrongdoing. Their representatives told the Wall Street Journal that Molchanova never told them she had been abused and “appeared to be one of Epstein’s assistants working through an LLC that Epstein set up for interior design purposes.” Indyke and Kahn deny knowing that their employer had arranged a sham marriage for Molchanova or used accounts registered in her name.

Epstein never helped Molchanova build a career in design, but he did try to place her in other jobs, including at Next Management, the modeling agency run by well-known businesswoman Faith Kates.
In a May 2015 email, Kates told Epstein that Molchanova had said in a job interview that she did not want to sit at a desk all day and had never worked in an office before. Epstein reprimanded her for turning down a receptionist job. ”[I] am angry,” he wrote.
Next Management told reporters it never had any relationship with Epstein. “Faith Kates’ multi-decade long, personal relationship with Jeffrey Epstein was completely and absolutely unknown to Next Management and its top executives,” the company stated in a statement. Kates did not respond to requests for comment. She left Next Management in late 2025, after the U.S. Justice Department published part of her correspondence with Epstein.
Epstein also arranged internships for Molchanova through his friends, including, she said, one with publicist Peggy Siegal in 2016. Molchanova said she felt out of place there, hampered by her poor English. “If he really wanted to help, he would have sent me to learn English,” she said. Siegal did not respond to requests for comment. She has previously said she did not know about Epstein’s “nefarious behavior” and that associating with him was a mistake.
Years of total dependence on Epstein took a severe toll on Molchanova’s physical and mental health. Her weight fluctuated, and Epstein criticized her for it, calling her fat. At her lowest point, she said, she thought about suicide, and Epstein would not let her see a therapist. Her mental health deteriorated further after a tabloid published photos of her with Epstein in 2016: “I remember thinking that I’m trapped forever, and my life is over.”
In 2017, Epstein’s lawyer drew up paperwork so Molchanova could dissolve her sham marriage. She describes the years that followed as an attempt to break free from what she calls a “cult.” She got a boyfriend she hoped to marry as a way out, but Epstein kept calling her back and the abuse continued. She never told her boyfriend what was happening, and the two eventually broke up.
Molchanova did not tell a friend about her dire situation until early 2019, and the friend helped her come up with a plan to fight back. That March, she emailed Kahn, Epstein’s accountant, asking why her credit history showed credit cards she had never opened. She also demanded to see her tax returns and be removed as a founder of JSC Interiors. Kahn replied that she could hire someone else to handle the tax returns but promised to send her the paperwork to leave JSC Interiors.
Around the same time, Molchanova sent Epstein an email accusing him directly. He responded by inviting her to Palm Beach, but she did not go. “I thought for sure, at that moment, someone would find me on the bottom of his pool if I go,” she said. Lesley Groff, Epstein’s longtime assistant, tried to persuade her to call him, and another young woman from his circle called her as well. Despite the pressure, she never returned to the “cult.”
In her interview with the Wall Street Journal, Molchanova recalled that she had nicknamed Epstein “little bear.” In June 2019, she painted a picture depicting the arrest and beheading of a bear, with no way of knowing that Epstein would be taken into custody on July 6, and that weeks later he would be found dead in his cell at a federal jail in New York.
