Rival cities vie to ‘poach’ international organisations from Geneva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:39:08 UTC
16:39:08 KST

Rival cities vie to ‘poach’ international organisations from Geneva
A UN funding crisis triggered by Donald Trump’s foreign aid cuts has set off a battle for diplomatic influence, with EU capitals and Gulf states competing to lure international organisations and staff away from Geneva, Swiss officials have warned.
Home to the European headquarters of the UN, dozens of international organisations, hundreds of non-governmental organisations and diplomatic missions, Geneva last year was confronted with its biggest test in decades after the Trump administration froze most US foreign aid, withdrew from the World Health Organization (WHO) and halted funding for several UN bodies.
At the same time many countries have been decreasing their contributions to the multilateral system and spending more on areas such as national defence.
    
        External Content    
    
        
    
The resulting budget crises have forced agencies to cut jobs, freeze hiring and look for cheaper locations, making high-cost Geneva an obvious target.
“International Geneva”, as the ecosystem is known, generates about CHF4 billion ($5 billion) of annual economic activity — according to foreign ministry estimates — and is home to roughly 450 international organisations and NGOs, as well as about 185 countries represented via permanent missions, according to government figures.
More
What’s next? Moving on after losing a job in International Geneva
Swiss officials say about 20 countries are trying to use the financial turmoil engulfing the multilateral system to bolster their own ambitions as diplomatic hubs. They identified Austria, France, Germany, Italy and Spain as well as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates as among those seeking to attract UN agencies or parts of Geneva’s international ecosystem.
“A lot of European countries have host-state ambitions and they want to use this moment of stress to strengthen their own position,” said one Swiss official with direct knowledge of the situation. “It is blatant poaching.”
“The sharp reduction in financial support in 2025 opened a real opportunity for a lot of challengers, particularly in Europe,” said Beatrice Ferrari, director of International Affairs at canton Geneva.
The WHO has proposed moving some headquarters functions to Lyon, France, as part of its restructuring. Unicef is relocating hundreds of posts to lower-cost cities including Rome, while the International Labour Organization (ILO) has said it will shift some staff and functions to its existing training centre in Turin.
More
Ripple effect of aid freeze becomes real in Geneva
The Swiss official said: “We’ve seen some member states offer a certain amount of money for every person they can move from Geneva to their city.”
Another Geneva-based politician said governments were increasingly carving out specialist roles rather than trying to replicate the city wholesale. Spain wants Valencia to become a centre for digitalisation and data, France is strengthening Lyon as a hub for international health governance and Paris’s education profile, Germany is building on Bonn’s environmental institutions and Berlin’s international role, while Vienna is seeking to expand its presence as a UN hub.
“They all want different parts of the ecosystem,” the politician said.
Among the Gulf states, Swiss officials see Qatar as the strongest challenger because it has established itself as a diplomatic broker. They pointed to Doha’s growing role in mediation, including over Gaza and in recent diplomacy involving Iran, and said it was combining that political influence with “very attractive financial offers” as it sought to become a bigger humanitarian hub.
More
Pressure eased on UN layoffs, official says in Geneva
Bern has responded with one of its largest host-state support packages in years. The federal government in June approved CHF269 million for International Geneva, citing the financial crisis facing UN agencies and “increasing competition between states” to host international organisations.
The package includes emergency funding for struggling agencies, investment in conference and digital infrastructure, a CHF78 million interest-free loan to renovate buildings used by international organisations, and support for Geneva’s ambitions in areas such as AI and other emerging technologies.
The effort extends beyond the federal government. Canton Geneva and the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, which controls Rolex, have created a CHF50 million fund to support International Geneva over five years. The canton has also earmarked CHF10 million for NGOs, while the City of Geneva has committed a further CHF2 million.
Swiss officials insist they are not trying to outspend rival host cities but to protect the concentration of UN agencies, diplomats, NGOs and researchers that has made Geneva one of the world’s leading centres for international co-operation.
They argue the economic benefits of relocation are often overstated. Lower salaries and rents elsewhere can be offset by the cost of recreating conference facilities, administrative support and diplomatic networks, while dispersing organisations risks weakening the collaboration that has made Geneva effective in tackling global problems.
More
US withdrawal from WHO puts global health in jeopardy
“There is fierce competition because of the US retreat,” said Vincent Subilia, a member of parliament for canton Geneva and director-general of the Geneva Chamber of Commerce. “But the federal government, the canton and the city have all stepped up to help fill part of the gap.
“Our high concentration of institutions means Geneva still offers the strongest and most unique international ecosystem.”
Nor is every government pulling back. Swiss officials said countries including China have stepped up their engagement with Geneva’s multilateral institutions, seeing an opportunity to wield greater influence as the US retreats.
Ferrari said six new countries had opened permanent missions in the past two years, including Belize and some Pacific island countries.
“The crisis is not over yet but Geneva remains the biggest centre and closest to decision makers,” she added.

- The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Monday that Tehran is planning to announce a maritime "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz where it intends to stop vessels attempting to transit the waterway without Iranian permission.
- The price of Brent crude, the international standard for oil, briefly hit a nearly seven-week high early on Monday, touching the $97 per barrel mark and continuing a trend from the previous week that saw it rise 8%. In the U.S., the average price of regular gas was $4.14 a gallon going into Labor Day weekend, nearly a dollar higher than last year and a record for any Labor Day weekend.
- Iran threatened Sunday to deliver a "more intense and more painful" retaliation after the U.S. struck three Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
Qatar says Gulf countries cannot rely on the U.S. alone for security
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said Monday the war with Iran had shown that Persian Gulf countries should not rely solely on their strategic partnership with the United States to maintain their security.
"We need to recognize in the Gulf region that the presence of international forces in the region and the establishment of a strategic partnership with the United States are extremely important, but they are not sufficient," Al Ansari said during a panel discussion at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi. "Self-reliance in the field of security is the only way forward."
"We need our partners and allies, but we cannot rely on them alone for our security," he said.
Qatar was one of the countries targeted on a regular basis by Iran in retaliation for U.S. strikes at the height of the war.
Tehran says Iran-Oman talks on Strait of Hormuz in "final stages"
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that negotiations with Oman regarding the future of the Strait of Hormuz had reached the "final stage."
The two countries sit on opposite sides of the strategic waterway and have been engaged in talks for months with the goal of reaching an understanding on how to manage commercial traffic through the strait in the future.
"Within the coming days, the understanding between Iran and Oman for a temporary route safe in the Strait of Hormuz will be registered with the International Maritime Organization."
Throughout the talks, both sides have suggested the possibility of charging fees for ships to transit the waterway, a notion the U.S. government has bristled at.
Emirati diplomat says restoring trust with Iran will be difficult but necessary
A top Emirati official appeared to extend an olive branch to Iran on Monday, saying that restoring trust with Tehran would be difficult, but necessary.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the United Arab Emirates president, also said Persian Gulf countries had failed to respond in a united fashion to Iran's attacks and threats during the U.S.-Iran war, with each country defending itself but not embracing a shared strategy.
Gulf countries bore the brunt of Tehran's retaliation for American strikes, with missiles and drone strikes hitting military targets as well as civilian areas on a regular basis at the height of the fighting.
"Geography leaves us no alternative to engagement, but we must distinguish clearly between rebuilding a necessary and functional relationship with Iran and rebuilding the trust that has been broken. The first is necessary. The second will be far more difficult," Gargash said at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi.
CBS/AFP
Iran warns South Korea against military deployment alongside the U.S.
Iran's foreign ministry on Monday warned South Korea against deploying military assets or getting involved in any other way with U.S. operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz, saying such a move would have "serious consequences."
On Friday, the South Korean government said it would consider taking part in naval operations, provided that its own military readiness was not compromised, but added that no decision had been made.
On Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei warned Seoul against succumbing to what he called "U.S. pressure and intimidation."
"Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences," he said in a post on X.
Tehran says it will announce new Strait of Hormuz "exclusion zone"
The new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Tehran plans to announce an "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Mohsen Rezaei's comments to Iran's state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the U.S. struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at U.S. warships.
The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and "will begin from the line of the U.S. naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said without providing more details.
CBS/AP
Price of oil climbs, as regular gas averages nearly a dollar higher than last year's Labor Day
The price of Brent crude, the international standard for oil, added another 67 cents, reaching $96.95 per barrel.
The average price of regular gas was $4.14 a gallon heading into the holiday, nearly a dollar higher than last year and well above the Labor Day weekend record of $3.82 from 2012, according to AAA motor club.
Prices shot up after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February and have not settled down since. Crude oil traffic through the key Strait of Hormuz has plunged, and Iran has refused to reopen the waterway.
Iran threatens "intense" and "painful" response to U.S. strikes on oil tankers
The speaker of Iran's Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, threatened on Sunday to launch swifter and more forceful responses to U.S. attacks, after Tehran targeted American warships in retaliation for U.S. attacks on tankers.
"The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end," said Ghalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that "any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response."
U.S. Central Command said Saturday it had "permanently disabled" three Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours," Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Interior Minister Quintin labels Leipzig drone incident “full-blown Russian attack”

2026-09-07

The foiled drone attack at Leipzig Airport was a full-blown attack rather than a “hybrid threat” says Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR). “We are in a kind of war,” he said, although, according to him, there are no precise indications of a similar attack on Belgium.
Interior Minister Quintin labels Leipzig drone incident “full-blown Russian attack”
“Findings from our services and partners point to Russian involvement in planning and execution of the foiled hybrid operation,” Mr Quintin’s German colleague said earlier last week, following a failed drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig Airport. Among other things, investigators found a drone carrying a powerful explosive. It failed to detonate due to a fault with the detonator.
In response, Germany closed a Russian consulate and a cultural centre. Russia described the allegations as “baseless and absurd”.
In a statement, Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said that there are “no concrete indications” of a similar threat in Belgium.
“That does not alter the fact that we have also had problems here. A few months ago, there were also drones here, but they were not loaded with explosives.”
“Our security services are, in any case, monitoring the situation closely. And they will continue to do so, in close cooperation with the security services of our neighbours.”
“This is not a hybrid threat, but an attack”
According to Quintin, the term “hybrid” threat does not do justice to the situation.
“I hate that word,” he says. “What happened in Leipzig was an attack. Full stop. We are in a kind of war.”
“We face cyberattacks every day. Cables are being cut in the Gulf of Finland, and it is clear that the Russians are behind it. These are attacks. They are waging a war against us.”
“We must have the courage to state the facts. That does not mean we should start a war with Russia ourselves, but our German partners have made it very clear that this was a Russian attack.”
According to Quintin, there is no cause for concern for the time being. “We must, however, be aware that we are living in a new geopolitical reality. That is why we must take measures.”
“First and foremost, we must ensure our security services function effectively, in close consultation with all our allies: our neighbours in Europe, but also the Americans. That way, we will certainly have the intelligence we need to protect ourselves.”
In addition, we must once again invest more in defence, Quintin concludes. “Over the past 10 to 15 years, this has not been done to a sufficient extent. Investment in the armed forces also strengthens our intelligence capabilities. Military intelligence services play a crucial role in gathering information.”

Hackers breached the Bitcoin platform company Liquid Network and stole approximately $320 million worth of bitcoin from its wallet. Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to Liquid Network, approximately 4,000 bitcoins may have been withdrawn from the wallet. The total amount of the stolen funds is estimated at approximately $320 million

It is noted that the funds were withdrawn through SideSwap, a settlement platform authorized to process withdrawals from the network, although the key used in the process was not compromised, Liquid Network added.

Israeli resident charged over ISIS ties, marking fourth in under two weeks

A 19-year-old resident of northern Israel was charged with membership in a terrorist organization on Monday, becoming the fourth person from the region indicted over alleged ties to the Islamic State in less than two weeks.
The concentrated run of cases includes two alleged plots to attack Israeli security forces and a former IDF soldier accused of training to join ISIS abroad.
Yaqoub Shibli, a resident of the northern village of Shibli, was arrested on August 16 in a joint operation by the Shin Bet and the Israel Police Northern District’s central investigative unit.
Investigators allege that Shibli expressed support for ISIS, watched material about the terrorist organization and pledged allegiance to it.
The prosecution filed the indictment at the Nof Hagalil-Nazareth Magistrate’s Court. The indictment follows three others filed against northern residents since August 28.
Various other cases of ISIS-affiliated arrests in Israel
In the first case, Haifa district prosecutors indicted a 16-year-old from the Galilee and Ibrahim Kaabia, 19, of Haifa after authorities alleged that both had pledged allegiance to ISIS and developed separate plans to attack security forces.
According to police and the Shin Bet, the minor searched online for instructions on making an explosive belt and intended to attack police officers and soldiers at the Temple Mount. Kaabia allegedly planned an attack against an IDF base in northern Israel.
Kaabia’s attorney, Suhad Aga-Dahla, denied that he had planned an attack. She said his exposure to ISIS material stemmed from curiosity and described him as a loyal citizen.
Five days later, prosecutors charged Khamis Su’ad, 30, of Huseiniya in the Galilee, with training or receiving instruction for terrorist purposes.
According to that indictment, Su’ad, who served in the IDF from 2017 to 2019, developed a growing identification with ISIS beginning in 2023. Prosecutors allege that he later decided to travel to Syria or Africa to join the organization, saved money for the journey, and viewed training material on combat, weapons, and the production of missiles and drones.
The four cases involve substantially different levels of alleged conduct, ranging from viewing ISIS material and pledging allegiance to preparing for attacks or training to fight abroad.
Police and the Shin Bet said they would continue acting against Israeli citizens seeking to operate on behalf of terrorist organizations.

About 50 firefighters fought the flames. Police sealed off a wide area, and the criminal investigation department is examining whether the fire was a crime or caused by a technical fault.
Hours earlier, on Sunday evening at around 10 pm local time (2000GMT), police mounted a major operation at the Niederrhein substation in Wesel, North Rhine-Westphalia, operated by energy company RWE, the daily Bild reported.
Officers found a hole cut in the security fence, indicating unknown people had entered the grounds. A police helicopter circled the sprawling site as officers searched the complex. Police did not immediately say whether technical infrastructure had been damaged or tampered with.
The two incidents come as authorities hunt a 48-year-old man from North Rhine-Westphalia suspected of a series of attempted sabotage attacks on Germany’s power network since last week. Investigators published a wanted notice with photos on Saturday and asked the public for tips.
A large search at the Hambach Forest west of Cologne was called off Sunday without finding the suspect, public broadcaster WDR reported.
Letters signed with the man’s name and sent to several newsrooms last week claimed responsibility for attempted attacks on power infrastructure near the Jaenschwalde and Schwarze Pumpe brown coal plants in Brandenburg, as well as at sites including Gohr, Bergheim-Rheidt, Dormagen and Weisweiler in North Rhine-Westphalia, ARD reported. India news: Several dead in Delhi building collapse
Published September 7, 2026last updated September 7, 2026
What you need to know

- 
	The building was located in South Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among Delhi University students

Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India on Monday, September 7.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
India's food warning labels challenged in court
Indian health activists have filed the first formal court objection to the government's proposed food warning labels, calling the plan an "industry-friendly loophole" that lets many unhealthy products avoid scrutiny.
The Indian government has proposed that a red hexagonal label be added if a food exceeds limits in at least two of three concerning nutrients: added sugar, salt or saturated fat.
Nonprofit group 3S And Our Health told the Supreme Court the proposal would let high-risk items slip through, as a product high in just one nutrient would not be flagged, the filing, as accessed by Reuters new agency, said.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also drawn criticism over exemptions for foods like honey and jaggery.
Health activists have been pushing for front-of-pack warning labels for years, but it remains unclear how effective they will be in their current form.
"After years of advocacy, and after the Supreme Court pushed the issue, FSSAI has accepted a front-of-pack warning. That fight is won. The next fight is not whether there will be a label, but whether the label will tell the truth," Dr Arun Gupta, paediatrician and Convenor, Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi) told Firstpost.
The Indian government intends to make rules stricter by having warning labels for each concerning nutrient in the second phase of the plan, a source told The Telegraph newspaper.
According to a study published in The Lancet journal, India had 180 million adults who were overweight or obese in 2021. The number is projected to rise to 450 million by 2050.
The case will be heard on September 10.
Drone scare at Amritsar airport prompts flight diversions: reports
Multiple suspected drones were spotted around the operational area of Amritsar's international airport Sunday night, Indian news agency ANI reported, prompting authorities to divert seven flights.
Airport Director Anirudh Kumar said the Air Traffic Control (ATC) unit received information from the Indian Air Force at around 9.45 pm local time regarding suspected drone activity over the airfield. This prompted all flight operations to be suspended for 90 minutes.
"Two of the flights were diverted to Chandigarh and five of them were diverted to Delhi," a Delhi airport official told the Hindustan Times.
Malaysia Airlines, Air India, Air India Express and IndiGo flights were among those diverted, local news agencies reported.
Amritsar's Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport is located about 30 kilometers (~18 miles) from India's border with Pakistan.
Reports suggested that the drones may have been flown locally, but the sensitive nature of the airport’s location prompted swift security action from all agencies involved.
Amritsar police told the Indian Express that the drones were flown during a sports tournament in a nearby village.
"These drones originated from the video recording of a sports tournament. Drones were used for this purpose without permission. It is not allowed to fly drones in 8 kilometres radius of the airport. We will take legal action in this matter," said Raja Sansi Station House Officer Gurpreet Singh.
At least 7 people killed as rescue efforts continue
The death toll has risen to seven after rescue personnel recovered another body amid the rubble of a five-story building in India's capital city Monday, a day after the nearly 50-year-old structure came crashing down.
The building was located in Satya Niketan, a popular student hub that houses hundreds of university students often living in crowded conditions. It is situated in close proximity to Delhi University's South Campus, making it a popular destination for students.
Local media reported that the building housed a private hostel.
In its latest update, Delhi Police said a total of 12 people had been rescued during the operation. Emergency crews say more people may be trapped in the rubble.
Rescue teams, including personnel from disaster agencies as well as fire and police teams, were using heavy machinery and sniffer dogs to locate those trapped.
Earlier, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), which is treating victims of the collapse, said its trauma center received 10 people: "Out of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while one patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to his injuries."
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta addressed the potential cause of the collapse, saying: "It is certain that there was water in the building's basement, and due to accumulation of water, due to ongoing repair work, the old building collapsed."
The police have registered a First Information Report (FIR) under Sections 105, 290 and 125(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (the official criminal code of India) against the building owners, local media reported. The specific sections relate to culpable homicide, negligence in the construction or repair of buildings as well as acts that endanger human life.

Jewish Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton targeted by armed assailant at campaign event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

16:32:48 KST

An armed assailant charged toward the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people before he was stopped by troopers, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said. Acton is Jewish.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol said in a statement that a man it identified as Patrick Havas, 38, forced his way through a crowd, knocking over multiple members of the audience as he moved toward Acton, the state's former public health director. He had a taser and two pistols, the statement said.
The Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after his arrest, and “no weapons were ever brandished or even removed from their holsters.”
Havas was taken to the county jail and booked on charges of disorderly conduct and two counts of assault, the highway patrol statement said, adding that no other details were available pending an investigation. Online court records didn’t yet list the case, and it wasn’t clear as of Sunday night whether Havas has an attorney.
Republican Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement that the man “tried to forcefully push himself” toward Acton as she was speaking at the fair in Canfield, in northeastern Ohio. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable," he added.
The attempted attack is the latest political violence to roil the United States. And the Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most high-profile races this year as the campaigns enter the final six weeks of campaigning before the election in November.
Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton.
Ramaswamy's campaign called the incident Sunday unacceptable.
“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement.
Addie Bullock, communications director for Acton's campaign, said in a statement that the suspect “lunged” at Acton. She said the Democratic candidate “will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”
The incident brought condemnation from Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who said on X that he and his wife were “disturbed by the attempted attack on Amy Acton today at the Canfield Fair. We are grateful for law enforcement’s quick response. There is no place for this kind of behavior, and it must never be tolerated.”
The country has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade. That includes the 2017 shooting at a Republican congressional baseball team practice in Alexandria, Virginia; the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of Democratic then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California; the 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump at a Pennsylvania rally during his presidential campaign as well as another on the president at this year's White House Correspondents' Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations last year of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk in Utah.
Federal political committees spent more than $40 million on expenses labeled as security during the 2023-24 campaign cycle, the most recent one for which data is publicly available, according a report released in April from the Public Service Alliance, a nonpartisan group that focuses on security for public officials.
Before running for governor, Acton was recruited by DeWine in 2019 to lead the Ohio Department of Health while serving as an associate professor of public health at Ohio State University. As the COVID-19 pandemic ramped up in early 2020, she was thrown into the state and national spotlight — becoming a source of comfort to many viewers of the governor’s daily news conferences.
For her service as health director, Acton earned the John F. Kennedy Library Foundation’s Profile in COVID Courage Award, the Columbus Foundation’s Spirit of Columbus Award and Ohio State’s highest alumni honor, the Alumni Medalist Award.
Her position as the face of the DeWine administration’s aggressive stance against the virus also earned Acton many enemies, among them Statehouse Republicans and average Ohioans who opposed pandemic restrictions.

Younger generations mostly richer than their parents: CBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:32:10 UTC
16:32:10 KST

Younger generations mostly richer than their parents: CBS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Younger generations in the Netherlands have generally ended up with more spending power and more wealth than their parents and grandparents did at the same age, according to national statistics office CBS.
Home ownership, however, is an exception. The generation born between 1970 and 1985 is the most likely to own a home at age of life, CBS found. The number of 25- to 35-year-olds still living at home has also risen in recent years amid the housing shortage and rise in house prices.
The youngest adults are behind on wealth, too: up to around the age of 30, millennials and Generation Z hold less than earlier generations did at the same age, as more of them stay in education longer and start earning later.
Over a full lifetime, though, younger generations appear richer. Purchasing power rose almost continuously between 1977 and 2024, so at nearly every age people had more to spend than the generations before them.
At 45, for example, people born between 1970 and 1985 had average purchasing power of €44,100 in 2024 prices – around 40% more than the baby boomers had at the same age.
Wealth has followed the same path, lifted mainly by rising house prices before falling back more recently with a rise in inflation. Millennials had the sharpest rise in their 30s of any generation.
Younger generations also spend a smaller share of their income on housing, CBS said, and are more likely to live in a flat.

Emergency crews recovered nine bodies from the rubble, including those of the two infants, while five people were injured.
Paramedics among those killed
In a separate attack in Kafr Rouman, an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle, killing two paramedics from the Islamic Risala Scout Association who were inside, according to NNA.
Israeli fighter aircrafts also carried out strikes on Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Arabsalim, where a house was destroyed.
NNA reported that the Israeli forces had issued an evacuation warning for a building in Deir al-Zahrani before Israeli fighter aircrafts destroyed it about 22 minutes later.
The reports come amid continued Israeli military offensive in southern Lebanon, where residential areas and civilian infrastructure have repeatedly been affected by strikes.
The latest casualties add to concerns over the impact of renewed violence on civilians in communities across southern Lebanon.

Fake Euronews video invents deadly shooting by Ukrainian soldier at NATO exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:23:42 UTC
16:23:42 KST

A fabricated report has used Euronews' visual likeness to falsely claim a Ukrainian soldier killed three NATO servicemen during a military exercise in Latvia.
A video impersonating Euronews has circulated online with the false allegation that a Ukrainian soldier shot and killed three NATO servicemen during a military exercise in Latvia.
The report claims that a soldier opened fire during NATO's Baltic Trust 2026 exercise, an event that did occur, killing three servicemen before taking his own life.
The shooting did not happen, and the video was not produced or published by Euronews.
The clip, which garnered more than 2 million views, was shared on X on 14 August and uses Euronews' name and visual style to make the invented story appear to come from a legitimate news organisation.
No corresponding report can be found on Euronews' website or its official social media accounts, whilst web searches found no credible news coverage of the alleged deaths.
Lies based on truth
The report incorporates one genuine detail: NATO's Baltic Trust exercise, which took place in the Latvian capital of Riga between 3 and 14 August.
The exercise focused on training and testing technology used to detect and counter unmanned aircraft systems, or drones.
Latvia's National Armed Forces explicitly denied that the alleged shooting had taken place after the fake Euronews report gained traction online.
“Such an incident has not occurred, and the exercises are taking place without incident,” the military said in a statement published on its official X account on 14 August.
“We inform you that this is a coordinated disinformation campaign – such an incident has not occurred, and the exercises are proceeding without incidents,” the statement said, implying the post was connected to a Russian influence operation. It added a hashtag saying "#RussiaAlwaysLies".
It's not the first time Euronews' identity has been connected to Russian-linked disinformation campaigns to spread false narratives, much of it targeting Ukrainians.
During the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics, a series of doctored Euronews videos falsely accused Ukrainian refugees and athletes of criminal or antisocial behaviour.
One video, viewed more than 114,000 times on X, falsely claimed that Ukrainian refugees had robbed a Euronews crew covering the Games.
Another alleged that Ukrainian supporters vandalised cultural sites in Milan following the disqualification of skeleton athlete Vladyslav Heraskevych.
In a separate case, doctored clips shared by a pro-Russian Telegram channel used apparent AI-generated voiceovers based on the voices of real Euronews journalists, with one manipulated report claiming that European pension systems were suffering because of government spending on Ukrainian refugees.
Such disinformation campaigns are designed to discredit Ukraine and undermine support from its allies amid Russia's invasion, as well as sow doubt about the work of legitimate news outlets.

War criminal Mladic’s funeral draws crowds, EU backlash in Belgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Crowds gathered in Belgrade on Monday for the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, as the European Union accused some in Serbia of glorifying a man convicted of genocide and other crimes during the 1990s war in Bosnia.
Mladic died in late August at age 84 while serving a life sentence in The Hague after being convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the Bosnian war.
Mourners began arriving at St. Luka Church in Belgrade at 7:00 a.m. (5:00 a.m. GMT) to pay their respects. Many kissed Mladic’s closed coffin as Serbian Orthodox priests recited prayers.
Police closed several streets around the church as crowds grew throughout the morning.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) reporters saw large crowds gathered outside the church, many wearing shirts praising Mladic. Aerial footage showed hundreds of mourners lining up to enter the church after the doors opened.
Serbian flags were displayed nearby, while a large banner stretched across the street bearing a message praising Mladic as a hero.
The banner read: “Welcome, General, thanks be to your mother for bearing a hero, so that Serbdom’s glory may return.”
The funeral came as Brussels criticized displays honoring Mladic, who remains a deeply divisive figure across the Balkans more than two decades after the end of the Bosnian war.
“I am here to see off the general, a national hero,” pensioner Radojka Visic, who had traveled from Bosnia’s Serb entity, Republika Srpska, told AFP.
“They couldn’t defeat us on the battlefield, so they sent him to prison and tortured him there instead,” Visic said, referring to the “international community.”
Mladic’s casket arrived in Serbia last week aboard a government plane. It was carried by six soldiers and draped in flags.
As it was driven from the airport in a motorcade, groups of young men held banners praising the former general, and some police officers were seen saluting as it passed.
Last week’s scenes drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who canceled a planned visit to Serbia on Friday, saying the “glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.”
Denis Becirovic, chairman of Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, called it “an act of identification by Serbia’s leadership with one of the worst killers in European history.”
“This has unforeseeable consequences for the future of the entire region,” he wrote on Facebook on Friday.
Mladic’s wartime atrocities during the breakup of the former Yugoslavia earned him the nickname “Butcher of Bosnia” in international media.
The 1992-95 war left around 100,000 people dead and displaced 2.2 million.
Mladic was the military figurehead of the Bosnian Serb leadership alongside former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
The United Nations war crimes court convicted him of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which Bosnian Serb forces killed around 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys in a U.N.-protected safe zone.
The atrocity was Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
Fadila Efendic, whose son and husband were killed in Srebrenica, told AFP earlier that it pained her “to know that his ideas are not dead.”
Mladic was also convicted of persecuting and forcibly expelling Bosnian Muslims and Croats, terrorizing civilians during the siege of Sarajevo and taking U.N. peacekeepers hostage during NATO airstrikes in 1995.
Mladic was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite the verdicts, he is still hailed as a hero by some Serbs, particularly in Republika Srpska, where his death was marked with vigils and gatherings.
Many people from the entity applied to travel to Belgrade for the funeral.
Mladic’s son, Darko, who is officially organizing the funeral, said he was “proud of the role” his father played.
On Saturday, around 300 people gathered at a commemoration for Mladic at a military facility in Belgrade, organized by an association of retired and active Serbian army generals.
Darko and other family members attended, as did Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic and officials from Republika Srpska, including President Sinisa Karan.
Speakers at the ceremony praised Mladic’s wartime role, describing him as a “towering figure both as a man and a soldier.”
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said tens of thousands of people were expected to attend the funeral and that the state would ensure the event passed “safely.”
He said he would not attend in person because of a prior engagement.

07:19:16 UTC
16:19:16 KST

The IDF began Operation “Kadmat Homa” (Advancing the Wall) in the sector of the 80th Division, near Eilat and the surrounding areas, the military announced on Monday, exactly a month before the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
The aim of the exercise is to improve the division’s capabilities and readiness in the face of a large-scale October 7-style surprise attack, based on the lessons drawn from the massacre.
All of the division’s forces will participate in the exercise, alongside Israel's air, naval, and additional security forces.
As a result, the military noted a noticeable increase in the movement of security personnel, aircraft, naval vessels, and vehicles in the Eilat area and along Israel's eastern border, but reassured that no security incident is taking place.
Israel Police said it is participating in the security exercise under the name Operation "Southern Wind," led by Israel Police's Southern District under the command of Southern District Police Commander Haim Bublil and District Commander Alon Kalfon.
Police from the Eilat district and the nearby region will be operating alongside security and emergency services.
As part of the exercise, the forces will practice responding to a range of complex extreme scenarios modeled after October 7, including responding to a surprise attack, developing security incidents, multiple simultaneous scenes, controlling traffic routes, maintaining public order, and providing a rapid, coordinated response.
Operation Dawn 2.0
Both Advancing the Wall and Southern Wind come on the tail end of the IDF's announcement of Operation Dawn 2.0 on Sunday.
Under the command of IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, Dawn 2.0 was a surprise exercise meant to test the heat-of-the-moment readiness and abilities of the military to deal with large-scale attacks, as part of the country's preparations to strengthen defense ahead of the holiday period.
As part of the exercise, surprise scenarios and multi-scene events will be practiced in all possible “theaters of war,” the military explained. Commanders from all units of the military were called up, forces mobilized, and the IDF's reserve capabilities are being assessed.

Herzog awards Israeli Presidential Medal of Honor to 11 distinguished figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:18:55 UTC
16:18:55 KST

President Isaac Herzog honored 11 prominent figures from a range of fields with the Israeli Presidential Medal of Honor during a ceremony at the President's Residence on Sunday.
Recognizing their lifelong dedication to the country, the ceremony highlighted the laureates' lasting impact on Israeli society through science, culture, academia, and public service.
The medal, established by president Shimon Peres in 2012, is awarded to those "who, by virtue of their skills, service, or in any other way, have made an exceptional contribution to the State of Israel or to humanity."
It is the highest civilian recognition awarded by the State of Israel and is presented to leading figures in Israel and abroad from the fields of government, culture, and public service.
This year's recipients were Yona Elian-Keshet, Prof. Hossam Haick, Prof. Mooli Lahad, Prof. Hefziba Lifshitz, Prof. Yossi Leshem, Abie Moses, Ziva Mekonen, Moshe Nissim, Rabbi Haim Sabato, Yehuda Eder, and Prof. Uriel Reichman.
President Herzog honors recipients, highlights Israeli unity
“Each and every one of you is a beacon in your field. Each and every one of you is a genuine, personal example of the power to make a difference, not only to the State of Israel and Israeli society, but to a great extent to the wider world as well," the president remarked at the ceremony.
"There are people here who simply changed the world, and there are certainly people here who made a decisive contribution to the good name of the State of Israel around the globe."
The president also addressed the ongoing changes in the country, including calling for unity during the election period.
"It is precisely amid our disagreements, precisely during an election period, that I will say again and warn again: elections are not a civil war! After the elections, we will all still be here, as sisters and brothers,” he said
Who are the 11 recipients of the 2026 Israeli Presidential Medal of Honor?
Five of the recipients were professors from various fields, including Prof. Hossam Haick, an internationally recognized scientist specializing in nanotechnology and biomedicine at the Technion's Wolfson Faculty of Chemical Engineering; Prof. Mooli Lahad, a psychologist and professor at Tel-Hai University who is an internationally recognized expert in resilience, psychotrauma, post-traumatic stress, and emergency intervention.
Prof. Hefziba Lifshitz of Bar-Ilan University's School of Education, a researcher specializing in the learning potential of people with intellectual disabilities; Prof. Yossi Leshem, professor emeritus at Tel Aviv University's School of Zoology, a prominent ornithologist and ecologist who has spent nearly five decades researching bird migration; and Prof. Uriel Reichman, a legal scholar, educational entrepreneur, and founding president and chairman of Reichman University.
In the field of social advocacy, the president honored Ziva Mekonen, a social activist and the founder and CEO of Mothers on Guard, which works against violence and racism targeting Ethiopian Israelis, as well as Abie Moses, who spent more than three decades advocating for victims of terrorism and bereaved families and has long served voluntarily as chairman of the Victims of Terror Organization.
For their work promoting the arts in Israel, Herzog also honored Yehuda Eder, a musician, producer, singer, educator, and cultural entrepreneur who founded the Rimon School of Music and serves as its president, as well as Yona Elian-Keshet, one of Israel's leading stage, film, and television actresses who also serves as chairwoman of the Israeli Union of Performing Arts.
Additionally, the president honored Moshe Nissim, a lawyer and former longtime Knesset member who served in several senior government positions, including justice minister, finance minister, industry and trade minister, and deputy prime minister, as well as Rabbi Haim Sabato, a rabbi, author, and co-founder and head of Yeshivat Birkat Moshe in Ma'ale Adumim.

"It seems they're just a few votes short of an absolute majority, but this is indeed a very worrying sign," Radoslaw Sikorski told Radio Vox FM.
AfD first far-right party at cusp of power since WWII
The AfD party surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, exit polls showed, putting a far-right party on the cusp of power at state level for the first time since World War Two.
While short of an overall majority, the AfD won 44% of the vote and delivered a drubbing to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives, reflecting the deep unpopularity of Germany's ruling coalition in a fracturing political landscape.
The AfD is already Germany's most popular party at the national level and is seeking to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.
"We have made history in this country," said Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, who attracted thousands to his campaign rallies and who repeatedly cast victory in the state as a first step towards securing national power in federal elections due in 2029.
"The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with us," Siegmund said.

Flights cancelled leaving Australians stranded as volcanic ash closes Indonesian airports
In short:
The eruption of Indonesian volcano Mount Anak Krakatau has seen flights in and out of Jakarta cancelled.
An Australian trapped in the region has told the ABC about the ash falling from the sky and "scratchy eyes".
What's next?
Qantas says services will resume when conditions allow, but Indonesian authorities have warned further eruptions are highly likely.
Liz Kendall has spent three days in a basic Jakarta hotel, watching ash fall from the sky and waiting to learn when she will be able to return home to Australia.
Ms Kendall, who lives in Mount Eliza in Victoria, was due to return to Australia on Saturday evening after a three-week sailing trip.
But her Qantas flight was cancelled after the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau sent volcanic ash across parts of Indonesia on Friday.
"We got the notification that they weren't going to be coming on Saturday, and here we sit," Ms Kendall said.
She said ash has been falling over the city.
"I have a burning throat and scratchy eyes,"
Indonesia's main international airport, Soekarno Hatta International, and seven others in the country remain closed.
Indonesia's transport ministry said about 170,000 passengers had been affected by flight cancellations.
"We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in a statement.
Qantas has cancelled its services to Jakarta from Melbourne and Sydney due to the volcanic ash.
A spokeswoman said meteorologists and operations teams were "closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta" and safety remained its "highest priority".
Ms Kendall said Qantas initially kept her informed by text message, but the updates had since stopped.
"I'm a little upset with Qantas because now they've stopped all communication,"
"I was on hold for a couple of hours, and they just said they'll be back in touch when flights resume, which might take a while."
A Qantas spokeswoman said multiple emails and text messages had been sent to Ms Kendall since her flight was disrupted.
'Not getting great updates'
Ms Kendall is staying in a Jakarta hotel costing about $47 a night.
"We are getting a bit discouraged that we're stuck here,"
"We're struggling with the language and not getting great updates."
Ms Kendall said some members of her group were considering travelling by train to another airport before attempting to fly through Bali, but she has decided to remain in Jakarta.
"If the wind shifts, that's not going to work either," she said.
Indonesia's volcano-monitoring agency said the most recent eruption occurred on Sunday evening and warned that further eruptions remained highly likely.
Ash has reached up to 20,000 feet on the Java side of the volcano and as high as 50,000 feet over Sumatra, according to Indonesian authorities.
Australian flights affected
Qantas operates direct services between Jakarta and Sydney and Melbourne.
The airline said flights QF39, QF40, QF41 and QF42 had been affected by the eruption.
Passengers who booked eligible Jakarta flights on or before September 5 for travel between September 5 and 11 will be offered fee-free refunds, travel credits or date changes.
Qantas said passengers should monitor its flight-status service or app for operational updates.
Singapore Airlines has also cancelled multiple services between Singapore and Jakarta.
Virgin Australia does not operate flights to Jakarta, while Virgin and Jetstar services to Bali have not been affected.
Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) has updated its advice for Indonesia, warning airports in affected areas may close at short notice.
Australians have been advised to monitor their flight status and check directly with their airline or travel provider before heading to the airport.
DFAT has also warned that volcanic ash may affect air quality and advised people with asthma or other respiratory conditions to take extra care.
For Ms Kendall, the wait could also carry a substantial personal cost.
She has a $2,500 ticket to Friday's NFL game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground but fears she will not be home in time to attend.
"I doubt it," she said.
"I would have to leave here by Wednesday."
Ms Kendall said she understood why Qantas could not operate in unsafe conditions, but wanted the airline to do one thing.
"Just keep me updated,"
"The first couple of days were maybe OK, and now it's three days. I might be here a while."

Members of the European Parliament call for EU law to protect workers from stress and mental health risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:15:44 UTC
16:15:44 KST

More than 840,000 people die each year from health conditions linked to psychosocial risks at work, according to the International Labour Organisation, as MEPs call for new EU legislation to better protect workers’ mental and physical health. The European Parliament’s Employment and Social Affairs Committee says work-related psychosocial risks can lead to occupational diseases and wants stronger measures to address stress, violence, harassment, bullying and discriminatory behaviour in the workplace.
The Committee on Employment and Social Affairs calls on the Commission to draft a law to protect workers from work-related psychosocial risks and stress at work.
MEPs have agreed on a series of recommendations for a new EU bill to ensure minimum requirements to prevent, eliminate or reduce work-related psychosocial risks which could lead to work-related stress, burnout, and mental and physical disorders. This proposal should be preceded by an impact assessment including an assessment of existing legislation.
MEPs are demanding binding obligations for employers to protect mental and physical health and to ensure safe and dignified working conditions. They also want the Commission and EU-countries to explicitly recognise that work-related psychosocial risks give rise to occupational diseases.
The request for a legislative initiative was adopted by 41 votes in favour and 12 votes against, with 4 abstentions.
Policies addressing violence and harassment
MEPs want employers to adopt and implement policies defining and prohibiting violence, harassment, bullying and discriminatory behaviour undermining workers’ dignity, physical or mental health, as well as early detection mechanisms and risk-based prevention protocols for third-party violence. They also say timely support is needed for workers exposed to psychosocial risks.
Psychosocial risk assessment and action plan
MEPs recommend employers carry out regular psychosocial risk assessments to evaluate factors such as excessive workload and high work intensity and adopt action plans with concrete measures. Significant restructuring or reorganisation, such as teleworking arrangements or the introduction of automated decision-making and automated monitoring systems, should be subject to a prior psychosocial risk assessment in cooperation with workers and their representatives, they say.
Employers should also ensure that the introduction of algorithmic systems does not impose excessive burden or monitoring of workers, and that human oversight is always ensured. MEPs also reiterate that workers have the right to disconnect from work.
Support for returning to work
Workers who have been absent from work due to work-related psychosocial risks should have the right to a supported and sustainable return to work, MEPs say. To that end, they recommend employers establish individual return-to-work plans, specifying factors such as adjustments to working time or work organisation and adaptations of a worker’s tasks or workload.
Injury or damage presumed to be work-related
Employers should ensure that, where a worker establishes that they have suffered injury or damage to health due to exposure to work-related psychosocial risk factors, it is presumed that the injury or damage is work-related, unless the employer demonstrates that it is not linked to the worker’s working conditions.
Quote
Rapporteur Estelle Ceulemans (S&D, BE) said: “This report represents a step forward, as it asks the European Commission for a legislative proposal to tackle burnout, depression, stress, and harassment. The prevalence of these issues is skyrocketing across Europe and are exacerbated by the increasing use of digital technologies and AI in the workplace. Addressing these structural work-related problems is not only an occupational health obligation but also an economic issue, costing €100 billion annually for work-related depression in the EU.”
Next steps
Parliament is expected to vote on this legislative initiative during its October I 2026 plenary session. The Commission will then have three months to reply, by either informing Parliament on the steps it plans to take or by giving reasons for any refusal to propose a legislative initiative along the lines of Parliament’s request.
Source: europarl.europa.eu

Far-Right German Party Ahead of Rivals in State Election, But Misses Majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD) is poised to finish ahead of rivals in a state election, coming closer than any other far-right party in the country to governing at a regional level since World War II.
The party won 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election on Sunday, according to provisional results. By comparison, center-right CDU, the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, won less than 20%. The state of 2.1 million people saw a record voter turnout of 77%.
But the party faces an uncertain path towards power. Without an absolute majority, it would need a coalition partner or support from lawmakers outside the party to form a government—something that German mainstream parties have thus far refused to provide.
Nevertheless, the surge in support for the AfD, which ran on a platform of restricting immigration, ending aid to Ukraine, and taking Germany out of the euro, is remarkable in a country where the legacy of Nazism has long kept the far right at the political margins. The party’s Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified by the state’s domestic intelligence as “right-wing extremist,” a designation that its leaders reject.
“We have made history in this country,” Ulrich Siegmund, AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said after polls closed.
“We’re taking our country back, it starts in Saxony-Anhalt,” he added. “A jolt is going through all of Germany.”
The result has already drawn global reactions.
U.S. President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the projected results without comment on Truth Social. Members of Trump’s Administration, including Vice President J.D. Vance, previously expressed public support for the party.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk, who spoke at AfD’s campaign launch last year, congratulated AfD co-leader Alice Weidel on the projected win. In response, Siegmund thanked him “for your support” and said he would “welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation.”
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted a screenshot of Trump’s post. He said in the caption,“Historic win for the pragmatic AfD that will put migration under control. The ruling Bidenthink coalition eviscerated,” referring to former U.S. President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The AfD is friendly to the Kremlin and has advocated for Germany to end support for Ukraine.
Invoking the collapse of the communist regime in East Germany and the fall of the Berlin Wall, Herbert Kickl, leader of the right-wing Freedom Party of Austria (FPO) said, “As of today, the strong wind of freedom from 1989 is blowing through Germany once again.”
Other European leaders expressed alarm over the result.
France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, said the win was a “grave moment in Europe.”
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said more bluntly, “In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany.”
What to know about Siegmund and the AfD
The AfD’s platform in Saxony-Anhalt ranges from tighter immigration controls to a sweeping overhaul of the state’s education system. Among its more controversial proposals is a policy of “remigration,” which is widely interpreted as mass deportation, although the party says it will prioritize deporting people with a criminal record. It has also called for segregating children of refugees and asylum-seekers in schools, and ending war refugee status for Ukrainians fleeing the war with Russia.
The party would largely be unable to enact many of its immigration policies in any individual state even if it can form a government, since many of its proposals would require federal action. But it could tighten policing and pursue changes to schools and cultural policy at the state level.
The party wants to steer schools and cultural institutions towards more traditional and nationalist values. It has also advocated revising history curricula to shift emphasis away from the Third Reich and for schools to ban rainbow flags. Instead, it wants schools to fly the German national flag daily, sing the national anthem at school celebrations, and teach more Russian language.
The AfD has also attacked Bauhaus, calling the influential school and design movement an “aberration of modernism.” Critics, including Germany’s culture minister, have said the AfD’s rhetoric echoes that of the Nazis, who forced the Bauhaus school to close in 1933.
Other proposals include establishing citizen patrols and imposing a moratorium on new wind farms.
The AfD capitalized on disillusionment with the political establishment and drew on regional and national pride, including “Ostalgie” or nostalgia for aspects of life in the former communist East Germany. That message found fertile ground in eastern strongholds, like Saxony-Anhalt, where economic disparities with western Germany persist decades after reunification. During the campaign, Siegmund frequently rode a blue Simson, a moped manufactured in the former East Germany, a move that drew criticism from the descendants of the Jewish family that founded Simson.
The Halle Institute for Economic Research in Germany has warned that the AfD’s anti-immigration policies could deepen Saxony-Anhalt’s labor shortage and cost the state billions in economic output. Merz has also argued that an AfD victory could turn away foreign investment from the state.
Founded in 2013, support for the AfD has grown significantly in recent years.
The AfD doubled its national vote share in 2025, and is the country’s most popular party nationally, polling at 28%, according to a recent INSA poll. At the same time, support for the federal government led by Merz, which is struggling to revive a sluggish economy, has fallen to historic lows. In the same INSA poll, Merz’s conservative party had 20% support. In Saxony-Anhalt, 87% of voters were dissatisfied with the federal government, according to an ARD poll.
Siegmund has said he wants to become state premier and eventually bring the AfD to victory in the 2029 national elections.
What the results mean for the AfD
While the election delivered the AfD a commanding victory, the party still lacks enough votes to govern alone. With 39 seats in the 83-member legislature, the party remains three short of an outright majority, and faces no obvious path to obtaining it.
Germany’s established parties have refused to work with the AfD, continuing their “firewall” against cooperating with the far-right. State premier Sven Schulze acknowledged defeat but his party, the CDU, said it would explore talks with other parties about forming a multiparty coalition.
The AfD could find unlikely support in the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, or BSW, which scraped into parliament with 5.3% of the vote. BSW has rejected the firewall and expressed a willingness to speak with the AfD, although it said it would not elect either Siegmund or Schulze as premier.
Siegmund has thus far ruled out leading a minority government or adopting an informal arrangement that would leave his government depending on unsteady support. “If necessary there’ll just be new elections, then we’d just get 50 or 55%,” he told ZDF on election night. He said, however, that he would be willing to work with individual lawmakers or parliamentary groups.
Thousands joined an anti-AfD demonstration on Saturday in the regional capital of Magdeburg. Some carried banners that read, “life is better without Nazis.” One protester, Laura Saalfeld, told AFP, “Whatever the results, the atmosphere will change. Far-right sympathisers will show themselves more openly on the streets.”

“The haze situation in Sarawak has not yet fully recovered, and the air pollution index (API) reading in several areas ... particularly Serian and Samarahan districts, is still at very unhealthy levels,” it said in a statement.
The federal government and the Sarawak state government will continue to closely monitor the situation, and residents in affected areas are advised to limit outdoor activities and to always comply with instructions from the authorities,” it said.
API figures in Serian passed the critical threshold of 500 on Friday, peaking at 519 with the town cloaked in a thick cloud of smoke.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API levels above 300 are classified as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.

A man accused of sexually abusing 361 children through social media platforms, including Snapchat, is due to go on trial in Finland on Monday, in one of the country’s largest child sexual abuse cases.
The man faces multiple charges over alleged offences committed against children aged 9 to 15 between 2019 and 2022, according to Finland’s National Prosecution Authority.
The public portion of the proceedings will begin at the Pirkanmaa District Court on Monday before the trial moves behind closed doors on Tuesday.
Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported that the alleged victims were boys from across Finland.
Police found thousands of images and videos
The investigation began after police discovered thousands of images and videos of unidentified children on the suspect’s mobile phone in 2022 while searching it in connection with another criminal case.
Police said the suspect allegedly contacted children through Snapchat and pressured them to send intimate images or videos and to carry out sexual acts.
He faces charges including aggravated sexual abuse of children, sexual abuse of children and aggravated distribution of an image depicting children in a sexual manner, according to the prosecutor.
The defendant partially admitted to the alleged offenses during the police investigation.
In December 2025, Finnish police said they were investigating a 27-year-old man in connection with 364 suspected sexual offenses against children.
Prosecutors subsequently decided not to pursue charges in three of those cases, leaving 361 charges before the court.
Trial expected to last through year-end
The scale of the case is reflected in the court schedule, with around 45 hearing days set aside for the proceedings.
The court expects the trial to continue for “at least until the end of this year.”
The case highlights the challenges authorities face in investigating online sexual exploitation, particularly when alleged offenders use social media platforms to target children across different parts of a country.

====================================================================================================

WMO warns wildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:08:00 UTC
16:08:00 KST

Wildfires and heatwaves are threatening to undermine global efforts to improve air quality, protect human health and safeguard ecosystems by producing microscopic pollutants that can remain suspended in the air, the World Meteorological Organization said Monday.
The United Nations weather and climate agency highlighted the close links between air pollution and climate change, which scientists say is contributing to more frequent and intense heatwaves and wildfires.
“Extreme wildfires are increasing, leading to big health consequences because of the high toxicity of smoke,” the WMO said in a statement accompanying its latest annual Air Quality and Climate Bulletin.
The agency said regulations in Europe and North America have helped reduce industrial and transportation emissions of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. However, exposure to PM2.5 from wildfires has increased, offsetting some of those gains.
PM2.5 consists of microscopic particles and droplets measuring less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter. Because the particles are so small, they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, posing a serious risk to human health.
PM2.5 is emitted by fossil fuel-driven industrial activities, farming, domestic heating and transportation, as well as by wildfires and dust storms.
The report said the world needs to better monitor air pollutants such as aerosols, including black carbon and microplastics, fine particles and ground-level ozone.
These pollutants “are not sufficiently monitored even though they are widespread and are potentially harmful to ecosystems,” the WMO said.
“(We need) complementary and coordinated policies on air quality and climate because they cannot be dealt with in isolation.”
“Air quality and climate change can’t be dealt with separately. If one worsens, the other does too,” Lorenzo Labrador, of the WMO’s Global Atmosphere Watch network of scientists, told AFP.
“In places where there are relatively powerful forest fires, we find a lot of fine particle pollution,” he said.
Microparticles generated by burning vegetation are “much more toxic” than those emitted by other sources, including car exhaust, he said.
They can harm the health of people and wildlife living far from the fire because they are carried by the wind, but their poisonous effects are not sufficiently taken into account in air quality assessments, Labrador said.
“Conventional risk models based on total PM2.5 concentrations may underestimate wildfire-attributable mortality by up to 93 percent,” the WMO said.
One study cited in the WMO bulletin said extreme fire-smoke events have tripled globally since the 1990s, contributing to nearly 100,000 additional deaths per year between 2010 and 2018, although that figure may be an underestimate.
Another source of air pollution that carries major health risks is ground-level ozone, which accumulates when temperatures rise, atmospheric conditions stagnate and solar radiation is intense, as seen during recent heatwaves in China, Europe and the southeastern United States.
“This increased exposure to ozone pollution has the potential to lead to tens of thousands of additional premature deaths,” particularly due to respiratory diseases, the WMO warned.
Another growing concern is aerosol particles, which can travel to oceans and continents far from their source.
They can alter the way the atmosphere reflects sunlight, change the chemical properties of land and water, and pollute otherwise clean environments.
“One example is the deposition of black carbon, or soot, on snow and ice, which reduces the amount of sunlight reflected by these surfaces and in turn can hasten the melting process,” the WMO explained.
Another example is microplastics, which form when plastics break down because of sunlight or other factors and are found virtually everywhere, including in the air, soil and oceans.
One simulation in the WMO bulletin estimates there are “51 million tonnes for land and 22 million tonnes for the ocean, which are in turn a source of microplastics for the atmosphere.”
“As plastic production and, critically, mismanaged plastic waste, continues to increase,” monitoring the airborne paths that carry microplastics from their source and deposit them in remote environments will be “crucial,” the report said.

Estonia's elderly more likely to use antidepressants than therapy for depression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

Estonia's elderly more likely to use antidepressants than therapy for depression
A new study has found that, depending on the age group, patients with mental health concerns are two to three times more likely to receive medication than therapy.
Professional mental health care largely comes down to prescribing medication, particularly for older people, according to a survey commissioned by the Estonian-Swedish Mental Health and Suicidology Institute and conducted by Norstat. Experts say this may be because medication is cheaper and more readily available.
As part of the "Depression-Free Tallinn" project, researchers surveyed 1,000 adults in Tallinn's Lasnamäe, Õismäe and Mustamäe districts about their attitudes and experiences. Rainer Mere, who is leading the research project, said one thing that immediately stood out in the results was the continued prevalence of prejudice, stigma and confusion about navigating mental health care.
"When we asked people whether they were willing to receive treatment and what kind of treatment they had received if they had sought help somewhere, it also emerged, particularly among older people, that their treatment tends to focus solely on medication and that they very rarely receive therapy," Mere said. "This is in contrast, for example, to younger people, who receive both medication and therapy."
Mere noted, for example, that people over the age of 60 use medication to treat depression three times as often as they receive psychotherapy.
"What we can infer from the figures is that older people are willing to receive help. In other words, they are not opposed to therapy, for example. When we looked at the figures, they would be willing to receive it, but perhaps it is simply not offered to them, they do not know to ask for it themselves or their doctor does not know to offer it to them," Mere said. "For some reason, they really are not getting into therapy."
Margus Tõnissaar, president of the Estonian Association of Psychologists, said the survey results were to be expected because while medication is inexpensive and more readily available, access to mental health services in Estonia is currently very difficult. The association is also concerned that the quality of services varies considerably.
"We want ordinary people to understand who is actually a psychologist and who is not," Tõnissaar said. "In our view, many of those who call themselves psychologists should not be doing so. From the standpoint of service quality, it is very important that in professions or services where a professional qualification is required, the person providing the service actually has that qualification. If they do not, they should not call themselves a clinical psychologist, counselor or sports psychologist."
He added that the landscape is currently very confusing for clients.
"I very much agree with what the researchers wrote: Mental health issues cannot be addressed through medication and therapy or counseling alone. It is a much more complex issue," Tõnissaar said. "It is also about how the community supports a person, how their family supports them and how we develop or foster the skills, including social skills, that can support people."
Mari Ader-Nobels, a mental health adviser at the Ministry of Social Affairs, said the government's goal is to improve access to psychological care so that people have a wider range of treatment options.
"In recent years, we have expanded opportunities for clinical psychologists to provide services while also working to ensure that there are enough of these specialists," Ader-Nobels said. "At family medicine centers, for example, mental health support can be provided not only by family doctors but also by mental health nurses and clinical psychologists and since last year also by counseling psychologists whose services are funded by the Estonian Health Insurance Fund. To increase the number of specialists, the Ministry of Social Affairs is also continuing to support the professional qualification year for clinical psychologists and counseling psychologists."
