Iran says to announce new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:06:55 UTC
16:06:55 KST

Iran says to announce new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days
DUBAI, Sept 7 - Iran said it will announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, as a weekend exchange of strikes on shipping sent oil prices higher on Monday.
The new restricted zone will begin from where the U.S. blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday in an interview with state TV.
Few details were provided on the plan, but Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone would be added to a sanctions list.
In addition, maps detailing passage routes for the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit largely closed to tanker traffic, would also be approved soon, Rezaei said.
"The maps of a new international corridor which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and in which Iran will have management have been agreed and should be signed in the coming days," he said.
"We will only commit to the Strait of Hormuz being open when they (the Americans) stop the sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran," Rezaei added.
Six months after U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran sparked the war, the conflict appears to be at a stalemate. A preliminary ceasefire accord reached in June has unravelled, and little progress has been made in diplomatic efforts to get the peace process back on track.
After a pause in military action for much of August, tit-for-tat strikes have resumed. U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, U.S. Central Command said, including one off Kharg Island, Iran's key oil export hub, following attacks by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on U.S. warships in the region.
Tehran has shown it retains the capability to attack U.S. interests in neighbouring countries and to shut down oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil supplies flowed prior to the conflict.
An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait per day in the past 10 days, the lowest since May, according to shipping data on Monday. That helped oil prices extend last week's big gains, with Brent crude up 0.8% above $97 a barrel.
SANCTIONS, OIL BLOCKADE SQUEEZE ECONOMY
Iran has said it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by U.S. sanctions that are crippling its economy.
However, the U.S. campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources have said.
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday that the U.S. should understand that the rules of the game have changed "before it is too late".
"From now on, any attack against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel.
Qalibaf said that alongside the military front, Iran’s main battle was now over production and people’s livelihoods.
He cited sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, adding Iranians could tolerate hardship but not mismanagement or inaction and expected the government to act quickly.
Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran planned to respond to U.S. economic pressure with reforms and rejected the notion that sanctions would cause it to change course, according to state media on Sunday.
“They speak of economic pressure and isolation, of breaking off financial ties and they think that by pressuring the economy of a country they can change the decisions of its people,” Madanizadeh said.
“I have to clarify one point: The responsibility of reforming Iran’s economy is with its government and people, not with the U.S. Treasury."
KHARG ISLAND HIT 550 TIMES IN PRIOR MONTHS, IRAN SAYS
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90% of its crude via its Kharg Island export hub before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
U.S. Central Command said on X that as of Sunday it had redirected 92 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two to ensure strict compliance with its blockade.
On August 31, U.S. President Donald Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being "blown to smithereens." Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
In an interview aired on state TV on Sunday, Iran's Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad said the island had been hit around 550 times in previous months but continued to operate.
Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up fuel prices, weighing on Trump's popularity as his Republican Party heads into elections in November when control of Congress is at stake.
However, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said oil was getting through the waterway.
"Our transits through the Strait are averaging over 9 million barrels a day now, and with the access pipelines that go around the strait, we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows. So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning that battle," he told CNN. REUTERS

Speaking in an interview reviewing the Oil Ministry’s performance over the past two years, Paknejad said the ministry continued development projects while managing the country’s strategic reserves, production imbalances, and challenges in the South Pars gas field.

Building collapses are frequent in parts of India during the rainy season from June to September. A similar incident occurred on Saturday after a three-storey building collapsed in northern India following heavy rain. No casualties were reported.

US envoy warns against developing conventions centre on Jewish cemetery site in Vilnius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

Any attempt to further desecrate the site of an old Jewish cemetery near Vilnius’ Concert and Sports Palace would face resistance, US Special Envoy for Monitoring and Combating Antisemitism Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun said.
“Any attempt to further desecrate this cemetery is shameful for the government of Lithuania and will be met with opposition,” Kaploun said in a letter to Culture Minister Lukas Alsys that he posted Friday on X.
“Any resolution which would recommend developing a conference center on the cemetery site would send a clear signal to Jews around the world that not only can cemeteries be desecrated but that the rich, 600-year history of the Jews in this country before the Nazi regime is… pic.twitter.com/0x1yHHBoR6
— Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun (@StateSEAS) September 4, 2026
The US official criticised Alsys’ statements about the future of the site of the former Šnipiškės Jewish cemetery and urged opposition to a proposal to develop a convention centre there.
Kaploun said a plan to develop a convention centre at the site would send a message to the global Jewish community that, in Lithuania, cemeteries can be desecrated.
“Claiming that the site’s fate remains ‘open’ […] risks legitimizing the ongoing and shameful attempts by members of the Seimas to further desecrate it,” he wrote.
The building, finished in 1971, stands on the site of the historic Šnipiškės Jewish cemetery. Jewish religious law places strict restrictions on disturbing Jewish graves.
The Sports Palace also holds symbolic significance in Lithuania’s modern history. In October 1988, it hosted the founding congress of the Lithuanian Reform Movement, Sąjūdis. It also lay in state several of those killed during the events of January 13, 1991, when Soviet forces attempted to suppress the country’s independence movement.
Alsys told BNS in an interview that discussions over the future of the Concert and Sports Palace are among the most contentious issues in Lithuania.
“On the one hand, we have a building that is strongly associated with the Sąjūdis movement, with the origins of independent Lithuania, with Lithuanian identity, with modern Lithuania and with the beginning of our statehood,” Alsys said. “On the other hand, we have the old Jewish cemetery next to it, which, according to Jewish traditions and customs, is subject to strict rules governing what can and cannot be done there. That also needs to be respected and addressed.”
Alsys said he hoped the two positions could be reconciled.
In May, the Seimas, Lithuania’s parliament, began considering a resolution proposing that the government adapt the Concert and Sports Palace into a congress centre while also commemorating the former Jewish cemetery and the Sąjūdis movement’s role in Lithuania’s independence struggle.
Part of Lithuania’s Jewish community opposes the convention centre proposal and would prefer to transform the building into a memorial to Lithuanian Jewish history.
Rabbi Sholom Krinsky, a representative of the Chabad-Lubavitch Jewish organisation in Lithuania, previously said a memorial at the site would also be unacceptable because the cemetery remains there. He called instead for the cemetery to be left undisturbed and enclosed by a wall.
Kaploun said in his letter that he had previously expressed his position to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius.
“Cemeteries are a sacred ground for all mankind. No self-respecting government, institution, or even community organization with claims to represent the needs of Jewish citizens can allow for their desecratetion,” he wrote.
Sinkevičius has said the building could become a place where Jewish and Lithuanian memory could coexist.
Under a previously approved plan, the renovated building would include conference facilities, a library, a cultural and information centre, exhibitions on the Sąjūdis movement, and a memorial and educational space dedicated to Jewish history.

Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:03:44 BST
16:03:44 KST

Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes
- Published
Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures.
Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses.
The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours.
Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop.
This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat.
There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war.
But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day.
In the seven days from Thursday 27 August, Kyiv endured 76 air raid alerts. The largest comparable number in 2022 was the week beginning 27 February when there were around 66 alerts.
Absolute comparisons are not possible because data gathered in the first few days of the invasion was sometimes incomplete. But the trend shown by the numbers is clear.
From the BBC's office, we hear the near constant rumble of air defences and drone explosions.
The more frequent Russian strikes are exacerbated by a second development, the use of newer and faster attack drones powered by jet engines. Some of these fly almost 370 mph (595 km/h), three times as fast the older Shahed drones driven by propellers, and are harder to shoot down. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched 2,800 fast drones in August, almost twice as many as in July.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones.
"You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said.
Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences.
Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones.
But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat.
"The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said.
"The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important."
Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses.
The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day.
When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts.
Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day."
Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally."
After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack.
Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation."
The constant air raids are a huge problem for businesses, many of which have to shut their doors every time a siren wails. We saw crowds of shop workers from Kyiv's biggest department store hanging around the streets during an alert, forced to leave their work place but not fearful enough to seek shelter.
There is also disruption to public transport. Some metro trains have to stop during an alert because they travel overground across the Dnipro river that bisects the city. This causes chaos for commuters who are forced to get on replacement buses.
To minimise this disruption, the government has agreed a new air-raid warning system with two different threat levels. A yellow warning to indicate a drone attack with less threat and fewer restrictions on work and travel. A red warning to indicate a more dangerous missile attack with more severe constraints on activity.
As ever, Ukraine is adapting to a yet another new threat. But the fear is that Russia's constant attacks now may leave the country and its capital less prepared for what many expect to be a tough winter as Russia shifts its attack back to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

De Lijn Ticket inspector injured after attack by passengers without valid tickets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:03:24 UTC
16:03:24 KST

Trade unions are calling on ticket inspectors at Flemish local transport company De Lijn not to carry out any ticket checks in the Antwerp region today. The action follows a serious attack on a ticket inspector at Berchem station in Antwerp on Saturday evening. This morning, the trade unions are meeting with De Lijn’s management for an emergency meeting.
Passengers without valid tickets attack and injure De Lijn Ticket inspector
The inspector was attacked on Saturday evening, after he had removed several passengers without valid tickets from a bus. According to the trade unions, the men then became aggressive and attacked the victim and his colleagues.
“Our colleague was severely beaten by the attackers,” says trade union representative Jo Van der Herten of the Christian ACV union. “It will take some time before he has fully recovered. But above all, we must not underestimate the psychological impact of such an attack.”
Showing solidarity
According to Van der Herten, the call to temporarily suspend checks today is, first and foremost, an act of solidarity with the affected colleagues. The action is focused primarily on the city of Antwerp.
“Our staff are on duty to support driving staff, but no checks will be carried out,” adds Van der Herten.
At 10 o’clock, the trade unions are holding an emergency meeting with De Lijn’s management. “We want the employer to do more to guarantee the safety of ticket inspectors. De Lijn expects us to raise 30 million euros through ticket inspections.”
“Firstly, that is not a realistic figure, but the pressure on staff is also too great. We are having to carry out these checks with ever-smaller teams. We expect De Lijn to prioritise safety first and the figures second.”
Bodycams on the way?
According to the ACV union, a team of four ticket inspectors is the absolute minimum for a ticket inspection on a bus. Even more staff would be needed on a tram. “The larger the vehicle, the larger the team needs to be.”
In addition, the trade unions are calling for the promised roll-out of bodycams to be implemented as soon as possible. “We are still waiting for a legislative framework. Bodycams will not, of course, solve all problems, but they can act as a deterrent and may be important for the burden of proof afterwards.”
Flemish Mobility Minister Annick De Ridder (Flemish nationalist N-VA) has announced that she is responding to the call for bodycams. She hopes that final federal approval for their use by inspectors and drivers will be granted before the end of this year, so that the roll-out can begin early next year.
In addition, the minister promised that by the end of 2027, all De Lijn buses must be fitted with CCTV. Today, this is already the case for 87 per cent of the buses managed directly by De Lijn and for 96 per cent of buses operated by other operators.

US Peace Push Gains Momentum, But 3 Ex-Ambassadors See Little Change in Putin’s Position
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:02:36 UTC
16:02:36 KST

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled from Moscow to Kyiv over the weekend for talks with Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky, but three former US ambassadors to Ukraine said the meetings have yet to show that Moscow is ready to shift its position.
On Monday, according to Radio Liberty, US ex-ambassadors to Ukraine said that despite the renewed diplomatic activity, there is still little evidence that Moscow is ready to make a settlement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Witkoff and Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv to meet President Volodymyr Zelensky. Witkoff described the discussions as constructive and said the US had heard “new ideas” from Moscow, while Kushner referred to a broader “peace package.”
Zelensky called his talks with the US envoys “very substantial” and said Ukraine was ready to move toward trilateral negotiations involving Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow. National security advisers from Britain, France, and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
The former ambassadors welcomed the renewed diplomatic effort but cautioned that increased activity should not be mistaken for actual progress.
William Taylor, who served twice as US ambassador to Ukraine, said the central obstacle remains Moscow rather than Kyiv or Washington. He said he had seen nothing to indicate that Putin had abandoned his maximalist demands.
Kyiv Builds Food and Water Reserves Ahead of Winter Amid Risk of Blackouts
John Herbst, a former US ambassador under President George W. Bush, called the current effort one of the most substantial US diplomatic initiatives in months, but said it remains unclear whether there is anything genuinely new behind it.
Geoffrey Pyatt, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine from 2013-16, likewise welcomed the renewed engagement while saying the fundamental issue is whether Russia is prepared to de-escalate.
What are Russia’s “new ideas”?
Witkoff’s claim that Moscow presented “new ideas” is one of the most closely watched elements of the weekend’s diplomacy. Neither he nor Kushner has publicly explained what those ideas involve.
For Taylor, the key test would be concrete military steps by Russia, including a cease-fire along the current front line, an end to long-range strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure, and arrangements covering shipping.
Without such measures, the language of new proposals could simply amount to a repackaging of Moscow’s existing demands.
The former ambassadors also stressed that previous suggestions of Russian willingness to compromise have often failed to produce concrete results, making the details of the latest talks particularly important.
A senior US administration official told Radio Liberty that Washington remains optimistic about another round of negotiations involving Russia and Ukraine.
The administration will assess the envoys’ meetings before deciding on the next steps, while the coming weeks could be used to develop a more detailed roadmap. The UN General Assembly could also provide an opportunity to continue the discussions.
Territory and security guarantees
Any potential peace deal would have to address two major unresolved issues: territory and Ukraine’s future security.
Russia continues to demand Ukrainian territorial concessions which Kyiv rejects, while Ukraine maintains that Russian-occupied territories remain sovereign Ukrainian land.
Taylor suggested that one possible approach could be to acknowledge Russia’s de facto control of roughly 19% of Ukraine without legally recognizing Russian sovereignty over those territories. Such an arrangement would effectively freeze the territorial dispute rather than resolve it.
However, Taylor said there is no indication that Putin is prepared to accept such a framework.
Herbst argued that Russia’s objectives go beyond territory, saying the Kremlin also seeks significant influence over Ukraine’s political direction – ambitions that would conflict with a settlement based on Ukrainian sovereignty and independence.
The two sides would also need to agree on security guarantees. Taylor said a credible arrangement could include European troops in Ukraine, supported by the US with air power, intelligence, and other capabilities. He also pointed to Ukraine’s eventual EU membership and, potentially, NATO membership as longer-term elements of its security.
For Kyiv, a cease-fire without credible deterrence could simply provide a pause before another Russian attack. At the same time, Moscow is likely to oppose Western security commitments that could strengthen Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
Europe’s role grows
The participation of British, French, and German security advisers in the Kyiv talks signaled a greater European role in the diplomatic process.
Witkoff said their presence showed that cooperation would be critical to reaching a settlement. Taylor argued that European involvement is particularly important because European countries would likely play a major role in any security arrangement for Ukraine and remain among Kyiv’s biggest sources of financial and military support.
For now, however, European governments appear to be involved mainly in consultations rather than formal negotiations. Their role could expand depending on what Washington proposes and what Moscow is willing to accept.
The talks are also unfolding while fighting continues, creating an important test of the claimed diplomatic momentum. A failure by Russia and Ukraine to maintain even limited restraint during negotiations would make a broader cease-fire more difficult to achieve.
No clear signal from Moscow yet
Ukraine has already indicated that it is ready for another trilateral meeting with Russia and the US. Zelensky said Kyiv would do everything possible to make such talks happen.
But there is still no clear public indication that Putin has agreed to meet with Zelensky and the US president.
For Taylor, that is the immediate benchmark: Washington needs a clear “yes” from Putin that Moscow is prepared to enter such negotiations.
Herbst said the next few days will show whether concrete details from the Moscow and Kyiv meetings emerge and how the three sides respond to them.
Pyatt welcomed the renewed US diplomatic effort but said the fundamental obstacle remains Putin’s willingness to de-escalate and his understanding of what Ukrainians want for their country’s future.

LONDON – British minister Emma Reynolds condemned hundreds of protesters who blocked streets in the English coastal city of Portsmouth late on Sept 6 to try to stop the arrival of migrants from France, calling them “thuggish”.
The gathering was the second anti-migrant demonstration in two days, after masked men disrupted traffic in the port of Dover on Sept 5, chanting “Stop the boats”, a reference to the vessels carrying asylum seekers across the English Channel.
“Perhaps the scale of the protest was something that we hadn’t seen before, but the police have brought this under control,” Reynolds, who is chief secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News on Sept 7, when asked about the protests in Portsmouth.
Successive British governments have faced accusations from opposition parties and anti-migration activists of failing to curb the numbers of asylum seekers coming to Britain, often in overcrowded, inflatable boats.
Reynolds said the numbers had fallen sharply to about 17,000 from Jan 1 to Sept 1, down 43 per cent on the same period in 2025.
Change from usual migrant route
The protesters, who were responding to calls from some far-right groups believed to be using messaging systems including Signal and Telegram, were reacting to the arrival of 140 migrants who had crossed to England.
“This is thuggish and intimidating behaviour,” Reynolds said.
When asked about how the protests seemed to be organised very quickly, she said that was “a concern”.
Donna Jones, police and crime commissioner for the area, said while the protesters were largely peaceful, the large size of the gathering meant the local force had to draft in officers from other regions to help.
The arrival of small boats in Portsmouth represents a change from the usual route taken by the dinghies, which tend to come ashore further east near Dover, where there is a large facility to receive migrants.
“Portsmouth and other parts of southern England are not set up to be able to take and deal with, not just the public order, but also the processing of these people coming into Britain illegally,” Jones told BBC Radio. REUTERS

British driver Ollie Millroy thanked rival Loek Hartog for saving his life after the Dutch racer stopped and pulled him from a burning Ferrari during a China GT Championship race in Shanghai on Saturday.
Millroy was involved in a multi-car crash on the seventh lap of the race and suffered five broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and finger, and a bruised lung.
"I am still alive tonight, entirely thanks to one man," Millroy posted on Instagram, describing how Hartog abandoned his own car and rushed to help before emergency crews arrived.

Car turned into a fireball

Race organizers said they would investigate the incident and address shortcomings in competition management, emergency response, rescue operations and medical support.

'Slow Water': Swiss farmers prepare for climate crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

‘Slow Water’: Swiss farmers prepare for climate crisis
Prolonged droughts and heavy rainfall are putting ever greater strain on Swiss agriculture. In canton Lucerne, a farmer is trying out various ways to retain more water in the soil, protect the ground and ensure fodder for his livestock. His farm is one of over 110 taking part in the "Slow Water" project.
From a hilltop on Urs Burri’s farm in Ellbach, a fine view unfolds over the rolling countryside in the Napf region of canton Lucerne, central Switzerland.
“It’s an oasis,” says Burri. “Isn’t it amazing?”.
On this day in late July, however, many meadows and pastures are yellow-brown, the grass stubby and withered. Amid this arid landscape lies a pond created by the farmer last spring. “Water is life,” he says. “There are dragonflies. Wild ducks sometimes come and swim here.”
Thanks to this pool and two smaller retention basins, which slowly release water through drainage pipes, the grass nearby is lush and green. Burri introduced these two measures to counter the increasingly frequent weather extremes, including the current drought.
“Nowadays rainfall is unevenly distributed,” he laments. “Sometimes it pours with rain, then not a drop falls for weeks on end.”
The climate crisis is threatening his livelihood. “As a farmer, the land is my capital. If it produces little or nothing, how can I feed my cows, which much of my income depends on?” he asks.
On the family-run biodynamic farm, Burri, who is in his 40s, keeps suckler cows, pigs, hens, turkeys, bees and dogs. There is also an orchard with some 80 fruit trees. The hilly landscape is made up of pastureland, hay meadows and a few fields for cereal crops.
>>Switzerland is not running out of water. But water resources are unevenly distributed, as we explain in this article:
More
Switzerland is water-rich. So why are 151 towns rationing it?
A paradigm shift for farmers
To counteract the changing conditions, characterised by long dry spells followed by torrential downpours, Burri has been part of the Slow WaterExternal link project for two-and-a-half years now. The initiative is backed by the Federal Office for Agriculture and co-funded by the cantons of Basel Country and Lucerne.
“The project focuses on two main aspects,” explains Oliver SchillingExternal link, professor of hydrology at the University of Basel and an expert at the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology (Eawag). “The first is to reduce erosion of the soil, which is a vital resource for agriculture. The second is to retain water in a given area for as long as possible, so it can be used when it becomes scarce, and farmers don’t have to resort to irrigation at once, for example by tapping into the water supply network.”
Around 110 farms in the pilot regions in the cantons of Basel Country, Basel City and Lucerne have signed up to the Slow Water project. “In the [central] Swiss Plateau region, water can be drawn from the big rivers, lakes and groundwater reserves. But in the Alpine foothills, the Jura and upland areas, during long dry periods there are no alternatives,” Schilling says.
“Retaining water represents a paradigm shift compared with recent history, when many marshlands were drained to make them suitable for farming,” he adds.
The project, which was launched in 2024 and is due to run until 2030, seeks to retain water in the soil for longer, reduce erosion and flood risk, and safeguard agricultural production in Switzerland.
The aim is to reduce the use of water from external sources by more than 30% in crop production and more than 20% in livestock farming.
To achieve this, Slow Water has identified 15 measuresExternal link, divided into two categories. On the one hand, hydrotechnical measures are used to collect, slow down or distribute water. These include ponds, retention basins, soakaways, infiltration trenches, adjustable drainage systems and keylines. Agricultural practices, on the other hand, improve the soil’s ability to absorb and store water through less invasive tillage, humus enrichment, undersowing, hedgerows and agroforestry systems.
Understanding which trees cows like
The Napf region is known for its distinctive, hilly terrain, made up of a conglomerate of layers of rounded pebbles, cemented together by fine matter and covered by a thin layer of humus. “Human survival depends on these 10–12 centimetres of soil,” Burri says. “Far too little is being done to protect them.”
His involvement in Slow Water is also driven by this conviction. He wants to avoid losing his source of income due to erosion at all costs, but the benefits extend far beyond his farm. “It is the wider community that stands to gain the most. By slowing down water runoff and promoting infiltration, we replenish springs and groundwater and reduce the risk of flooding,” he points out.
“It is easier to divert water when it is gushing from a spring – all you need is a spade. To divert a raging torrent, however, you need a digger at the very least,” he says.
To date, the farmer has implemented various climate adaptation measures, including keylines. “These are furrows around 40 centimetres deep, dug horizontally along the contour lines. They promote water infiltration, slow erosion, retain water and channel it towards drier areas,” he explains.
He has also planted forage trees on the raised edges of the keylines. On the one hand, their roots stabilise the soil and the foliage provides shade; on the other, the plants supply the animals with minerals. “At this point, we need to work out which tree species the cows like,” he says.
Burri emphasises the importance of knowledge-sharing amongst farmers and teamwork between science and practice. The Slow Water project follows a participatory, bottom-up process. “The ideas drawn up in the office do not always pass the test on the ground. It is important to discuss them and combine them with the farmers’ know-how,” he says.
Benefits of water retention
The pastures and meadows on Burri’s farm are dotted with sensors that measure rainfall, soil moisture, water levels and runoff, both in the places where measures have been taken and those left in the original state, which serve as control areas.
“The effects of the measures are not immediately apparent, and it may take years to see any real impact,” says Schilling, who is providing scientific support for the project in Ellbach.
The research team uses models that can simulate the entire water cycle: in the soil, on the surface and in the water table. “Our aim is to produce a national map showing which measures yield the best results in the different regions of Switzerland. We are already very close to achieving this,” the expert says.
Meanwhile, Burri is already seeing the first positive effects in the spots where water retention measures have been introduced, such as on a steeply sloping pasture that is very exposed to the sun. “Here, the soil is still soft and will absorb the water more effectively the next time it rains, meaning less erosion,” he says.
Drainage water from another bit of land is channelled down the slope through a perforated pipe and collected in a well. This is beneficial not just for the grassland but also the fruit trees, which Burri planted together with his father some 20 years ago.
Hopes for a better autumn
Burri knows that working with nature means being confronted with moments of uncertainty such as these, when all one can do is look on, powerless, as the heat scorches the meadows. However, he is neither fatalistic nor pessimistic. He is hoping for a late summer and a good autumn ahead for farming.
“With enough rainfall and high temperatures, we can still bring in enough hay to feed the livestock throughout the winter, without having to sell any of our animals,” he says.
At his side is his son, who is training to be a farmer, and it is to him that his final thoughts turn. “For future generations, I want to leave a land that is, if not better, at least as good as what I received from those who came before me.”
Between April and June 2026, Swiss precipitation reached just 56% of the 1991 to 2020 average. Taking July into account too, the drought is comparable to those of 1976, 2003 and 2018. Taking July into account as well, the drought is comparable to those of 1976, 2003 and 2018.
The prolonged period of low rainfall is having a profound impact on Swiss agriculture. Milk production has fallen by up to 30%External link in some regions, including the canton of Fribourg, the Bernese Seeland, Jura and Central Switzerland.
In addition, cases of fever and diarrhoea have been reported in cows, stemming from a virus never before detected in Switzerland and mainly transmitted by small biting insects. It leads to a drop in milk production.
The shortage of grass was already forcing many farms to dip into their winter reserves as early as July and to sell some of their livestock. In June and July, around 70,000 cattle (excluding calves) were slaughtered, compared with just over 60,700 in the same period in 2025. This represents an increase of over 15%, according to the Swiss meat industry association, Proviande.
The cost of crop irrigation is estimated at several thousand francsExternal link (several thousand US dollars) a week. Farmers’ associations are therefore calling on major retailersExternal link to help cover the outlay and be more flexible regarding compliance with product quality standards (size, shape and appearance).
Around 1,100 farms have already reported drought damage to the insurance organisation Schweizer HagelExternal link, which protects the agricultural sector from the effects of extreme weather. Summer crops, above all potatoes, maize, sugar beet and sunflowers, as well as pastures, have been hit much harder than winter crops such as wheat and barley, according to Urs Schuler, head of crop insurance at Schweizer Hagel.

Fifty years of the Maison d’Ailleurs: a mecca for science fiction fans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Fifty years of the Maison d’Ailleurs: a mecca for science fiction fans
From prison to sci-fi wonderland, Yverdon's Maison d’Ailleurs is more than a museum – it’s an adventure.
“Science fiction is important because it nourishes people. Human beings are creatures who recount their lives, their thoughts and their imaginations,” says Frédéric Jaccaud, director of the Maison d’Ailleurs in Yverdon-les-Bains.
The building housing the science fiction museum was built in 1806, originally as a prison. Since 1991, it has housed a vast collection of fantastical works: books, comics, magazines, newspapers, films and computer games. These form the basis for the museum’s exhibitions.
“We follow a thematic approach based on the world of the imagination – on everything that mankind has devised since it began telling stories,” explains Jaccaud.
Science fiction has always been a trailblazer
Sci-fi used to be a niche phenomenon, says Jaccaud: “In the 2000s, and now in the 2020s, science fiction has been and remains very popular, predominantly in cinema and US comics.
“The genre enriches and enlivens our world because it influences contemporary thinking. The technology that surrounds us today is often inspired by concepts devised as far back as the 1950s.”
Video calls, moon landings, virtual reality headsets and telemedicine, for example, all appeared in science fiction literature long before they became a reality. Conversely, says the director of the Maison d’Ailleurs, the present day inspires new imaginings among today’s science fiction authors.
A donation as a starting point
The Maison d’Ailleurs’ journey began in 1975, when French author Pierre Versins donated his vast collection to the town of Yverdon. Versins, a Resistance fighter who had survived Auschwitz, wrote the well-known Encyclopédie de l’utopie, des voyages extraordinaires et de la science-fiction. He did not want his books and documents to be divided up after his death.
The Maison d’Ailleurs offers 300 square metres of exhibition space. This year, the town of Yverdon is providing a grant of CHF620,000 ($761,956) to the museum’s supporting foundation. This funding covers 3.4 full-time posts and the running costs. Its influence extends far beyond the region, says Frédéric Jaccaud.
Over 10,000 people visit the museum each year, including 100 school classes. In addition, numerous researchers in the fields of literary studies and design carry out research using the collection, which now comprises 120,000 objects.
At first, he ran his museum from his three-room flat. In 1991, the town of Yverdon made the former prison available and, since 2008, the museum has also had an additional floor for the Espace Jules Verne in the neighbouring former casino.
This is where the museum’s small permanent exhibition is housed: objects from a collection dedicated to the visionary French author, also donated by collector Jean-Michel Margot.
Not a museum for the masses
The Maison d’Ailleurs is well established in the museum landscape, explains its director. Its themes are “a bit like Art Brut”.
So it is less a museum for the masses and more of an adventure – aesthetically, but also in terms of the visions that the fantastical brings to the fore. It is a unique space for reflection and exhibition.
The exhibition ‘Expedition inside Peeters’ (on display at the Maison d’Ailleurs until January 2027) showcases 200 works from every creative phase of the Geneva-based comic artist Frederik Peeters.
“A tremendous talent of international renown,” says Frédéric Jaccaud. “He creates not only a fictional, fantastical body of work, but also one that is enormously diverse.”
This diversity is showcased in the current exhibition.

From grey skies to heatwaves: climate drives Swiss abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

From grey skies to heatwaves: climate drives Swiss abroad
Every year, many Swiss choose to settle abroad for a better climate. In the past the main motivation was often to escape the country’s long grey winters. But increasingly severe heatwaves, such as that of summer 2026, may encourage more Swiss citizens to leave.
“I live on the central coast of California. When someone asks us why we chose to live here, we always say there are three reasons: the climate, the climate, the climate. No, I’ll never go back to Switzerland,” says Gabrielle Robbins-Essig, as part of a debate launched among Swissinfo readers across our platforms.
More
In the past, people fled the grey weather
For many years, the typical Swiss emigrant was someone fed up with the long winters and damp weather of the Swiss Plateau, in search of a pleasant, predictable climate all year round.
“We emigrated to Southern California ten years ago because we’d had enough of the bad weather in Switzerland. San Diego has one of the best climates in the world, with glorious sunshine for over 300 days a year,” writes Mike Vetter.
Also based in Southern California, Marianne Shintaku did not leave her home country for climatic reasons. But she admits it has now become one of the main reasons she chooses to stay: “I hate the damp and the cold, so the Californian climate has clearly become the reason I stay here.”
In Costa Rica, Agnès Vetsch is delighted with the decision she made 20 years ago: “I’m never cold anymore. And I don’t regret my choice.” “I don’t miss the fog and winter slush of the Aargau plateau,” adds Pascal Leutwyler, who now lives in Ontario, Canada.
Heat as a new reason for leaving
Escaping the grey Swiss weather may soon no longer be the primary motivation for all those seeking a more pleasant climate. With Switzerland ranking among the ten countries in the world that are warming the fastest, rising temperatures could well become a major reason for emigration within a few years.
For Norbert Roth, this is already a reality. Climate change is one of the main reasons that prompted him to leave Switzerland: “The heat, the frequent thunderstorms, the heavy hailstorms…” He now lives on the North Sea coast.
Andrea Wildi has come to the same conclusion. Unable to bear the summer temperatures in Switzerland any longer, she chose to settle in Ireland. “I moved to a more temperate climate. I only go to Switzerland during the summer months if it’s absolutely necessary,” she says.
More
Why Switzerland is among the ten fastest-warming countries in the world
Countries better equipped
Paradoxically, some people living in parts of the world where temperatures are significantly higher say they cope better with the heat than they did in Switzerland, largely thanks to suitable infrastructure.
“In Florida, we’re used to the heat, but also to air conditioning. It surprises me a bit to see how much people complain about the summer heat in Switzerland, which seems perfectly bearable,” says Ruth Härri.
In Sicily, a region that has nevertheless been hit hard by climate change, Monique Staehli has no plans to leave either: “Sicily is suffering greatly from climate change (wildfires, water shortages)… But here, I have the sea on my doorstep and we’ll soon have air conditioning in every room, powered by solar panels. We also have a shaded garden. In Switzerland, it would be difficult for me to put such solutions in place and I’d suffer more from the heat,” she explains.
Retiring to a warm country where the cost of living is cheaper undoubtedly enables some Swiss Abroad to better protect themselves against periods of extreme heat. This allows them to invest in suitable equipment and facilities – a level of comfort they might not otherwise afford in Switzerland.
Some regions are more affected than others
Of the approximately 840,000 Swiss Abroad, nearly two-thirds live in Europe, a continent particularly affected by global warming. However, this does not yet seem to be having a massive impact on the lifestyle choices of the Swiss Abroad worldwide.
Speaking from Canada, Kati Lyon-Villiger puts the scale of the phenomenon into perspective: “Climate change is much less noticeable here than in Switzerland. The snow simply takes a bit longer to arrive.”
The weather isn’t everything
Despite the appeal of a milder climate, nostalgia and family ties sometimes matter more than the weather.
“I emigrated to Australia 28 years ago to escape the fog and the grey, dreary winters. Climate-wise, it was an excellent decision: the climate in Western Australia is exceptional. But as the years go by, I miss my brothers and sisters more and more,” says Verena Edmondson-Siegenthaler.

The 79-year-old actress has been vocal with her support for Palestine amid the ongoing conflict in Gaza and shared that her activism carries professional consequences. Susan Sarandon has shared that her support for Palestine has led to her losing film roles and that parts of the film industry continue to shun her over her activism.
The 79-year-old American actress spoke at the Venice Film Festival about how her stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza has affected her work: "In terms of the power structure, I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still.”
The Oscar-winning actress noted that despite losing out on film roles she feels "the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America in our politics".
She added: “That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really understood that.”
Recent opinion polls have shown a distinct softening in US support for Israel since the start of the Gaza war in 2023. According to a July survey from Pew Research Center, US public opinion toward both the Israeli people and the Israeli government has grown increasingly negative and Americans now view the Palestinian people nearly as favourably as they view the Israeli people.
Sarandon was attending a press conference for her upcoming film The Echo Chamber, and thanked director Andrea Pallaoro for not "listening to the warnings" from those opposed to her working in cinema.
The veteran star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Thelma & Louise and Dead Man Walking has been one of Hollywood's most outspoken pro-Palestinian campaigners, alongside others like Joaquin Phoenix, Javier Bardem, and Marc Ruffalo, and was dropped by her talent agency UTA in 2023 after remarks she made while attending pro-Palestinian rallies one month after the Hamas attack on Israel.
Her words anchor themselves in growing fears regarding Hollywood blacklisting,and follow comments made by George Clooney, who came to the defence of Mark Ruffalo following accusations of antisemitism.
Speaking at the Venice Film Festival, where he received the festival’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, Clooney defended Ruffalo’s right to criticise the proposed $111bn Paramount takeover of Warner Bros Discovery.
“I worry when a big company swallows up another company,” Clooney said. “I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.”
He continued: “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. We’re not going to ban speech. I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important, right? In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works.”
He added: “There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in … I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.”
Ruffalo had previously expressed concern regarding the proposed studio merger over its potential consequences for Hollywood, while also turning his criticism on the family behind Paramount. David Ellison, the company’s chief executive, is the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison. Ruffalo accused the Ellison family of being complicit the “genocide” of Palestinians, arguing that it was “built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle”.
Ruffalo highlighted Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military, and his comments prompted a backlash from Paramount, which accused him of invoking antisemitic tropes.
Ruffalo rejected the accusation and more than 170 Jewish artists, academics and public figures subsequently signed an open letter defending the actor, warning against attempts to silence criticism of Israel or the proposed merger.
The open letter titled “Enough!”, signed by the likes of Joel Coen, Joaquin Phoenix, Ilana Glazer, Todd Haynes and Hannah Einbinder, read: “We are Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals, faith leaders and thinkers who have, in response to the outrageous smear campaign against our respected colleague Mark Ruffalo, a simple message to share with the world: Enough!”.
“Enough with the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism against those who are brave enough to point out the obvious: that the assault on the Palestinian people and the assault on our liberties at home are deeply interconnected, and there is nothing antisemitic about recognizing that fact.”
The letter notes that the proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers Discovery will “destroy thousands upon thousands of livelihoods” and “further consolidate the oligarchic control of our media” as part of a “larger project of tech-driven domination.”
“Larry Ellison and his partners have never been shy about trumpeting - and one they themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors,” the letter reads.
The letter ends with the signatories stating that they “stand proudly with Mark Ruffalo, and with all decent people who are bravely rising and speaking truth to power.”
Susan Sarandon stars in The Echo Chamber, which is one of 21 films competing for Venice’s Golden Lion award. The prize will be presented on 12 September.

More than 1 million users affected in Mathspace data breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:53:31 UTC
15:53:31 KST

More than a million people, including students, school staff, and parents have been affected by a data breach across Australia and New Zealand.
Learning provider Mathspace says "unauthorised parties had accessed an internal reporting system" and the exposed information included names and email addresses.
What's next?
The compromised reporting system has been taken offline and individuals who are affected are being contacted.
More than a million people, including students, school staff, and parents, have been affected following a data breach at Mathspace, according to the learning provider.
The company said, in a blog post, "unauthorised parties had accessed an internal reporting system used by Mathspace" and the exposed information included names and email addresses.
It said the attackers accessed the system between August 10 and August 27 during a period when a security patch had not been installed.
Mathspace said "attackers exploited a security vulnerability" in its self-hosted installation of software.
"We're truly sorry this happened and are taking steps to prevent similar breaches in the future," the company said.
"Protecting the information entrusted to us by students, families and schools is our responsibility."
Mathspace confirmed a total of 1,079,819 people were affected in Australia and New Zealand.
The hackers exported information that included user IDs, usernames, first names, last names, email addresses, countries, time zones, user types, email-verification status, last-active date, last-login date and date joined.
But the company said not every person had all those fields of data stolen.
Mathspace make clear that no academic records, learning activities, results, assessment records, passwords (hashes), authentication tokens, SSO credentials, or API credentials were exposed.
"The exposed data did not include records linking user accounts to their schools," the blog said.
Mathspace advised people to:
Check unexpected messages independently
Do not disclose passwords or verification codes in response to a message
Use a unique password for each account.
It also urged people to watch for unusual account activity, and if anybody wanted to report suspicious messages or activity they should contact data-breach-response@mathspace.co.
The compromised reporting system has been taken offline.
Mathspace said it had contacted schools, cyber security authorities and education departments and was now contacting affected individuals.
The company said it did not yet know who was responsible for the breach and had found "no evidence so far" that the stolen information had been published, shared or sold.
Steve Hunter, director of engineering, APAC, at cybersecurity and AI company Arctic Wolf, said the Mathspace incident highlighted how difficult it could be for organisations to keep on top of software vulnerabilities.
"Rather than playing 'Whack-a-Mole' every time a new vulnerability appears, organisations need to take a more risk-based approach," he said.
"The priority should be knowing what systems and software you have, understanding where the biggest risks sit, and having a clear process for acting when a critical security warning comes through."

Berlin (dpa) – German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt outlined plans to increase the country’s defences against hybrid Russian attacks following a recent failed drone attack at a major airport in remarks to the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild tabloid.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks involving explosive-laden drones targeting airports, agents operating in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality,” Dobrindt said.
He predicted that the attacks would increase but said Germany could defend itself.
The newspaper reported on specific plans to improve protection against drones and hacker attacks, citing information from the Interior Ministry.
The airspace over critical transport hubs, airports, railway stations, and Berlin’s government district was reported to be fully protected against drones by means of “new, rapidly deployable units,” it said.
Companies operating critical infrastructure, such as water utilities, electricity providers, and defence contractors, are also to be given legal authority to actively defend themselves against drones.
A national protective shield known as a “Cyberdome” is to be established, comprising a dense network of digital sensors designed to detect and intercept attempted hacker attacks.
A drone laden with explosives was intercepted at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Ukrainian transport aircraft in August.

Singapore retail sales growth slows to 1.5 pct year-on-year in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:52:07 CST
15:52:07 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's retail sales growth moderated to 1.5 percent year-on-year in July, from 4 percent in June, the Department of Statistics said on Monday.
On a seasonally adjusted month-on-month basis, retail sales increased 0.9 percent in July, it said in a statement.
Total retail sales were estimated at 4.4 billion Singapore dollars (3.47 billion U.S. dollars), with online sales accounting for 15.4 percent, down from 16.4 percent in June.
Recreational goods led growth among retail industries, with sales rising 13.9 percent year-on-year, followed by watches and jewelry at 11.1 percent, mainly on higher sporting goods and jewelry sales.
Sales of computer and telecommunications equipment increased 5.1 percent.
However, food and alcohol sales fell 5.1 percent, while department store sales declined 3.5 percent year-on-year. ■

Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 11, state news agency says
BEIRUT, Sept 7 - Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town early on Monday killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon's state news agency said.
Israel has intensified its bombardment of south Lebanon in recent days despite a June ceasefire that was meant to halt fighting between the Israeli military and Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. At least seven people were killed in Israeli strikes on Sunday.
Just after midnight, Israeli warplanes hit a residential building in the town of Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon, killing nine people including two children, and wounding five more, Lebanon's National News Agency reported.
A separate Israeli drone strike on a civilian vehicle in the town killed two medics inside the car, it said.
The strikes on the town came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions on the strikes, including whether it was aware of the presence of medics and children at the strike locations and why no evacuation warning was issued.
A spokesperson for the Israeli military issued a separate evacuation warning just after 2:00 a.m. local time (2300 GMT on Sunday) for areas around a building in another town in southern Lebanon where it said it would strike Hezbollah facilities.
Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on March 2 — two days after the start of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran — triggering an Israeli air and ground offensive.
The ceasefire saw violence decrease dramatically, but Israeli troops occupying swathes of southern Lebanon have continued razing villages in the self-declared security zone. Israel's military has continued carrying out strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without evacuation warnings. REUTERS

VIENTIANE, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese medical support team participating in the China-Laos "Peace Train-2026" joint humanitarian medical rescue exercise arrived in the Lao capital Vientiane on Sunday morning.
The team will conduct a 17-day joint exercise and medical service program with the medical support team of the Lao People's Army.
Bouasing Inthavong, deputy director of the General Logistics Department of the Lao People's Army, joined representatives from both sides in attending a warm welcome ceremony.
Song Caiping, captain of the "Peace Train" medical team, said at the ceremony that the Chinese participants had completed 11 rounds of intensive medical skills training before departure and had conducted realistic combat drills en route.
Bouasing expressed gratitude for the assistance China has provided to Laos in the health sector in recent years. He said that, with the continued and in-depth development of the "Peace Train" series of activities, medical support exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries have established a sound mechanism and system, marking a new stage in mutual trust and cooperation in the medical field between the two sides.
According to a member of the Chinese command and coordination group for the joint exercise, this year's exercise is being held against the backdrop of the 65th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Laos, the "China-Laos Friendship Year," and the fifth anniversary of the opening of the China-Laos Railway. It is the sixth time the two militaries have held this series of joint exercises.
The exercise will further enhance the two militaries' capabilities in joint command, joint rescue, and joint prevention and control in medical support, demonstrating their deep military friendship and mutual trust while continuing to build a model for bilateral military cooperation and exchanges.
Following the exercise, the medical team will travel to Vientiane, Savannakhet, Champasak, and Attapeu provinces to provide medical services, including specialized diagnosis and treatment and academic lectures.
These activities are expected to further deepen strategic mutual trust, expand practical cooperation, and promote medical exchanges between the two militaries toward more comprehensive, in-depth, and regularized development. They will also contribute to advancing the building of a China-Laos community with a shared future toward higher standards, higher quality, and higher levels. ■

Police Chief Superintendent Mel Adams told reporters that the scene was confronting for first responders and asked for anyone who witnessed the aircraft hitting the ground to contact investigators immediately.
Local media reported that the aircraft had taken off from a nearby airport around 10 minutes before crashing.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said it has deployed a team of three investigators to examine the wreckage, recover components and interview witnesses and involved parties. ■

Good morning, readers. Angela Skujins here holding the pen for this week’s newsletter, where a seismic regional election in Germany’s east has seen the far-right, anti-migration Alternative for Germany (AfD) sweep to power, with the blow ricocheting as far as Berlin.
No alternative: With voters turning out in droves, preliminary end results from Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt ballot show the AfD securing 43.8% of the vote, representing 39 seats of the 83-member state parliament.
Although this is short of an outright majority, with the official results expected Monday night, it is already being interpreted as a major loss for Merz’ centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU) party. This is a party that has led the region of Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years, but only scraped through 17.2% of the votes.
Nothing short of a disaster: AfD co-chair Alice Weidel told CNN she expects Merz to be out by Christmas. The German chancellor has so far stayed out of the spotlight, but is expected to front-up to his cabinet today in the capital for crisis talks.
CDU member of the German Bundestag Günter Krings just admitted to Europe Today that this was a "devastating result" and "the perception and credibility of our party is a low". Asked about how this impacts the European Union, he said the right would feel "emboldened". "The European Union also should ask, 'What did we contribute to this anger, and what do we have to change?'" Watch.
Interesting to note: European Council President António Costa will be in Berlin on Wednesday and will hold court with Merz. It’s part of Costa’s tour of the capitals — a weeks-long voyage around the member states aiming to collect intel from leaders about their hopes, desires, and gripes with the state of EU affairs. The election results could factor into these talks.
Officially, though, it has to do with the EU’s multi-annual financial framework, aka the long-term budget. As an aside, keep an eye on his Thursday meeting with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, where the Ceuta migration crisis could widen.

But what if the money were moved from Euroclear into an EU-owned custodian?
The idea is gaining traction as a potential solution to break the political deadlock. Jorge envisions what the custodian could look like.
Brussels watches Serbia: The funeral of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić is expected to take place today in Belgrade without state honours or the presence of government officials, despite a Serbian cabinet minister initially vowing to give the “Butcher of Bosnia” a burial with "all military and state honours".
As Mared Gwyn reports, the the optics around Mladić’s funeral have already sparked outrage in Brussels, with the EU’s Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos on Friday delaying her planned trip to Serbia, an EU candidate country, saying that the “glorification surrounding his (Mladić’s) death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.”
Mladić died in late August while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Bosnian war. His body was returned to Belgrade last Thursday on a government plane, his body draped in the Serbian flag, in the presence of a cabinet minister.
Kos said that the events surrounding his funeral and commemoration would be an “important test” in terms of Belgrade’s alignment with EU values, a key requisite in its bid to join the bloc. “The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable,” she said on social media.
Straying close to the red line: While no state funeral will be held, Serbia’s Justice Minister and the President of Bosnia’s Serb-majority Republika Srpska joined tributes to Mladić over the weekend at the state-owned Army House in Belgrade, according to local media.
A diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Euronews that any commemoration by Serbian state officials would be completely unacceptable and inevitably weaken the support for the country's EU bid among member states. Brussels had been pushing to open talks on economic growth and competitiveness under Chapter 3 of the accession process.
“Anyone even considering opening Cluster 3 will think twice,” the diplomat told Euronews. “It seems very unlikely that anyone would want to push for that now.”
Hungary, out of the wilderness? The European Parliament is on track to bring Budapest from out of the cold by reversing what is known to be the EU’s “nuclear option”. Article 7 is a legal mechanism that allows the EU to suspend certain rights for a country if deemed necessary. In Hungary’s case, it was triggered in 2018 to assess violations of EU values and alleged democratic backsliding during the government of former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.
With Péter Magyar at the helm, the country is revising several laws from the Orbán era, which is prompting Parliament to reconsider its position. But will this be the good news story Budapest is looking for? Vincenzo Genovese has answers.

Yours truly wrote an article about how the trip coincides with Brussels reforming its much needed Arctic policy, particularly when it comes to military and economic threats. I have the story below.
EU races to rethink Arctic policy as the global power grab continues
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is completing her two-day whistlestop tour of the Greenlandic capital, Nuuk, on Monday to further European Union-Arctic relations — and gather intelligence as the European Union maps out a new Arctic Policy.
When the policy's first iteration was published in 2021, it made little reference to growing security threats. Instead, the then-EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell emphasised climate change, raw materials and geostrategic influence as central to the document.
But in the years since, the European Commission has admitted the policy needs an urgent revamp to address the changing security and defence environment in the region — a more militarised Russia, for one thing, as well as China's effort to expand its economic footprint as melting ice opens new Arctic Sea routes. The site of the Lin Family Murders:  Gikong Presbyterian Church
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:49:44 UTC
15:49:44 KST

In a quiet backstreet off Section 3 of Xinyi Road in Taipei City sits an unassuming prayer space: Gikong Presbyterian Church. However, in 1980 this tranquil spot was the scene of an event that shocked Taiwanese society: the murders of family members of veteran pro-democracy activist Lin I-hsiung, who then lived at this address.
In the wake of murder
On February 28, 1980, during the military trials of defendants in the case arising from the Kaohsiung Incident—a violent clash between pro-democracy protestors and the Kuomintang government in late 1979—Lin I-hsiung was being tried at the Military Law Division of the Taiwan Garrison Command, and his wife Fang Su-min was attending the trial. That day, around noon, Fang tried to call home several times, but there was no answer, so Lin I-hsiung’s secretary Tien Chiu-chin was asked to go to the family home and check things out.
When Tien arrived, she found the family’s eldest daughter, Lin Huan-chun (today Judy Linton) lying inside the house with multiple stab wounds. Huan-chun was rushed to the hospital and fortunately survived. When police, family, and friends later entered the home’s basement, they found the murdered bodies of Lin’s mother Lin Yu A-mei and his seven-year-old twin daughters Liang-chun and Ting-chun. The case has never been solved.
After the homicides, the Lin home remained under surveillance. As the site of multiple murders, the property could also not readily be rented out or sold. It was only in 1982 that the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan bought the building and converted it into a religious space.
In the course of creating this church, many people came forward to contribute money but were unwilling to leave their names. Some even just threw their contributions into the basement. This reflected the oppressive social atmosphere of the White Terror at the time.
From residence to church
According to Wang Ming-tse, one of the pastors at Gikong Church, the name “Gikong” (Mandarin yiguang), meaning “light of justice” or “light of righteousness,” derives from the Bible, Psalms 89:14–15, and expresses the hope that “the light of God’s justice will shine down on this place.” The desire is to prevent such an atrocity from ever occurring again.
Since its founding, Gikong has continued to stand by the side of victims and their families, and to show concern for the disadvantaged and social issues. In 2014, Lin I-hsiung’s hunger strike to call for a halt to construction of the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant also took place here.
Through successive renovations, Gikong has endeavored to preserve some traces of the old Lin home. A few red bricks left over from conversion of the building have been placed beneath a crucifix, to remind people that this is the former Lin family residence as well as a church. A commemorative piano remains at the entrance to the first floor; according to the church, Lin’s three daughters all used to play it.
As for various rumors, such as one claiming that bloodstains were left on the stairs and were later covered up with carpeting, Pastor Wang says that some of these stories were passed down among early churchgoers by word of mouth and are hard to either verify or disprove. His solution is to tell the different versions of the church’s history when giving tours and allow each visitor to form their own understanding of the truth.
From memory to public space
Memories of the Lin Family Murders are also preserved at the Chilin Memorial House in Yilan County. Lin I-hsiung and Fang Su-min founded the Chilin Education Foundation in 1991 in hopes of using cultural and educational activities to cultivate a better understanding of Taiwanese society and concern for public affairs among citizens.
In 1993, the foundation transformed the home where Lin grew up in Yilan County into the Chilin Memorial House. It commemorates Lin’s mother and his twin daughters, displaying funeral scrolls, elegies, and some personal belongings. In 2001, it was registered by the county as a historic building.
In 2025 Gikong Church was designated by the National Human Rights Museum as a “site of significance for transitional justice.” A plaque was formally unveiled on April 5, 2026, making the church the first site in Taiwan approved by the government under new rules calling for ordinary citizens to initiate applications for this designation.
Gikong Church is the place where the Lin Family Murders occurred, whereas the Chilin Memorial House preserves family memories and historical materials. From two different perspectives, the two institutions keep people aware of the same stretch of history.
Where history happened
Today, the church not only holds services and gatherings, it also offers tours to visiting groups from home and abroad. Pastor Wang, who has served at Gikong for five years, says that through his interactions with victims of political repression and their families, he has gradually come to understand that period of history and also comprehend that “faith and life must be linked together.” He says: “Victims’ families aren’t looking for you to give them a clear-cut answer, but simply need someone who will listen to them.”
In the transformation from the Lin family home to Gikong Church, the light of justice represented by the church’s name has pierced through a historical tragedy and come to shine on the freedom and democracy that Taiwan enjoys today. It also illuminates the hope that people feel for peace and the future.

Easton says China doubtful of US 'Hellscape' concept in Taiwan Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:49:18 UTC
15:49:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Beijing is concerned about the US’ “Hellscape” drone strategy to defend Taiwan in an invasion but is convinced it has not come to fruition yet, Ian Easton, an associate professor at the US Navy’s China Maritime Studies Institute, said in a CMSI report.
The US Pacific Command first used the term Hellscape in August 2023 to describe what a conflict in the Taiwan Strait would look like in the future, Easton said. That same month, the command announced the Replicator Initiative, which seeks to quickly deploy thousands of drones that could make the hellscape strategy a reality.
On June 10, 2024, PACOM Commander Admiral Samuel Paparo described the hellscape strategy as massive swarms of unmanned weapons targeting Chinese forces, per the report. “I want to turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape using a number of classified capabilities so I can make their lives utterly miserable for a month, which buys me the time for the rest of everything,” Paparo said.
Later that month, Chinese defense ministry spokesman, Senior Colonel Wu Qian, said that “some Americans” wanted to use Taiwan to contain China and flood the Taiwan Strait with drone swarms, calling them “extremely psychotic.” Wu claimed America would end up abandoning Taiwan.
In July 2024, Ren Guozheng, an expert on Taiwan affairs at the PLA Academy of Military Science, wrote that the hellscape strategy was part of American cognitive warfare and the US was trying to scare China with its plans and operations, according to Easton.
A Taiwan affairs program in China discussed the hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative during one episode that same month. The host, Li Hong, said the US was militarily inferior and called Paparo’s remarks “full of provocative intent.” She suggested America was in decline and could not keep up with the PLA.
In August 2024, another military affairs program about the Hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative was aired. Commentators said that US unmanned systems could be easily countered with electronic jamming and cyberattacks. They claimed that PLA air defense units could shoot down the drone swarms.
Despite Chinese propaganda dismissing the Hellscape strategy, many Chinese military experts are taking it seriously and respect its basic idea of using large numbers of cheap drones, seeing it as important for future warfare, Easton said.
In August 2025, the PLA Navy’s top magazine, Navy Today, published an article linking Hellscape to several US Navy advances in different types of unmanned surface vessels. “Its current state of equipment development is comprehensive, focused on actual warfighting, and cutting edge,” it said.
In January 2025, Shipborne Weapons, a China State Shipbuilding Corporation military magazine, called the Hellscape plan a “threat” and said shipborne laser weapons could be a potential countermeasure to swarms of unmanned vessels and unmanned aerial vehicles. It argued that missiles like the Hongqi-9 and Hongqi-16 were too expensive. One shot of a solid-state laser weapon would only cost a few thousand RMB.
Additionally, lasers are not limited by ammunition and are faster and more accurate. They can also destroy anti-ship missiles that are impervious to electronic jamming, the magazine said.
In a Modern Weaponry report, authors said the Replicator Initiative was a work in progress and not yet battle-tested. They said it was “basically still conceptually immature.”
The authors said the US would need to transport huge numbers of drones close to Taiwan, which would strain limited long-distance logistics and put ships within range of PLA missiles. “This means the ‘Replicator’ plan’s large numbers of unmanned systems could be destroyed before they can even be deployed,” the report said.
Easton pointed out that while Chinese propagandists are dismissive of America’s Hellscape plan, Chinese military experts take asymmetric warfare seriously and are worried about the increased US military support to Taiwan. He added that the experts view drone swarms as integral to future warfare.
