Hungarian Media Tycoon’s Firm Formed Dubai Subsidiary While Under Investigation at Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Reported by
Hungarian media tycoon Gyula Balásy broke down in tears in a May television interview, stating authorities had frozen the accounts of his companies, which had received lucrative public relations contracts under the administration of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Following that admission, the National Investigation Bureau of the Emergency Police released a statement about its investigation into “suspicion of fraudulent misrepresentation in connection with overpriced contracts.” The investigation involves the National Tax and Customs Administration, and has been active since at least April in 2024.
Corporate records obtained by OCCRP and Átlátszó reveal that one of the companies that had its accounts frozen created an offshore firm in 2024, as the investigation was ongoing.
In October 2024, the records show, Balásy’s New Land Media formed a subsidiary in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) city of Dubai.
Balásy also owns a luxury apartment in Dubai, according to property records.
He began the process of buying the apartment for approximately 3.2 million UAE dirhams (roughly $870,000) in May 2023, according to leaked property records obtained as part of the Dubai Unlocked project. The land registry shows that the purchase was officially completed in 2025.
Also in 2025, Hungarian corporate records show that New Land Media provided approximately 1.3 billion forints (nearly $4.2 million) in long-term loans to a subsidiary. New Land Media’s records list only two subsidiaries at the time — the Dubai firm and another based in Hungary. The Hungarian subsidiary’s financial statement for 2025 does not record receiving the loans.
In his response to questions from reporters, Balásy did not clarify whether the funds went to the Dubai subsidiary. The Dubai firm is involved in “Education & Training Computer Software,” according to its UAE business license.
While the investigation into Balásy’s companies is more than two years old, authorities did not freeze the accounts until Orbán was ousted in national elections this April, after 16 years in power. Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has made moves to investigate the misuse of public funds under the previous government.
In a response to questions about the Dubai apartment and the transfer of funds from New Land Media to a subsidiary, Balásy said: “I do not wish to comment on the details of the individual transactions.”
“We are fully cooperating with the competent bodies of the Hungarian state and the investigative authority,” he said. Cooperation has included providing “all requested information and documents.”
“I strongly reject any allegation or suggestion that I have absconded or hidden any assets,” Balásy added.
There is no evidence that the transfer of funds or the purchase of the Dubai apartment were illegal, and the ongoing Hungarian investigation has not resulted in any charges against Balásy.
But Balásy is now facing even more scrutiny. On September 1, Hungarian authorities raided the premises of several of his companies. The action came after Átlátszó revealed that toy vehicles distributed during political campaigns appeared to be overpriced.
Balásy did not respond to a request for comment about the raids.
Controversial Campaigns
In April 2024, Hungary’s chief prosecutor revealed that the National Investigation Bureau of the Emergency Police had launched a probe into alleged “misappropriation of funds and other crimes” by firms that received state communication contracts.
Six months later, in October 2024, the same firms under investigation — owned by Balásy — won another major state communications framework agreement worth up to 75 billion forints ($243 million). Balásy’s companies continued to receive Hungarian state contracts until Orbán lost elections.
During Orbán’s tenure, Balásy’s companies won contracts from the National Communications Office for coordinating advertising campaigns, media buying, event organization and public outreach projects for government institutions.
His network of advertising and event-management companies — collectively known as Lounge Group — designed and distributed the government’s political and ideological campaigns for more than a decade. Some campaigns were criticized for vilifying migrants, Ukraine, the European Union, and LGBTQ+ communities, along with American-Hungarian billionaire George Soros.
New Land Media is the unit of Lounge Group that specializes in media planning and buys advertising space across television, radio, print and outdoor billboards. It decided where and how often government ad campaigns would run. Reporting by Átlátszó and other Hungarian media shows it overwhelmingly spent that public money on pro-Orbán media outlets.
New Land Media has served as a main contractor for government communication and state-backed campaigns overseen by the Cabinet Office, which was headed by Antal Rogán and includes the National Communications Office.
The Hungarian police and the National Tax and Customs Administration both said they could not provide further information about ongoing investigations.
Frozen Funds
Last week, Magyar’s administration initiated the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which is tasked with investigating the alleged misuse of public funds under Orbán’s government.
Magyar had launched his political career with a 2024 live interview on the YouTube channel Partizán in which he broke with Orbán’s ruling Fidesz party, and lambasted its alleged systemic corruption.
Among his claims in that interview, Magyar said he had quit as CEO of the state-owned student loan center because he refused to continue signing severely overpriced government communication contracts with the Balásy companies.
Balásy has not responded directly to Magyar’s allegations. However, he told OCCRP and Átlátszó: “All transactions between my companies, or between my companies and external parties, have been and are taking place within a strictly controlled, approved legal and financial framework in accordance with the laws in force at all times.”
Setting the scene in 2024 for his future run for prime minister, Magyar vowed to root out what he alleged was cronyism. He also promised to dismantle the state-controlled public media network built by Orbán and his associates, which he called a "propaganda machine.”
Balásy’s companies were central to the Orbán government’s public relations strategy.
In a television interview in May this year, Balásy said Hungarian authorities had frozen bank accounts linked to his companies — including those connected to New Land Media.
A teary-eyed Balásy offered to hand over control of his business empire to the Hungarian state, insisting that he had “nothing to hide” and had done nothing unlawful.
In a Facebook post in response, Magyar appeared to suggest that the action against Balásy's companies was part of a broader effort to dismantle the patronage system built under Orbán. Quoting his 2024 interview, he wrote: "This system could collapse much faster than many people think."
The following day, the National Bureau of Investigation confirmed in a statement that it had frozen company bank accounts as part of an investigation into the alleged misappropriation of public funds and money laundering.
The National Bureau of Investigation said it was also conducting a separate probe based on suspicion of allegedly "overpriced contracts" related to the group of companies.”
It is not known if the Dubai subsidiary, or Balásy’s apartment in the city, are part of the investigation. Balásy declined to clarify whether authorities had questioned him about either.
“I do not wish to comment on the details of my private investments,” Balásy said in his emailed response to questions. “However, I consider it important to state that all my investments — whether in Hungary or abroad — are made in full compliance with the relevant laws and tax regulations.”
The OCCRP Research and Data team contributed research.

Taiwan cooling suppliers target thermal resistance with new designs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:56:55 UTC
14:56:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Thermal resistance between AI chips and cooling plates is emerging as a new challenge for the cooling industry, with Taiwanese companies pursuing new designs to improve heat dissipation, CTEE reported Monday.
In conventional AI chip designs, heat generated by a chip passes through thermal interface material (TIM), a metal lid covering the chip package, and another TIM layer before reaching an external cold plate, where coolant carries the heat away. Each additional interface can increase thermal resistance while also creating challenges related to coating thickness and material aging, according to Pocket Securities.
As AI chips consume more power, Auras Technology Co. is seeking to reduce the number of materials and interfaces that heat must pass through before reaching the coolant. The company said microchannel technology will become increasingly important.
Microchannel technology creates tiny channels within the metal lid covering the chip package. Coolant can then flow through the lid itself, bringing it closer to the chip and reducing the distance heat must travel, according to Sinotrade.
Auras said the designs require precise control of coolant flow and hot spots. The shift is also pushing cooling companies further into chip packaging, requiring changes to packaging equipment, manufacturing processes, and yield management.
Jentech Precision Industrial Co. is developing a removable-lid design for Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra platform. The approach allows part of the metal lid covering the chip package to be removed during system assembly, eliminating the second TIM layer and enabling the cold plate to sit closer to the chip.
Jentech also plans to eventually combine vapor chamber and microchannel technologies to bring cooling closer to the chip’s main heat sources.
Asia Vital Components Co. is pursuing cooling systems that cover a larger area and cool both sides of the chip. Some of its newer designs extend cooling from the front of the chip to the back of the motherboard.
Which approach gains wider adoption will ultimately depend on decisions by AI chipmakers and cloud service providers. Industry players expect microchannel technology to enter mass production as early as 2028.

French mechanical elephant parade draws 150,000 in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:56:32 UTC
14:56:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei Arts Festival’s opening outdoor spectacle, “Three Elephants Pass...,” concluded its second and final procession in Shilin on Sunday (Sept. 6).
Guided by glowing red torches, three massive mechanical elephants paraded alongside mechanical phoenixes and a tin-soldier band through busy streets and night-market arcades.
Accompanied by bagpipes and double-reed instruments, performers representing five continents marched alongside tens of thousands of spectators, turning Shilin into an immersive outdoor theater.
According to the Taipei Performing Arts Center (TPAC), the two-day event drew more than 150,000 visitors, while official livestreams attracted over 220,000 views.
Produced by French street theater company Compagnie Oposito, the performance drew on Taipei’s local history.
The procession’s precise 7:14 p.m. start time honored 1914, the year Taipei’s first zoo was established. For longtime residents, the parade also evoked memories of 1986, when crowds lined the streets to watch animals being relocated from Yuanshan to Muzha.
Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs Commissioner Tsai Shih-ping (蔡詩萍) said the record turnout resulted from long-term cultural cultivation rather than a short-term campaign.
Tsai said the effort began in 2025 after local borough chiefs proposed revitalizing the commercial district. The city subsequently collaborated with TPAC on a multiyear initiative to promote urban regeneration through the performing arts.
Tsai said sales for vendors at Shilin Night Market doubled over the weekend compared with typical days, demonstrating a successful connection between public cultural policy and the local economy.
Founded in 1982, Compagnie Oposito is a pioneer of European street theater.
Co-founder Jean-Raymond Jacob maintains that “the street is both a battlefield and a stage,” emphasizing that the urban environment is a living component of the work rather than merely a backdrop, according to TPAC.
Jacob likened adapting productions to “mixing anise liqueur with water,” noting that while cities, laws, and physical spaces vary, the core structure and rhythm remain intact.
TPAC said Jacob’s choreography relies on geometric concepts such as circles, straight lines, and M-shaped formations. The troupe adapts the performance to each city by recalculating travel times based on distance, road conditions, and slopes.
Technical director Veronique Charbit highlighted the logistical realities of outdoor productions, saying tools suited to indoor stages often fail on uneven street pavement. Charbit works closely with local authorities in each host city to review safety protocols and mitigate risks.
Jacob cited the troupe’s past work “Blue Skins,” which explored the Black experience in France by inviting actors to share their stories and control their choreography, attire, and music rather than reproduce societal stereotypes.
For the Taipei production, the troupe partnered with Taiwanese groups Sun Son Theatre and Hsuan Yu Music, along with dozens of local volunteers, to adapt the performance to its setting.

Germany’s anti-Russia stance helped drive AfD election victory – expert
The German government’s increasingly hostile stance toward Russia, mounting economic problems, and concerns over migration have helped propel the Alternative for Germany (AfD) to a historic election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, Professor Vladislav Belov, head of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Center for German Studies, has told RT.
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than doubling its result from the previous state election, according to official preliminary results. It is set to hold 39 of the state parliament’s 97 seats, falling short of the 49 required for an absolute majority.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has led Saxony-Anhalt’s coalition government since 2021, finished a distant second with 17.2% and 15 seats. Sven Schulze, the party’s lead candidate and outgoing regional head, conceded defeat and congratulated the AfD on its success.
Speaking shortly after polls closed on Sunday, Belov recalled his earlier assessment that the anti-Russian positions adopted by German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt would benefit the AfD among certain groups of voters.
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024, entered the Saxony-Anhalt parliament for the first time after securing 5.3% of the vote.
“I did not expect the BSW to cross the 5% threshold, so congratulations to Sahra Wagenknecht,” Belov said, describing its performance as another surprise and attributing the result to the party’s “broad peace-oriented position.” “Sahra said that right-wing extremists were those who wanted war and militarization. That also resonated with voters.”
Belov argued that the campaign had been unusually dominated by federal issues, despite voters formally electing a state parliament.
“For the first time, the AfD presented itself not merely as a protest party but as a party with governing competence,” he said, identifying migration, education, and Saxony-Anhalt’s economic and political situation as key campaign issues that other parties had failed to address.
The predominantly rural state is also home to a sizeable chemical industry that has been affected by higher energy costs since Germany abandoned inexpensive Russian pipeline gas. Unemployment stood at 8.1% in July, compared with 6.4% nationwide.
Belov attributed the Greens’ result to tactical mobilization rather than voter support for their policies. He described the ‘Taktisch Wählen’ initiative, which used door-to-door canvassing and an online tool to encourage support for the SPD or Greens in order to block an AfD majority, as “scandalous.”

====================================================================================================

An unmanned army: Hezbollah terrorists are using UAVs to hold off  Israel’s superior forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:53:47 UTC
14:53:47 KST

In late August, Israel resumed active strikes on positions held by the Shiite movement Hezbollah inside Lebanon — a response to FPV drone attacks against Israeli soldiers. Cycles of escalation keep repeating themselves in the region: despite ceasefire agreements between Israel and the Lebanese government, Hezbollah fighters continue to attack Israeli forces, and Jerusalem’s response results in civilian casualties, leading to further rounds of fighting. Importantly, Hezbollah’s countermeasures against the IDF now involve the use of fiber-optic-guided drones of the sort developed on the battlefield in Ukraine. The use of this relatively accessible, highly effective technology allowed Hezbollah to retain its ability to fight in the face of Israel’s undeniable military superiority.
What is happening in southern Lebanon
On Aug. 27, following an attempted drone attack on IDF troops near the Ali al-Taher ridge, Israeli aircraft carried out a series of strikes on facilities belonging to Hezbollah near Nabatieh. Military warehouses are reported to have been hit; a woman was killed, and other civilians were injured.
Two weeks earlier, three Israeli soldiers had been severely injured by a drone strike in the same area, and the airstrikes carried out in retaliation for that incident killed not only Hezbollah fighters and commanders, but also at least 11 civilians, including women and children (according to the Israeli side, some of them were relatives of the killed militants).
Similar “cycles of escalation” have accompanied the talks on conflict settlement in southern Lebanon in recent months — negotiations that are themselves part of the broader process of ending the conflict between the U.S.-Israeli coalition and Iran.
The Lebanese theater of operations is one of the key topics in the negotiations. Back in 2024, Israeli authorities announced their intention to “dismantle the terrorist infrastructure” and “liberate” Lebanon from the influence of Hezbollah, which remains Iran’s most valuable and dangerous asset on its “external perimeter.”
Israel’s stated goal in Lebanon is to free the country from Hezbollah’s influence
On Oct. 1, 2024, Israeli forces launched a ground operation into Lebanon aimed at limiting the Shiite movement’s combat capability — the third such war in recent decades (the first two being in 1982 and 2006). A ceasefire was reached at the end of November 2024.
Then, on March 2, 2026, Hezbollah resumed rocket fire on Israeli territory following the death of Iran’s supreme leader Ali Khamenei in a missile strike by the U.S.-Israeli coalition. In response, the IDF continued its ground operation in Lebanon.
A ceasefire was announced on April 16, but fighting continued yet again. With U.S. mediation, an agreement between the Israeli and Lebanese governments was signed on June 26, providing for a partial withdrawal of IDF units from several areas in the south of the country while maintaining an Israeli presence until Hezbollah is disarmed.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem refused to recognize the agreement and stated that armed resistance would continue. Notably, the particularities of the Lebanese political system make it impossible to implement any settlement agreement with Israel without the support of the Shiite community.
Drones vs. IDF
At the current stage of the war in southern Lebanon, fiber-optic-guided FPV (first-person view) drones have become Hezbollah’s main means of countering Israeli forces. As many as 33 incidents involving Israeli military deaths and injuries in southern Lebanon were recorded from March to July 2026, with FPV drones used in more than half of them. By some estimates, they have curtailed Israel’s offensive capabilities by up to 80%.
Observers note Hezbollah appears to be in the early stage of what is known as a reconnaissance-strike loop: drones first conduct aerial reconnaissance, followed by launches of fiber-optic FPV drones at identified targets. If the use of drones can be scaled up and incorporated into a strategy for countering Israeli forces, this would create a long-term threat with no clear solution.
In a sense, Hezbollah has successfully exploited a gap in Israeli operational capability that stems less from technological asymmetry than from differing speeds of adapting doctrine to technological progress in warfare.
Hezbollah is successfully adapting to technological progress in warfare
Notably, before the April 16 ceasefire, videos of drone attacks showed hits on static objects or combat vehicles, and despite the agreement, on April 26 a Hezbollah FPV drone struck a tank, killing one Israeli soldier and wounding six others, and more drones came close to successfully attacking an Israeli helicopter that had arrived to pick up the wounded.
It appears that drones have become central to the attrition strategy Hezbollah has adopted against Israeli forces. Speaking with The Insider, Israeli military expert David Gendelman notes the similarities between the southern Lebanese theater of operations and the battlefield in Ukraine:
“FPV drones have proven to be an extremely cost-effective weapon on the Russian-Ukrainian front, which is why millions of them are now being used there, partially replacing the roles of artillery, anti-tank guided missiles, and air power. And this is happening in a symmetric war between two regular armies. Such weapons will be all the more effective in the asymmetric war that Hezbollah is waging against Israel’s regular army.
The Russian and Ukrainian armies are world champions at countering FPVs, with years of experience, and they still suffer several hundred casualties from them every day, because just as there is no wonder weapon, there is no counter-wonder-weapon either. There is a set of partial solutions, in both troop training and technical means, that reduces losses but does not bring them to zero.
The same is true of other types of weapons for which no ‘wonder shield’ has been found either. FPVs are no exception. Just as artillery, anti-tank guided missiles, small arms, and other battlefield tools remain with us, FPVs are here to stay too — this is now a new reality we have to live with.”
Hezbollah’s rocket and missile stockpiles — mostly short- and medium-range ones — have shrunk from roughly 100,000 to 25,000 since 2023, and drones have proven to be an extremely flexible and effective alternative, well-suited for use by small combat cells operating within a decentralized command structure.
Comparing the active periods of fighting in Lebanon from October to November 2024 and from March to July 2026, Hezbollah’s use of FPV drones for attacks on Lebanese territory rose from 0 to 214 cases (21% of all attacks), and the use of conventional suicide drones rose from 21 cases (6%) to 244 cases (24%).
In attacks on Israeli territory, the use of FPV drones rose from 0 to 16 cases (1% of all attacks), and suicide drones from 176 (14%) to 343 (31%). According to calculations by the Israeli research center Alma, from the announcement of the ceasefire on April 16 through June 21, 2026, Hezbollah carried out more than 1,163 attacks, with 637 involving the use of various drones.
Why the IDF was unprepared for drone warfare
The first serious incident involving Hezbollah drones occurred on Oct. 13, 2024, when a Sayad-107 suicide drone struck a dining hall at a Golani Brigade base in Binyamina. Four soldiers were killed, and more than 50 were injured. The drone approached the target from the Mediterranean Sea, evading detection by Israeli air defense systems. Still, Hezbollah’s systematic shift to FPV drones as a primary weapon is likely linked to the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, which disrupted the supply route of traditional missiles. So far, Israel has not found a reliable answer.
David Gendelman points out that the resulting asymmetry in drone use and countermeasures is explained primarily by organizational differences between the two sides:
“The experience of the Russian-Ukrainian war was studied by both Hezbollah and the Israel Defense Forces. The difference was that Hezbollah, as a relatively small, non-bureaucratic structure, adopts and masters innovations like FPVs quickly and doesn’t need a large quantity right away to start carrying out attacks.
For the IDF, the main issue wasn’t so much adopting FPVs themselves, which was also happening, but countering FPVs. And that is a far more labor-intensive process, because protective measures need to be introduced everywhere, tactics need to be changed everywhere, budgets and man-hours need to be allocated to everyone for this, and time and resources are limited. On top of that, the war has continued on multiple fronts since 2023, diverting resources to other urgent matters. Plus they had to deal with the traditional bureaucracy of regular armies and large organizations in general.
As a result, by the start of the latest war with Hezbollah, the Israeli army had spent several years studying Ukraine’s experience and writing recommendations on implementing the lessons learned, but they had adopted practically none of the tactics against FPVs — and only began doing so once the war had already started.
Hezbollah sporadically used FPVs, including fiber-optic ones, in 2024, and even in this current round of hostilities in 2026 the daily number never exceeded a few dozen — nothing comparable to the thousands per day in Ukraine. But due to poor preparedness, even such a small number led to undesirable losses… And we had to implement rapidly, on the fly, all those measures that the army had included in the guidelines years earlier based on Ukraine’s experience, adapting them to our own conditions given differences in terrain, the theater of operations, the forces and resources of the two sides, and so on.
Protective netting, shotguns, field training for troops, countermeasure tactics, acoustic, optical, and radar warning systems, electronic warfare, and various interception tools — all of this is already being put into practice, but there are limits to what we can speed up. Developing new tools, testing available ones, approval, procurement, distribution, training, deployment — once the decision is made, things move forward, but the decision itself came years too late.”
The FPV drone threat has already resulted in operational changes. Some IDF units have shifted to operating at night, although it is known that militants are trying to equip drones with thermal imaging cameras. No changes are yet apparent at the organizational level.
What’s next
Changes in Hezbollah’s tactics show just how quickly the processes of adoption and adaptation happen in wartime. Just a few years ago, the group relied mainly on unguided rockets, anti-tank guided missiles, and classic fixed-wing drones. Now, their mass use of commercial fiber-optic drones is rendering Israeli electronic warfare countermeasures useless. The cost of these new guided munitions starts at $300–400 per unit, and many components can be 3D-printed on site or sourced from civilian-grade parts.
The conflict in southern Lebanon shows how quickly innovations are adopted during wars
Improvised munitions and a guerrilla-style organization — with drone crews hiding in mountainous terrain or residential areas — pose a challenge to the foundation of Israeli military doctrine, which is built on unconditional technological superiority over neighboring state and non-state military-political actors.
Unlike in Ukraine, in southern Lebanon FPV drones serve as a cheap weapon in a low-intensity war, preventing Israel from establishing stable control over the “buffer zone” it created, and thereby serving as a tool of pressure on Israel both within Lebanon’s domestic context and regionally, in Iran’s interests. By some estimates, there are fewer than 100 trained drone operators in all of southern Lebanon, but even this quantity allows Hezbollah to sustain its activity.
Israel is working on interceptor drones and combined systems based on laser technology and electro-optical systems, along with so-called “smart sights” for firearms that significantly increase the chances of hitting a drone. The IDF, for its part, is procuring multi-pellet ammunition and special anti-drone shotguns as a last line of defense and adopting protective netting based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine. Overall, according to Gendelman’s assessment, due to various constraints Hezbollah will not be able to scale up its use of FPV drones to Ukraine’s level and, as the IDF rolls out various countermeasures, the threat will largely be neutralized. But it will not be eliminated entirely.

Five killed as Amazon cargo plane crashes in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:49:54 UTC
14:49:54 KST

A Prime Air cargo plane is seen at Miami International Airport after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport in Miami, Florida, on Sept. 6, 2026. (Photo by AFP)
At least five people were killed and five others injured when an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport, struck several vehicles and caught fire on Sept. 6, authorities said.
The Boeing 767-300, operated by cargo carrier 21 Air, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it left the runway at around 2 p.m. local time and crossed a nearby road.
Miami-Dade County officials said three of the injured were in critical condition, while the other two sustained less serious injuries. The identities of the victims were not immediately released.
It remained unclear whether those killed were aboard the aircraft or in vehicles hit by the plane.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah said the pilot and co-pilot were trapped in the cockpit following the crash, while several people were also trapped in vehicles. More than 200 emergency personnel responded to the scene.
Images showed the aircraft resting on its belly beside a roadway, with black smoke rising from its largely intact fuselage.
Amazon said it was “heartbroken” by the deaths and would cooperate with the investigation.
The National Transportation Safety Board sent a team to Miami to determine the cause of the crash. Flights at the airport were suspended for several hours following the accident.

Estonia shuts border crossing after 2 Iranian nationals attempt entry from Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

Estonia shuts border crossing after 2 Iranian nationals attempt entry from Russia
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) said Sunday evening it temporarily closed a border crossing in southeast Estonia. The checkpoint has since been reopened.
The PPA said it made the move, at the Luhamaa checkpoint in Võru County, after two Iranian nationals repeatedly tried to enter Estonia without grounds for stay.
"We closed the Luhamaa border crossing earlier than usual today. During the course of today (Sunday – ed.), two Iranian citizens have repeatedly been attempting to enter Estonia from Russia via the Luhamaa border crossing. However, they had no grounds for crossing the border, as both destroyed their travel documents immediately after arriving from Russian territory," the PPA announced.
The pair had continued to attempt to cross the border after being sent back and after Russian authorities were informed of their actions.
"We informed the Russian authorities of the incident, but the Iranian citizens were allowed to continue their attempts to enter Estonia. We consequently temporarily closed the Luhamaa border crossing. The border crossing will remain closed until the Russian Federation has resolved the situation on its side," the PPA statement went on.
Border patrol personnel issued the pair, a man and a woman, with bans on entering Estonia and returned them to the Russian Federation.
Luhamaa and Estonia's other border crossings with the Russian Federation are only open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. The PPA had closed the checkpoint a couple of hours earlier than its regular shutdown time Sunday.
Attempts at illegal immigration by Iranian citizens have reportedly risen since July, prompting an unequivocal response from Estonian authorities to head off eastern border crossings becoming vectors for illegal immigration into the EU.
Editor's note: This piece was updated to note the re-opening of the border crossing at Luhamaa.

KOSGEB offers SMEs loans of up to 30 mln liras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:47:05 UTC
14:47:05 KST

Türkiye’s Small and Medium Enterprises Development Organization (KOSGEB) has opened the third 2026 application round for its Capacity Development Support Program, offering eligible businesses loans of up to 30 million Turkish Liras.
Applications, which opened on Aug. 22, will close on Sept. 15, KOSGEB said.
The program supports investments intended to increase productivity, resilience, production capacity and market reach, as well as projects involving business expansion and digital transformation.
Eligible expenses include machinery, equipment, molds, software, personnel, consultancy, training, certification, testing, marketing, design and working capital linked to an approved project.
The program is open to SMEs operating in manufacturing, telecommunications, computer programming and consultancy, information technology infrastructure, data processing, hosting and research and development.
Applicants must be registered and active in the KOSGEB database, hold an up-to-date business declaration and qualify as a small or medium-sized enterprise.
Businesses are generally required to meet fast-growth criteria. The requirement will not apply to companies holding a Techno-Entrepreneurship Badge or taking part in designated supplier-development partnerships.
The loan ceiling is 20 million liras for fast-growing companies and Techno-Entrepreneurship Badge holders. It rises to 30 million liras for eligible suppliers in the defense, aerospace and space sectors.
Defense projects must hold certification under the Industrial Competence Evaluation and Support Program. Loan ceilings will range from 25 million to 30 million liras depending on the certification level.
Projects may run for 24 months, while loans will have a maturity of 36 months. KOSGEB will cover 20 percentage points of borrowing costs and provide access to guarantees through the Credit Guarantee Fund.
Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the program, launched in 2025, had provided 3,938 SMEs with access to 64 billion liras in financing.

Saudi Arabia in advanced talks to join Türkiye’s KAAN project: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:46:07 UTC
14:46:07 KST

Saudi Arabia is in advanced talks with Türkiye over possible participation in the country’s KAAN fifth-generation fighter jet program, according to a report, as testing of the aircraft’s new prototypes continues.
London-based news outlet The New Arab said Riyadh was exploring ways to join the program, led by Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ). No agreement has yet been announced.
TUSAŞ General Manager Mehmet Demiroğlu said at the World Defense Show in Riyadh in February that long-running talks with Saudi Arabia had been elevated to “the highest level.”
Demiroğlu said the options under discussion ranged from a direct purchase to extensive participation in the program.
The cooperation model would depend on Saudi Arabia’s requirements, planned order and industrial capabilities, he added.
KAAN completed its maiden flight on Feb. 21, 2024.
Its P1 prototype began taxi tests on July 31 as part of ground trials ahead of further flight testing.
Development work is also continuing on the P2 prototype.
The aircraft is being developed with low-observability features, internal weapons bays, advanced mission and sensor systems and electronic warfare capabilities.
TUSAŞ says KAAN is intended to gradually replace the Turkish Air Force’s F-16 fleet beginning in the 2030s.
The program currently relies on U.S.-made General Electric F110 engines, while Türkiye is developing the indigenous TF35000 engine for later versions.
The New Arab said integrating a domestic engine, radar and electronic warfare systems would strengthen Türkiye’s strategic autonomy and improve KAAN’s export prospects.
A potential Saudi partnership could involve procurement, joint production or broader participation in the development program, but the structure of any agreement remains undecided.

AfD wins record vote in Saxony-Anhalt, falls short of majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:46:00 UTC
14:46:00 KST

Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany won a record victory in Sunday’s election in Saxony-Anhalt but fell short of the majority it needed to govern alone, leaving the eastern state facing potentially lengthy negotiations over its next government.
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than doubling its 20.8% showing in the 2021 election and marking its strongest performance in any German state election. It won 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament in Magdeburg, three short of the 42 needed for an outright majority, according to preliminary official results after all ballots were counted.
The result was a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his center-right Christian Democratic Union, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years. The CDU won just 17.2%, its worst result in the state and less than half of the 40 seats it secured in 2021.
The outcome also fell short of the AfD’s goal of securing enough seats to form Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II. Mainstream parties have ruled out forming coalitions with the AfD, meaning the party’s victory does not automatically translate into control of the state government.
"We have achieved exactly what we set out to achieve. We have made history in this country," AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told public broadcaster ARD.
Siegmund, 35, said voters had sent a message that "things cannot carry on like this" and described the result as a signal to the national government in Berlin.
"A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz," Siegmund said. "Every day this man is in the chancellery is one too many."
He said the AfD was prepared to work with politicians who supported its demands for a major change in policy, whether through a parliamentary group or individual lawmakers. If no governing arrangement could be reached, he said, "if necessary, there will just be new elections."
The AfD’s national co-leader, Alice Weidel, called the result "sensational" and said the party had received a clear mandate to govern.
But other parties quickly rejected any prospect of cooperation.
Franziska Hoppermann, the CDU’s national general secretary, said the party would maintain its refusal to work with the AfD.
"AfD is a right-wing extremist party," she said, citing its positions on the euro, Russia and German society. "We will not work with them."
The Social Democrats finished third with 9.3%, followed by the Greens with 8.9% and the Left Party with 8.6%. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, or BSW, won 5.3%, just above the threshold needed to enter parliament. The Free Democrats, who were junior partners in the outgoing state government, received 2.6% and failed to win seats.
The CDU will hold 15 seats, while the Greens, SPD and Left Party each won eight. The BSW will hold five seats.
Those numbers offer no straightforward route to a governing majority. A coalition involving the CDU, SPD and Greens would control 31 seats. Adding the Left Party would bring the total to 39, still three short of a majority.
The AfD could reach the 42-seat threshold only with support from the BSW. The BSW could potentially support an AfD-backed candidate, back a CDU candidate or abstain. Under state election rules, a third vote for governor requires only a plurality, adding another layer of uncertainty to the coalition negotiations.
Party leaders are expected to outline their positions this week, with exploratory talks likely to begin in the coming days.
Saxony-Anhalt, a state of about 2.1 million people west of Berlin, has become one of the AfD’s strongest areas of support. The party is particularly popular in the former communist east, where economic and demographic challenges have fueled discontent with Germany’s political establishment.
The AfD is the largest opposition party in Germany’s national parliament. Its rise has alarmed mainstream political parties, which have maintained a so-called firewall against cooperation with it.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch as a proven right-wing extremist organization. Authorities have cited what they describe as racist and ethnically based views within parts of the party, including hostility toward migrants from Muslim-majority countries.
The AfD rejects accusations of extremism and says the classifications are politically motivated.
The party has campaigned heavily on immigration, including its call for a "remigration" policy involving the deportation of immigrants. Siegmund has made what he calls a "deportation offensive" one of his priorities and has called for ending incentives that he says encourage people to come to Germany and take advantage of its social welfare system.
The party also supports allowing home schooling, which is generally not permitted in Germany, and wants to prevent schools from officially raising the rainbow flag while requiring them to display the German national flag.
On foreign policy, the AfD opposes German support for Ukraine and wants sanctions against Russia lifted, although state governments do not have the authority to determine national foreign policy.
The party has also proposed withdrawing Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about what it describes as disinformation.
The election drew unusually high interest, with turnout reaching 77.8%, compared with 60.3% in 2021. It was the highest turnout in the state since German reunification in 1990.
The result nonetheless leaves the AfD in an unusual position: It has won a commanding share of the vote but remains dependent on other parties it has sharply criticized and that have publicly rejected governing with it.
There has been a recent precedent for an AfD election victory not leading to an AfD-led government. In neighboring Thuringia, the AfD won a state election in 2024 but remained out of government after a CDU-backed minority administration took power.
Saxony-Anhalt’s next government will have significant responsibilities, as Germany’s 16 states oversee areas including education and parts of domestic security. State governments also have seats in the Bundesrat, Germany’s upper house, which must approve certain federal legislation.
Saxony-Anhalt has limited influence there because it controls just four of the Bundesrat’s 69 votes.
For Merz, the election represents another warning about the strength of the far right and a damaging result for a party that has dominated state politics for more than two decades.

Heavy rainfall hit eastern Japan and elsewhere on Monday, with the weather agency urging maximum vigilance against landslides on Niijima and Oshima islands, south of Tokyo, and a woman dying in Iwaki in the northeast after her car became submerged.
The Japan Meteorological Agency issued a special landslide warning for Niijima after more than 480mm (19 inches) of rain fell there over 24 hours, the largest amount since local records began.
Heavy rain also hit eastern Japan including Tokyo from the early hours of Monday, disrupting train services and forcing some school closures. The weather agency issued a Level 4 landslide alert on its five-point scale for parts of Chiba and Saitama prefectures, neighbouring the capital.
The agency also warned that rainbands capable of bringing localised torrential downpours over prolonged periods could develop in the northeastern Tohoku region as a seasonal rain front moved north.
A woman in her sixties was declared dead after being found unresponsive in a submerged car at an underpass in Iwaki, Fukushima prefecture, according to the local fire department.

Witches, tapestries and a suspended horse: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:45:10 UTC
14:45:10 KST

From the museum loan of the century, to the bewitching return of Practical Magic — here's what to look out for this week.
September is in full swing, and we're ringing in the autumn vibes with a line-up of events and new releases that will give you goosebumps.
From the Bayeux Tapestry's first appearance in the UK in nearly 1,000 years, to the provocative works of Maurizio Cattelan, and spellbinding magic of Practical Magic 2, this week's offerings conjure all kinds of wonder and awe.
There's also the release of indie band Bloc Party's new album, along with a new teen drama Netflix show that calls for evenings spent snuggled under blankets — hot drink in hand, remote in the other.
Keep scrolling to find out more.
Exhibitions and events
Maurizio Cattelan: Night
When: 10 September - 7 March 2027
Where: Neue Nationalgalerie (Berlin, Germany)
Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan has become a mischief maker within the art world. From his banana duct-taped to a wall, to a child-sized statue of Hitler in prayer, to an 18-karat gold (and fully functional) toilet that was installed at the Guggenheim — his creations have proven polarising, but also often funny, inspiring, and always challenging. One particular theme that runs throughout his career is the tensions between innocence and violence, and how we balance our identities with the collective discomfort of historical memories. This is the focus of the Neue Nationalgalerie's latest exhibition, which brings together some of Cattelan's most seminal works, along with new and never-before-seen commissions. Find out more here.
The Bayeux Tapestry
When: 10 September - 11 July 2027
Where: British Museum (London, UK)
Nearly 1,000 years ago, the Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux. It has not been seen in Britain since — until now.
Following an unprecedented agreement with France, the 70-metre-long tapestry, which depicts the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings and Normal Conquest of England in 1066, has been transferred to the British Museum. It's a once in a lifetime event that allows visitors to see in person a piece of astonishing medieval history; a representation of one of, if not the most, defining moments of the England's past. It's also estimated to have cost the UK around €20 million to transport and exhibit the tapestry — a worthy investment judging by the ticket sales so far. Find out more here.
Bonus highlight: Timeless Tintoretto, a showcase of the works of Jacomo Robusti, opens at the Musée Jacquemart-André in Paris on 11 September.
Movies
Practical Magic 2
Where: Cinemas
When: 11 September
Midnight margaritas, anyone? The iconic Owen's sisters (Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman) are back — 28 years after they first appeared on screen in what has become a cosy classic among Halloween-loving Millennials. The plot centres around a centuries-old family curse: Any man the witches fall in love with is doomed to die. While seemingly broken by collective love at the end of the first movie, the sequel grapples with its seeming return, as Sally's (Bullock) daughters reckon with its consequences and the emergence of their own powers. Based on Alice Hoffman's The Book of Magic, it's a return to that nostalgic '90s fall feeling — suburban streets, candlelit laughter, black cats in lap — and a cinematic world where whimsy and women rule.
To find out more about other upcoming movie releases this autumn, take a look at our preview list here.
Bonus highlight: A new documentary about Britpop band Oasis, Don't Look Back in Anger, is released on 11 September. Stay tuned for our full review later this week.
TV series
Crew Girl
Where: Netflix
When: 10 September
Netflix's new sports drama follows a teenage elite rower named Teagan Tao (Miku Martineau), who relocates to a small town with her mother following a family scandal. However, after joining an all-boys varsity crew as their coxswain, she finds herself in even more uncharted waters: navigating being an outsider, school rivalries, romantic dramas and the strain of emotional grief. A throwback to teen dramas of the late 2000s/early 2010s, it's perfect binge-watch material as the colder nights set in.
Bonus highlight: A police dispatcher (Patrick Brammall) sets out on an all-consuming quest to find his missing daughter in Apple TV+'s compelling new drama, Last Seen. Stream from 9 September.
Music
Bloc Party: Anatomy of a Brief Romance
When: 10 September
The seventh studio album from British indie band Bloc Party arrives after an almost 4 and a half year hiatus, which followed their polarising last, release 'Alpha Games'. A lot has happened in that time — especially in frontman Kele Okereke's life. After his 11 year relationship ended, he began a whirlwind romance with someone else, the intensity of which forms the crux of the band's latest songwriting. From the percussive punchiness of 'Coming on Strong' to the jittery harmonies of 'Love Bombs', each track takes listeners through the highs and lows of falling for someone: from excitable infatuation to crushing disappointment to difficult but necessary realisations.
To find out more about other upcoming albums this autumn, take a look at our preview list here.
Bonus highlight: British musician Simon Charles Green, who goes by the stage name Bonobo, releases his eighth studio album on 11 September, 'Distance in Static'.

South Korea's ruling party Monday called for strengthening the country's "independent" security capabilities, citing the possibility of a shift toward a "freeze-first" approach to the nuclear weapons program of longtime rival North Korea.
Kim Min-seok, the leader of the Democratic Party, made the call in his policy address to the National Assembly session, Seoul-based Yonhap News reported.
"The days when South Korea could depend solely on the United States are over," Kim said, adding that Washington is choosing to become "a tough negotiating partner rather than a generous big brother."
His remarks follow a series of recent US moves, including President Donald Trump's decision to scale back joint military drills with Seoul.
Kim emphasized the need for Seoul to facilitate dialogue between the US and North Korea.
"Considering the possibility that the United States and North Korea may achieve a dramatic improvement in relations and if by any chance, a 'freeze-first, resolve-later' approach could be adopted on the North Korean nuclear issue, South Korea must strengthen its independent security capabilities in advance," he said.
Kim added that South Korea should consider whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's "two-state" policy could be used to promote peaceful coexistence rather than dismissing it entirely.
Last month, Trump expressed his intention to meet Kim later this year and ordered the scaling back of a major South Korea-US exercise.
Trump also argued that the allies' drills are costly and can send a "totally inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang.

China may have secretly supplied Russia with components for attack drones - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
Jilin Chemical Fiber Group may have supplied Russia with 46 tonnes of carbon chemicals for the production of attack drones. The US and Ukraine confirmed the authenticity of the documents.
The Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group may have secretly supplied Russia with materials necessary for the production of kamikaze drones. This is evidenced by internal documents of a Russian company concerning shipments, obtained by Politico, reports UNN.
Details
According to transportation and customs documents, at the beginning of 2026, the Chinese company disguised the delivery of 46 tons of carbon-fiber-based chemicals to a subsidiary of Russia’s "Rosatom." The subsidiary, among other things, produces key components for kamikaze drones.
Politico notes that Chinese components have long been found in Russian drones shot down in Ukraine. At the same time, the new documents describe in detail for the first time the direct delivery of materials essential for UAV production from China to Russia.
The United States and Ukraine confirmed the authenticity of the supply documents
The documents from Russian sources were collected by the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation. According to a U.S. government representative, the U.S. House Select Committee on China examined them and deemed them "authentic."
A Ukrainian official also told the publication that the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine had examined the documents and confirmed their authenticity.
It is noted that "the Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group did not respond to numerous requests for comment."

A massive fire at a market in the village of Babuda in Indonesia’s Central Papua province has claimed the lives of eleven people, six of them children. The fire spread from the market to surrounding buildings destroying around 40 homes and shops.

Ukraine marks Military Intelligence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:37:00 UTC
14:37:00 KST

Ukraine marks Military Intelligence Day
According to Ukrinform, Ukraine's Military Intelligence Day was established by a presidential decree on September 7, 2022.
It is observed annually on September 7.
The holiday recognizes the important role military intelligence plays in protecting the country's national interests. In the challenging conditions of open aggression, Ukraine needs effective and proactive intelligence capable of providing timely, objective and reliable intelligence, as well as accurate assessments to help the country's leadership make important national security decisions.
Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi congratulated military intelligence personnel on their professional holiday.
"Dear military intelligence officers! Brothers in arms! You are the first to see what the enemy tries to hide. Your intelligence forms the basis of commanders' decisions, and the lives of others depend on its accuracy. I know the value of this work. There is no room for chance in it," Drapatyi said.
According to him, most of what intelligence officers do will never become public, and that is precisely the price of their profession – a price that cannot be measured in awards.
Drapatyi thanked intelligence officers for work that often goes unseen, but without which there would be no success on the battlefield.

Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:36:24 UTC
14:36:24 KST

Sydney captain Callum Mills will miss the remainder of this year's finals campaign and the majority of next season as scans confirmed an ACL tear in his right knee.
Mills hurt his knee in the first quarter of Sydney's 53-point win over Brisbane on Saturday afternoon.
What's next?
Mills is set to meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.
The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.
Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.
Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.
Loading Twitter content
Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.
It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.
Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.
This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.
The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.
Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.
Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.
Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.
Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.
Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

Rain continues in Latvia, monthly precipitation norm already exceeded in many areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:36:24 UTC
14:36:24 KST

Although the new week will begin with slightly drier weather, with rain expected only in some areas and lighter winds, conditions will change from Tuesday afternoon as new cyclones strengthen their influence. Rain will spread across a wider area, while winds along the coast will become gusty. The weather will remain relatively warm, with daytime temperatures reaching +16°C to +21°C, according to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
On Monday, the 7th of September, skies will be partly cloudy. Brief rain is expected in some areas overnight, with locally heavy downpours and thunderstorms also possible. From midday onwards, clouds will continue to bring rain in places. During the night and early morning, fog will thicken in some areas, mainly in the west, reducing visibility.
Light to moderate westerly winds will prevail. Overnight temperatures will range from +8°C to +11°C, with warmer conditions along the coast at +11°C to +16°C. During the day, temperatures will reach +16°C to +21°C.
On Tuesday, sunny spells will alternate with clouds, bringing rain to some areas overnight and to many western regions in the afternoon. Fog will develop in places during the night and morning, mainly in eastern areas.
Light to moderate southerly and south-westerly winds will prevail, becoming gusty along the coast during the day.
Overnight temperatures will fall to +10°C to +14°C, while the far eastern regions will be cooler at +8°C to +10°C. Daytime temperatures will rise to +18°C to +22°C.
On Wednesday, cloud cover will increase, with sunshine appearing only occasionally. Rain is expected across many areas overnight and in some places during the day. Winds will continue to blow from the south and south-west, with gusts reaching up to 14 m/s along the Gulf of Riga coast overnight. Temperatures on Wednesday night will remain between +13°C and +17°C, while daytime temperatures will reach +17°C to +22°C.
For the remainder of the working week, Latvia’s weather will continue to be influenced by cyclonic activity. New precipitation zones will cross the country, while winds will become gusty on some days. Temperatures are not expected to change significantly and will remain broadly similar to those recorded at the beginning of the week.

Ukraine’s Experience in Insurance Supervision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

Ukraine’s European integration has been accompanied by a profound transformation of its financial sector. One of the key areas of reform has been the introduction of risk-based insurance supervision and modern standards of financial regulation.
Zhanna Dryha, doctor of Economic Sciences and professor in the Department of Law, Public Management and Administration at Zhytomyr Polytechnic, combines academic research with practical experience in the insurance sector and financial regulation. She beings a particular focus on insurance reserves, internal control, risk management, and emerging AI-based supervisory tools.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, she discusses Ukraine’s transition to risk-based insurance supervision, the importance of reliable data and internal controls, and how her research on insurance reserves has evolved into a broader framework for financial regulation and AI governance.
Kyiv Post: You have more than 20 years of professional experience in insurance and financial regulation, and since 2011 your research has focused on insurance regulation, internal control, and risk management. During this time, the financial sector has changed dramatically. In your view, what has become the main challenge for modern financial regulation?
Zhanna Dryha: Over the past 20 years, the financial sector has changed more rapidly than in many previous decades. Digitalization, artificial intelligence, automated financial services, and digital assets have significantly expanded the capabilities of financial institutions while also creating new risks. That is why the key issue today is not simply the adoption of new technologies, but the ability to ensure effective risk management, robust internal controls, and trust in the financial system. These are the issues at the core of my research.
China Lures Russia’s Far East Firms With Cheap 3% Loans
Today, the Ukrainian insurance market is undergoing one of its most sweeping reforms. What has fundamentally changed, and why are these changes important, not only for Ukraine but also for European integration?
Zhanna Dryha: We are talking about a transition from formal compliance with regulatory requirements to a risk-based model in which insurance reserves are treated as economic obligations that must be appropriately assessed, verified, and backed by assets of sufficient quality. NBU Resolution No. 157 details requirements for insurers’ governance systems, internal control, internal audit, and accounting for insurance contracts. The significance of these changes can be viewed from three perspectives:
The first is political. Ukraine has committed to carrying out institutional reforms, increasing transparency, and implementing modern mechanisms of financial regulation as part of its cooperation with the EU, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and other international partners. The fewer the opportunities for manipulation, the greater the confidence of international financial institutions and investors.
The second is economic. Insurance serves as an essential component of the risk-management infrastructure. If insurance reserves exist only formally and are not backed by high-quality assets, the risk of non-performance is ultimately transferred to policyholders, businesses, and the state, reducing the country’s financial stability and investment attractiveness.
The third is technological. Reliable, verifiable, and traceable data form the foundation of modern financial supervision. Without such data, the digitalization of the financial sector, the automation of control procedures, and the secure integration of artificial intelligence into financial regulation, risk management, and supervisory processes are impossible.
You describe risk-based regulation as a modern supervisory model, yet your research began long before the current reforms – almost 15 years earlier. How did it all start? Did your experience working at UNIQA serve as the starting point for your research?
That’s correct. This research began with my practical work in the insurance sector, where I saw that an insurer’s reliability depends not only on the size of its insurance reserves, but also on the quality of the assets backing them, the effectiveness of internal controls, and coordination among actuaries, finance professionals, and internal auditors. This led me to view insurance reserves not as an isolated accounting issue, but as part of a broader system of risk management and financial stability.
At the time, professional practice lacked comprehensive methodologies for simultaneously assessing asset quality, liquidity, risk concentration, compliance with insurance obligations, and internal control effectiveness. This methodological gap prompted the research program I have developed since 2011 in insurance reserves, risk management, and internal audit.
At what point did this research extend beyond insurance and become the foundation of your academic and teaching activities?
Zhanna Dryha: My research on insurance reserves formed the basis of my PhD dissertation, “Accounting and Internal Control of Transactions Involving Insurance Reserves,” which I defended in 2014 at Kyiv National Economic University (KNEU). As the research progressed, it became clear that insurance reserves were closely linked to risk management, asset quality, internal control, internal audit, and the financial stability of non-bank financial institutions.
I therefore continued this work at Zhytomyr Polytechnic State University, where it was further developed in my doctoral dissertation, “Accounting, Analysis, and Audit of the Activities of Non-Bank Financial Institutions in a Risk Environment.” My university work since 2016 allowed me to transform practical observations into a coherent research program, expand my teaching activities, and establish a distinct research direction integrating accounting, internal control, auditing, risk management, and financial regulation.
Over the years, your research framework has evolved through more than 70 scientific publications, five monographs, and a series of original methodologies. How has this framework developed, and which result do you consider the most significant?
The central result of my academic work has been the development of a comprehensive risk-based framework for accounting, internal control, and internal audit built around the analysis and management of risks associated with insurance reserves. I later expanded this framework by integrating forensic early-warning mechanisms, creating a broader system aimed at strengthening insurers’ financial stability.
This framework has been incorporated into teaching materials for approximately 15 academic disciplines and translated into a series of original methodologies, certain elements of which have been registered as works protected by copyright. It also provides a methodological basis for the safe integration of artificial intelligence and digital assets into the governance, internal control, and financial regulation of non-bank financial institutions.
Many of the ideas you developed appear to have preceded elements of the National Bank of Ukraine’s current risk-based model. To what extent is that the case?
The foundations of this research direction took shape between 2011 and 2014 and formed the basis of my PhD dissertation. Even at that stage, my research developed risk-based approaches to the assessment of insurance reserves, actuarial verification, asset quality, and internal control. These findings were developed and published before the current reform of insurance supervision, and corresponding principles were later reflected in the requirements of the National Bank of Ukraine concerning the assessment of insurance liabilities, the quality and diversification of assets, internal control, and audit.
One practical outcome of this stage was the QLDCR (Quality–Liquidity–Diversification–Counterparty Risk) model, designed for the comprehensive assessment of the quality of assets backing insurance reserves.
Between 2016 and 2021, I continued to develop this research direction as part of my doctoral research. This led to the IAEAS (Internal Audit Effectiveness Assessment System) methodology for assessing the effectiveness of internal audit within a risk-based management system, followed by the FEWS (Forensic Early Warning System) methodology, which integrated accounting, internal control, internal audit, actuarial assessment, forensic analysis, risk management, and prudential supervision to support the early detection of financial manipulation and threats to insurers’ financial stability.
In preparing my Regulatory Note in response to the NBU Discussion Paper on the responsible use of artificial intelligence, I applied my original AI-PRIC (Artificial Intelligence Prudential Risk Integration and Compliance Methodology), which integrates AI into corporate governance, risk management, internal control, internal audit, and prudential compliance. Together with my other methodologies, AI-PRIC has been registered as a work protected by copyright, providing documentary evidence of my authorship.
Your early research focused on insurance reserves, while today you work on AI governance. How did this transition occur?
The transition was a natural extension of the same research framework. My early work examined how reliable data, asset quality, internal controls, and audit mechanisms can identify and mitigate financial risks. As financial institutions became increasingly digital, these same issues extended to automated decision-making and artificial intelligence.
AI-based supervision depends on data discipline – completeness, quality, structure, clear accountability, and audit trails. NBU Resolution No. 157 and related regulatory changes help establish this foundation, enabling tools such as automated detection of anomalies in reserves, concentration monitoring, identification of risk patterns in claims, and continuous auditing. My methodologies demonstrate how regulatory data, internal audit, and early-warning technologies can be integrated into a unified digital supervision framework.
We often talk about drawing on international experience. Could Ukraine’s experience also be relevant to international insurance companies and regulators?
Ukraine provides a relevant case study of how risk-based regulation can be implemented amid heightened uncertainty and rapid institutional change. The methodological approaches I developed for insurance reserves, internal audit, and risk management have been applied in professional settings involving international companies and organizations, including UNIQA, UNIVERSALNA, part of Fairfax Financial Holdings, and BDO, while Chubb has expressed interest in their further development.
These approaches are not limited to a single jurisdiction. They can be adapted by international insurance groups and financial regulators seeking to strengthen financial stability, transparency, and the reliability of controls. Ukraine’s ongoing regulatory reform therefore offers not only practical experience but also solutions that may be transferable across jurisdictions.
If we were to look back on your work 10 years from now, what would you like to see as your main legacy – academic publications, trained professionals, or practical changes to insurance supervision?
I would not separate these outcomes. For me, scholarly impact occurs when an idea moves beyond a publication, is applied in practice, developed through further research, and carried forward by other specialists. That is how a lasting research tradition develops.
Together with international colleagues, we founded GIDAFS (Global Institute for Digital Assets, Financial Security, and Public Governance), bringing together scholars and practitioners from the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and Ukraine in financial security, financial regulation, internal audit, risk management, digital assets, and AI governance.
In 2026, at the International Consortium on Governmental Financial Management (ICGFM) conference in the United States, I presented my approach to managing AI risks in financial monitoring. I subsequently further developed this work in expert recommendations submitted to the National Bank of Ukraine in response to its discussion paper on the responsible use of artificial intelligence in the financial market.
These areas share one objective: protecting the financial security of users of financial services. I believe individual financial security contributes to the stability of financial institutions and, ultimately, national financial security. In 10 years, I would like to see my research-based solutions applied in practice and further developed by other specialists to strengthen financial security and the resilience of the financial system.

Facing a criminal case over an anti-war post, hospice founder Lida Moniava says she’ll leave the Lighthouse Charity Foundation’s leadership but not Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:35:12 UTC
14:35:12 KST

Facing a criminal case over an anti-war post, hospice founder Lida Moniava says she’ll leave the Lighthouse Charity Foundation’s leadership but not Russia
Lida Moniava will step down as director of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation, which operates a children’s hospice, and leave its board, according to a post published by her friends on her Telegram channel.
“I will have to step down as director of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation and leave the board. But I believe my colleagues will be able to keep the hospice running without me,” Moniava’s friends wrote on her behalf. Moniava herself is barred from using the internet.
Moniava said the investigation into her case will continue for the next couple of months before the case goes to trial. For now, she said, there are still “a few months of life left to finish things up and try to put arrangements in place at the Lighthouse Charity Foundation so that the hospice can keep running without me.”
Moniava said (through her friends):
I’m getting a lot of advice to leave the country. I understand that everyone is worried about me and wants me to be okay. It’s very hard to upset everyone like this, but I’m still not going to leave Russia. I can’t really explain this except from a Christian perspective. I understand all the risks: I’ve been through a 6 a.m. search, shivered in a gloomy cell, spent time in handcuffs, done squats naked in front of officers of Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service, and been bounced around on a bench in a prison van with a vomit bag in hand. Now I live with an ankle monitor. But it really matters to me to stay in Russia during this difficult time.
Lida Moniava was detained on September 2 on charges of spreading “fake news” about the Russian military. The criminal case was prompted by a post on her Telegram channel published in February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The post read: “For a year now, my country has been sending missiles, tanks, and soldiers to Ukraine. For a year now, innocent people have been dying because of it.”
After spending a night in a temporary detention facility, Moniava was brought to court, where a judge imposed restrictions on her activities while the case is pending. The court barred Moniava, a co-founder of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation, from going outside between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., communicating with witnesses, and using the internet.
