Exclusive: MEPs on track to end article 7 'nuclear option' against Hungary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

MEPs are on course to end the long-standing measure, which was introduced over alleged violations of EU values under Viktor Orbán’s government. A mission to Hungary in October would assess the progress of Péter Magyar’s administration, with a final decision expected in early 2027.
The European Parliament is on track to end the long-running Article 7 procedure, the EU’s so-called “nuclear option" against Hungary, which was launched in 2018 over concerns about violations of EU values under then-prime minister Viktor Orbán.
With Péter Magyar now leading the Hungarian government, the country is revising several laws dating back to the Orbán era, prompting the Parliament to reconsider its position, according to several MEPs and officials who spoke to Euronews.
“Hungary has completed many reforms that bring the country into closer alignment with the EU," said a senior MEP from the European People’s Party (EPP), the Parliament’s largest political group. "I see it as reasonable that the procedure ends soon, and I hope it will,” he added.
The EPP is among the political forces prepared to push for the withdrawal of Article 7, in a bid to secure a political victory for Magyar’s Tisza party, which is a member of the party.
The Article 7 procedure is an exceptional measure that can ultimately strip a country of its voting rights if a serious breach of EU values is established. MEPs triggered it against Hungary in 2018, citing concerns over judicial independence, corruption, media freedom and fundamental rights, as well as the rights of minorities and migrants.
A fact-finding mission to Hungary is planned for late October, with meetings scheduled with institutions, stakeholders, authorities and NGOs to gain a comprehensive picture of the rule of law situation in the country.
MEPs taking part in the mission will then draft a report and are expected to recommend withdrawing the procedure if they conclude that EU values are no longer being violated. Some Parliament officials say this could happen as soon as December, while Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, who is leading the file, expects the report to be ready in early 2027.
“There is a whole checklist with criteria which we will assess: one of the elements is the withdrawal of the anti LGBTI+ law,” she told Euronews.
Strik referred to a controversial piece of legislation on minors' protection which restricts children’s access to books, films and other content promoting or depicting a deviation from biological sex, gender transition or homosexuality.
So far, the Hungarian government has not repealed the law, nor has it announced its willingness to do so.
The final decision to withdraw the procedure requires a two-thirds majority, meaning at least 480 of the Parliament’s 719 lawmakers must vote in favour of ending it.
Left-wing groups such as the Greens and The Left could oppose the withdrawal, while conservatives and far-right forces are expected to back it, having consistently viewed Article 7 as an unwarranted intrusion into national politics. The European Conservatives and Reformists, Patriots for Europe and Europe of Sovereign Nations together account for almost 200 MEPs.
With the EPP’s 184 lawmakers likely to back the move, the centrist Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and liberal Renew Europe groups will be crucial to the decision. Both acknowledge Hungary’s progress but stress the need for a thorough assessment that takes into account the full body of legislation.
Renew will discuss the issue at its first meeting of the new parliamentary season in Paris next week, MEP Sandro Gozi told Euronews.
“The end of the procedure should be based on real changes; otherwise we give the impression it is just a political decision,” he said.
The procedure has been triggered only twice in the EU’s history: by the Commission against Poland in 2017 and by the European Parliament against Hungary the following year. In neither case has it reached the sanctions stage, which requires unanimous support from EU member states to suspend a country’s voting rights.
The procedure against Poland was closed in 2024, after a coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk replaced the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) government, bringing the country back in line with the Commission's requests on judicial independence.

As assisted dying bill returns to Commons, families recall loved ones’ battle to ‘go out on own terms’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The feeling, said Sarah Burns of her sister’s last days, is one of overwhelming guilt.
“You feel really guilty, and helpless,” she says. “Because we knew what she wanted. We really did know. But we couldn’t do anything.”
When time eventually ran out for Elise Burns, a 52-year-old woman who worked in publishing, the circumstances were “absolutely her worst nightmare”. Initially treated for breast cancer and subsequently diagnosed with terminal secondary cancer, which had spread to her liver, lungs and bones, Elise had campaigned passionately for the assisted dying bill, daring the peers who ensured it ran out of time to “look me in the eye”.
As part of the Dignity in Dying campaign, she was one of eight terminally ill people who appealed directly to MPs in powerful videos, filmed by the world renowned British photographer and director Rankin.
She died on 22 July – the second of the eight terminally ill people who featured in the Rankin videos, which were filmed in May, to go. The first, Keith Williams, a 77-year-old former welder who became a social worker, died of lung cancer on 16 June, having also been denied, according to his son, his desperate wish to “go out on my own terms”.
The controversial bill, reintroduced by Lauren Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, returns to the Commons for a second reading on 11 September. Andy Burnham has already said he will not vote to avoid influencing the emotional debate.
Burns will be at the Commons, carrying the baton for her sister, who was from Faversham, and was one of the last people Edwards heard from before reviving Kim Leadbeater’s private member’s bill, bringing it back to parliament after it foundered under the weight of hundreds of amendments by peers in the Lords.
“I would simply like the chance to put a human dying face to what this debate really means for terminally ill people like me,” Elise Burns wrote to Edwards. “For me this is not about politics or ideology, it’s about dignity, compassion and the possibility of having some choice at the end of life.”
After her secondary cancer diagnosis, Elise wanted to “live life to the full” but also started talking seriously about Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic. “She said all along ‘I do not want a painful death’. And literally every day was painful,” said her sister.
In the end, the speed of events deprived her of that choice. At the beginning of July, just two months after shooting her Rankin video, she developed an infection and was hospitalised. Sixteen days later, she was moved to a hospice, dying two days later.
“The hospice was incredible, trying to make her as comfortable as possible, all the time,” said Burns. “But legally there is only so much they can do. They all knew her wishes.”
The family were left feeling utterly helpless.
More than 100 cross-party peers have written to MPs urging them to send the bill back to the House of Lords so that it can complete its passage through parliament.
The signatories, including the former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell, the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson, said the upper house’s failure to pass the legislation in the previous session had let terminally ill people and their families down and blocked a measure which had public support.
They accused a minority of peers who had opposed the backbench bill of filibustering after hundreds of amendments tabled by just seven opponents meant it ran out of time.
They wrote: “As even opponents of the principle of assisted dying in the Lords have acknowledged, the elected chamber has every right to ask us to do this. The overwhelming majority of the public – who vote for you but do not vote for us – expect the same.
“And the many terminally ill people and their families who are depending on parliament to pass this long overdue change to the law should not be asked to wait any longer than absolutely necessary for us to come to a decision.”
Marc Williams, Keith Williams’ son, has written directly to Burnham, describing the circumstances surrounding the death of his father, who was a committed campaigner for the bill.
“Dad could have chosen to fly to Switzerland to end his life, but he would have needed to go in November to ensure that he was still fit enough to be able to travel and to endure the loneliest journey imaginable,” Williams, a civil servant, told the prime minister. For the “dignified death” he sought, his father “would have been forced to end his life prematurely”.
Keith Williams, who was a canoeing instructor from Tonyrefail, the Rhondda, was diagnosed in 2023 with prostate cancer and undergoing radiotherapy, which left him with distressing long-term side effects. Last October, he was diagnosed with lung cancer and pulmonary fibrosis. He died on 16 June.
“Dad had some red lines. He wanted to die at home. He was: ‘I want to go out on my own terms. I am desperate to go out on my own terms at home.’”
He shot the Rankin video in early May. Within days he was in hospital struggling to breathe. On returning home, his wife, who suffers from arthritis, was now physically unable to care for him, “much as she wanted to”, said Williams. He was moved to a hospice and died the following week.
“He wasn’t just in pain,” his son said. “He was suffocating to death. The pain, they could give him medication for, but no one could breathe for him.”
Four days from death, a physiotherapist gave him a pint of water and two straws, telling him to exercise his lungs by blowing through the straws, said Marc. “He was four days away from dying! It was ridiculous.”
“He didn’t want any of that. He was ready a long time before that to say goodbye and have his peace.” His children and grandchildren could do nothing but sit and watch him deteriorate because “there is nothing you can do”.
His father was “chuffed to bits” about the bill being back. “Because he wanted it for us,” said Williams. “Obviously it was too late for him, but that’s what he wanted all along, for other people.”

  Additional reporting by Pippa Crerar

Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously? | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The gap between what is being inflicted on Palestinians and the appropriate reaction on the part of the international community has always been vast. But now it yawns so wide that it swallows reality itself. As arms export licences for Israel from states such as Germany surge, talk of harsher measures and sanctions on the part of other European countries remains talk. People continue to be killed in Gaza, Palestinian families remain besieged in the West Bank, and the Israeli political right has been removing all doubt that these violations are intentional, by telling the world of its hopes and plans.
A sample from only the past few days. On Thursday, Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, detailed a scheme for the illegal ethnic cleansing of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip. He also posted an AI-generated video, now deleted, of Palestinian men entering a conveyor belt into detention, emerging emaciated and tearful. Also a few days ago, the defence minister, Israel Katz, stated that the country was “organised and prepared” to expel Palestinians from Gaza “by every way possible”.
This macabre theatre continues to unfold, its performances less plausible by the day. The Board of Peace promises Gaza will be “redeveloped for the benefit” of its people, while the notion that those same Palestinians in Gaza cannot be allowed to thrive is expressed by Israeli politicians with consistency and a frequency that makes a mockery of the declarations. Last month, the former head of Israel’s national security council, Giora Eiland, pointed out the fact that Israel’s acceptance of Donald Trump’s 15-point plan was a matter of temporary military tactics, rather than long-term peace. “Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt, it’s better for us that it be destroyed for generations to come,” he said.
Moshe Feiglin, previously a “far-right outcast” according to the Times of Israel, is now within reach of a cabinet position as a result of an alliance with the finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party. In a recent interview, Feiglin said that those who didn’t want to leave Gaza should be compelled to by “every way possible. We’ll shut off his water pipes, for example.”
This sort of talk, from within the very ranks of government, is often dismissed as unrepresentative of the Israeli state and, as there are elections ahead, is written off as the lurid but ultimately unserious rhetoric of electioneering. But people such as Ben-Gvir and Katz are not fringe voices, they are ministers with high-impact executive briefs – security and defence – that they have indeed used to push policy that matches their statements.
Ben-Gvir has reopened the underground Rakefet prison, one closed in the 1980s for being inhumane. He has successfully pushed for the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of terror attacks, and celebrated the legislation with a noose-themed cake. Torture and sexual abuse in Israeli prisons are widely documented, the latter earning Israel a spot on the UN’s sexual violence in war zones blacklist. As Ben-Gvir himself is fond of saying, “we promised, we delivered”.
Katz has approved the biggest settlement expansion in the West Bank in decades and justified the move on the grounds that it “prevents the establishment of a Palestinian state that would endanger Israel”; he recently advanced legalisation of outpost settlement farms in the West Bank, and instructed the IDF to hand over law enforcement in the West Bank to the Israeli police, which is a stealth move towards annexation.
As the Knesset member Ahmad Tibi wrote in Haaretz earlier this year, a fiction exists at the heart of Israeli politics, where politicians’ efforts to explain and justify policy to international opinion proceed as though “the racism and extremism now driving government policy exist only on the margins”. When really, it lies at the heart of the state.
And if some of the more extreme statements are just electioneering, what does that say about the parameters of discourse in the country if your campaign is mass ethnic cleansing? What does that say about not only the future of Gaza, but all Palestinians in occupied territories who are labouring under home demolitions, militant settlers and the de facto annexation of the West Bank?
Even if these figures are a minority, both in terms of the seats held in the Knesset and the relative number of people who have voted for them, they still hold the levers of power, there is no substantial domestic mobilisation against them, and the rest of the system is unable or unwilling to stop them. The distinctions around how big their constituency may be or how representative they are of Israelis in general matters not a jot to the fate of Palestinians over whom they have been given executive dominion.
The question now is, why are these people not being taken at their word? Why is there no sense of urgency and outrage. Why are these policies and stated goals from the Israeli state not taken seriously and met with appropriate sanctions, trade and arms embargos, and international censure? There is a wild asymmetry when it comes to the perceived potency of Israeli rhetoric and action. “From the river to sea”, for example, as expressed by Palestinians and their supporters has become stigmatised and its use censured. But the most extreme interpretation of that phrase, that it means only one sovereign people in the mentioned land, is commonplace in Israel.
The founding charter of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party states that “between the sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty”. Netanyahu himself last week attended a gathering at a religious-Zionist yeshiva, nodding along to a Kahanist song belted out by the attenders. “Remember me, please, give me strength just this time, O God, to take revenge, if only for one of my two eyes, on Palestine,” they sang, adding “May their name be erased!” “There are no more red lines,” was how a Haaretz writer described the scene.
The international community has averted its eyes as red lines are trampled over. This can only be a combination of cowardice and acceptance, barely obscured by feeble statements of condemnation here and there, and grounded in the belief or resignation that Palestinian lives shall be consigned to hell. The facts are clear and plentiful. The Israeli right has a plan and a sense of direction, one that it has nursed for a very long time, and now given nourishment by the 7 October attacks.
Some may not be realisable (ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza is limited by the fact there are no countries that can or will receive them), but much of it is. The direction of travel is clear and there have been some huge successes so far. There is a line connecting the hundreds of thousands of Palestinians expelled or forced to flee in 1948 and today. The security and carceral state that Palestinians exist in, the destruction of their homes and infrastructure, the settlement and fracturing of their territories, and the extension of Israeli sovereignty over them in ways that dehumanise and oppress, all serve to ensure that a future in which Palestinians are free, let alone thriving in self-governance, never emerges.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Starwatch: Waning crescent moon gets close to brilliant beacon of Jupiter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

Those already out and about at 5am this week will be rewarded with a beautiful waning crescent moon approaching Jupiter, while Mars watches on from a little further away.
The chart shows the view looking east from London at 5am on Tuesday. The waning moon will be easily visible with about 10% of its visible surface illuminated. The brilliant beacon of Jupiter will be close by. The two are drawing together ahead of a conjunction later that day when the moon will pass less than a degree north of the giant planet. For comparison, the moon appears to be about half a degree wide in the sky.
Unfortunately, the conjunction itself takes place at 7.11pm, after both objects have set from the UK. The following morning offers another opportunity, with the moon now on the other side of Jupiter.
Mars adds to the scene. Look upwards and to the west and the red planet will be identifiable because of its colour. Mars lies in Gemini, while the moon and Jupiter are in neighbouring Cancer.
From the southern hemisphere the pairing is also visible before dawn, with the moon and Jupiter generally appearing higher in the morning sky.

Cheese pie, seed crackers and prawn rolls: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for cooking with filo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

I love this gossamer-thin pastry for its lightness and crunch, not least because it can be used for both sweets and savouries. Once, on a trip to Athens, I learned how to make filo from scratch: it needs to be rolled very, very thin, so, unless you are skilled with a rolling pin, it’s hard and time-consuming. Luckily there are good ready-made varieties out there (if you’re using the frozen variety, make sure it’s fully defrosted). And always keep the pastry you are not working with under a damp cloth, because it dries out very quickly and will probably crack.
Cheese and spring onion pie (pictured top)
This boasts four varieties of cheese and a ruffly top of crisp, golden filo that requires no complicated technique.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 1 hr, plus cooling
 Serves 6
300g feta, crumbled
250g firm ricotta, crumbled
200g halloumi, grated
150g gruyere or a sharp cheddar, grated 
150ml single cream
  3 eggs
  25g chives, finely chopped
25g dill, finely chopped
25g flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
1 large bunch spring onions (8-10), trimmed and finely sliced
Finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
Nutmeg
  Sea salt and black pepper
  125g butter, melted 
8 sheets filo
  Sesame seeds, to scatter
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. In a large bowl, combine the cheeses, cream, eggs, herbs, spring onion, lemon zest and a good grating of nutmeg, then season to taste.
Line the base of a 20-23cm cake tin with baking paper and grease the sides with melted butter. Lay a sheet of pastry in the bottom of the tin, allowing the excess to hang over the sides. Brush generously with butter, then lay on another sheet of pastry at a slight angle, so it doesn’t completely overlap the first sheet, and brush that with butter, too. Repeat until you have six filo sheets covering the base and sides of the tin.
Spoon the filling into the pastry base and flatten it out with the back of the spoon. Brush another piece of pastry with butter, fold it in half and lay it on top of the filling, tucking in the excess pastry. Repeat with the last sheet of pastry, then fold in all the overhanging filo to create a lovely textured top. Brush with the remaining butter, sprinkle over the sesame seeds, then bake for 45 minutes, until golden. Leave the pie to rest and cool for 15 minutes before serving.
Seeded filo crackers
These require no dough making or rolling: they’re simply made by layering ready-made filo pastry. They have an addictive crunch, and are ideal for swiping through your favourite dips.
Prep 5 min
 Cook 20 min, plus cooling
 Serves 6
1 tbsp fennel seeds
  1 tbsp caraway seeds
  1 tbsp coriander seeds
  2 tbsp sesame seeds
  2 tbsp nigella seeds
  1 tsp pul biber
  ½ tsp onion powder
  1 tsp flaky sea salt
  4 sheets filo pastry
  100ml extra-virgin olive oil
In a mortar, lightly crush the fennel, caraway and coriander seeds, then stir in the sesame and nigella seeds, pul biber, onion powder and salt.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put a sheet of baking paper the size of your baking tray on a work surface, and top it with a sheet of filo. Brush with olive oil, then lay over a second sheet of filo, pressing it down lightly to get rid of any air pockets, and brush with oil. Repeat with the remaining two filo sheets, brush the top with the remaining olive oil and scatter over the spiced seed mix generously and evenly, pressing it in gently, so it sticks.
Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into strips, triangles or squares – whatever you like – then slide the baking paper on to a baking tray and bake for 10 minutes. Leave to cool on the baking sheet to crisp up, then serve with your favourite dip.
Saffron prawn boreks
With the addition of saffron, these crisp prawn rolls feel rather lavish. Perfect to pass around at a party with a glass of something fizzy.
Prep 15 min 
 Cook 40 min, plus cooling
 Makes 16 small boreks
2 tbsp olive oil
  1 onion, peeled and very finely chopped
1 red pepper, halved, pith and seeds removed, and flesh finely chopped
1 carrot, coarsely grated 
1 green bird’s eye chilli, finely chopped
½ tsp pul biber
1 pinch saffron threads, steeped in 1 tbsp warm water for 5-10 minutes
200g raw prawns, peeled, deveined, half blitzed in a food processor, half roughly chopped
25g coriander, leaves very finely chopped
Finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon
Sea salt
4 sheets filo
75g butter, melted 
1 tsp fennel seeds mixed with ½ tsp pul biber, to garnish
Put the oil in a pan on a medium heat, then saute the onion, pepper and carrot until soft but not coloured. Add the green chilli, pul biber and saffron, stir-fry briefly, then take off the heat and tip into a bowl. Leave to cool slightly, then stir in the blitzed and chopped prawns, coriander, lemon zest and juice, and season with salt.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. On a clean surface, lay out a filo sheet and brush it with melted butter. Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into four equal rectangles. Spread a log of the filling mix along the short end of one rectangle, leaving a 1½cm gap on each side, then roll up the pastry, tucking in the ends to secure the filling. Put the roll seam-side down on a lined baking sheet and brush with more melted butter. Repeat with the remaining three sheets of filo and filling, then sprinkle over fennel seed and pul biber mix.
Bake for 15-20 minutes, until golden brown and crisp, and serve hot or at room temperature

Bereaved parents to give evidence at independent review of Sussex maternity services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

Susan Cacciacarro was almost 37 weeks pregnant with her daughter Chiara when she woke up one morning in 2021, unable to feel her baby kicking.
“My belly just didn’t feel right,” she said. “I didn’t feel any movements.”
Chiara, her first child, had been diagnosed with a hole in her heart during a 20-week scan. Since then, Cacciacarro’s pregnancy had been classed as high risk and the growth of her baby had been regularly monitored in hospital.
But when a 34-week scan revealed Chiara had lost weight over the previous two weeks, maternity staff at Worthing hospital in Sussex did not make a plan to expedite her birth, which was planned to take place at 39 weeks.
On the day Cacciacarro woke up and realised Chiara was not moving, she rushed to the hospital, which is run by University hospitals Sussex NHS foundation trust.
Staff were unable to find the baby’s heartbeat and Chiara was delivered stillborn. “I’ve never felt so devastated and so crushed,” Cacciacarro said. “Your world turns upside down and suddenly it’s black.”
She is among the bereaved parents who will give evidence at a major independent review into maternity and neonatal services in Sussex, led by the senior midwife Donna Ockenden.
The review launched on Saturday with a public meeting in Brighton after months of campaigning by bereaved Sussex families. In February, a joint investigation between the New Statesman and the BBC revealed the deaths of at least 55 babies might have been avoidable if they and their mothers had received better care from University hospitals Sussex.
Ockenden, an expert on maternity safety, led the landmark review into maternity care at Shrewsbury and Telford and another into maternity services at Nottingham University hospitals NHS trust. She is also chairing a review into maternity and neonatal services at two Leeds hospitals.
At the meeting on Saturday, Ockenden discussed the review’s terms of reference with the families who will be most affected by it. “We need to get the finer details right to make sure that no family is left behind,” said Cacciacarro, who is now a mother of two. “I felt robbed when we lost Chiara … I’m hoping this review will provide answers to all harmed and bereaved families.”
As well as accountability and transparency, she said what was most important to the families was that the review brought about an improvement in the safety of maternity care services. “We definitely don’t want other families to go through this.”
When her appointment was announced, Ockenden said it was an honour to be asked to chair the review, which is expected to investigate more than 1,000 maternity and neonatal cases dating back to 2018.
“I am absolutely aware of the responsibility I have to the families and babies across Sussex,” she said. “My priority will be to listen carefully to harmed and bereaved families and to engage comprehensively across communities and with staff ‘on the ground’ here in Sussex.
“We will proactively reach out to ensure that the voices of seldom-heard families are heard through this review. It is vital that the scope of the review now reflects the experiences of families and enables a thorough and meaningful examination of care, so that improvements can be made as the review progresses.”
The bereaved campaigners, who are members of the Truth for Our Babies group (TFOB), are urging other affected families to come forward and participate in the review.
Dr Andy Heeps, the chief executive of University hospitals Sussex, said: “Our thoughts remain first and foremost with the families whose babies have died or who have suffered harm when receiving care in our hospitals.
“We welcome Donna Ockenden’s review and remain committed to fully supporting the process so families can get the answers they need, and we take any possible opportunity to learn and improve. Our overriding priority is always to provide the safest possible care for mothers and babies – that is why our maternity teams have implemented many positive changes in recent years, and why we will work with the review team to find new ways of making our services better, and safer, still.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sympathy are with Susan [Cacciacarro] and all women and families who were failed by maternity services in Sussex.
“Through the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, increased investment in maternity safety, and the wider reforms following the previous Ockenden and Amos reviews, we are working to ensure families receive safer, more compassionate and more consistent care in every part of the NHS.”

The Big Question: Is timber the secret to affordable housing in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:14 UTC
14:00:14 KST

Europe is scaling up its timber industry, but unsustainable growth could prove disastrous.
According to the European Commission, the construction sector is responsible for over 35% of the EU’s total waste generation.
The greenhouse gas emissions from material extraction and the manufacturing of construction products, as well as the construction and renovation of buildings, are estimated to produce 5-12% of total national GHG emissions.
“The global construction sector has doubled its carbon footprint in the last three decades and is set to double it again by 2050,” Dr. Subhra Bhattacharjee told Euronews.
But with more than two million homes needing to be built every year across the bloc to meet current demand — a 25% increase on current construction — how do we balance ever-growing urban spaces with our environmental targets?
In this episode of The Big Question, Dr. Bhattacharjee, director general of the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) joined Angela Barnes in the studio to discuss whether Europe can scale up its sustainable timber industry and achieve its construction goals.
Are timber homes safe?
With deadlines looming and environmental policy tightening, a clear shift towards the use of timber is under way in Europe. Historically, unlike the US, Europeans have usually opted for concrete, steel and brick.
But do timber constructions offer quality, value for money and safety? Do they pose a fire risk as wildfires blaze across the continent in the summer?
“There need not be a quality compromise, because recent innovations in engineered wood creates stronger and more versatile structures,” Subhra explained.
“And it gives you a material that is both weather resistant, fire resistant, lighter, and yet stronger. So quality compromises need not to be there.”
And Subhra is confident it’s only going to get better as innovation continues.
Are timber homes expensive?
The processes around constructing with timber are much cheaper than traditional techniques used in Europe, so, in theory, those savings can be passed on to the buyers. Subhra suggested the cost can be up to 25% lower than those for traditionally constructed homes.
“The cost differential comes because first, the transportation costs are lower - it's lighter to handle. Your on-site labour costs are lowered because you can bring in prefabricated structures and that results first in the buildings or the construction getting done faster, but also lowering your insurance costs for the duration of the construction.”
For home-owners themselves, insurance is taking a little longer to catch up, however.
“The insurers need to be educated about the new timber products - the engineered timber products which are fire resistant and which can hold up against fire risks.”
That work is ongoing, Subhra explained, with constructors, production companies and insurers now communicating more closely than before. This shift is gathering pace, and in areas where fire risk is lower, insurance rates are already starting to stabilise.
“So it is only a matter of time before the insurance industry catches up,” she continued.
Is timber good for Europe’s economy?
According to Eurofer, the steel sector generated approximately €152 billion in gross value added and directly employed 293,000 people in 2025. And so, does a scale-up of the timber industry mean a decline in the steel industry?
“Given that housing needs are growing very fast I don't see the potential for a full out downturn,” Subhra predicted.
“What would be an ideal scenario would be low-carbon cement, recycled steel and construction timber complementing in bringing down the carbon footprint of the entire sector and contributing to low-cost housing that is needed.”
And even with some reductions in the steel industry, the growth potential for timber is an exciting economic prospect.
“North America and Europe are the two markets where timber construction is growing faster than anywhere else in the world. It is a $5 billion (€4.32bn) market that's growing at 10% on average per year. So the potential is huge.”
In addition, the green economy is expected to create around 1.5 million new jobs, including those needed to replace retired workers.
“In the green construction sector, specifically the timber construction sector there will be the need for increased skilled labour. Skilled labour means higher income, higher wage labour. So, the employment potentials are large.”
“But once you trace it down the supply chain, in terms of the manufacturing of engineered wood, in terms of the needs for more responsible forest management, rural economies are likely to get revitalised. There's potential across the entire supply chain from the forest floor all the way up to the building,” she concluded.
The Big Questionis a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.
Watch the video above to see the full discussion about Europe’s timber industry.

Inside the world’s first solar ambulance transforming remote healthcare even when the sun goes down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Solar ambulance Stella Juva could transform access to healthcare in regions that lack reliable infrastructure, electricity and fuel.
The world’s first solar-powered ambulance has officially taken to the road, in what has been described as an “important first step towards the future of sustainable healthcare”.
Students from Solar Team Eindhoven at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands have developed Stella Juva – a road-legal ambulance that operates as an electric vehicle (EV) powered by fully integrated solar panels.
Energy generated from the sun is stored in a 50 kWh battery, allowing the ambulance to safely keep driving and deliver healthcare in remote areas – which often lack reliable infrastructure, electricity and fuel options – even when the sun has gone down.
Unlike traditional ambulances that pick patients up and transport them to a hospital, Stella Juva brings healthcare directly to people in need.
“When a healthcare professional arrives at a dispensary, they are able to extend solar panels from the side of the ambulance,” Yarno Basten of Solar Team Eindhoven tells Euronews Earth.
“This helps generate extra energy and provide shade for delivering healthcare. While stationary, the ambulance generates more solar energy than the medical equipment uses. This means that healthcare workers can keep using medical equipment at all times.”
World’s first solar ambulance takes to the road
During its first practical test, in collaboration with the international health organisation Amref Health Africa, Sella Juva covered more than 800km driving around various field locations in the Narok region of Kenya.
At one point, the team spent six hours travelling on challenging roads to reach a remote field location in Mosiro.
“During the end challenge in Kenya, the solar ambulance tackled rough off-road terrain,” Basten says. “During this off-roading, the toelink broke down, which connects the front wheels to the steering mechanism.
“Luckily, this part was designed as the first part to break. Within just half an hour, the team was able to exchange it with a new piece, so that Stella Juva was able to finish her journey.”
An ‘energy independent’ ambulance
Stella Juva is equipped with medical equipment that is urgently needed by health organisations in remote locations, such as an X-ray machine, ultrasound, Automated External Defibrillator (AED) and cooling equipment for vaccines.
During a two-day test, the solar ambulance proved that it could have provided medical care to approximately 200 people.
While stationary, Stella Juva generated more solar energy than it consumed while using all of the medical equipment simultaneously. Researchers say that this shows the ambulance can operate in an “energy independent manner”, allowing healthcare workers to keep using medical equipment at all times.
“It is really great for the team to see the potential of Stella Juva in practice,” says team manager Mathijs van Gerven. “Not only to drive sustainably, but also to be able to provide fully independent care. Especially in remote areas where energy is often scarce, this can make all the difference.”
‘The potential impact could be enormous’
“In Narok, long distances and unreliable electricity still make quality healthcare difficult to access,” says Geoffrey Sadera, a project lead of maternal and child health at Amref Health Africa.
“Stella Juva can bring not only health workers to remote communities, but also the power and medical equipment needed to examine and diagnose people on the spot.”
For example, during a single outreach, Stella Juva could provide an ultrasound scan for up to 40 pregnant women. This could be a literal life-saver in Narok and nearby counties, which face high levels of maternal and child mortality.
“If we could deploy Stella Juva in these areas, the potential impact could be enormous: we could identify risks earlier, intervene sooner and ultimately save lives,” Sadera says.
Following the successful test, the research team hopes that its impressive results will inspire companies, social organisations and governments to tackle societal challenges. It says they are open to parties who want to explore scaling up the invention.

====================================================================================================

On Lithuania’s border, Europe is chipping away at refugee rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

People began entering the EU from Belarus in the summer of 2021. They were soon routinely subjected to pushbacks – and that has continued ever since. Swedish journalist Thord Eriksson travelled to Lithuania, where the interior minister wants border guards to be allowed to open fire on people crossing the border.
The gravel road runs between rolling fields before disappearing into dense forest. It could have been out in the countryside somewhere in the Stockholm region, if it weren’t for the fence. It glints in the August sun, topped with thick coils of razor wire. With only a few gaps, the four-metre-high structure runs the entire 1,250-kilometre stretch that separates the EU from Belarus, from Latvia in the north to Poland in the south, with Lithuania in between.
Recently, right-wing populists across Europe like Italy’s neo-fascist prime minister Giorgia Meloni, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, and AfD chair Alice Weidel in Germany held up Spain as a threat to the EU and to freedom of movement.
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk held up his own country’s border regime – essentially identical to Lithuania’s – as a model, saying Spain must follow Poland’s example if Schengen is to survive.
Exactly what Tusk’s example means in practice is not something the countries along the border are eager to show. No one – not even journalists or aid organisations – is allowed near the fence without a permit. In Lithuania the restricted zone is five kilometres wide, in Latvia two kilometres, and in Poland up to four kilometres. Anyone who defies the ban risks a fine.
“You’d better take over, they tend to be more cooperative when a woman is driving,” says Mantautas Šulskus, braking his worn Mitsubishi to a stop.
He is the field coordinator of the organisation Sienos Grupė, the Border Group, which he also helped found in 2021 in response to the humanitarian crisis. Now he swaps places with 24-year-old volunteer Vaiva Vinskaitė, a graphic designer who describes herself as a full-time refugee activist.
The purpose of the trip into the restricted zone is to see the places associated with 32-year-old Samrin from Sri Lanka, one of the border’s victims.
“There are cameras everywhere, so there’s no doubt the border guards already know we’re in the area.” After a while Vaiva parks by the roadside and we walk across a field to a steep slope above the river Neris.
It was on the riverbank below that Samrin was found dead in August 2022. Five days earlier, Lithuanian border guards had subjected him to a so-called pushback, forcing him out of the country and into Belarus.
Lithuania was the first country along the Belarus border to see people entering from its eastern neighbour, in the summer of 2021. They came through the forests and crossed a border then marked only by posts stuck in the ground. The same development soon followed in Latvia and Poland. There was talk of instrumentalised migration, invasion and hybrid war – the same terms now being used about those who entered Ceuta.
It is speculated that the incident in the Spanish exclave was staged by Morocco. The parallels were easier to see in 2021: Alexander Lukashenko, who has ruled Belarus with an iron grip for nearly three decades, had already threatened to let migrants through to the border. The trigger was the sanctions the EU imposed after the country’s rigged 2020 presidential election and the brutal violence inflicted on those who dared to protest.
The method was simple: start granting visas to people who would not normally be granted them. From the capital, Minsk, to Lithuania – the nearest stretch of the EU border – was then just a 150-kilometre trip. A border guard has told Politico what happened to those who, for whatever reason, changed their minds and wanted to go back to Minsk:
“If they chose to return, they were detained by the Belarusian side and treated like animals. Anyone who tried to return was dragged back to the border – and they were beaten.”
The situation initially drew extensive media attention. Reporting teams from around the world travelled to Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. Since then, media interest has faded, not least after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but people are still making it across the border.
According to official statistics, Lithuania has so far this year forced nearly 1,100 people to return to Belarus, and since 2021 the total has reached just over 25,000. The figures should be treated with caution, however, since most people have made several attempts to enter Lithuania and are therefore counted more than once. The “invasion” is consequently smaller than Lithuania, Latvia and Poland make it out to be.
Since 2021, the three countries have described their actions as self-defence against an outside attack. But it is not Lukashenko who feels the resistance – it is the people who have seized the chance to avoid the deadly crossing of the Mediterranean in order to enter the EU.
Among Šulskus and others critical of the country’s pushbacks, the name Ylva Johansson carries a particular weight, he explains. In 2021, the former Swedish Social Democratic minister and member of parliament was the EU’s commissioner for home affairs, which included responsibility for migration. And since Lithuania was the first to notice the border crossings, that is where she travelled in early August of that year.
“It doesn’t seem to be people in need of protection, but rather other kinds of migrants,” she told TT news agency.
Until then, people who made it into the country had been stopped and placed in accommodation centres that were often makeshift and full, but they at least had a roof over their heads, food, and had their asylum claims investigated. After that, the practice that still applies today became established: anyone who crosses the border is forced straight back out and given no opportunity to seek asylum.
“People may not remember Ylva Johansson’s name, but they do remember that the EU commissioner was here and that she was convinced pushbacks were an option. That’s when they began,” says Šulskus.
The day before the trip into the restricted zone, I visit a border station just south of Vilnius. It is located in Šalčininkai District, where a strip of Lithuanian territory juts into Belarus and is surrounded by the neighbouring country on every side except the northwest. This is where the first border crossings began to be noticed, according to Žydrūnas Vaikasas, the station’s chief, a solidly built man with a hard stare.
“First came Chechens, and after a few days groups started showing up from countries like Afghanistan, Pakistan and India.”
Five years ago there were cameras and patrolling border guards. Since then the fence has been built and more modern technical equipment installed – an essentially impenetrable structure, according to Vaikasas.
Earlier this summer Lithuania got a new interior minister, Social Democrat Martynas Katelynas, who previously belonged to the country’s nationalist National Alliance party. Since taking office he has said that border guards should have the right to shoot at people trying to enter the country. Vaikasas declined to comment on the proposal.
“But of course we follow whatever legislation is decided,” he says, with translation help from non-commissioned officer Vytautas Makauskas. Like his boss, he was dressed in military green, but he also carried a Glock 19 in a holster.
Since 2021, border guards have mainly received military training, Vaikasas said. In late July, Lithuanian media reported the discovery of a tunnel dug from the Belarusian side – a new way of entering the country that the border chief seemed to take in stride. Sensors along the border pick up the vibrations caused by digging.
“That’s how we know that an attempt like that is going on somewhere near here right now. We just haven’t found it yet, but we will.”
Later it turns out that the tunnel was actually found on the same day as my visit.
Another tunnel discovered this past spring had been the way into Lithuania for several people.
“There were 37 of them, from Afghanistan, but they were caught and forced to return”, Vaikasas said.
These pushbacks sounded self-evident when Vaikasas spoke about them. He insisted firmly that the border patrols have the law on their side.
That’s only partly true.
The pushbacks that have been carried out routinely since 2021 were formalised in 2023 through a law passed by Lithuania’s parliament – similar decisions have also been made in Poland and Latvia. Under international law, however, it is not clear-cut that people seeking protection can be sent away without their situation being assessed. The decision was accordingly criticised by, among others, Amnesty, which described the law as a green light for torture.
UNHCR has also criticised Lithuania’s pushbacks. “We do not think that people should be used as pawns in a political chess game,” Annika Sandlund, head of the UN refugee agency for the Nordics and the Baltics, told the Lithuanian news agency BNS late last year. She stressed that those affected have a right to individual asylum processes – even if they have been exploited by Lukashenko and are alleged to be part of a planned hybrid attack.
“That does not mean they are not refugees. It is a separate determination that looks at the situation in your country of origin, not how you arrived.”
The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg has had three open cases since 2021 and 2022 concerning the conduct of Lithuania, Latvia and Poland respectively. The case concerning Lithuania involves four Cubans who in 2021 felt forced to leave their home country after taking part in a protest against the government. They travelled to Moscow and on to Belarus, and in March 2022 crossed into Lithuania for the first time. Over the course of a week they made repeated further attempts, but were forced back each time, sometimes at gunpoint, they claim.
The four were eventually let into the country, allowed to seek asylum – and granted refugee status.
There is no clearer illustration of the problem with forcing people to leave a country without investigating their grounds for staying. Lithuania, Latvia and Poland have nonetheless argued before the European Court for their right to carry out pushbacks. Other countries, including Norway, Finland and Denmark, have submitted written filings backing that position.
Sweden, by contrast, has kept a low profile, but backed a statement this past winter arguing that the European Convention on Human Rights should not fully apply to people coming over from Belarus, on the grounds that they should be regarded as part of a hybrid attack. The statement, signed on Sweden’s behalf by Minister for Justice Gunnar Strömmer, called among other things for a restricted application of Article 3 of the Convention: “No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”
The written statement was addressed directly to the European Court, which is expected to rule before long in the three cases concerning the Belarus border. The message was clear: states’ interests should take precedence over individuals’ human rights.
I asked border guard station chief Vaikasas how he thinks about the risk that people turned away, like the Cubans, have legitimate asylum claims. No danger, he assured me – it is assessed right at the border, so genuine refugees are not at risk of being pushed back.
The claim that border guards, on the spot, carry out individual assessments of complex personal accounts and geopolitical circumstances is of course not plausible. When I pointed that out, he fetched a binder and quickly showed me a form filled in by an Ahmad from Pakistan who had been at the border and had no identity documents.
According to the head of the border station, everyone who is stopped fills in one of these forms. He insisted forcefully that this is sufficient basis for deciding whether someone should be forced out of the country.
“We do everything the law requires us to do.”
Those who are forced back end up in limbo, since on the Belarusian side they are just as unwelcome as in Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. There are cases of people getting stuck in the border zone for long stretches of time, and in winter having to sleep outdoors. From the summer of 2021 to March 2024, a total of 116 deaths were confirmed along the three countries’ border stretches, though the true number is most likely far higher. Many are never found.
Samrin could have been one of them. He is buried near Vilnius airport – the tail fins of planes rise above the treetops at the edge of the field where his grave lies. The fact that he rests beneath a stone bearing his name is thanks to his wife, Sanooja.
The first thing he did after eight days of trying to get into the country was call her to say he was unharmed. Then came a draining silence. Sanooja understood something had happened, but she didn’t know that her husband had been reported by the manager of the hotel in Vilnius where he had checked in, and that he had then been forced out of the country again.
She called border guards, police, and organisations such as UNHCR and the Red Cross, but nowhere could she get information about what had happened to Samrin.
After four and a half months, she was contacted by Sri Lanka’s foreign ministry, which had received information from Interpol that he was dead. His body had been in Lithuania the whole time, after being found by the river.
Sanooja decided the remains would not be taken back to Sri Lanka. That wasn’t only because it would have been expensive. Other reasons weighed even more heavily.
“As Muslims, we believe that even dead bodies can feel pain. I felt broken that he was in the mortuary, feeling the cold for four and a half months,” she explained to journalists who have documented deaths at the border.
Instead he was laid to rest in the section of the cemetery marked out as Muslim, with graves facing Mecca, while the surrounding Catholic graves run east–west. Sienos Grupė raised money for a headstone.
Lithuanian border guard service put no resources into investigating deaths and keep no statistics on bodies that are found. Unmarked graves simply appear, and it falls to activists like Mantautas and Vaiva to do their best to piece together who is buried there.
Right next to Samrin’s grave are two such graves, with no name or marker – just mounds of earth surrounded by weeds. Vinskaitė searches an app to try to find details, but comes up empty. Everything remains unclear.
But one thing is beyond doubt: The border claims victims.
At least every other month, people contact Sienos Grupė asking about missing relatives, says Šulskus.
“The fact that pushbacks are used means people risk dying. The danger is just as great now as it was before.”
Migration as a political pressure tool
Using migration as a political pressure tool is not new. Since the UN Refugee Convention was adopted in 1951, the method has been used on average once a year, according to American researcher Kelly M. Greenhill, author of the book Weapons of Mass Migration: Forced Displacement, Coercion and Foreign Policy.
How the phenomenon is described and responded to has changed, however. The previously little-used term “instrumentalised migration” truly took hold in 2021, when it was used by Belarus’s neighbours Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. Both the rhetoric and a tacit acceptance of pushbacks and suspended asylum rights spread quickly to other parts of the EU, not least the European Commission.
Earlier this summer, the EU’s regulation on addressing crisis and force majeure situations in the field of migration and asylum came into force. It treats instrumentalisation as a crisis that justifies extraordinary measures. Pushbacks, however, are not explicitly named in the legal text as such a measure.
Rhetorically, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen took a major step when, in a statement at the end of 2024, she not only spoke of instrumentalisation at the EU’s border with Belarus as a threat, but also about “weaponisation” of migration.
In an analysis from Germany’s Hertie School, migration researchers conclude that the alleged crisis, and the methods it is said to justify, are generally undermining the rights of migrants and refugees across Europe.
The article was originally published by the Swedish outlet Dagens ETC on August 12, 2026.
Thord Eriksson is a journalist and author writing a book about the situation at the EU’s border with Belarus.

“I love this country so much, and I love the people of this country so much,” he added.
“I want so much to achieve things with this country, to be successful in this way. My team and I put everything we have into making this happen.”

“I am incredibly proud of this team,” Erdem said. “The crowd was amazing, the support was amazing. If it weren’t for their pressure, we couldn’t have brought it to 3-2.”
Erdem also dedicated the hard-fought victory to the broader legacy of Turkish women, linking the triumph to the nation’s history.
“Along the path opened to us by the Republic, we showed what Turkish women can achieve,” Erdem said. “Turkish women will always continue to dream, fight, and win. This trophy belongs to all of us! Today, the capital of Europe is Istanbul! Thank you everyone.”
The championship marks another milestone in a golden era for Turkish volleyball, cementing the program’s absolute dominance on the European stage.
“This team fights until the last ball and never gives up,” Turkish Volleyball Federation (TVF) President Mehmet Akif Üstündağ said.
“This team is this country’s team. Everyone must embrace and support this team. Because they are role models for the youth, exemplary people, and they have given us every possible pride. Next up is an Olympic medal.”

AFL introduces contract training limits in bid to curb concussions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:56:54 UTC
13:56:54 KST

The AFL is set to introduce weekly limits to contact training in both the men's and women's competitions from 2027.
All clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide vision of sessions to the AFL upon request.
Measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes per week, including 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.
All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.
The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.
Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.
From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.
Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.
Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.
Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.
These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.
Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.
The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.
In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.
Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.
There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

Leading Turkish business organizations have welcomed the government’s Medium-Term Program (OVP) for 2027-2029, saying it provides a roadmap for the economy and places emphasis on production, exports and sustainable growth, while stressing the importance of improving companies’ access to finance.
Istanbul Chamber of Commerce (İTO) Chairman Şekib Avdagiç said the program’s comprehensive focus on promoting production and exports, as well as attracting global investment and talent, was a positive step.
Avdagiç said concrete and permanent mechanisms that facilitate access to financing for manufacturing and exporting companies would contribute to achieving the program’s targets.
“The disinflation program should be implemented with determination, and the room created by that process should be translated into a gradual normalization of interest rates,” he added.
The Türkiye Exporters Assembly (TİM) Chairman Mustafa Gültepe highlighted that the new program presented a more cautious framework that takes into account global uncertainties and current economic conditions.
Gültepe said it was important that the program attached special importance to preserving the production and export capacity of the manufacturing industry and addressed support for financing, working capital and labor-intensive sectors in a more concrete manner.
“Our expectation for the coming period is that the financing, cost, market access and competitiveness measures included in the program will be strongly reflected in practice,” he said.
Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEİK) Chairman Nail Olpak said the program was important because it sets out the economy’s roadmap for the next three years and provides guidance for the business community’s future planning.
“The emphasis placed on the quality of growth in order to achieve sustainable growth targets is very important,” Olpak said.
“A growth structure based on productivity gains, high value-added production, strong exports and qualified employment will increase our economy’s resilience against external shocks,” he added.
Olpak said access to financing on appropriate terms was among the key factors that would make the program’s success tangible for businesses.
“Meeting the working capital needs of our production and export companies, improving maturity and cost conditions in investment loans, and supporting the transformation investments of SMEs are of great importance,” he said.
Olpak also welcomed the inclusion of the “Economic Security and Resilience” heading in the program for the first time.
“Global challenges have brought the concepts of security and resilience to the forefront in many areas,” he said.
Olpak said the heading reflected a holistic approach covering stronger energy and natural gas supply security, food security and agricultural resilience, increased domestic production in critical technologies, and the strengthening of family, social and physical resilience.

Armed assailant attacks Ohio Democratic candidate during campaign stop
Patrick Havas, 38, arrested with weapons after injuring several at Ohio Democrat Amy Acton’s campaign stop.
An armed assailant in the United States attacked the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people, campaign officials said.
The individual lunged at Acton as she was speaking on Sunday. Acton was unharmed after the incident, campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement.
The suspect, Patrick Havas, 38, was arrested with multiple weapons after knocking volunteers to the ground, according to a statement from Mahoning County Democratic Party chairman Chris Anderson.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol, which made the arrest, said Havas had two pistols and a Taser before he was stopped by troopers.
Police officers from Mahoning County said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after the incident.
Havas was booked on charges of disorderly conduct and two counts of assault at the county jail, but no other details were available pending an investigation, the highway patrol added.
The suspect knocked down two older adults during the incident, Sheriff Jerry Greene told local NBC outlet 21 News.
Ohio Governor Mike DeWine condemned the attack in a statement and said Ohio police at the fair quickly responded to the incident at the Mahoning County Democratic booth. DeWine, a Republican, is unable to run for re-election because of term limits.
Acton’s Republican opponent in the general election, Vivek Ramaswamy, called Sunday’s attack “completely unacceptable” in a campaign statement. Ramaswamy, leveraging national name recognition and alliances with the tech industry and President Donald Trump, has raised record funds and spent on advertisements criticising Acton.
Federal political committees spent more than $40m on security during the 2023–2024 campaign cycle, according to the most recent publicly available data cited by the nonpartisan group Public Service Alliance.
A Trump-backed political group recently announced it will spend $10m on television and digital advertisements in the state of Texas ahead of the upcoming elections. Trump said he planned to spend up to $500m to help Republican candidates in their races.
The Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most closely watched in this year’s midterm elections. Campaigns are entering the final six weeks before the election on November 3.
The attempted attack is the latest in a string of political violence cases in the US, which has seen a rise in similar incidents over the past decade.
In 2025, Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark Hortman, were assassinated at their home. The husband of former Democratic House of Representatives Speaker Nancy Pelosi was assaulted in 2022.
Trump was also the target of two assassination attempts during the 2024 presidential campaign, while an armed man attempted to breach security at this year’s White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner, where the president was in attendance.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has slowed to its lowest level since May, with an average of 10 commodity ships transiting the waterway per day over the past 10 days, Reuters reports, citing shipping data by Kpler.
 
 
 The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sunday, down from more than 15 on Friday and nearly 13 on Saturday. Only two vessels passed through the strait on Saturday, while six went through on Sunday. 
 
 
 Kpler data showed that one very large crude carrier and three bulk carriers entered the strait on Sunday, while no very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have exited since Wednesday.
 
 
 Separately, LSEG data showed that a tanker carrying refined products from a Saudi port attempted to leave the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday but turned back, Reuters reported.
 
 
 The slowdown comes amid heightened maritime tensions following a new round of US and Iranian attacks on tankers. The UK’s Maritime Trade Operations Agency says 27 projectile attack incidents have damaged vessels operating in and around the strait since July 6.

Germany’s far-right AfD wins a historic 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but falls three seats short of a governing majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:43:09 UTC
13:43:09 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- Europe
- Germany: Far-Right AfD falls just three seats short of solo majority in strongest-ever regional performance
Germany: Far-Right AfD falls just three seats short of solo majority in strongest-ever regional performance
Germany’s far-right AfD wins a historic 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but falls three seats short of a governing majority
The far-right Alternative for Germany party surged to a historic victory in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt, securing its strongest-ever regional performance but falling just short of the absolute majority required to form the country’s first far-right state government since World War II.
Final results show the party, known as the AfD, winning 39 seats in the 83-member regional parliament. The tally leaves the nationalist movement three seats shy of the 42 needed to govern alone in the eastern state.
Despite the shortfall, the result represents a massive electoral shift, with the party capturing nearly 44% of the popular vote and doubling its previous standing in the state.
The Christian Democratic Union, which previously led the state coalition, suffered severe losses, slumping to roughly 17% of the vote. Because all established mainstream parties have repeatedly pledged to maintain a strict "firewall" against coalitions with the far right, the election outcome plunges Saxony-Anhalt into profound political fragmentation and uncertainty.
The triumph of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, where its local chapter is officially designated as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has sent shockwaves through Germany’s Jewish communities and drawn close scrutiny from Israel.
For Jewish leaders in Germany and observers in Jerusalem, the AfD's rise raises acute safety and historical concerns.
'The policy of AFD when it comes to Israel is the same as the German radical left- catastrophic,' expert on German-Israel relations Melody Sucharewicz told i24NEWS.
The Central Council of Jews in Germany has consistently warned that the party harbors xenophobia, historical revisionism, and antisemitic undercurrents that threaten Jewish life.
Prominent leaders within the party have routinely sought to downplay Nazi-era atrocities, downplayed Germany's Holocaust remembrance culture, and pushed nationalist platforms that alienate minority populations.
Officials in Jerusalem have historically maintained a policy of official non-engagement with far-right European parties with roots or elements tied to revisionist stances on the Holocaust.
The expansion of the AfD’s political footprint in state capitals tests the stability of Germany’s post-war democratic consensus, which has long served as a bedrock of strong German-Israeli bilateral relations and a guarantor of protection for local Jewish institutions.
As political leaders in Magdeburg begin arduous negotiations to explore alternative governing alliances, the election shows a deepening political divide between eastern and western Germany.
While the AfD’s victory demonstrates its formidable grass-roots strength, the remaining political parties now face the challenge of cobbling together a broad coalition to keep the far right out of power.

Germany’s right-wing AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election with record 43.8% vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:40:47 UTC
13:40:47 KST

Ayhan Simsek
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Germany’s right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt with a record 43.8% of the vote but fell short of a majority to govern alone, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) slumped to a historic low of 17.2%, according to preliminary official results.
The state election authority said all ballots had been counted. The AfD more than doubled its 20.8% result from 2021 and posted its strongest showing in any German state election. It won 39 of 83 seats in the Magdeburg parliament, three short of the 42 needed for an outright majority. With all other major parties ruling out a coalition with the AfD, the outcome pointed to political uncertainty and long talks on forming a government.
              Turnout was 77.8%, up from 60.3% in 2021 and the highest in the state since German reunification.
“We have achieved exactly what we set out to achieve. We have made history in this country,” AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told public television.
He said cooperation was possible “only with those who support the AfD’s demand for a clear change in policy,” whether that came “through a parliamentary group or through individual deputies.” Asked what would happen if no partner emerged, he said: “If necessary, there will just be new elections.”
The Social Democrats (SPD) finished third with 9.3%, one of their weakest showings in the eastern state. The Greens followed with 8.9% and the socialist Left Party with 8.6%. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) passed the 5% threshold with 5.3% and entered the new parliament. The Free Democrats, junior partners in the outgoing government, missed the threshold with 2.6%.
Merz’s CDU took 15 seats, down from 40 in 2021. The Greens, the Social Democrats and the Left Party won eight seats each, and the left-wing populist BSW won five. The other parties together hold 44 seats.
The numbers offer no clear path to a governing majority. A coalition of the CDU, SPD and Greens would hold 31 seats. Adding the Left Party would lift that bloc to 39, still short of 42. The AfD could reach a majority only with BSW support. The BSW could back an AfD candidate, support a CDU-backed contender or abstain. In a third ballot for state premier, only a plurality is required.
Party leaders are expected to set out their positions this week, with initial exploratory coalition talks likely to begin in the coming days.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s regional branch as a proven right-wing extremist organization, saying parts of the party promote a racist, ethnic understanding of national identity that is incompatible with the country’s democratic constitutional order. Mainstream parties have cited that assessment in maintaining a refusal to govern with the AfD.

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten to undermine air quality: UN weather agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:39:00 UTC
13:39:00 KST

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten to undermine air quality: UN weather agency
- Wildfires and heatwaves driven by climate change are increasing air pollution, making it harder to meet global air quality goals, the UN's World Meteorological Organization warned.
- Wildfire smoke raises harmful pollutants like PM2.5 and ground-level ozone, linked to respiratory and heart diseases, even in regions with otherwise clean air.
- The report urges better monitoring of pollutants such as black carbon and microplastics and highlights that extreme fire-smoke events have tripled since the 1990s, causing many deaths.
AI generated
GENEVA – Pollution from increasingly intense wildfires and heatwaves could undermine global efforts to improve air quality and protect human health, the United Nations’ weather agency said on Sept 7, warning that climate change is making it harder to meet international air quality goals.
In its annual report on air quality and the climate, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said air pollution and climate change are closely linked and should be tackled through coordinated policies rather than in isolation.
It warned that meeting the World Health Organization’s air quality guidelines will become more difficult because extreme wildfires are more likely to occur in the future.
Wildfires are becoming a growing source of harmful air pollution even as regulations have reduced emissions from industry and transport in many developed countries, the WMO said in its report.
“No matter how clean your city or your region is... if you have a lot of pollution brought about by wildfires, that has the potential to negatively impact air quality in those regions as well,” Lorenzo Labrador, scientific officer at the WMO, told Reuters.
The report highlights the growing impact of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, and ground-level ozone, pollutants linked to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
It also calls for improved monitoring of pollutants and aerosols, including black carbon and microplastics, which it said remain poorly tracked despite their widespread presence in the atmosphere.
The year 2026 has been marked by extreme heat and destructive wildfires across parts of Europe, including Spain, France and Greece. The WMO has said that extreme heat is becoming more frequent, intense and longer-lasting as the planet warms.
The new report said PM2.5 concentrations in 2025 were above long-term averages in northern Canada, parts of Russia and western-central Africa due to heightened fire activity, while north-western Spain was a hot spot following exceptional late-summer fires.
A study cited in the report found that extreme fire-smoke events have tripled globally since the 1990s and may have contributed to nearly 100,000 additional deaths annually between 2010 and 2018.
Particulate matter from wildfires is particularly harmful because it comes with a host of toxic chemicals, Labrador said, adding that inhalation causes body-wide inflammation that can lead to pulmonary disease. REUTERS
