Ulrich Siegmund: from CDU member to AfD lead candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:07 UTC
13:00:07 KST

Ulrich Siegmund is the AfD's leading figure in Saxony-Anhalt: 35, media-savvy and aiming to be minister-president. At the next state election he wants to lead his party into government.
Ulrich Siegmund was born on 25 October 1990 in Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt. The now 35-year-old has been a member of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since 2016 and, since August 2022, has co-chaired the AfD parliamentary group together with Oliver Kirchner. In 2025, he was chosen as the AfD’s lead candidate for the 2026 state election.
His professional path did not start directly in politics. Siegmund trained as a wholesale and foreign trade clerk. He then studied business psychology and business administration, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree.
Before entering politics, Siegmund made his money in fragrances. In 2014, at the age of 23, he founded a company in the field of scent marketing. The firm sold fragrance oils, scent accessories and scenting technology, and offered consultancy services in marketing and sales. Siegmund’s studies in business psychology and business administration were also directly linked to his business: his bachelor’s thesis examined the psychological impact of scent marketing on purchasing behaviour.
In 2014, Siegmund and a business partner founded the company "Berlin duftet". The idea was to use targeted ambient scents to make, among other places, BVG and S-Bahn stations more pleasant and thereby reduce stress, aggression and vandalism. In a report by WELT at the time, Siegmund said he was thinking, for example, of a relaxing scent such as lavender.
Particularly interesting is that Siegmund, at the time, pointed to experiences in New York, where busy train stations were subtly perfumed with vanilla. He drew on studies suggesting that pleasant smells can improve people’s mood.
Siegmund was initially a member of the CDU before switching to the AfD. He joined the AfD at the age of 24. Two years later, he entered the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament for the first time.
The social media politician
Today, Siegmund is one of the best-known AfD politicians in Germany. He owes a significant part of his success to his social media strategy. More than 400,000 people now follow him on Instagram; on TikTok, he has more than 763,500 followers, making him one of the most-followed politicians in Germany.
Siegmund often comes across as friendly, easy-going and close to ordinary people, posing for photos with supporters and relying heavily on his election campaigns at family festivals, citizen dialogues and personal encounters.
International media often describe him as the AfD’s "sunny face". The Financial Times portrays his campaign as deliberately community-oriented and family-focused.
Siegmund is calling, among other things, for a far more restrictive migration policy, deportations and a fundamental change in state policy.
His family and other private details
Siegmund is married and has a daughter. His wife, Julia, has also already appeared on camera, though not in a political context. She featured in the VOX wedding docu-soap "Zwischen Tüll & Tränen", where she was looking for her wedding dress for her marriage to Ulrich Siegmund.
For his party, he works extensively with concepts such as home, security, family and change.
In 2017, Siegmund left the Catholic Church. Its values, he says, he carries "in his heart", but he rejects the German institution behind them. In his office hangs a portrait of Otto von Bismarck from nearby Schönhausen, beneath the sentence: "An idea that is right cannot be lied away in the long run."
His older brother sits on Tangermünde’s town council as an independent. His mother died in an accident in 2019.
Controversies in the media
In 2026, Siegmund’s father, Andreas, came under scrutiny for "nepotism". The 66-year-old works in the parliamentary office of AfD MP Thomas Korell in the Bundestag. He had previously worked for other AfD MPs. Siegmund defended in principle the hiring of relatives and party friends and pointed out, among other things, that it was difficult for the AfD to find good people because anyone working for the party is stigmatised.
A widely reported media controversy involving Martin Sellner and Ulrich Siegmund also centred on a meeting near Potsdam in November 2023. Siegmund took part in the gathering, at which Austrian right-wing extremist Martin Sellner spoke about "remigration". By this, Sellner meant not only the return of foreigners obliged to leave the country, but also measures against "non-assimilated citizens" with a migration background.
Siegmund subsequently described his participation as private and explained, in essence, that mere attendance at a lecture does not imply agreement with its content.
On Abgeordnetenwatch, Siegmund was asked in January 2024 whether he distanced himself from Sellner’s "master plan for remigration". His reply was: "The accusations must be rejected."
The Saxony-Anhalt Office for the Protection of the Constitution, a department of the CDU-led Interior Ministry, classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch on 7 November 2023 as a "proven right-wing extremist endeavour". The grounds cited included anti-Muslim, racist and antisemitic statements by AfD officials and elected representatives.
However, the classification is legally disputed and under review by the courts. The AfD is challenging it; the proceedings are currently suspended.
Siegmund has also managed to turn to his advantage the fact that SPIEGEL’s mid-August cover dubbed the lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt "Germany’s most dangerous man". In the election campaign, he signed piles of copies of SPIEGEL with his photo on the cover, which are being auctioned on eBay for sky-high sums.
From state MP to potential minister-president
Siegmund’s political rise has occurred in just a few years. In 2016, he entered the state parliament for the first time; in 2022, he and Oliver Kirchner took over the chairmanship of the AfD group. In 2025, the party placed him at the top of its state list for the 2026 election.
Now it is about far more than another parliamentary seat: Siegmund wants to become minister-president of Saxony-Anhalt. However, he has himself said that he will only govern if the AfD alone commands an outright majority.
If the AfD does indeed win a governing majority, Siegmund could become Germany’s first AfD minister-president.

One House, Many Climates: When Greenhouse Design Enters the Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

A greenhouse is a building designed to create one climate inside another. By controlling sunlight, heat, and ventilation through its enclosure, it produces conditions that differ from those outside. Traditionally, that controlled environment was designed around plants. In housing, the same principle is increasingly being used to shape spaces for people.
Bringing greenhouse construction into a house offers more than additional enclosure. It can create sheltered spaces without conditioning them like conventional interior rooms, capture solar heat when it is useful, provide ventilation when temperatures rise, and extend the periods of the year when certain areas of the home remain comfortable to occupy.

Von der Leyen visits Greenland amid Trump pressure
September 7, 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Greenland for a two-day visit as the European Union plans a major boost in investment in the region amid threats of US annexation under President Donald Trump.
Alongside the EU investments, she is expected to announce closer political ties with the autonomous Arctic territory which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The European Commission head arrived in Greenland's capital Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
In a post on X, Von der Leyen said the EU is committed to "contributing to a safe, peaceful Arctic and to the security of Greenland."
What does the EU investment package include?
The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:
- critical minerals,
- satellite communications
- renewable energy
Von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details.
Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.
Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?
Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.
Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."
Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.
His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.

Viet Nam, 81 years of independence: from renovation process to stepping confidently into a new era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:52:33 UTC
12:52:33 KST

Viet Nam, 81 years of independence: from renovation process to stepping confidently into a new era
TEHRAN- On 2 September 1945, President Ho Chi Minh, the revered leader of the Vietnamese people, proclaimed to the world the birth of an independent and free VietNam. This historic day has since become the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam. From that historic milestone, independence and self-reliance have remained guiding principles throughout the cause of national defense and development. Eighty-one years may not be a long period in the history of a nation, but they represent a proud journey for Viet Nam – from a country that had just regained its independence, through years of extremely difficult war, to an economy with a GDP of more than US$ 500 billion.
With an indomitable spirit and extraordinary determination, we fought to defend our national independence and achieved lasting peace and national reunification in 1975. In just four decades of the Renovation process (1986–2026), rising from the ashes of war, with an exhausted economy and under a policy of encirclement and embargo, Viet Nam, drawing on its national intellect and aspiration for renewal and prosperity, together with the support of international friends, has emerged as a dynamic country deeply integrated into the global economy.
In 2025, Viet Nam’s GDP grew by 8.02%, bringing the size of the economy to US$ 514 billion. GDP per capita exceeded US$ 5,000, while the poverty rate, according to the United Nations standard, fell to just 1.3%. Also last year, total import and export turnover reached US$ 910 billion, while Viet Nam attracted nearly US$ 38.5 billion in foreign investment. VietNam welcomed over 21 million international visitors, the highest number ever recorded. Viet Nam has trade relations with 230 countries and territories, and diplomatic relations with 195 countries, including 30 countries with which it has established strategic or comprehensive strategic partnerships.
Throughout the process of national development, VietNam has remained steadfast in pursuing the goals of national independence and socialism, while consistently pursuing the Renovation policy, continuously renewing its thinking and approaches to development and maintaining political stability. It has always placed the people at the centre, ensuring that economic development goes hand in hand with social equity and that no one is left behind.
As a country that has experienced many wars, VietNam cherishes every moment of peace and makes every effort to preserve it through diplomacy and dialogue. Viet Nam pursues an open foreign policy and seeks to be a friend to all countries, regardless of their political systems, while proactively and actively engaging with the international community. Throughout its development, it has consistently regarded national independence and sovereignty, the right of peoples to self-determination, and the preservation of national identity as principles that cannot be compromised.
Today, the world is undergoing rapid and unpredictable changes, creating new opportunities for development while also presenting considerable uncertainties and challenges for all countries. The achievements of more than four decades of Renovation have given Viet Nam the foundation and confidence to enter a new era of development, with a clearer understanding of the strengths that need to be harnessed and the limitations that need to be overcome, so as to propel the country into a new era of national advancement.
Viet Nam enters a new era of development
The 14th National Congress of the Communist Party of Viet Nam, held in January 2026, set the goal of making Viet Nam a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income status by 2030, with annual GDP growth of 10% or higher.
To achieve these objectives, Viet Nam is pursuing three strategic breakthroughs. First, it is focusing on accelerating institutional reform, streamlining administrative procedures, strengthening decentralisation and continuing to streamline the state apparatus. Second, it is promoting a new growth model based on science and technology, innovation, digital transformation and a green economy. Third, it is improving the quality of human resources, accelerating investment in strategic infrastructure, while identifying tourism as a key economic sector.
Viet Nam will continue to deepen its external relations, promote international integration and diversify partnerships and engagement across different regions of the world, thereby expanding its development space and enhancing the autonomy of the economy. The Middle East is an important region, with a strategic geopolitical position, abundant energy resources and dynamic development. Recent tensions in the region have affected regional security, energy markets and international transport routes. Viet Nam hopes that the Middle East will achieve peace and long-term stability at an early date through negotiations and dialogue, on the basis of respect for national sovereignty and the principles of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.
53 years of maintaining the bridge of friendship between Viet Nam and Iran
Viet Nam and Iran established diplomatic relations on 4 August 1973, just a few months after the signing of the Paris Peace Accords. From the very beginning, the two sides based their relations on enduring principles: respect for independence and sovereignty, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs, and the assurance of each other’s legitimate interests.
Although geographically distant from one another, VietNam and Iran are both countries with long histories that attach great importance to independence, sovereignty and national identity, while seeking to expand their economic relations with the world. Both countries hold important geopolitical positions. VietNam is an active member of ASEAN, with an extensive network of economic linkages across the Asia-Pacific. Iran lies at the heart of the Middle East, at the crossroads of major global flows of energy and trade.
Over the past 53 years, Vietnam has consistently attached importance to developing friendly, mutually beneficial cooperation with Iran, regarding Iran as one of its important partners in the Middle East.
The two countries have maintained political trust and cooperation in the economic and cultural spheres, while strengthening exchanges of delegations and people-to-people ties. A particularly significant milestone came in 2023, when the two countries marked the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations through a series of commemorative activities and high-level exchanges. The two countries have also maintained effective cooperation at multilateral forums.
In April 2026, in his congratulatory message to General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam To Lam on his election as President of Viet Nam, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian noted that the bilateral relationship held great potential and should continue to be deepened and broadened in line with the interests of both countries. In July 2026, when receiving Iranian Ambassador to Vietnam Akbar Ghasemi Ali Abadi, who presented his credentials, General Secretary and President To Lam proposed four areas for further promoting Viet Nam - Iran relations: strengthening political trust; prioritising economic cooperation; creating breakthroughs in science and technology; and expanding cooperation in culture, education and training, and tourism. These orientations provide an important basis for the relevant agencies of the two countries to implement multifaceted cooperation programmes in the years ahead.
Trade has always been a priority area of cooperation. The economic structures of Viet Nam and Iran are highly complementary. Viet Nam has strong export sectors, including products that rank among the world’s top exporters such as rice, coffee, pepper, cashew nutsand garments, as well as other competitive products including seafood, processed food, consumer goods, electronics and industrial products. Iran has considerable strengths in a number of sectors, including industry, construction, pharmaceuticals, materials, minerals, fruit and meat products.
Despite the above-mentioned difficulties, bilateral trade turnover has continued to grow year on year: US$133 million in 2022, US$ 164 million in 2024 and US$170 million in 2025. This demonstrates that there remains considerable room for cooperation between the two countries, not only in trade, but also in other fields of cooperation.
In the new era of development, Viet Nam - Iran relations should be carried forward not merely through the memories of more than half a century of friendship, but through new connections in the fields of the economy, science and technology, education, culture and people-to-people exchanges. In the period ahead, as the regional situation improves, we believe that relations between the two countries will be further strengthened across a wide range of areas, in a manner commensurate with their considerable potential.
On the occasion of the 81st anniversary of the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nnam, we would like to express our sincere appreciation to the State, Government and people of Iran for their sincere and effective support for Viet Nam’s national development over the years.
May the friendship between our two countries continue to flourish, for the cooperation and prosperity of our two peoples, and contribute to peace, stability and development in the region and around the world.

Volcano in Indonesia erupts, canceling hundreds of flights and stranding thousands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:46:51 UTC
12:46:51 KST

Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and frequently experiences eruptions due to its location along the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Indonesia kept several airports closed and shifted schools to remote learning on Monday though a volcanic eruption that halted 2,300 flights and coated areas with ash was subsiding.
The continuous, 25-hour eruption of Anak Krakatau that produced a fountain of lava and a boom heard 700 kilometres away ended on Sunday, the country's Geological Agency said.
But it remained active on Monday with moderate, intermittent eruptions, dark ash emissions and small, localised earthquakes, the agency said in a statement.
Weather was obscuring visual observations of the eruption.
AirNav Indonesia said tests showed volcanic ash present in the airspace around Jakarta and several other cities, prompting authorities to close eight airports until 6 pm on Monday, including the four commercial airports managed by state-owned operator InJourney Airports: Jakarta's international airports of Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma, Husein Sastranegara in West Java and Radin Inten in Lampung on the southern tip of Sumatra.
The closure disrupted about 2,300 flights and affected 268,539 passengers at the four airports managed by InJourney Airports, the company said.
The eruption’s impact extended beyond air travel. The government authorised schools in areas affected by volcanic ash, including in Jakarta, West Java, Banten and Lampung provinces, to temporarily move to online learning at home to reduce students’ exposure to ash.
“The probability of additional eruptions in the coming days remains high,” said Lana Saria, head of the Geology Agency.
“The main hazards include volcanic bombs, heavy ashfall and possible lava flows if sustained eruptive activity resumes," she said.
Anak Krakatau is a volcanic island in the Sunda Strait between Indonesia's main Java and Sumatra islands. Its name means “child of Krakatau,” and the volcano is the offspring of the infamous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
An eruption of Anak Krakatau in 2018 caused a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java.
Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water.
Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and frequently experiences eruptions due to its location along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” the ring of seismic faults around the Pacific Ocean where most global seismic activity occurs.

What to Know About the Miami Plane Crash That Killed 5 People
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:45:19 UTC
12:45:19 KST

At least five people were killed and five others were injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway upon landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon.
Miami-Dade County officials said in an evening press conference that 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon, crashed into several vehicles shortly before 2 p.m.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said they are investigating the incident.
"The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
Nantel said the company’s “deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Amazon contracts out its cargo flights.
The incident has impacted operations in “America’s busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers,” according to the Miami airport’s website.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on social media that travelers should anticipate significant delays and potential flight cancellations. A full ground stop had earlier been issued but was lifted about three hours later. Authorities said ground delays are expected until early Monday.
Here’s what we know so far.
How it unfolded
According to the FAA, Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during the news conference that the crash happened at around 1:58 p.m. Data from tracking site Flightradar24 shows that the plane had a speed of nearly 130 mph when it left the usable portion of the diagonal runway.
It’s unclear what caused the plane to overshoot, and the NTSB and FAA are investigating. The airport’s runways and taxiways were closed, and the aircraft was left disabled at the northwest end of the airport. Some of the runways were later reopened.
According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, more than 60 units and approximately 200 personnel responded to the scene, arriving at the airport “to find an airplane that had stopped beyond the airport operational boundary with heavy flames and smoke showing.” Photos and videos from the scene showed black smoke billowing from the plane.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue chief Raied Jadallah said in the news conference that several people were trapped in their vehicles.
“What we found was a very complex situation here,” Jadallah said, and added that responders also conducted search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped in the aircraft.
What we know about the victims
Jadallah said there were a total of 10 people involved in the crash: five were killed, three are in critical condition and were transported to the trauma center, and another two were transported to a local hospital. It was not clear on Sunday evening whether those killed and injured were on the plane or on the ground.
What we know about the carrier and the plane
North Carolina-based cargo airline 21 Air began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024. The company was founded in 2014.
Keith Winters, the airline’s CEO, said in a statement on their website that they were “devastated by the accident” and that the company’s “deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Flightradar24 data shows the plane involved in the crash was a 32-year-old Boeing 767. The aircraft model is used for both passenger travel and freight delivery. The first Boeing 767 flew on Sept. 26, 1981, and started commercial operations in 1982 with United Airlines.
Amazon’s cargo flight history
Amazon Air’s cargo network oversees more than 100 aircraft and over 250 flights daily. It contracts all of its cargo flying to other operators. In its fleet are Boeing 737 and 767 planes, as well as the Airbus A330.
Citing details from aviation analytics firm Cirium, the New York Times reported that 21 Air runs eight planes for Amazon Air, while Air Transport International operates about 40 planes, and low-cost carrier Sun Country Airlines operates 22.
It’s not the first plane crash involving Amazon Air. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a cargo plane flying from Miami to Houston, crashed into Texas’s Trinity Bay. All three people onboard were killed, and a subsequent federal investigation attributed the crash to pilot error.
Sunday’s incident is the latest high-profile crash involving a cargo aircraft in the U.S. Last November, more than a dozen people were killed after a UPS plane crashed into an industrial area in Louisville, Ky. shortly after departing Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.

Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".
Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.
The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.
Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.
The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.
In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.
Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.
Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.
As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.
"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.
"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.
"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.
"In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before."
As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.
"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.
"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."
GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.
The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.
Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.
Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.
"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.
"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.
"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

Global investors and startups should consider establishing a foothold in the Greater Bay Area given its unique combination of strengths in finance and innovation, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Monday.
He was speaking at the opening of the inaugural Co-Development and Investment Conference, which brings together around 300 investors and more than 500 startups alongside industry leaders and academics in the Greater Bay Area.
The six-day event starts at Hong Kong Science Park before moving on to Dongguan and Hangzhou for its final four days.
“For global investors in a world overshadowed by geopolitics, the requirement is twofold: stability and security on the one hand, attractive returns on the other,” Chan said.
“For innovators and entrepreneurs, capital alone is not enough. They need an industrial ecosystem, a steady supply of talent and access to the full range of innovation resources.
“Nowhere is the combination of finance and innovation stronger than in the Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao Greater Bay Area.”
Chan called Hong Kong a “magnet” for global talent and a hub for fast-rising innovation, making it a natural complement to sister Greater Bay Area cities that excel in advanced manufacturing, commercialisation and scaling.
The city, he added, is also building a capital ecosystem tailored to support startups and drive innovation.
These efforts are already bearing fruit, Chan said, pointing out that the technology sector's share of turnover on the Hong Kong bourse has risen from 15 percent to 47 percent over the past decade, with overall turnover growing more than eightfold.

AfD wins big in German regional election, falls short of outright majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:25:51 UTC
12:25:51 KST

AfD wins big in German regional election, falls short of bid to become first far-right party to lead a state since WWII
The far-right Alternative for Germany party surged to a resounding victory in a regional election Sunday, but fell a little short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country's first far-right state government since World War II.
The party of Germany's unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany's candidate for governor said that "we have written history" and the party had a clear mandate to govern.
Ulrich Siegmund, 35, told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this." He said that "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz."
Alternative for Germany, or AfD, was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with AfD.
Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund said it wouldn't engage in "games" such as a minority government. But it wasn't evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it.
A first state government would be the biggest prize in the anti-migration party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with a national government that has yet to persuade voters that it can get the country's sluggish economy moving.
Whether or not AfD ends up governing, the result is a blow to Merz, whose center-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn't yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.
AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.
Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is one of several classified as a proven right-wing extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, which points to members' denigration of migrants from Muslim countries, among other things.
The party talks of "remigration," a politically charged term for the deportation of immigrants. Its leader in a neighboring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.
AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism and says they're politically motivated.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.
That was far ahead of Merz's Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2% — losing about half its support — and won 15 seats. The center-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece.
The BSW party, which has said it wouldn't elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticizes the "firewall" against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats.
Turnout was very high at 77.8%. AfD appeared to have won over many people who didn't vote at all five years ago.
AfD's national co-leader, Alice Weidel, described the result as "sensational." She said the party's "hand is outstretched to all who want to make Saxony-Anhalt better and move Germany forward." It may hope to attract defectors from other parties.
Schulze congratulated AfD on becoming the state's strongest political force and said that "we as the CDU will also have to deal with this result," without specifying how.
Franziska Hoppermann, the national general secretary of Merz's party, rejected backing off its refusal to deal with AfD.
"AfD is a right-wing extremist party. It wants to leave the euro; that would be economic downfall ... it works closely together with Russia, it wants a completely different social model," she said. "We will not work with them."
Once previously AfD won a state election but didn't end up governing. That was two years ago in neighboring Thuringia, where a CDU governor took power with a minority government, but AfD was much further short of a majority there.
Any attempt by Schulze to put together an alliance against AfD would be delicate because it would require at least some tacit support from the Left Party, a hard-left party with which the CDU refuses to form coalitions.
Germany's 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system.
Siegmund has listed among his top priorities "a deportation offensive" and dropping incentives for people to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about "disinformation."
AfD in Saxony-Anhalt wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag, which it says "stands for the devaluation of the family," and ensure they fly the national flag.
It opposes taxpayers' money being "given away" to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.
The 16 states' governments also sit in Germany's upper house of parliament, which has to approve some government legislation. The influence there of Saxony-Anhalt, one of the smaller states in a nation of 83.5 people, is limited — it controls four of the 69 votes.

Feature: Connected by algorithms and shared interests, young Chinese build social lives across screens and streets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:25:26 CST
12:25:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- "Anyone want to bike this evening? Not for speed. Just enjoy the breeze and stop whenever we get tired."
After finishing work on a recent Friday, Chen Jiahao, 26, a programmer in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, posted this invitation on Xiaohongshu, a popular Chinese app for sharing lifestyle tips and hobbies.
It didn't take long for people to start leaving comments.
That evening, three strangers met and set off along a bike path near a local river. They rode at an easy pace, taking in the view and stopping now and then to chat about work and things they had been watching or reading lately.
More than two hours later, they parted and headed home.
"I wasn't really looking to make a new friend," Chen said. "Sometimes you just feel like doing something on the spur of the moment, and it's nice when you happen to find someone who wants to do the same thing."
This encounter lasted an evening. That was enough.
It points to a broader shift in how young Chinese are building their social lives -- and perhaps to what they now expect from one another.
For generations, friendships grew almost by default out of the places and communities people shared: school, work, neighborhoods and family. But as young people move more often, live more independently and spend more time online, those old settings no longer necessarily determine who enters their social lives.
Liu Shengzhi, a professor of communication at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said young people increasingly connect online over shared interests and then take those relationships offline, sometimes in more fleeting forms: someone to eat with, walk with or watch a movie with.
Their social lives are becoming more lightweight, activity-based and modular, according to a 2026 social trends report by an institute under Soul, an AI-powered immersive social platform in China, in collaboration with Fudan University.
Liu described such lighter forms of socializing as a response to modern urban life, where maintaining traditional, close-knit relationships can demand considerable time, money and emotional energy.
This shift is hardly unique to China. Sociologists often describe the broader process as social atomization, which can leave people feeling isolated and lonely, but can also give them greater freedom, autonomy and private space.
What may be changing, experts say, is not young people's desire for connection, but the terms on which they seek it. They want to find "their people," but without giving up their own space.
Sometimes a simple connection remains just that.
Sometimes it becomes something more.
For Maggie Gong, 35, the large online group for bouldering enthusiasts has largely fallen by the wayside. She now mostly makes plans in a group chat with two people she climbs with regularly.
The user-interface designer, who lives in Chengdu in southwest China's Sichuan Province, picked up the sport as a way to get out of the house. Working mostly from home, she had spent a lot of time sitting alone when she came across bouldering videos online.
"Bouldering is a bit like solving a problem with your body," Gong said. The sport makes it easier for her to get a sense of her climbing partners' personalities.
Those who insist on finding the best way up may call out the next move as their partner climbs. Others prefer to work out a route on their own and are more open to different solutions.
"It requires trust. For a few minutes, quite literally, your safety is in someone else's hands," she said.
For Li Xinyu, 25, who works at a bank in Dalian, Liaoning, shared interests have provided something more enduring: a reason to stay.
She decided to settle in the northeastern city after graduation, in part because she had found like-minded friends online through her interest in animation and comics.
Li often hangs out with these friends at comic conventions, dressed in cosplay, taking photos and browsing "guzi" shops. The term "guzi" is a Chinese phonetic rendering of "goods" and refers to merchandise associated with anime, music, gaming and other fandoms.
People may differ in age, education or profession, but a shared passion can give them a sense of belonging that might otherwise be hard to find, Li said.
The rise of these casual ties in China is not simply because young people want them. Young people elsewhere do this, too. What may set China apart is a growing digital and physical infrastructure that is lowering the barriers to turning online interests into offline activities.
Algorithms that sort and connect people by interests, location and online behavior have made social discovery far more efficient and precise, allowing young people to find each other at little cost, said Liu.
The physical environment matters, too. In Shanghai, a former cement plant has been turned into a cultural and commercial complex where young people can bring their pets, grab a drink, stroll along the waterfront or visit an art gallery. In Chengdu, an elevated cycling path runs through a shopping mall and connects with cycling routes around the city.
Meanwhile, real-name verification, reputation systems and the growing overlap between online communities and offline activities can make meeting a stranger feel less like a leap into the unknown.
Behind this trend lies a clear commercial logic.
As user growth plateaus, China's internet platforms are looking for ways to keep people engaged for longer. Interests can serve as a gateway, taking users from content to conversation, commerce and eventually offline experiences.
Douyin and Taobao have increasingly integrated content, commerce and payments, while Soul has introduced a feature that enables users to quickly form groups around shared interests and activities.
In Kunming, the capital city of southwest China's Yunnan Province, where the feature was piloted, the platform completed the full chain -- from posting a request and forming a group to organizing an offline activity and making a payment -- in less than a week.
Soul said the pilot showed that when platforms make it easy for people to find others who want to do the same thing at the same moment, young people are surprisingly willing to take those connections offline.
Even so, lightweight connections cannot replace deeper ties that offer emotional intimacy, unconditional acceptance and long-term commitment, said Liu.
A survey of 1,333 young people by China Youth Daily found that 81.6 percent considered deep relationships necessary, though 71.4 percent said they felt it had become harder to maintain them.
Gong has noticed the limits of online connection.
Connecting with someone online via a shared interest can make a first encounter easier, she said. But it cannot do the work of a relationship.
"Whether two people can build on that initial connection still depends on their personalities, values and the rhythms of everyday life," Gong said.
The ease of finding a companion online also comes with risks. Users have reported being abandoned midway through trips, falling victim to online scams, or even facing verbal or physical abuse.
Li tends to choose busy public places, like shopping malls and exhibition halls, for first meetings with people she has met online. She also lets friends know where she is going and what she plans to do.
"And I'm especially cautious when money is involved, whether it's buying tickets for someone or sharing a hotel room," she said. "Just because you hit it off with someone online doesn't mean you should immediately put your trust in a stranger."
There is another, less obvious risk.
The same algorithms that make it easier to find people like you can also make the world around you look increasingly like you, Chen said.
After he searched a few times on his phone for cycling routes and activities, his feed increasingly showed him the same narrow slice of the world: people roughly his age, interested in similar activities and talking about similar things. Even the destinations they visited began to converge.
Chen said he tries not to let the feed dictate who he meets. He chats with potential companions a little longer, asking about the details to see whether they are actually a good fit. Sometimes he also searches for things far outside his usual interests, or follows activities recommended by other people, simply to throw the algorithm off his trail.
"An algorithm can help me find someone to bike with tonight," he said. "But I don't want it deciding who I spend time with over time." ■

Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House of Representatives by 229 seats to 206, while putting the Senate at a knife-edge 50-50.
Republican leaders have nevertheless decided that the answer is more Trump, not less.

ONT Field is located near Ontario International Airport and incorporates an aviation theme throughout the ballpark. MLB reported that the venue is about 64 kilometers from Los Angeles. Israel must fight harder to keep its doctors in the country - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:07:11 UTC
12:07:11 KST

Israel is losing doctors at an alarming rate. It should be doing everything possible to keep them. But it should also recognize an opportunity: Israel can recruit more Jewish doctors from around the world to make aliyah.
The Jerusalem Post recently reported that 1,370 Israeli doctors left the country for more than a year between 2023 and 2025, a 94% increase compared with the equivalent period a decade earlier.
Not every doctor who spends a year abroad is gone for good. Physicians leave for fellowships, research, specialist training, and other reasons before returning. But the trend should concern policymakers. After accounting for returning physicians, Israel recorded a net loss of 509 doctors in 2023 and 2024, roughly five times the annual average of the previous decade.
The government’s first responsibility is obvious: Find out why doctors are leaving and give them reasons to stay.
Israeli physicians work under enormous pressure. The healthcare system must offer competitive conditions, professional advancement, adequate staffing, and a sense that young doctors can build their futures here.
Israel's two-pronged path toward doctor retention
But retention should be only half of Israel’s strategy. The other half should be recruitment.
Israel is the national home of the Jewish people, and Jewish communities worldwide contain doctors, nurses, researchers, therapists, and other healthcare professionals. Some already dream of making aliyah. Others might consider it if Israel made the process easier and they saw a clear opportunity to contribute.
Israel already has an International Medical Aliyah Program, run by Nefesh B’Nefesh with the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, Health Ministry, and Jewish Agency. Its goal is to facilitate the aliyah of 2,000 physicians by 2029 by streamlining licensing and helping doctors find placements.
The government should expand and accelerate that effort.
That means removing unnecessary barriers to recognizing foreign qualifications, expanding professional Hebrew programs, helping immigrants find placements, and assisting families with the practical difficulties of moving countries. Israel should also strengthen incentives for immigrant doctors willing to practice where shortages are most severe, particularly in the North and South.
There is ample precedent.
Former waves of aliyah provide a historical blueprint
Successive waves of aliyah have transformed Israel demographically and professionally. Immigration from the former Soviet Union brought thousands of doctors and nurses, alongside scientists, engineers, musicians, and academics. Their contribution to Israeli medicine, science, and technology is difficult to overstate.
There are encouraging signs. More than 1,100 North Americans made aliyah through Nefesh B’Nefesh in August alone. Approximately 2,700 had arrived since the beginning of 2026, and the organization expects more than 4,000 by year’s end. The current wave includes doctors and nurses.
Imagine a Jewish doctor in New York, Toronto, London, Paris, or Melbourne wondering whether Israel might someday become home. Israel could actively make the case: We need you. We will help you navigate licensing, learn professional Hebrew, and connect with hospitals and communities where your skills can make a difference.
That is not merely immigration policy. It is national planning.
None of this should become an excuse for ignoring why Israeli doctors are leaving.
It would be absurd to recruit a physician from New Jersey while failing to address the conditions driving a physician from Jerusalem abroad. A successful healthcare strategy must make Israel attractive both to the doctor considering aliyah and the Israeli medical student deciding where to build a career.
Nor should aliyah be viewed merely as a mechanism for filling labor shortages. People make aliyah for reasons of identity, family, community, faith, Zionism, and belonging. They are citizens building lives, not numbers on a manpower spreadsheet.
But Zionism has always involved matching individual aspirations with national needs.
Israel needs doctors. There are Jewish doctors around the world who may want to make Israel their home. Connecting the two is a natural proposition for a country that prides itself on creative solutions to difficult problems
The physician crisis is a warning and a call to action
The rise in doctors leaving Israel should serve as a warning and a call to action.
Israel must fight harder to keep the medical professionals it has. At the same time, it should open the door wider to those who want to join them.
A brain drain demands a brain-gain strategy. For Israel, part of that strategy may be waiting in Jewish communities around the world.

25 years on, America seeks to keep 9/11 memories alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

25 years on, US seeks to keep 9/11 memories alive
- The US marks 25 years since 9/11, focusing on preserving memories as many younger Americans did not experience the attacks first-hand.
- The 9/11 Memorial & Museum emphasises education and outreach to engage younger generations, with volunteers sharing personal stories to deepen understanding.
- More than 9,400 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses, and the trial of alleged mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is set for 2028 at Guantanamo Bay.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A quarter of a century after the era-defining attacks of Sept 11, 2001, the United States is eager to keep alive the memory of a trauma that is fading as the proportion of Americans who did not experience it first-hand grows.
US President Donald Trump will pay his respects at the Pentagon rather than in New York, where the attacks by hijacked passenger planes on the World Trade Center towers claimed the largest number of the 2,977 total victims recorded on that day.
But Vice-President J.D. Vance and Trump’s four living predecessors – Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, as well as Republican George W. Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks – are all expected at the Ground Zero site in Lower Manhattan on Sept 11.
The anniversary commemorates a watershed moment for the US and the world.
“Many in my generation remember exactly where we were on that horrific day,” said Beth Hillman, 59, president of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum and a US Air Force veteran.
Yet today, “100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember” the tragic events.
Young people ‘more inquisitive’
After placing major emphasis on the duty to remember, her institution is now focusing on outreach, education and engaging younger generations.
Trained volunteers, including first responders, connect with audiences who have learnt of the disaster solely through their parents or school.
“Even if you were alive but not here or have a connection, it’s a lot easier to understand the magnitude of what took place,” Logan Miller, a 32-year-old who lost an uncle and a grandfather as a result of the attacks, told AFP.
Making sense of Sept 11 is “a little tougher for that next generation”, he added.
Miller is one of many volunteers sharing their experiences at the museum, which gets 2.4 million unique visitors a year, or through video clips.
Young people are “more inquisitive” and ask more questions than their elders, who Miller said sometimes hesitate to challenge him for fear of causing offence.
“I wasn’t born at the time and yet, it was important for me to be here, to do this trip,” said 22-year-old Ignacio Gaete, a Chilean visiting the museum and memorial featuring two large recessed pools within the footprints of the Twin Towers.
Gaete said that while young people do not have visceral memories of Sept 11 like his father does, “I think it can transcend generations”.
But that transcendence requires preservation and education, according to Holly Kafka, visiting Manhattan from Chicago with her husband.
“Our younger generation... they’re always in this little rat race, keeping up with social media,” the 61-year-old said. “We have to stop them and say, ‘Come here and experience it’.”
Deaths from illnesses linked to attacks
As they do every year at Ground Zero starting at 8.40am local time (8.40pm Singapore time), the time shortly before hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower, relatives will read the long list of their loved ones’ names.
In the evening, two beams of light will project skywards from Lower Manhattan, symbolic of the towers.
Nineteen Al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four planes on that nearly cloudless day in 2001.
Two jets slammed into the World Trade Center, causing the iconic 110-storey buildings to collapse.
A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth – which apparently had targeted the US Capitol or the White House – crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.
Beyond those killed on Sept 11, more than 9,400 other people have died from illnesses related to the attacks, according to the federal programme established to provide medical care to those affected.
The trial of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, alleged mastermind of the attacks and a top lieutenant of Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, was recently scheduled for June 2028 at the US Navy base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
He has been detained there for 20 years.
Trump, 80, has confirmed he will skip the Ground Zero event and instead speak at the Pentagon on Sept 11.
The New York Times reported it was because Trump would not be allowed to deliver remarks at the site, which has strictly banned speeches so commemorations there could remain non-partisan.
Trump dismissed the reporting as “made up”. AFP

Europe cannot afford to lose the race for biomedical innovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Europe cannot afford to lose the race for biomedical innovation
As clinical trials and investment increasingly turn elsewhere, European patients are missing out on breakthrough treatments. Policy can make a real difference here.
Europe stands at a crossroads. For decades, it led the world in pharmaceutical research, delivering medical advances that have transformed the lives of millions. But that leadership can no longer be taken for granted. U.S. trade policies toward the pharmaceutical industry, including tariffs and Most Favoured Nation pricing, underscore the urgency of Europe’s response, while China is advancing at unprecedented speed.
Fina Lladós
The figures speak for themselves. Europe led the launch of new medicines in the 1990s but lost that lead to the U.S. in the following decade and, by 2024, to China as well. Over the past 20 years, the EU’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development investment has fallen significantly, while the proportion of clinical trials conducted in Europe has also declined sharply.
This is particularly alarming in the fields that will shape the future of medicine. Advanced therapies, personalized treatments, and solutions for genetic diseases and certain cancers are increasingly being developed elsewhere. Every clinical trial that moves away and every patent filed outside Europe mean a real loss of knowledge, skilled jobs and opportunities for Europeans.
This is not a theoretical risk. The pandemic exposed how reliance on external supply chains can threaten access to essential medical products, underscoring why the pharmaceutical industry is now recognized as strategic for Europe’s competitiveness, security and autonomy. A strong biopharmaceutical industry is therefore not only an economic asset; it is essential to health security and to Europe’s ability to respond to future crises.
Every clinical trial that moves away and every patent filed outside Europe mean a real loss of knowledge, skilled jobs and opportunities for Europeans.
Much of Europe’s declining appeal can be explained by developments across the Atlantic. The U.S. represents a much larger share of the global pharmaceutical market and has long offered stronger incentives for innovation, steadily attracting research investment. New measures to reinforce domestic production and draw further investment to the U.S. risk accelerating this trend. For Europe, the message is clear: strengthening our own regulatory and fiscal incentives for innovation is no longer optional — it is urgent, and it is entirely in our hands.
Greater competitiveness also requires faster and fairer access to treatments by removing unnecessary restrictions. Access to innovation is not only an industry issue; it is also a societal one. Scientific investment must reach patients, because better health also strengthens the economy.
Europe still has an exceptional scientific and academic base, but it has not always translated that knowledge into innovation that delivers wellbeing and social progress on the same scale. The priority now is to build a life-sciences ecosystem that translates research into tangible solutions for citizens.
Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation.
Spain illustrates this paradox clearly. It is Europe’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical market and a leader in clinical trials, yet patients still wait too long for approved treatments. Scientific excellence does not automatically translate into timely access; closing that gap is a challenge for all of Europe, not Spain alone.
Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation. Intellectual property protection is central to this. Weakening it will not sustainably lower medicine costs; it will only reduce the incentive to research and develop new treatments in Europe.
Europe’s competitiveness also depends on its ability to attract and conduct clinical trials, where scientific ideas become treatments and much of biomedical innovation’s economic value is created. Faster approvals, harmonized procedures across member states and stronger research infrastructure would make Europe a far more attractive destination for global investment.
Europe also needs an ambitious industrial policy to expand and modernize its biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. Research and industry reinforce each other, and advanced therapies, personalized medicine and AI-driven drug discovery require industrial capabilities that Europe must build now.
This is why the forthcoming European Biotech Act matters. If it reduces unnecessary administrative burdens, improves access to venture capital and creates real regulatory sandboxes for advanced therapies, it could send the strongest signal yet that Europe is serious about global competitiveness. This opportunity must not be weakened by half-measures.
Policymakers must now act with urgency: protect and reward innovation, remove barriers to faster access, strengthen Europe’s industrial and research base, and make biomedical innovation a strategic priority.
AI can accelerate the discovery of new molecules, optimize clinical trials and enable more precise medicine, provided it is supported by modern regulation that ensures transparency, data protection and human oversight. The European Health Data Area could be decisive if Europe guarantees interoperability, simplifies procedures, and fosters public trust. Together, these tools can accelerate research, improve data-driven decision-making, and ultimately benefit patients and society.
In an aging society, biomedicine and new technologies are delivering increasingly complex treatments that can also reduce broader public costs, such as those linked to sick leave. Yet healthcare systems remain underfunded and rarely account for the wider social value of biopharmaceutical innovation.
Europe’s biopharmaceutical industry and wider life-sciences ecosystem have enormous potential to invest, innovate and grow. But that potential must be consistently recognized and supported at the European level. Policymakers must now act with urgency: protect and reward innovation, remove barriers to faster access, strengthen Europe’s industrial and research base, and make biomedical innovation a strategic priority. This is not only about competitiveness, it is also about ensuring European patients can benefit earlier from the treatments of the future and that Europe can respond autonomously to the health challenges ahead. The choice is clear: Europe must act now.

AI data centres are less thirsty now, tech giants say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

AI data centres are less thirsty now, say tech giants
NEW YORK – Data centres are running into a wall of public anger in the United States over their thirst for water and power.
The tech giants spending billions of dollars on them say the water part, at least, is solvable.
Data centres are the warehouses full of computer servers that run the internet and, increasingly, artificial intelligence.
The computers get hot and keeping them cool takes water.
US chip giant Nvidia said in a June report that it can eliminate water consumption almost entirely at some facilities when deploying DSX, its newest system for designing and managing AI data centres.
It is a bold claim and one that the industry is under mounting pressure to make good on.
In 2025, data centres consumed 222 billion litres of water worldwide for cooling, according to consultancy Rystad Energy.
Without adaptive measures, the figure could nearly triple to 644 billion litres by 2030, Rystad estimates. Steps to limit the growth could keep it under double.
Nvidia’s new method uses a closed-loop cooling system in which liquid flows directly through the servers, as close as possible to the chips, whose temperature can rise above 80 deg C.
The problem is that “there’s a pretty direct trade-off between how much water is used and how much energy is used” for temperature control, said Andy Masley, an independent researcher who covers AI and data centres.
Cutting back on water use usually means more power as the liquid in those sealed pipes still has to be cooled down somehow, usually by blowing air over it – and that takes electricity.
Nvidia gets around some of this by letting the liquid enter the servers warmer than usual, at 45 deg C.
Most other closed-loop systems ran at about 32 deg C in 2024, according to the Uptime Institute, which certifies data centres.
By starting with warmer water, Nvidia does not need to pump in cooled air year-round.
Josh Parker, Nvidia’s head of sustainability, said “simple fans circulating the air” are often enough, although sometimes, a mix of methods is needed.
At sites in extreme climates, or during a heatwave, chill airflow or water evaporation is still necessary.
Public relations
Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Meta told AFP that they also use closed-loop systems, which they said involve no net water loss.
The two cloud computing giants, which have been expanding their already huge data centre footprints, used more water overall between 2022 and 2025, but the water-use efficiency improved by 25 per cent at Microsoft and 37 per cent at AWS, according to their most recently released sustainability reports.
There is no industrywide consistency, however, in how companies report data on so-called environmental, social and governance (ESG) efforts.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX, now a major player in data centres after it acquired his AI company, xAI, has never published an ESG report.
In June, ratings agency MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG score.
Ren Shaolei, an engineering professor at the University of California, Riverside, said that “because water is generally much cheaper than electricity”, companies have less incentive to cut water use on cost grounds alone.
There are incentives, Ren said, but they have more to do with public relations amid the growing backlash to data centres across the US.
Another obstacle is that upgrading an older data centre to newer, less thirsty technology is expensive.
This may matter less than it sounds.
Older data centres are smaller and less powerful than the enormous new ones being built now, so they need less cooling in the first place, said Minh Khoi Le, who leads data centre and hydrogen research at Rystad.
And the water a data centre uses directly is only part of the story.
Water is used to generate the electricity that powers the data centre and to manufacture its chips and servers.
In the US, that hidden water use can be twice the amount a data centre consumes on its own. AFP

Israel loses 1,370 doctors in three years as brain drain intensifies: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:34:59 UTC
11:34:59 KST

Zein Khalil and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
At least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025 according to a new study by Tel Aviv University, highlighting a deepening brain drain from the country’s medical sector.
The findings were published Sunday by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The study classifies doctors as having left if they spent more than 270 days abroad during their first year away and did not subsequently remain in Israel for more than three consecutive months.
Prof. Itay Ater, one of the study’s authors, said economists had warned since 2023 of an accelerating departure of skilled professionals amid Israel’s political and security turmoil.
He said concerns first emerged during the government’s judicial overhaul push and intensified after the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the war that followed.
Researchers focused particularly on doctors over 45, who have typically completed specialist training and play a central role in training younger physicians.
One in five doctors who left Israel during the three-year period was over 45, a trend the study described as worrying.
The losses were particularly pronounced in several specialties.
Some 116 ophthalmologists, dermatologists and ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialists left Israel, equivalent to 6.2% of physicians in those fields, while 188 surgeons – around 6% of the total – also departed.
The Tel Aviv area recorded the highest departure rate, with 5.4% of doctors leaving, according to the study.
The findings follow a report by the Israeli Finance Ministry last week showing that around 24% of specialist doctors in public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Another 25% have already passed retirement age but continue working amid shortages in medical staff.
Ater warned that the trajectory, rather than the current situation alone, was the greater concern, saying the trend could worsen after Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27.
The study adds to broader signs of rising emigration from Israel.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country between 2023 and 2025 for at least three months, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have linked the rise in departures to the war, high living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken judicial powers.
A Kantar poll for KAN in August found that around one in five Israelis had considered emigrating over the previous two years, while 12% said the outcome of the upcoming election could affect their decision to remain in the country.

Taiwan finds new uses for agricultural waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:33:04 UTC
11:33:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is turning agricultural waste into new products as part of efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with the initiative generating NT$150 million (US$4.7 million) in output, according to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The drive toward net-zero agriculture began in 2022, when the ministry unveiled a strategy to cut emissions by 2040. Since then, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said the program has helped develop 49 products made from agricultural waste.
A total of 19 companies have joined the initiative, with combined investment reaching NT$320 million as businesses seek ways to put materials that would otherwise be discarded to new uses.
One example is yarn made from discarded oyster shells by a textile company in Tainan. The firm has also combined oyster shell powder with recycled plastic bottles to produce functional fibers, according to CNA.
Agricultural waste can also be reused as an energy source. A dried longan farm in Tainan, for instance, processes pruned branches and other dry wood from its grounds into biomass pellets. The pellets are then burned as fuel to dry longan.
Chen said cutting emissions from agriculture requires more than reducing energy consumption. Changes in farming and livestock practices are also needed, including measures to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation and livestock manure, as well as nitrous oxide emissions linked to fertilizer use.
Farmers have increased their use of nitrogen fertilizer to boost crop yields. However, excess nitrogen can be released as nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that traps nearly 300 times more heat than carbon dioxide, according to the Agricultural Technology Research Institute.
Taiwan’s agricultural sector emitted about 6.5 billion kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024, accounting for approximately 2.38% of the country’s total emissions. The figure includes emissions from crop production, livestock, forestry, and fisheries, according to the Climate Change Administration.

BERLIN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- The United States advanced directly to the quarterfinals of the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup on Sunday while China secured a place in the quarterfinal qualification round, after both teams won in Group D.
The U.S. survived a stern challenge from Italy to win 55-52, while China came from behind to defeat Czechia 74-70 in overtime earlier in the day.
Team USA led 23-8 early in the second quarter after a 12-0 run spanning the first two periods. Italy responded with a zone defense and gradually erased the deficit before moving ahead 50-48 with 4:29 remaining.
The U.S. answered with seven consecutive points. Breanna Stewart, who had missed her first eight shots, hit a jumper to put her team ahead 51-50. Jackie Young then added a layup, and Chelsea Gray extended the lead to five.
Italy still had a chance to force overtime, but Cecilia Zandalasini missed a 3-pointer at the buzzer. Young led the United States with 10 points, while Zandalasini scored a game-high 14 for Italy.
Team USA shot just 29% from the field and made only one of their 12 3-point attempts, but improved to 2-0, guaranteeing first place in Group D and a direct quarterfinal berth.
China trailed 64-59 with 27 seconds left in regulation time before completing a dramatic comeback. Luo Xinyu hit a 3-pointer to cut the deficit to two, and after Czechia missed two free throws, Yang Shuyu drove for the tying layup with three seconds remaining.
Luo opened overtime with another 3-pointer before Han Xu scored off an offensive rebound to give China a 69-64 lead. China protected its advantage to seal its first victory of the tournament.
Han finished with 22 points, 14 rebounds and four assists, while Yang added 18 points and five assists.
China and Italy, both 1-1, are guaranteed top-three finishes and will meet Monday to decide second and third place in Group D. Czechia was eliminated after suffering its second consecutive defeat.
In Group C, Australia and Belgium both secured at least a place in the quarterfinal qualification round after recording their second victories.
Australia defeated Türkiye 87-71 after leading for 38 minutes, 41 seconds. Ezi Magbegor scored 21 points on 10-of-14 shooting, while Steph Talbot contributed 17 points, five rebounds and five assists.
The Opals led by 10 points at halftime and stretched their advantage to as many as 20 in the fourth quarter.
European champion Belgium followed with a 76-64 victory over Puerto Rico. Julie Allemand narrowly missed a triple-double with 11 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists, while Maxuella Lisowa-Mbaka scored a team-high 16 points off the bench.
Imani McGee-Stafford led Puerto Rico with 25 points and 13 rebounds.
Australia and Belgium will meet Monday, with the winner taking first place in Group C and advancing directly to the quarterfinals. Puerto Rico and Türkiye will contest the group's remaining qualification-round berth. ■

Doan Ritsu (L) of Eintracht Frankfurt vies with Arijon Ibrahimovic of FC Augsburg during the German first division Bundesliga football match between Eintracht Frankfurt and FC Augsburg in Frankfurt, Germany, Sept. 6, 2026. (Photo by Ulrich Hufnagel/Xinhua)
BERLIN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Augsburg scored four second-half goals to rally past Eintracht Frankfurt 4-1 on Sunday, moving top of the Bundesliga for the first time in the club's history.
Eintracht went ahead after six minutes when Jonathan Burkardt headed home from Younes Ebnoutalib's cross.
The hosts controlled much of the opening half, with Mario Gotze directing play and Ebnoutalib repeatedly causing problems. Augsburg goalkeeper Finn Dahmen denied Can Uzun, Raphael Onyedika and Ebnoutalib.
Augsburg's only clear chance in the first half came from Fabian Rieder's free kick, which went narrowly wide in stoppage time.
The match changed immediately after the restart. Arijon Ibrahimovic, making his Augsburg debut, headed Marius Wolf's delivery into the far corner in the 46th minute.
Augsburg struck again less than two minutes later. Goalkeeper Noah Atubolu appeared to have Ibrahimovic's effort under control but spilled the ball, allowing Robin Fellhauer to turn it home.
Atubolu denied Michael Gregoritsch in the 58th minute but was beaten seven minutes later when substitute Alexis Claude-Maurice curled a shot into the far corner.
Rieder completed the scoring in the 89th minute with a free kick from 24 meters into the top corner.
The victory followed Augsburg's 3-0 win over Schalke and leaves the club with six points and a 7-1 goal difference. Eintracht has one point from its opening two matches.
"Conceding two goals straight after halftime is very bitter. I don't really know what happened," Burkardt said. "Augsburg was clearly more mature in the second half."
Augsburg hosts Bayer Leverkusen next Saturday, while Eintracht visits Mainz.
Also on Sunday, Mainz crushed Hamburg 5-0, with Phillip Tietz scoring twice after Sheraldo Becker and Phillipp Mwene had put the visitors in control. Ransford-Yeboah Konigsdorffer completed the rout in stoppage time. ■

Sochi oil depot reportedly erupts in flames again days after Ukrainian strikes

2026-09-07

11:29:33 KST

An oil depot in the Russian city of Sochi appeared to reignite on Sept. 7, three days after being struck by Ukrainian drones, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Videos posted by Sochi residents on social media appear to show the oil depot, owned by Russia's state energy company Rosneft, ablaze and billowing smoke. The Russian monitoring Telegram channel ExileNova+ reports that authorities are asking local residents to close their windows due to heavy smoke in the coastal vacation destination.
At the time of publishing the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports nor the extent of the damage caused.
It was not immediately clear as to what caused the oil depot to reportedly reignite. Russian Air raid alerts in the region were not activated ahead of the blaze.
The latest fires come days after Ukrainian forces launched several waves of attacks against targets in Sochi on Sept. 3-4, including a naval drone strike on a Russian vessel.
Known as Russia’s "Second Capital," Sochi is home to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s official summer residence. Considered a winter playground for Russia’s elite, the city is located approximately 650 to 700 kilometers (400 to 435 miles) from the Ukraine border.
For months, Ukraine has conducted a sustained campaign of drone and missile strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Damage to energy facilities has prompted Moscow to impose export restrictions as domestic supplies have tightened and long queues have formed across the country.
Ukraine's General Staff announced on September 4 that two major Russian oil facilities have suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in August. 
Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, located about 800 kilometers (nearly 500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was shut down due to damage suffered in a Ukrainian drone attack on Aug. 26. The facility is Russia's fourth-largest oil refinery and second-largest gasoline producer, processing around 15-17 million metric tons of crude oil annually. 
The General Staff also said the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Slobidka, Leningrad Oblast, had suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes on Sept. 1. Located about 850 kilometers (nearly 530 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the facility is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for exporting crude oil and petroleum products.
