At least five killed in New Delhi building collapse

Kushner refrains from saying is US will toughen pressure on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:03:28 UTC
05:03:28 KST

WASHINGTON, September 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has refrained from saying whether the United States is going to increase pressure on Russia if no visible progress is made toward settling the Ukrainian conflict in the foreseeable future.
"There's no such thing, you know, in the world as forever enemies or forever allies," he told a news conference after talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev, answering a relevant question.
According to Kushner, Trump is looking at the Ukrainian conflict through the prism of the "idea of what the best outcome could be and what benefits all people." "You know, President Trump comes from the business world. In the business world you think about things in the context of win-win," he said. "War is negative sum, you know. Everyone loses from war, whereas you know business and peace is positive sum, and hopefully you can find big benefits from that in a big way."
"Our role is to try to be the ones who are pursuing the peace," he stressed, adding that attempts to settle the conflict in Ukraine are "a very important and noble pursuit."
"And we're going to keep doing it with everything we have," Kushner noted. "And President Trump obviously has a lot of different ways to play it, but he's always focused on what are the best interests of America and the United States.".

In France, the far-right leader wants Ukraine to pay for Europe&apos;s aid - Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

In France, the far-right leader wants Ukraine to pay for Europe's aid - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Jordan Bardella, leader of the "National Rally," is demanding guarantees of repayment for aid to Ukraine. He proposes spending funds only on European weapons.
The president of France’s far-right party "National Rally," Jordan Bardella, called for replacing unconditional support for Ukraine with relations under which France would receive something in return. If his political force comes to power, financial and military aid to Kyiv could be provided under new conditions. Bloomberg reports this, writes UNN.
Details
According to him, the difficult state of French public finances requires Paris to receive some return for military aid to Kyiv. The 30-year-old politician is considered one of the most likely candidates for the post of prime minister of France if Marine Le Pen wins next year’s presidential election. At the Ambrosetti Forum in Cernobbio, Italy, Bardella said that France has serious problems with public debt and the budget deficit.
We are drowning in debt. We are drowning in deficits. And it is irresponsible to take on spending commitments and promises of financial support for a country without any guarantees
Bardella stressed that the current approach needs to be completely reconsidered. He spoke positively about the policy of the United States, which demands certain commitments from Ukraine in exchange for support. As an example, the politician mentioned agreements granting the United States access to Ukrainian natural resources, including rare-earth materials, as part of guarantees related to loans and other aid.
At the same time, Bardella assured that France would not abandon Ukraine if Marine Le Pen wins; she is the "National Rally" candidate for president after Emmanuel Macron. However, he proposed changing the mechanism for providing support. In particular, Ukraine could guarantee that financial aid received from European states would be used to purchase military equipment exclusively from defense-industry companies in those countries.
As the publication notes, French President Emmanuel Macron has sought to coordinate Europe’s response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and strengthen France’s position as one of Kyiv’s main allies and a leader of the Western bloc. Bardella’s position differs substantially. His views on international politics and the economy are much closer to Trump’s approach.
Bardella also criticized the European Union’s regulatory policy. He took a position close to that of the American president and major U.S. technology corporations, whose influence the EU has sought to limit with new rules in recent years. In the politician’s view, France could use its significant nuclear-power capacity to attract data centers needed for the development of artificial intelligence.
We remind you
National Rally Vice President Louis Aliot promised to halt aid to Kyiv if Le Pen wins the election. The leader of the National Rally’s parliamentary group has already announced her participation in the presidential race.

- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in business circles, NABU and SAPO had detained Kropyva.
- On the same day, NABU and SAPO announced that they had uncovered a criminal organisation which investigators say was headed by the head of a department at the Prosecutor General's Office. Members of the organisation are suspected of regularly taking bribes from scam call centres and laundering the proceeds of crime. According to Ukrainska Pravda, the person in question is Serhii Kropyva.

The psychological effects of padel and pickleball, according to science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:00:38 UTC
05:00:38 KST

Pickleball participation was associated with greater happiness, life satisfaction, social integration and lower depression, while padel was more closely studied in relation to confidence, anxiety and mental fatigue, according to a systematic review published in Frontiers in Psychology.
Physical activity is widely linked to better mental health, yet many people do not meet recommended activity levels. Padel and pickleball have attracted attention because they are social, relatively accessible and can be played across a range of ages and skill levels. Padel is played on an enclosed court where the ball can rebound from the walls, while pickleball uses a smaller court, a perforated plastic ball and slower-paced play that emphasizes strategy and interaction.
The researchers conducted the review because most previous studies had concentrated on physical fitness, injuries and sporting performance. Less was known about whether these sports were related to mental health and wellbeing. The review ultimately revealed a stark divide in the existing literature: padel has mostly been studied in competitive settings, while pickleball research has frequently focused on recreational play among older adults.
Led by Lena Lauxtermann at the University of Vienna, the researchers searched for studies published through October 8, 2024. Of 71 records screened, 14 studies were included, representing 1,403 participants. Eight padel studies included 538 people and six pickleball studies included 865. Women represented 42% of the overall sample, or approximately 589 participants.
The pickleball findings were mainly linked to wellbeing. Participation was associated with greater happiness, stronger social connections and higher life satisfaction. One study found that happiness was positively related to participation, while another linked more serious involvement in pickleball with lower depression. Social integration appeared particularly important for female players. During the COVID-19 pandemic, reduced opportunities to play were associated with increased loneliness and poorer mental health, suggesting that the social contact provided by the sport may be part of its benefit.
The padel studies focused more on athletes’ performance-related emotions. Higher-level players generally reported greater self-confidence and lower physical symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety also changed according to ranking, gender, match stage and whether players won or lost. Mental fatigue increased across consecutive matches and was linked to slower reactions and poorer accuracy. Motivation sometimes rose during mentally demanding matches, which may help explain why players continued performing despite feeling mentally tired.
The findings suggest the two rapidly growing racket sports may offer different mental-health benefits, but stronger research is needed to determine whether playing them directly causes improvements.
The authors summarized: “Padel studies primarily target performance aspects like self-confidence, anxiety, and mental fatigue, while pickleball research highlights wellbeing gains in life satisfaction, happiness, and social integration.”
Some limitations are to be noted. The results should not be interpreted as proof that either sport prevents depression or anxiety. For example, many studies relied on self-reported experiences, and all of the included studies were observational rather than randomized controlled trials. Padel research also overrepresented elite and competitive players, while pickleball research focused mainly on older adults. Additionally, the available research was geographically narrow, with all included studies originating from just three countries: the United States, Spain and Finland.
The study, “Padel, pickleball and wellbeing: a systematic review,” was authored by Lena Lauxtermann and Brendon Stubbs.

The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:00:14 UTC
05:00:14 KST

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.
New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.
“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …
“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:
- 
  Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
- 
  Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
- 
  Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
- 
  Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.
Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.
Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.
Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.
Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.
Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.
The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.
The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.
The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.
Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.
“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”
There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.
Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.
Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”
Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.
But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.
Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).
More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”
Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.
“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”
She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”
Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.
“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”
Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”
- 
  The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
September 6, 2026
On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.
In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.
DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.
Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.
Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots
Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.
A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."
The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.
Verdict: False
There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.
They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.
The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.
Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.
Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system
Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud
Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.
"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.
Verdict: False
DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.
The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.
Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".
One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."
Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.
"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.
DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.
Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections
Did Halle start counting ballots too early?
Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.
Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".
Verdict: Misleading
The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.
Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.
The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."
The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.
Edited by: Sarah Steffen

Iran will declare a ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz in coming days: security chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:53:02 UTC
04:53:02 KST

Iran plans new ‘exclusion zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz after ship attacks
Iranian security chief threatens sanctions on transit ships as US blockade and tanker strikes escalate tensions
The new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on Sunday said Tehran plans to announce an “exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Mohsen Rezaei’s comments to Iran’s state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the US struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at US warships. Experts called the launches a dangerous escalation after Iran’s previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.
The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and “will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei said. “Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list.”
It is not clear where Iran defines the location of the weekslong US blockade, which is aimed at Iranian ports and keeping Tehran from shipping out its oil. The US military has said over 20 warships are supporting the blockade, which as of Sunday had redirected 92 commercial ships and disabled three.
The US has been introducing new measures to increase the economic pain on Iran after negotiations collapsed and no end to the intermittent fighting appears in sight. Meanwhile, Iran continues to attack some ships trying to transit the strait, which has become an important source of leverage for Tehran in the war that began February 28 with US and Israeli strikes.
Iran earlier Sunday said it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the US military dismissed as a “total lie”.

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure
TEHRAN – The Iranian authorities on Sept 6 announced they were raising the price of petrol for heavier consumers, as the United States steps up sanctions seeking to isolate the country’s economy.
Iran’s quota system prices petrol in three tiers – 1,500 tomans per litre for a consumer’s first 60 litres in a given month, 3,000 tomans per litre for their next 50, and 5,000 tomans per litre after that. The toman is an informal unit equivalent to 10 Iranian rials.
On Sept 6, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said the price for the third tier would double to 10,000 tomans (about 5.7 Singapore cents).
“The rate will increase to 10,000 toman rials from the morning of Sept 8,” Mohajerani said in remarks carried by state media.
“Different numbers were mentioned in expert meetings, but because the President had promised the people, the rate of 10,000 tomans was set,” she added.
She later clarified that the price of the first and second tiers would not be changed.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making any changes to pricing politically sensitive.
The development comes as the Iranian currency was trading on the black market on Sept 6 at more than 2.2 million rials to the US dollar, according to websites that track the rate.
Before the start of the Middle East war on Feb 28, the rial traded at around 1.7 million to the dollar, and in late April it hit what was then a record low of 1.8 million.
Late in August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, hoping to use financial pressure to hasten the end of the war.
The new measures build on a sanctions regime by the US and allies that has been in place since 2018, when President Donald Trump withdrew from an international deal struck with Tehran on its nuclear programme.
The US has also put Iran’s ports under a naval blockade, attempting to reduce its oil exports to zero. AFP

'Now measured in the millions': The common process being used to scam Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:35:54 UTC
04:35:54 KST

in brief
- Scammers are exploiting the growing use of CAPTCHAs to trick people into running malicious code outside their browser.
- An expert has practical tips on how to minimise your risk.
CAPTCHAs are meant to protect our online infrastructure from bots. Scammers, however, are turning them against us.
Cybersecurity experts have seen a rise in fake CAPTCHA scams, with the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) releasing a warning this week about the ruse.
The fake CAPTCHAs direct internet users to input code outside of their browser, which grants hackers access to the device and, in some cases, browser session information.
The scams often ask them to paste a script into a computer's terminal, allowing the attacks to bypass anti-malware security systems.
Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at UNSW School of Computer Science and managing director of the Digital Lies & Cyber Literacy Foundation, said the ability to bypass anti-malware protections made fake CAPTCHA scams particularly dangerous.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"You haven't got very many of the protections of the operating system working for you," he told SBS News.
Previously, CAPTCHAs were commonly required for creating online account. However, they're now common when making the first connection with a website, greatly increasing the number that internet users are asked to complete.
Pearce attributes this to "the explosion of AI agents online" as websites attempt to prevent artificial intelligence from going through them.
The increased prevalence of CAPTCHAs means it's easier for dodgy ones to slip through.
Pearce said he'd "expect it more on slightly dodgier websites" but hackers "can try and hijack your connection so that you get that when you're trying to get to a normal website".
Pearce also said the number of fake CAPTCHA attacks "are now measured in the millions".
How to avoid fake CAPTCHAs
According to Pearce, it's now much harder than it used to be for criminals to leverage a person's internet connection against them.
Major browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Edge have used significant resources to make themselves "about the safest piece of technology there is on your computer", Pearce said.
He said users should be suspicious if a CAPTCHA asks them to type something or leave the window.
"If it's actually asking you to type some random thing on your keyboard, you should immediately start getting suspicious," Pearce said.
"Be very wary of anything that might take you out of the safety of the web browser."
He says that, if something feels off, internet users should ask themselves: "Why? Why do I need to do this?"

Veena feared she would be a resentful grandmother. One rule stopped this
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:31:43 UTC
04:31:43 KST

What does grandparenting look like today? Insight explores whether the demands on modern-day grandparents are keeping them physically fit and mentally well, or if the younger generations’ wants and needs are being prioritised to the detriment of grandparents. Watch Insight episode Grandparenting Tuesday 8 September at 8.30pm on SBS or SBS On Demand.
Veena Gopinath recently became a grandmother to twins. When she found out her daughter was pregnant, Veena was excited for her, but not for herself.
"It wasn't a joyful instant emotion in any way, shape, or form," the 56-year-old told Insight.
"I was like, 'Oh my God, how am I going to do this?'"
The Sydney-based small business owner says her feelings about becoming a grandmother were strange.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"In my mind, I was still young and our son had just finished school.
"So, life was just becoming more fun for me — I had time and money and resources to look after myself."
When Veena became a mother 32 years ago, her parents put their lives on hold to help her adjust to motherhood.
"Both my parents came from India, and they stayed for 12 months ... I was totally pampered."
"That was the message I was given — to be a grandparent like that — and it was a really tough act to follow ..."
Deciding she didn't want to put herself through the same thing, Veena set clear boundaries with her daughter four months after she gave birth.
"She doesn't expect anything more than what I offer," Veena said.
"I have said that I will never commit to regular babysitting for her."
But there are a few exceptions to this boundary.
"If they want to go on a date night, I'll help them out because that's important for their marriage; and then if there are urgent or emergency things, of course I'll help."
"My view is that they need to find resources and create their own babysitting and money to handle those things. It's not my thing to help them out."
The tipping point
Myra Hamilton is a sociologist at the University of Sydney whose research focuses on gender, work and care.
She says that grandparents who set clear boundaries around what they're willing to do regarding childcare are less likely to experience negative impacts on their health and financial security. She says grandparents providing occasional or regular childcare has its benefits.
"[It] actually can be positive for grandparents' mental health, their mood; it can be positive for their physical health, their fitness or their balance or mobility; and some studies even find that it can be positive for cognitive health ..."
But the sociologist said there is a "tipping point" when it's no longer beneficial.
"Our own research has found what we call a tipping point of about 13 hours of childcare per week ..." she said.
"That's when you started to see things like they were less likely to say they felt they had a choice, they were more likely to feel obligated, they were less likely to enjoy providing the childcare."
Prioritising family
Unlike Veena, Fiona Ninnes has a standing agreement with her daughter, who is a single mother working full-time, for regular childcare.
But prioritising grandparenting responsibilities has meant personal sacrifice for the retired teacher and her husband — including her no longer having time to participate in community theatre and having to relocate.
The couple used to live in the Southern Highlands, 90 minutes' drive from Sydney, but had to downsize to a Sydney apartment when the commute to babysit became too taxing.
"It's affecting our hip pocket, but we don't have the petrol costs ... because we can now jump on a train.
"I don't know if it's exactly balanced, but we're happy with it."
The 67-year-old minds her five-year-old and two-year-old grandchildren every Tuesday afternoon and all day Wednesday.
"Both of them have had a lot of health issues ... They were both going to daycare but had to be withdrawn because of the health issues.
"[My granddaughter] was constantly in hospital. If a child [got] a cold, she would get pneumonia."
When she's not babysitting, the retired teacher likes to spend time with other family members — including her four other grandchildren.
"But if one of our other [grandchildren] is in hospital, then yeah, I can often feel like I'm a piece of string stretched in too many different directions."
When that happens, Fiona knows it's time to take a step back to stave off burnout.
"If I've done 10 days straight and I'm absolutely exhausted because it's 24/7, I have to say, 'Okay, well, you've got a nanny coming in'."
"Even though I absolutely adore spending time with them ... it is exhausting."
'I didn't want to take money from my own daughter'
Like Fiona, Kaaran Moody also provides regular childcare for her daughter Christine, who transfers Kaaran some money each week as a token of appreciation.
"I told her I didn't want money for looking after him because I just love him, and I love her, and I wanted them to get ahead financially.
"But she insisted on paying me whether I wanted it or not."
While Kaaran says she felt very guilty for accepting the money, she says it is helpful.
"I didn't want to take money from my own daughter, especially because we never had a hand when we were young parents, and we wanted to give her what we'd never had.
"But at the same time, I wouldn't have been able to afford petrol. And I was able to take him to activities ... buy him toys, games and books."
The 56-year-old and her daughter worked together as early childhood educators at an Adelaide childcare centre before Kaaran offered to mind her grandson at home and stopped working.
When Christine returned from maternity leave, she would drop her son off in another class at the daycare and work in the other, which proved difficult.
"He wasn't eating; he wouldn't sleep; and she would come into the room, and he would just be really distressed, wanting her to cuddle him," Kaaran said.
"And she couldn't because she's literally at work."
Grandparenting in Australia
For grandparents who provide regular childcare in Australia, 70 per cent change their working hours, 50 per cent reduce their working hours, and one in five reports changing jobs to accommodate their childcare responsibilities, a 2020 survey by the University of Sydney found.
The survey also reported that one in three grandparents believed providing childcare to their grandkids negatively impacted their finances — by working less and earning less super, and through the direct costs of childcare, such as buying nappies and baby food.
Hamilton notes that childcare can be expensive, hard to find a placement, sometimes not culturally appropriate, and often "not flexible enough".
"When you ask grandparents why they're providing regular childcare, the most common reason they provide is to support their adult children in paid work," she told Insight.
"Especially their adult daughters and daughters-in-laws — supporting them to invest in their careers."
Hamilton said that grandparenting is often gendered — with grandmothers being more likely to take on childcare duties. And these duties are often taken on during a time when some older women are also trying to work and save for their financial future.
The sociologist says that men and women often take on different roles in providing care for grandchildren.
"Grandmothers are more likely to provide routine childcare tasks (like bathing, feeding, and putting the child down for a nap) ... Whereas grandfathers are more likely to be involved in things like transporting the grandchild to and from daycare or play-based tasks."
"And we also find that more of the hours that grandfathers spend providing childcare are spent with the grandmother also present, whereas grandmothers are more likely to be providing that care on their own."
'It's probably not a natural role'
Before becoming grandparents, family lawyer Franco Pomare expected that he and his wife would take on traditional grandmother and grandfather roles.
"I would've thought my wife would've taken on the greater role," he said.
"I would eventually slow down at work and I would pick up the slack."
However, Franco's wife, Lydia, had a stroke five years ago, which left her with limited mobility, cognitive impairment and memory loss.
"The heavy lifting I think, is normally done by a grandmother," the 66-year-old said.
"But that hasn't occurred."
Franco has reduced his hours at his family practice, where he works with his daughter Gabriella, to be a more involved grandfather.
He does school pick-ups for his six-year-old grandson and spends more time at home with his wife and her carer, who look after Gabriella's two-year-old daughter.
"It's probably not a natural role," Franco said.
"But I'm adapting to it."

The EU could lose 300,000 industrial jobs due to competition from China
Kyiv • UNN
Eurometal forecasts the loss of 300,000 jobs in the EU by the end of 2026 due to competition from China. The association is preparing a protest in Brussels.
Job cuts in the EU’s manufacturing sector will surge if Brussels does not stop the "colonization" of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry business association warns. The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
Eurometal forecasts the loss of 300,000 manufacturing jobs by the end of 2026 due to intensifying competition from China, which currently has a record trade surplus with the bloc of €1 billion per day.
As a result, the Eurometal association plans to hold a protest in Brussels near the headquarters of the European Commission, using 10 symbolic coffins bearing messages about competitiveness, industrial jobs, and European factories.
European manufacturers are concerned that Brussels is failing to notice the destruction of industry caused by China’s integration into component supply chains. Eurometal President Alexander Julius notes that China seeks to control key value chains rather than simply be a raw-materials supplier.
The problem is compounded by the fact that European companies are burdened by high carbon-emissions taxes and tariffs on steel imports, while Chinese components are not subject to such charges, making fair competition impossible against the backdrop of an undervalued yuan.
Despite the political rhetoric, businesses will continue buying cheaper products from China in the interests of shareholders.

Wreckage and ruin at site of wedding hit by alleged US strike

Wreckage and ruin at site of wedding hit by alleged US strike
KUHESTAK, Iran – Outside a home in southern Iran, family photos, appliances and household items were piled in a courtyard, pulled from the wreckage of what the authorities said was a US strike that killed five people as they gathered to celebrate a wedding.
The bride and groom had not yet arrived when the blast tore through the Mallahi family’s home in Kuhestak on the night of Sept 1, according to relatives who spoke to Iranian media.
But dozens of women and children had already gathered in the compound, waiting for the festivities to begin.
The extent of the destruction was stark, according to AFP journalists who visited the area on Sept 6 under the supervision of the Iranian authorities.
The ceiling of one of the rooms had completely collapsed, and walls in a hallway had deep cracks.
All of the windows had been shattered, while the kitchen area was in shambles.
Abandoned shoes, many of them dressy women’s sandals, were piled up in one room, while a gaping hole the width of a double-doorway was blown in the wall of another.
Part of the building’s exterior wall was blackened by fire.
The dead included a four-year-old child and three women, one of whom died later in hospital, as well as one man, with nearly 70 people wounded.
Homes evacuated
Kuhestak, a small coastal town more accustomed to the sound of the surf in the nearby Strait of Hormuz, was rocked by the thunder of explosions as the US carried out a wider bombardment of southern Iran on Sept 1.
On Sept 6, workers were cutting away the remains of a telecommunications tower that was knocked down in the attacks.
The tower, about 15m high, had stood near the town’s port, and was about 100m from the house where the wedding was taking place.
A technical and administrative building in the same complex was also seriously damaged.
Many pieces of shrapnel could be seen in surrounding areas, including at a shop near the tower, and several houses have been evacuated.
At the Kuhestak port, the pier and a large barge were also damaged.
The Iranian authorities have blamed the United States for the attack on the wedding ceremony, with the judiciary saying the US used precision-guided munitions and the Foreign Ministry calling it a “war crime”.
Washington has not accepted responsibility for the attack, but has said it is investigating and does not target civilians intentionally.
US officials said the military had targeted communications and other military infrastructure in the area. AFP

The Greens have also secured a place in the state’s parliament with around 8.5-9%. The Free Democratic Party received only around 2-2.5% of the vote and will lose its seats in the state parliament.
The voter turnout was 80%.

Germany's far-right AfD wins state election in Saxony-Anhalt but falls short of governing majority — preliminary official results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:08:00 UTC
04:08:00 KST

What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
- The European press calling the results an "unsettling new page in German history"
Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.
Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD
Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."
Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.
Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."
For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.
It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.
AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'
Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.
He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.
Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.
She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.
This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.
Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."
Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.
AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference
In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state.
Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.
Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.
Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.
Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.
After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.
Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.
Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."
Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.
"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."

Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'
Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."
Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"
After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era.
Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."
Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now
Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.
After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.
Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory
The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.
The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.
International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'
Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.
New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.
In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.
Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."
And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."
Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory.
"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."
"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.
Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'
Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.
"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.
Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.
She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."
The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.
"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.
AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win
According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.
AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."
At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.
"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."
If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.
Is coalition without AfD possible?
The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."
That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.
Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.
Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?
Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.
The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.
But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.
The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.
Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.
Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:
- Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
- Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
- Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
- Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
- Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
- Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats
Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.
According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.
WATCH: "Migration alone no longer explains the party’s rise"
Historian Katja Hoyer says the AfD's breakthrough was fueled by a more upbeat campaign around Ulrich Siegmund, while mainstream parties struggled to offer a positive vision of change.
CDU fails to win a single direct mandate in Saxony-Anhalt state election
As a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU, the party came away empty-handed in the individual constituencies.
The CDU failed to win a single direct mandate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
According to preliminary figures from the state election authority, CDU candidates were defeated in all 41 constituencies.
Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidates prevailed in 38 constituencies, including lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Genthin. Candidates from the Left Party won the remaining three constituencies: one in Magdeburg and two in Halle.
In the 2021 state election, the CDU won direct mandates in 40 of the 41 constituencies, while the AfD won one.
In Germany, voters have two votes. The "first vote" determines the winner of a constituency and the direct mandate. The "second vote" determines the distribution of seats among parties in the state parliament.

Woman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian first
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:00:12 UTC
04:00:12 KST

A woman has been buried in a coffin made from mushrooms in New South Wales in an eco-friendly first for Australia.
Carolyn, whose surname was withheld for privacy reasons, was laid to rest on Friday by friends and family at Springwood Cemetery in the Blue Mountains. She was aged in her 70s.
The mushroom coffin, created by the Dutch firm Loop Biotech, was grown from mycelium – the root network of fungi – and hemp fibres.
The coffin is grown in mould in a climate-controlled room, taking just a week to fully form. Once buried, it takes about 45 days to become part of the soil.
The process is akin to composting, as the body and coffin gently biodegrade and transform into nutrient-rich soil in far less time than a traditional wooden casket, which can take up to 50 years to break down.
Carolyn’s husband, Donald, said picking the mushroom coffin aligned with his wife’s values of giving back.
“She was always there to help others. It feels very true to who she was that even after her death, she can still do something for others while giving something back to nature,” he said.
While Carolyn is the first to be buried in the coffin in Australia, Loop Biotech’s founder Bob Hendrikx said there had been thousands of others across Europe and the US.
“Five years ago when I started, there was lots of interest from Australia,” Hendrikx said. “It was a little bit harder to ship overseas [at the time].”
Hendrikx hopes the mushroom coffins, which weigh about 30kg each, could improve the sustainability of the Australian funeral sector by shortening the decomposition process.
“It’s about giving back to nature: we have the mushroom, which is grown and dissolves into nature, but the actual benefit is that … it’s enriching the soil,” he said.
“The body needs to just return to nature and let nature do what it’s done best forever.
“If a kangaroo dies in the forest, it’s just going to be part of the cycle of life.”
Dr Hannah Gould, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Melbourne, believes people are becoming increasingly interested in environmentally friendly farewells.
“As people perhaps become less religious, other kinds of values or community groupings become more important, and one of those that we’ve seen is eco-death.
“This idea that perhaps that you don’t go up to heaven after you die, you return to the earth, has been an increasingly popular narrative around death and dying.”
While about 70% of Australians choose to be cremated, it has a substantial environmental impact: the emissions from a typical cremation are estimated to be equivalent to 125kg of carbon dioxide.
In recent years options such as alkaline hydrolysis (a cremation-like process that uses water instead of fire), natural burials without embalming, and even shallow burials have become available. A natural burial uses a cardboard coffin with rope handles and will emit less than 10kg of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to PlanetMark analysis.
Gould believes that as Australians are living longer and more people are dying from prolonged illnesses, more time is being spent thinking about how to depart and farewell loved ones.
“They’ve maybe seen or organised a funeral for their parents and it hasn’t gone so well,” she said. “And they’re now deciding that they want to do things differently. So we’re seeing a huge rise in funeral planning.”

Zelensky warns war likely to continue into winter after US talks

US envoys have ‘more effective proposals’: Ukraine official
KYIV - Washington’s envoys have brought new, “more effective” proposals on ending the war with Russia to Kyiv and President Volodymyr Zelensky is meeting them again in a trio format, a senior Ukrainian presidential official told AFP on Sept 6.
Earlier on Sept 6, Zelensky had said the war with Russia looked likely to continue into winter.
While both he and the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had given upbeat assessments of the talks, neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the conflict.
But the senior presidential official told AFP: “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective. They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part.”
Earlier on Sept 6, Witkoff and Zelensky had both given upbeat assessments of the talks, even if neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the conflict.
Witkoff, who is President Donald Trump’s business ally, and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow – the latest of several visits to the city.
The visit to Kyiv on Sept 6 was their first to the Ukrainian capital, which has been enduring deadly Russian strikes for more than four years.
Zelensky said: “We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter – and this is how it appears at the moment.”
Zelensky also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, but did not elaborate.
The Ukrainian leader repeated his call that only a meeting between the two leaders could solve territorial issues.
Thanking the US envoys for their visit, Zelensky said on X: “The main thing is to achieve peace for Ukraine – a dignified, reliable, and lasting peace.
“We are directing all our efforts toward this.”
‘On same side’
Moscow occupies large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and the Kremlin told the Americans on Sept 5 that it was feeling “confident” it would advance more.
Moscow has said it wants not just the territories it occupies but the land it claims as Russian to be recognised as its own – terms unacceptable to Kyiv.
Witkoff said both sides would need to compromise, adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place.
“We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged, and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.”
Kushner added: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.”
Witkoff and Kushner travelled to the region hoping to revive the Trump administration’s push for peace in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation.
British, French and German representatives attended a separate round of the talks.
Zelensky said he was grateful the Europeans were there, adding: “Here we are all on the same side.”
Like all visiting officials, the American delegation had arrived by train, with “Peace Express” written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station.
Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Russia launched its invasion in 2022.
Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other’s capitals during the US envoys’ trip.
‘Substantive plans’
Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
A White House official said in a statement to AFP that in Moscow the envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”.
Without elaborating, the Kremlin said the Americans “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine, and Russia increased deadly strikes this summer.
Since Putin launched the invasion in February 2022, the war has dragged on with no end in sight.
In Kyiv, few people appeared to believe in a breakthrough.
Nataliia Lipekh, 67, said it was “absolutely necessary (for them) to be here” and to see that “our land is already soaked with this blood and that we need some help”.
“At the moment, I have no grounds for hope,” said 29-year-old Yaroslav, saying he had seen “far too many of these negotiation processes”.
Despite the ceasefire pledges for the capital cities, fighting continued elsewhere.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it had shot down 258 drones.
Ukraine said on Sept 5 that 10 people were killed by Russian strikes, including an 11-year-old boy. AFP

Germany to Create Comprehensive Measures to Counter Russian Sabotage and Cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:49:54 UTC
03:49:54 KST

Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior plans to establish a comprehensive set of measures to counter Russian sabotage, including cyberattacks.
Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told this to Bild.
The security plan calls for the rapid deployment of special units in strategically important cities across the country — Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, Leipzig, Hanover and Cologne.
They are to provide comprehensive protection against drones in the airspace over critical infrastructure, airports, railway stations and the government district of the capital. In addition to interception, their duties will also include neutralizing explosive devices.
“Hybrid attacks involving drones carrying explosives targeting airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks and sabotage of our infrastructure — this is our daily reality. These attacks will intensify, but we can defend ourselves,” the minister said.
Under the security plan, drone protection in the near future will be provided not only by the federal police but also by critical infrastructure operators, including energy companies and defense contractors. They will be given legal authority to actively repel drone attacks.
In addition, Germany also plans to create a national protective shield, known as the Cyberdome.
According to the minister, the network is to detect and block attempts by hackers to launch attacks at an early stage.
The security plan is being developed amid Russian hybrid threats. On August 5, a drone equipped with explosives was found near a Ukrainian An-124 Ruslan transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport during the night. Militarnyi reported on the incident.
On September 1, Germany officially accused Russia of the attack involving the Ukrainian An-124 in Leipzig.
On September 2, German law enforcement authorities confirmed that a Russian-born man with a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen who also holds a Russian passport were involved in the planned attack.
On September 3, amid Russia’s attempted sabotage in Leipzig, Germany strengthened cooperation with Ukraine and drafted a plan to expand its military contingent in Lithuania.

Trump administration appeals again to US Supreme Court over mail-in voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:47:03 UTC
03:47:03 KST

Trump administration appeals again to US Supreme Court over mail-in voting
How the nation’s highest could rules could have major implications in this year’s midterm elections.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has made another appeal to the Supreme Court to allow new restrictions on mail-in voting ahead of the midterms in November.
Two days after a federal judge blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Trump’s executive order, the administration on Sunday escalated the matter to the country’s highest court, asking justices to temporarily allow the agency to track mail-in ballots and decide whether they could be rejected. The ongoing legal battle comes even as some states have already begun sending out postal ballots.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail
- list 2 of 3Top US general says no plans to deploy troops for 2026 midterm elections
- list 3 of 3What’s behind the vote-by-mail controversy in the US?
US District Judge Indira Talwani issued an order on Friday that said Trump’s directives, which would grant the federal government power over the handling of mail-in ballots, are likely unconstitutional. In the US, elections – including ones for federal office – are carried out by states.
The judge also criticised the timing of the executive order’s implementation, writing that, with just two months until election day, it “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail”.
But in its emergency filing on Sunday, the Trump administration countered Talwani’s ruling: “Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalise the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail”.
US Solicitor General John Sauer, who argues cases before the Supreme Court on behalf of the federal government, said Trump’s order would not seize control of states’ right to administer elections, but would only impose “reasonable preparation requirements” for mail-in ballots.
“[The rule] requires States to upload the name, address and barcode information of intended recipients of ballot mail in an online portal — information that election officials would necessarily already possess to send ballot mail under the Rule to those recipients,” Sauer wrote in the filing. “The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures.”
Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson set a deadline of Wednesday for responses to the Trump administration’s request.
Sunday’s filing marks the third time the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene. The court recently allowed the plan to move forward but did not rule on whether it was legal.
With control of the US Congress up for grabs in November, how the Supreme Court rules on the appeal could have major implications.
Despite voting by mail himself, Trump has long sought to limit it during his time in office, falsely claiming that it is ripe with fraud. Opponents say the president’s motivation is simpler, arguing that Democrats vote by mail more than Republicans.
An analysis conducted by the States United Democracy Center found that many voters, no matter their political affiliation, cast their ballots by mail. The research found that one in four registered Democrats and one in five registered Republicans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election.

‘We are family’: EU chief in Greenland to sign partnership deal
