Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:07:08 UTC
01:07:08 KST

German far-right AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election, falls short of majority
Party hails ‘historic’ result, but it is not immediately clear whether it will be able to form a government.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to preliminary results.
AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote, according to preliminary official results. That is more than twice the 17.2 percent for the incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” said AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “We have made history in this state.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed the “historic” result, which has given the far-right party a clear mandate to govern, though it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.
Merz did not make a statement on Sunday evening on the election results. The German leader left the CDU’s head office, the Konrad-Adenauer-Haus, after 10pm local time (20:00 GMT).
“The reality is the AfD has got the lion’s share of the votes in this election, according to the exit polls. But the question is: is it enough to get them control of the state? Right now, we cannot say for sure,” reported Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane from Magdeburg in eastern Germany.
The latest projections gave the AfD 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats, leaving it three short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Siegmund said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties’ will, he stressed.
The AfD has never participated in a governing coalition in Germany’s 16 states, nor in its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the “firewall”.
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s national co-leader, claimed the result showed that voters had rejected the governing coalition’s policy.
The mainstream parties “were voted out, or rather, the voters delivered a clear verdict, and I can only encourage them to recognise that the ‘firewall’ has been definitively rejected by the voters today,” Chrupalla told broadcaster ARD.
Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD branch has been classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by the state’s domestic intelligence agency, a designation the party rejects as politically motivated.
Blow to Merz’s authority
Sunday’s result is another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has declined as his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy.
His centre-right CDU came a distant second. Incumbent Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze congratulated the AfD and acknowledged that the result had hit his party hard, saying, “We’re going to have to live with this result”.
Schulze later said he did not intend to cooperate with the AfD, although he initially declined to give a clear answer when asked whether the CDU’s firewall would remain in place.
The projected parliamentary arithmetic would make forming a government exceptionally difficult. Schulze could attempt to assemble an alliance involving several parties, though the CDU has traditionally ruled out formal cooperation with both the AfD and the Left (Die Linke) party.
AfD has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany, as well as lingering resentment about the enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden an East German-produced Simson Schwalbe bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermunde, with his wife in tow.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting undocumented migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
AfD’s agenda
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes promises to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on Hitler’s Third Reich.
To replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking population in the small state of 2.1 million.
The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Thuringia state Interior Minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily newspaper.

US withdrawal from Iraq will be watched closely by Iran-backed militias, Kurds - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:57 UTC
01:04:57 KST

The US is to meet a September 30 deadline for withdrawing from Iraq, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported on Sunday.
It was one of several reports that indicate the US is committed to taking away air defense systems from the Kurdistan Region. The full details of this are unclear and hard to confirm. What matters is not necessarily if it is accurate, but that people will think it is happening.
Rudaw wrote, “The United States will withdraw its defense systems from the Kurdistan Region along with its remaining troops by the end of September under an agreement with the Iraqi government, a senior Iraqi security official said on Sunday.”
The report noted that “Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, told Rudaw that the withdrawal includes all defense systems, including remaining ones in Erbil, adding that the phased removal of troops and military equipment has already begun.”
Araji said, “On September 30, coalition forces will completely withdraw from Iraq, and this is the implementation of the agreement made between the previous government and the global coalition…The American side has expressed its full readiness to implement the agreement and withdraw by the specified deadline.”
US pressuring Iraq to control militias
This comes as the US is also pressuring Iraq to rein in Iranian-backed militias and disarm them. So far, none of the militias have disarmed. It doesn’t seem possible that any weapons will be collected in September. If no militias were disarmed in the last months, why would they hand over their guns now?
Instead, what they will do is put more conditions on disarmament. Some may also claim they already put their guns under “state control.” Most of the militias are part of the Baghdad-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). As such, they will claim the PMF controls their weapons already. This is a kind of bait and switch.
Rudaw said there is progress with the militias. “Araji said discussions with the armed groups were moving in a positive direction.”
Araji said, “After the withdrawal of the coalition, an agreement will be reached on a comprehensive mechanism to place all weapons under the control of the state and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.” He added that “discussions are proceeding very well and there is positive understanding.”
It’s worth noting that the militias were supposed to hand over their weapons by September 30. Now the handover is overdue. This is how the can gets kicked down the road.
For the Kurdistan Region, this is a problem because the militias and Iran have already targeted the region with more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks since February 2026.
Iran has even targeted the offices of the Kurdish Regional Government’s prime minister and president. Iran is indicating that it wants to strike at dissident groups in the Kurdistan Region and also that it can do as it wants.
Not clear if air defenses will remain
In the past, reports said that US and coalition air defenses had downed some of the drone attacks. It is not clear if some of the defenses will actually remain. The US has a large consulate in Erbil. It is logical that the US will want to defend it. The consulate, as well as a UAE consulate, has been targeted in the past.
Yet, Rudaw said, “the US has already relocated eight Patriot surface-to-air missile batteries to Jordan, while Britain has transferred its Rapid Sentry system to Cyprus.”
The report added context, noting the “US and British forces have defended Erbil airport and surrounding areas using anti-missile and counter-drone systems stationed at the base. Despite those defenses, at least five American soldiers and contractors have been killed in attacks in recent months, Rudaw understands.”
The report also names five Iranian-backed militias as refusing to disarm. These include Kataib Hezbollah, Sayyid al-Shuhada and Harakat al-Nujaba. Kataib Hezbollah is believed to be the most dangerous in terms of its threat and close ties to the IRGC.
In 2020, when the US killed IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, he was riding with Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Muhandis was also killed.
Kataib Hezbollah killed three Americans in Jordan in a drone attack in 2024. It has also attacked Saudi Arabia. The militias, such as the three mentioned above, often play a role in the “Islamic Resistance” in Iraq, which has carried out attacks on Israel, the US, and others in recent years.

Israel should consider changing Hatikvah as its national anthem - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:57 UTC
01:04:57 KST

Several countries have changed their national anthems. In Australia, where I was born and raised, we used to sing the British national anthem of “God Save the Queen,” which underwent a slight change in previous years, depending on the gender of the monarch.
In April 1984, the anthem was officially changed to “Advance Australia Fair.”
In New Zealand, they have two national anthems, one of which is “God Save the King” and the other being “God Defend New Zealand,” which is in tribute to the indigenous Maori population.
Prior to the end of apartheid, South Africa also had two national anthems, but in 1997, abandoned both, and adopted a new anthem.
Other countries wishing to correct historic grievances or bowing to a change of regime have also altered existing anthems or brought in new ones.
In Russia, for instance, the anthem has been changed at least three times. The present anthem is sung to the same tune as that of Soviet times, but the lyrics were changed in December 2000.
Prior to the fall of the Berlin Wall and the reunification of Germany in November 1989, the East Germans had a different anthem to those of the West Germans. The East German anthem was “Risen from the Ashes,” whereas in West Germany they sang “Germany Above All,” omitting some of the Nazi-era lyrics.
For Jews, the world over, Israel’s national anthem “Hatikvah” – the Hope – which was originally a poem written in 1878 by Naftali Herz Imber, is the universal national anthem. The melody was adapted from a Moldavian folk song by Romanian immigrant Samuel Cohen. The lyrics speak of the Jewish people’s longing to return to Zion.
Most national anthems are in tribute to the country or the nation as a whole. But “Hatikvah” is clearly the anthem of the Jewish people and does not take into account the minorities who are also part of the nation of Israel.
Making Israel's national anthem more inclusive
A major step toward making Israel more acceptable to the Arab world would be to change the anthem to something in which the lyrics would be more neutral and could apply to any sector of the population. “Jerusalem of Gold” comes close, but includes the Temple Mount in the text. Though unofficially Israel’s second national anthem, it would have to be altered slightly so that another expression could be found for Temple Mount which has both political and religious connotations.
Whether “Jerusalem of Gold” replaces “Hatikvah” or whether a new song is composed, what remains important is change in order to make the national anthem inclusive.
Debates on this subject go back to long before the establishment of the state.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, who was Ashkenazi chief rabbi under the British Mandate, wrote a possible alternative to “Hatikvah” under the title of “HaEmunah” (“The Faith”). This was fine for religious Jews, but not for the rest of the population.
The debate on the anthem has been going on for more than a century, with agreement yet to be reached. Non-Jews respectfully stand to attention when “Hatikvah” is played, but cannot bring themselves to sing about the Jewish soul and Zion.
Jews in other countries often face a similar problem in hospitals run by Catholic orders. Almost every room in such hospitals features a crucifix on the wall and a portrait of the Virgin Mary.
Even secular Jews feel uncomfortable in such an environment, but most of the Catholic hospitals are really good, and the nursing staff amazingly kind and considerate.
It’s not quite the same, because hospital stays are relatively brief and seldom repeated. But many events attended by non-Jews begin or end with “Hatikvah,” which was inspiring on the road to statehood, but is no longer suitable when we have a state
If we want everyone to sing the anthem with pride and a sense of belonging, we must agree to change.

Gaza mourns 100 victims, mostly children, found under rubble

Breadcrumb
Gaza's Zeitoun neighbourhood mourns 100 victims, including 70 children, found under rubble
Large crowds gathered in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood on Sunday to attend a solemn mass funeral for 100 people whose remains were only recently retrieved after they were killed in the Gaza War.
Their bodies were recovered from under the rubble of destroyed homes in the neighbourhood and were taken to the Baptist Cemetery, in a scene which highlighted the scale of the tragedy endured by Gaza’s residents during the genocidal war.
The funeral was organised by the Zeitoun Neighborhood Families Association in coordination with the General Directorate of Civil Defence and the Missing Persons Committee.
Relatives of those found were in attendance while mourners carried photographs of the deceased and banners bearing tribute to them.
Civil Defence teams that had carried out the recovery and transportation of the bodies also took part in the funeral.
Gaza Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said that of the 100 victims, 70 were children.
Before the funeral began, an atmosphere of grief filled the area. Family members gathered to take a final look at the remains of their loved ones after waiting so long to learn of their fate.
Some were in shock, unable to comprehend that the long search had finally ended with coffins bearing the names of the people they loved.
Bassal said that the operation to recover the bodies had been about returning victims to their families and giving them the right to say goodbye and bury their loved ones.
“How long will Gaza remain in this pain? How long will a father raise his children for years, only for them all to die in a single moment? Why are innocent people being killed? And how long will Gaza continue to bleed?” he asked in anguish.
Bassal said that the Civil Defence still need to search for approximately 8,000 people under the rubble, despite limited resources and a total absence of support from the world.
Omar Nofal, representing the Missing Persons Committee said, “Behind every body found is a name, a family, and a story that has waited a long time.”
Nofal emphasize that the bodies of those killed had been under the rubble for three years but said that this was “not a failure on the part of Civil Defence, but a failure of humanity, and of a world that constantly boasts about human rights, children's rights, and women's rights.
“But the only truth is that, in this world, rights belong to the powerful, and the law that prevails is the law of the jungle.”
“Civil Defence did not recover a single weapon from beneath the rubble, but it recovered nearly 70 boys and girls,” Nofal added. “It recovered colourful dolls and little teddy bears, while more than 8,000 people remain beneath the rubble to this day.”
After the farewell speeches, mourners carried the coffins and the funeral procession moved through the streets of Gaza City toward the Baptist Cemetery.
At the Baptist Cemetery, families and mourners gathered around the bodies for the final time before the burial ceremonies began. The coffins were lowered one after another into the graves, while family members stood at their edges, taking their final looks before the victims were laid to rest.
For the Zeitoun neighborhood, the funeral was not so much the end of the story as a collective recovery of a part of its memory, while other families continue to wait to learn the fate of their missing loved ones.

Israel election panel allows parties to track who has voted in real time ahead of High Court review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:39 UTC
01:04:39 KST

The Central Elections Committee voted on Sunday to allow party representatives inside polling stations to report in real time which voters have cast ballots, restoring - for now - a central part of parties’ Election Day turnout operations ahead of the October 27 election.
The information at issue does not reveal how anyone voted, which remains secret. What it does do is tell parties whether a particular person has voted or not. Campaigns can compare that information with their databases and concentrate calls, messages, home visits, and transportation efforts on likely supporters who have not yet reached the polls.
Sunday’s decision is not the final legal word. The High Court of Justice will resume hearing Likud’s petition at 8 a.m. on Wednesday, after the parties update the court on the committee’s decision.
The full committee approved the proposal by 19 votes to 11, with three abstentions, departing from the position of committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, who ruled in August that transferring identified voter information to political parties was prohibited.
Under the committee’s decision, the reporting will be allowed only under restrictions: Information may not be transferred from special polling stations, parties may not record when an individual voted, and the data may be used only to encourage voter turnout.
Special polling stations are those where voting is conducted using double envelopes, including polling stations in prisons and hospitals, military polling stations, and specially accessible polling stations intended for people with limited mobility.
Information must be destroyed after the election
The information may not be transferred to another party or outside body and must be destroyed after the election by the parties themselves, a CEC spokesperson confirmed.
It remains unclear whether the ban on transferring the information to an outside body also applies to companies operating parties’ voter-tracking applications.
The proposal was presented by attorney Ilan Bombach, who represents Likud in the proceedings. The committee is composed primarily of political-party representatives, with seats allocated according to the factions in the outgoing Knesset; the coalition holds a majority.
The court has not ruled that Sohlberg lacked the authority to impose the original ban. Instead, an arrangement approved last Thursday transferred the underlying question to the full committee for a fresh decision, with Sohlberg’s rulings placed before it as his legal opinion.
The State Attorney’s Office will represent Sohlberg at Wednesday’s hearing, while the committee’s legal adviser will represent the full committee, according to the spokesperson.
That allowed the court to bypass the authority dispute for the time being. Now that the committee has permitted the practice, the central question is expected to become whether its decision complies with privacy and election law.
Wednesday’s hearing will proceed as though the court has already issued a conditional order requiring the respondents to justify their position. In practical terms, that allows the case to move directly into substantive review without another preliminary stage.
Likud has argued that this system has operated openly for several election cycles and is essential to its ability to bring supporters to the polls. It said Sohlberg’s original prohibition was imposed after parties had already planned their campaigns around the practice and that aggregate turnout figures could not replace identified reporting.
The privacy concern extends beyond the secrecy of the ballot
Sohlberg, the attorney-general, and the Privacy Protection Authority took the opposite position. They argued that information entrusted to polling-station officials for administering and supervising the election cannot be repurposed for political-party operations without legal authorization.
Sohlberg found that whether a person voted, when they voted, and the circumstances of their vote constitute personal information. He ruled that the fact that parties had used the information in previous elections did not make its transfer lawful.
The privacy concern extends beyond the secrecy of the ballot. Information showing that someone voted at a hospital, prison, women’s shelter, or another special polling station could reveal sensitive details about that person even without disclosing their vote. Sunday’s decision seeks to address that concern by excluding special polling stations and prohibiting the transfer of voting times.
Critics maintain that identified information from ordinary polling stations can also become sensitive when combined with party databases. In communities with predictable voting patterns, even the fact that a person voted may support inferences about their political views. Real-time access can also expose voters to targeted pressure or repeated approaches before polls close.
Sohlberg had proposed an alternative under which the committee would publish aggregate turnout figures for every ordinary polling station at least four times on Election Day, without identifying individual voters. Sunday’s decision instead preserves identified reporting under the new restrictions.
The parties must now explain to the High Court how the committee’s decision affects their positions. The justices may then determine whether the safeguards are sufficient or whether identified voter reporting remains incompatible with privacy and election law.

New report flags widespread failures in Canadian universities’ antisemitism response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:32 UTC
01:04:32 KST

B’nai Brith Canada has launched its Canadian Campus Climate Report Card, an institutional accountability initiative designed to evaluate the state of Jewish life and the climate for Jewish students on university campuses as the new academic year gets underway.
The initiative is part of B’nai Brith’s broader Project Accountability, which operates on the principle that academic institutions must be held accountable for the environments they foster and for how effectively they respond when students face antisemitism, harassment, or discrimination.
The initial launch features a pilot assessment covering four universities where students have reported particularly hostile social climates: York University, the University of Toronto, Queen’s University, and McGill University.
Unlike traditional incident trackers that catalog instances of antisemitism, the report cards evaluate 28 criteria across three core categories: administrative policies and actions, campus conduct and climate, and Jewish life on campus.
The methodology combines student surveys with a qualitative review of university policies, anti-hate measures, course offerings, and the availability of kosher dining and Jewish services. Each criterion is weighted equally across the categories.
Initial findings from the pilot program highlight that while all four institutions demonstrated strong traditional Jewish life indicators, such as active student groups, chaplaincy support, and religious services, the campus climate and administrative response metrics yielded widespread red scores.
Administrators received poor marks for their handling of antisemitic incidents
At McGill University, York University, and the University of Toronto, administrators received failing or critical marks regarding their handling of harassment, event disruptions, and transparency in reporting antisemitic incidents.
“The goal isn’t simply to hand out grades,” said B’nai Brith Canada’s CEO Simon Wolle in a press release on Wednesday. “It is to give students, parents and the community a clearer picture of what is happening on campus. We want to recognize where universities are getting it right, identify where they’re falling short, and help universities do better.”
Wolle added, “Our Report Cards must serve as an impetus for Canadian institutions to revise their policies, where they fall short, and improve programming if it is insufficient to meet the needs of Jewish students.”
B’nai Brith intends for the report cards to serve as an ongoing benchmark to push Canadian tertiary institutions to tighten their policies and enforce anti-hate codes.

Israel’s next leader must be ambitious for Israel, not themselves - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:04:14 UTC
01:04:14 KST

On October 27, Israelis will once again choose a government.
We will spend the coming weeks arguing about Gaza, Iran, the haredi draft, the economy, judicial reform, the Palestinians, and the consequences of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks. We will scrutinize party platforms, coalition possibilities, and opinion polls.
But perhaps we should be asking: What sort of person wants to be prime minister in the first place?
It is a peculiar ambition. The hours are appalling. Privacy mostly disappears. Every mistake becomes public property. Your appearance, your family, your finances, and sometimes even your choice of lunch become legitimate subjects for discussion. Roughly half the country may regard you as the person qualified to save the nation, while much of the other half regards you as the person most likely to destroy it.
Why would anybody want the job?
Many politicians still motivated by public service
Political psychologists have been asking versions of this question for years, and their findings are fascinating. Research into “political ambition” suggests that politicians are not simply power-hungry egomaniacs, as the popular stereotype would have it. Many are strongly motivated by public service. Studies of political candidates have found genuine evidence of what psychologists call “self-transcendence,” the desire to improve society and help others.
That is worth remembering in an age when cynicism about politicians comes so easily.
But alongside the desire to serve sits something else: the desire to influence. Political leaders tend to have a greater “need for power” than the rest of us. Again, that is not necessarily bad. If you are convinced that your country is heading in the wrong direction, it is perfectly reasonable to want the authority to change course.
Then there is a third characteristic: unusually strong self-belief. Research has associated political ambition with traits including extraversion and grandiose narcissism. That does not mean that every politician is a narcissist, still less that we should diagnose politicians we dislike with psychiatric disorders.
It means something simpler. To seek the premiership requires an extraordinary degree of confidence in yourself.
Israel has almost 10 million inhabitants. To seriously aspire to become prime minister requires believing that, among all those people, you possess some combination of judgment, ability, and vision that makes you particularly suited to lead them. Most of us never have that thought.
Those who do are, almost by definition, psychologically unusual.
Pirkei Avot (Ethics of the Fathers) understood the danger long before anyone invented political psychology. Shmaya teaches: “Love work, hate authority, and do not become overly familiar with the government.”
“Hate positions of power.” It is a striking instruction. Judaism clearly does not oppose leadership. The Torah is filled with leaders. Jewish communities cannot function without people willing to take responsibility.
The warning is not against exercising authority. It is against falling in love with it. And that distinction ought to matter to us as voters. Does a candidate want power because there is something that they believe desperately needs doing, or has acquiring and retaining power become the objective itself?
How can we possibly know? Not from campaign advertisements. Every candidate will assure us that they seek office only out of devotion to the people of Israel.
We have to watch their behavior. How does this person react when contradicted? Can they admit a mistake? Can they tolerate talented people around them, or does everyone eventually have to demonstrate personal loyalty? Do they distinguish between criticism and betrayal? Do they listen to advice that they do not want to hear?
When something goes badly wrong, is the first instinct to ask, “What did I get wrong?” or “Whom can I blame?”
Perhaps above all: can this person distinguish between what is good for the country and what is good for his or her political survival?
This is not an argument for timid leadership. In fact, Pirkei Avot gives us the opposite warning as well. Hillel says: “In a place where there are no people, strive to be a person.”
The traditional commentators understand this, among other things, as an instruction to step forward when nobody else is capable of taking responsibility.
Leadership sometimes requires enormous confidence. Moses’ humility did not prevent him from confronting Pharaoh. David’s greatness did not consist of avoiding difficult decisions. There are moments when standing back is not modesty but cowardice.
So Judaism presents us with a beautiful tension. Do not crave leadership. But when leadership is needed, do not run away from it.
Perhaps that is exactly the personality we should be looking for in October. Someone who wants the job enough to do it, but not so much that possessing the job becomes an end in itself.
Someone confident enough to make terrible decisions under pressure, but humble enough to wonder whether somebody else might know better. Someone strong enough to withstand public hostility, but not so insulated from criticism that they stop hearing it. Someone ambitious for Israel, rather than merely ambitious for themselves.
Our electoral system encourages us to think primarily about parties. Formally, we vote for lists rather than directly for a prime minister. In reality, personalities dominate Israeli elections. Faces stare at us from billboards. Campaigns revolve around leaders. Pollsters constantly ask which individual is “most suitable” to be prime minister.
If personality is already part of the election, we should examine it more seriously. Not whether we like the candidate, or if they gave a good speech, or if they performed brilliantly in a television interview.
Character is revealed most clearly when things go wrong. How did this person behave after failure? How did they treat an opponent once the cameras were switched off? Did they keep people around who disagreed with them? Have they ever publicly accepted responsibility for anything?
These questions matter in every election. In Israel in 2026, they matter enormously.
The next prime minister will inherit a country still carrying the wounds of the October 7 massacres and the Israel-Hamas War that ensued. Israeli society remains divided, bereaved, and exhausted. Enormous decisions lie ahead concerning security, the economy, the haredi draft, our relationship with the Palestinians, our relationship with the wider world and, perhaps most difficult of all, our relationship with one another.
Policies matter enormously. But policies do not make decisions. People do. Sometimes, the intelligence is incomplete, advisers disagree, and every option carries terrible risks.
What remains is the person; their judgment, temperament, humility, courage, and ego. Their capacity to listen; their ability to say, “I was wrong.” So by all means, before October 27, let us ask our politicians what they intend to do. But perhaps we should spend more time asking who they are.
Shmaya warned us to distrust the love of power. Hillel reminded us that good people must sometimes step forward and exercise it. Somewhere between those two teachings lies the leader that Israel needs.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD secures huge lead in key vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
- The European press calling the results an "unsettling new page in German history"
Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.
Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD
Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."
Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.
Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."
For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.
It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.
AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'
Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.
He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.
Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.
She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.
This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.
Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."
Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.
AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference
In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state.
Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.
Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.
Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.
Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.
After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.
Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.
Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."
Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.
"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."
What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?
Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'
Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."
Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"
After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era.
Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."
Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now
Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.
After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.
Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory
The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.
The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.
International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'
Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.
New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.
In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.
Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."
And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."
Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory.
"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."
"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.
Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'
Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.
"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.
Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.
She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."
The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.
"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.
AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win
According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.
AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."
At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.
"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."
If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.
Is coalition without AfD possible?
The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."
That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.
Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.
Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?
Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.
The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.
But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.
The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.
Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.
Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:
- Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
- Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
- Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
- Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
- Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
- Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats
Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.
According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.
WATCH: "Migration alone no longer explains the party’s rise"
Historian Katja Hoyer says the AfD's breakthrough was fueled by a more upbeat campaign around Ulrich Siegmund, while mainstream parties struggled to offer a positive vision of change.
CDU fails to win a single direct mandate in Saxony-Anhalt state election
As a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU, the party came away empty-handed in the individual constituencies.
The CDU failed to win a single direct mandate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
According to preliminary figures from the state election authority, CDU candidates were defeated in all 41 constituencies.
Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidates prevailed in 38 constituencies, including lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Genthin. Candidates from the Left Party won the remaining three constituencies: one in Magdeburg and two in Halle.
In the 2021 state election, the CDU won direct mandates in 40 of the 41 constituencies, while the AfD won one.
In Germany, voters have two votes. The "first vote" determines the winner of a constituency and the direct mandate. The "second vote" determines the distribution of seats among parties in the state parliament.

Escitalopram reduces impulsivity and anger in women with severe premenstrual irritability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:34 UTC
01:00:34 KST

A study of women suffering from severe premenstrual irritability and anger found that escitalopram reduced their irritability and anger in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Participants on escitalopram also demonstrated a lower frequency of anticipatory responses and greater consistency in response speeds in a sustained attention test. The paper was published in Psychological Medicine.
The menstrual cycle is a recurring biological process in which hormonal changes prepare the body of a woman for a possible pregnancy. It is commonly divided into the menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, and luteal phases. The cycle begins with menstruation, when the uterine lining is shed and menstrual bleeding occurs. Ovulation occurs around the middle of the cycle, when a mature egg is released from the ovary. The last is the luteal phase, during which progesterone becomes dominant and the uterine lining is maintained in preparation for a possible pregnancy. If pregnancy does not occur, estrogen and progesterone levels fall toward the end of the luteal phase, leading to the beginning of a new menstrual cycle.
For some women, these hormonal changes are accompanied by recurring emotional, behavioral, and physical symptoms that become particularly pronounced before menstruation. These changes, called premenstrual symptoms, are thought to be linked to normal fluctuations in sex hormones across the menstrual cycle. In more severe cases, the symptoms may form part of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD. In this disorder, several symptoms repeatedly emerge during the luteal phase and largely disappear after menstruation begins.
Studies have shown that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, a type of medication used to treat depression, can be effective in reducing the symptoms of PMDD within only a few days. This suggests that serotonin, a neurotransmitter affected by SSRIs, might play an important role in premenstrual symptoms. It seems to be particularly effective in reducing irritability, anger, and rapid mood shifts.
Study author Maria Gröndal and her colleagues conducted a study in which they examined possible cognitive components of impulsivity in premenstrual irritability. They also examined the women’s sustained attention and the effects of intermittent treatment with escitalopram, a widely used SSRI.
Study participants were 27 women suffering from severe premenstrual irritability and anger, selected from an initial pool of 203 prospective participants. Participants were included in the study if they showed at least a 50% increase in irritability/anger symptoms from the follicular phase to the luteal phase of a menstrual cycle, and had a mean rating of irritability/anger over a threshold study authors defined over the last 5 days of the menstrual cycle. Participants’ average age was 33 years. 85% of them had a university degree. Participants received 1000 SEK (around $100) for each of their three lab visits, plus reimbursement for travel or loss of income.
The study extended over three of the study participants’ menstrual cycles. The first cycle did not involve any intervention. In cycles 2 and 3, participants were randomly assigned to either receive 20mg of escitalopram per day during the luteal phase of cycle 2 and placebo (an identically looking pill with no effects) during the luteal phase of cycle 3, in a single-blind design, or to receive these same treatments in the reverse order (placebo in cycle 2, escitalopram in cycle 3).
Participants completed a sustained attention test (the Conners Continuous Performance Test 3 – CPT 3) twice, once in the luteal phase of cycle 2 and once in the luteal phase of cycle 3. They also completed an assessment of impulsivity twice – once in the follicular phase and once in the luteal phase of the cycle when they were receiving placebo. Participants also rated their symptoms on a daily basis using an online survey. The symptoms they rated were irritability/anger, depressed mood, mood swings, and tension/anxiety.
Results showed that participants reported significantly higher levels of negative urgency (the tendency to act impulsively when experiencing negative emotions) during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle compared to the follicular phase. They also showed lower levels of sensation seeking. There were no differences between phases of the menstrual cycle in the other two aspects of impulsivity (lack of premeditation and lack of perseverance).
On the sustained attention test, perseverations (anticipatory, repetitive, or random responses) were significantly higher during the placebo cycle than during the escitalopram cycle. During the menstrual cycle when participants were receiving placebo, they also showed greater variability in their response speeds. In other words, escitalopram reduced participants’ anticipatory responses and made their reaction speeds more consistent. Escitalopram treatment also caused a significant reduction in self-rated irritability, anger, and mood swings in the luteal phase.
“The current study showed that intermittent treatment with escitalopram during the symptomatic luteal phase of the menstrual cycle may have a beneficial impact on specific aspects of impulsivity and inattentiveness in women with severe premenstrual irritability and anger. Moreover, our findings showed that self-reported urgency increased, whereas self-reported sensation seeking decreased in the luteal versus the follicular phase, suggesting that different facets of impulsivity may be of different significance to premenstrual complaints,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about premenstrual disorders and ways to treat their symptoms. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a very small group of women, selected for severe premenstrual irritability and anger. Results of studies involving larger groups of women may not be identical.
The paper, “The effects of intermittent escitalopram treatment on impulsivity and inattention in women with premenstrual irritability and anger,” was authored by Maria Gröndal, Christin Englund, Jakob Näslund, Karl Ask, Elias Eriksson, and Stefan Winblad.

Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:09 UTC
01:00:09 KST

Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.
Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.
The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.
Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.
School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.
One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.
Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.
“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.
“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”
EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs, according to official data.
The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt.
Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.
During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.
“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.
“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.
“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”
Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”
Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.
Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”
Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.
Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”
The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.
William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.
Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”

‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:00:09 UTC
01:00:09 KST

Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.
Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.
Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).
The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.
“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.
Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.
“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”
The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.
But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.
“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.
“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”
Simon Essex, the executive head of Thomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.
“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.
“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”

Alcott Weiin Beijing
Radically rewriting world and Chinese history without solid proof could threaten China’s international image and national identity, a leading Communist Party journal has warned.
There has been a growing trend to promote a less Western-centric view of history in recent years, while Beijing has also been keen to promote the idea that Chinese civilisation has a long and continuous history.
But at the same time, the so-called pseudo-historical school – which has cast doubt on the origins of Western culture or claimed key scientific advances originated in China – has become increasingly popular in some circles.

“The extreme pseudo-historical claims proliferating online continue to spread overseas and have already damaged our country’s ‘academic discourse power’ and cultural image abroad,” the article said.
Some of the most eye-catching theories have cast doubt on key aspects of ancient Greek history, which risk damaging Beijing’s relationship with Athens and other governments.

Ukrainian Armor Masters Production of Running Gear Components for Novator-2 Armored Vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:56:06 UTC
00:56:06 KST

Ukrainian Armor has mastered the production of some running gear components for the Novator-2 armored vehicle: control arms, rods, bump stops and bushings.
Ukrainian Armor told Militarnyi about this.
The vehicle is based on a Ford F-550 chassis that is additionally reinforced: the company strengthens the frame and axles and installs reinforced shock absorbers and stabilizers.
At the same time, the company develops and manufactures some running gear components itself, namely control arms, rods, bump stops and bushings.
The Novator-2 is a specialized Ukrainian armored vehicle developed based on experience gained from the combat use of the first version of the Novator.
The vehicle is primarily designed to transport a combat unit. It can carry 10 service members — a driver and nine troops. Compared with its predecessor, the armored vehicle features reinforced front and rear suspension, an improved steering system, enhanced mine protection and an enlarged armored compartment.
The first prototype was unveiled in September 2023 at the MSPO international defense exhibition in Poland. In January 2024, the vehicle’s tests were publicly shown. The National Guard of Ukraine received the first production batch in early July 2024.
The vehicle is equipped with a 6.7-liter eight-cylinder diesel engine producing 300 hp, as well as an automatic transmission.
The vehicle has a curb weight of about 9,660 kilograms and a payload capacity of up to 3,340 kilograms. It is equipped with run-flat tires, allowing it to continue moving after the tires are damaged.
The armored hull provides ballistic protection at STANAG 4569 Level 1, which provides protection against 7.62×51 mm NATO Ball M80 rounds at a distance of 30 meters.
Mine protection meets STANAG 4569 Level 2a/2b. The vehicle is designed to protect the crew if a charge equivalent to up to 6 kilograms of TNT detonates either under a wheel or beneath the hull. Special mine-resistant seats with five-point safety harnesses are also installed to reduce the impact of the blast on the crew.
Based on the standard chassis, Ukrainian Armor has developed several specialized armored vehicles: the Novator-2S armored ambulance, the Novator C2V, and the Novator-2 Krechet for coordinating air defense units and assets.

Long-term proteges and verifiable reality must be jettisoned for Saving Private Nige | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:42:10 UTC
00:42:10 KST

We’ve all been there. It’s a lovely summer’s day and you just want a bit of me time. A quiet lunch of champagne and oysters. As you do. Anything to get away from having to pretend you are interested in the people of Clacton. Hell, it’s bad enough being expected to actually visit Clacton – who in their right mind would want to do that? – let alone having to talk to the little people who live there.
So, you’re just minding your own business when who should turn up but two of your closest mates in politics – or contractors who you’ve barely heard of, as you prefer to call them – saying they have been having meetings with an American donor and his son who have already given you more than £30,000 for an opinion poll you have commissioned and now want to bung you another £500,000. And these guys would like to meet you.
The cheek of it. Two strangers, one of them even a foreigner, who want to take up an hour of your time. And all you’re going to get for it is half a million quid. Who do they think you are? Don’t they know the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne stumped up a £5m gift? Admittedly, several hundred Cameo users have bought you for £80 a pop, but that was at least a few months ago. Things have changed. Besides, that wasn’t really being bought. More a short-term rental.
These wasters are basically insulting you. But you’re a tolerant kind of guy. You choose to indulge them. If you have a fault it’s that you’re never chippy and are unfailingly polite. Everyone tells you that. So you go along with them even though they have nothing of value to offer you. Yes, Yes. That’s fascinating. Thank you so much. But all along, you’re not really listening at all. You’re just zoning out. Trying to chill out in the sun. All you’re really thinking is of getting the first train out of Clacton.
Over the past few days, Reform have been in a tailspin over the Channel 4 News sting that appeared to show the party was intensely relaxed about breaking the law by taking money from overseas. First, they tried to style it out. It was a hoax. Nothing to see here. It was an establishment plot carried out by anti-establishment climate protesters. Go figure. Then, as the net closed in, they started to panic. No one had a clear line on anything. Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s long-term protege, and James Orr, the lawyer turned Cambridge academic turned Reform head of policy, left the party. Anything to buy some breathing space. All that mattered now was Saving Private Nige. Everyone else was expendable.
So for his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that was recorded on Saturday but broadcast on Sunday morning, Nige was keen to distance himself from any allegation of wrongdoing. That person in the film that people said was him? It was actually an avatar. Who knows how many versions of Nige might be in play at any one time? He’s a very busy man.
But whichever Nige it had been, he was certain that he hadn’t been listening as the people around him were discussing in some detail not only how they exactly planned to break the law but how they had done so in the past. I mean, that was just pub talk. Who doesn’t like to boast about apparently criminal behaviour over a couple of drinks?
Laura K seemed rather taken aback by this. She wasn’t the only one. Because it turns out Nige is capable of holding down his part in a conversation when he isn’t even listening. What a gift that must be. Most of us distinctly remember him saying, when the talk turned to the polling, that Nige insists he had no idea he had been funded by foreign money, that the polling had been “amazing”, had provided “bang for buck” and “it had worked – boom”. Perhaps he was just talking in his sleep. Or had had his brain hacked by the establishment. He even made a point of thanking the donors.
Not that they were donors, of course. Maybe that was the bit that hurt the most. The realisation that the offer had never been genuine. Then came the distancing. Jukes and Orr had been “injudicious at best”. That would suggest that at worst they might have been … maybe that’s one for the lawyers.
What you had to remember was that Nige had never been close to Dan. Had never really liked him. Come to think of it, he had no idea why he had allowed him to be his right-hand gofer for the last 10 years. As for James, he was just an ingenu. A dreamer. It was totally unreasonable to expect someone who had trained as a finance lawyer to know anything about … er, the law concerning party funding. And it was just daft to think that a Cambridge ethics professor should behave ethically. Orr’s thesis had been on “divine lawmaking”. Perhaps breaking the law had been God’s will.
Dan and James had just been freelancing. They didn’t really work for Reform. So any alleged law breaking was one step further removed from Nige. Besides, as Reform leader, it wasn’t his job to be the compliance officer. Even though no one apparently knew the rules governing party donations better than him. He was the world’s leading expert. That was by the by. His job was just to be the frontman. To smile and shake a few hands. He had just been doing what he had been told.
Yes, said Laura, by now totally confused. But you did appear to be up to speed as the potential donor outlined how a scheme like that would be breaking the law and told him, “it’s all above board”, she said. Worried that she might be losing the plot. No, said Nige. What he had said was: “Is it all above board?” Except he hadn’t. He had definitely said it as a statement. Still, that cleared up one thing. The reason he hadn’t been listening was because he had hearing difficulties. One that made him turn every sentence on its head. Hopefully the police will take that into consideration if they get round to starting an investigation. Nige could do with a break.

Niger military accuses France of orchestrating failed mutiny: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
